author: Clare Hymer
title: ‘Major Opportunity’ for UK Unions to Recruit Workers As New Rules Take Effect
content:
Trade unions could see a boost in membership due to 

new workplace rights

 that come into force today.




As of 30 October, union representatives have the right to request in-person or digital access to workplaces where at least 21 people are employed – even if the union isn’t recognised by the employer or it has no members there.




This will make it easier for organisers to reach workers shut out of collective representation in order to speak to them about demanding better pay and conditions.




Until today, bosses could keep unions out of many workplaces by simply refusing access. Now, if talks to negotiate an access agreement fail, the Central Arbitration Committee – an independent government body – can force employers to agree, with penalties for breaches reaching £500,000.

 




Andrea Egan, general secretary of Unison – Britain’s largest trade union – said the new laws presented “a major organising opportunity”.




“For decades, employers have used every trick in the book to prevent unions getting into workplaces,” 

she wrote in a blog post

 earlier this month. “They know organised workplaces shift the power dynamic so that workers have a real voice through recognition and collective bargaining and they don’t want that to spread. 




“The new access rights provide a significant reset of industrial relations.”




After peaking at 13.2 million in 1979, union membership in the UK plummeted as a result of deindustrialisation and anti-union legislation introduced by Margaret Thatcher’s government.




The new rules, which form part of Labour’s Employment Rights Act 2025, could be particularly helpful for unions wanting to reach workers in the private sector, where 

just 12% of employees

 are unionised.




Other reforms taking effect today strengthen protections for workers taking part in industrial action. 




A separate requirement for bosses to inform staff of their right to join a union is due to come into force on 1 January 2027.

author: Adetokunbo Abiola
title: Nigeria’s AI Ambitions vs. The Regulatory Void–Who Protects the Citizens?
content:
Last year, scammers launched a deepfake videos of popular Nigerian social media influencer, 

Martins Vincent Otse

, through a fraudulent Facebook campaign. The cybercriminals superimposed a fabricated AI-generated audio on a genuine video of Otse from early 2024.




Martins Vincent Otse




In the cloned voice, Otse introduced an online chatting scheme where viewers could earn up to $1,000 monthly. By cloning the influencer’s face and reputation, the scammers not only harmed Otse’s reputation as a respected influencer, they also preyed on the poverty of many Nigerians, tricking them into becoming a member of an online platform created to appropriate their personal information and savings.




On 

October 5

, to show that the issue still mattered, the Nigeria Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) warned organisations and staff against sharing sensitive data with public AI tools.




As the federal government shapes  its National Artificial Intelligence Strategy with the aim to leapfrog development, doctors and nurses use clinical Al tools without standardised verification methods and companies run systems without Al oversight structures. Banks move transactions to automated and Al-driven solutions to combat soaring transaction fraud and manage financial risk, while




87.5 percent

 of  fintech companies now deploy Al for automated fraud detection. In theory, the 

Nigeria Data Protection Act

 gave citizens the right to object to automated decision-making; in practice, the abuse of enforcement renders it non-justiceable when Al systems cause harm.




For instance, during the lead up to the 2023 presidential elections, a simulated audio clip went viral, purportedly featuring 

former Vice President Abubakar Atiku

 and other members of his party  discussing plans to rig the election. Fact checkers labelled the audio false and generated by artificial intelligence tools. Investigations opened, but there was no prosecution. Defamation laws exist in Nigeria, but none existed to assign blame for the creation of a lie by generative models.




In another instance, unverified screening AIs missed the detection of over 

1,247 tuberculosis cases

, as well misclassified 

342 high-risk pregnancies

, with 

186 preventable patient deaths

 linked to Al diagnostic errors. The tools involved were not registered as medical devices by the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control ( NAFDAC), but registered as “wellness” apps.




Driven by the Ministry of Communications and NITDA, the National AI Strategy sets normative ambitions — to align AI deployment with human rights. But with internet penetration now at 

68.3 percent penetration

 at 

148.2 million

 subscribers, that ambition is no longer aspirational; the state has a functional duty to protect citizens from algorithmic harm at scale.




The issue remains implementation. NITDA has put together a draft 

Al Code of Practice

, and the Nigerian Data Protection Commission is enforcing data protection. But broader analytics from NITDA suggest that more than 

56 percent

 of government IT projects fail to meet expectations due to procurement, design and implementation flaws. This exposes sensitive consumer data to hackers, increasing the risk of identity theft and digital fraud from design flaws.




In the UK and EU, high-risk AI systems are subject to mandatory pre-deployment conformity assessments. In Nigeria, where banks now use AI-powered tools to identify and prevent fraudulent transactions, no equivalent requirement exists for auditing models against local fraud patterns before they go live.




This institutionalises systemic weaknesses. Angela Olusola was a 46-year-old mother of three. After an unaudited AI flagged her successive transaction as suspicious fraud behaviour, it froze her account. Unfortunately, she lacked financial buffers, with the 48-to-72-hour account freeze meaning she could not buy food, pay her transport fares or restock her business. Since she lived from hand-to-mouth, the algorithm error triggered an immediate poverty crisis.




Algorithmic biases in micro-lending are not abstract. A poor trader who uses a cheap phone and constantly changes SIM cards is flagged as “high risk”. The algorithm sees her behaviour as an indicator of low financial standing or attempts to cheat, resulting in instant loan rejections.




The training data is heavily skewed to salaried, urban, Android users in Lagos.




Because the algorithms are fed historical datasets consisting mostly of formal salary earners of people belonging to this class, the AI learns to flag the variable income streams of the informal majority as a “high risk of default,” effectively shutting them out. If any person’s dataset deviates from those of salaried, urban, Android users in Lagos, the AI treats  this as high-risk indicators or fraudulent tendencies, leading to exclusion.




With time, automated errors force the poor into the cash-only economy, their financial security stripped from them, leaving them at the mercy of inflation and crooks.




A second, quieter weakness may be happening at the other end of the value chain. Google and Microsoft have started collecting Nigerian data to improve their Large Language models (LLMs). Projects like Meta and the Gates Foundation’s African Next Voices 

use local hubs

 to clean up voice data. The average Nigerian spends a lot of their monthly income on these bundles, paying for the network connection required to give their data away for free.




Who owns a Nigerian’s voice when it is used to train voice cloning? The local hubs sign release forms, meaning the ordinary Nigerian surrenders their voice ownership rights, their voice becoming an asset of the funding enterprise. Nigeria doesn’t benefit from this, since it has no data trust, no licensing regime for foundation models trained on its digital identity. We give them the raw materials, we shoulder all of the risk, and we spend a lot of our money purchasing the product.




Another weakness is state power. The federal government of Nigeria has spent over 

$470 million

 to purchase Al-driven cameras with automated license plate and facial recognition. Many note that these systems operate in a legal vacuum. In the absence of Al-specific laws, this brings a situation where the ordinary citizen’s everyday life could be constantly logged, analysed and stored.




Nigeria does not need to ban AI to protect her citizens. It needs to carry out three basic things that other African nations are already considering.




Addressing dataset bias is now a technical necessity, if it wasn’t in the past. Since current models are trained predominantly on salaried, urban, Android users in Lagos, they systematically misclassify the 

76.7 percent

 of Nigerians in the informal sector. Funding localised datasets would correct this distributional skew while lowering adaptation costs for indigenous tools.




A constitutional remedy is required on the issue. Section 37 of the 1999 Constitution, which guarantees privacy, must be amended to expressly cover biometric and digital video metadata. Without that, state procurement of surveillance AI will continue to operate in a regulatory vacuum.




Mandating consumer-protection-by-design in fintech is now imperative. A significant share of automated loan rejections among low-income borrowers stems not from actual default risk but from unadjusted device-proxy metrics — such as SIM swapping to secure network coverage — being misread as fraud signals.




Without these interventions, Nigeria’s AI ambitions risk not halting underdevelopment but automating it. Martins Vincent Otse’s video was flagged as fake—saving many people from taking part in the online chatting scheme. For many  without that information, losing money becomes final.




The central question is not whether Nigeria should pursue AI development, but how liability is distributed when these systems fail. Currently, that burden is borne disproportionately by ordinary citizens.




The post 

Nigeria’s AI Ambitions vs. The Regulatory Void–Who Protects the Citizens?

 appeared first on 

African Arguments

.

author: CMI Argentina
title: “No vendan el Estatuto”: el gremio de prensa reclamó al Senado que trate en comisión los proyectos para proteger el periodismo
content:
Sindicatos de prensa de todo el país, representantes de las carreras de comunicación y organizaciones de la sociedad civil se movilizaron este jueves 29 al Congreso de la Nación para reclamar que traten los diversos proyectos legislativos para actualizar o prorrogar el Estatuto del Periodista Profesional (Ley 12.908), cuya derogación fue establecida por la regresiva Reforma Laboral del gobierno nacional de ultraderecha a partir del 1 de enero de 2027.







“Senadores, diputados: NO VENDAN EL ESTATUTO DEL PERIODISTA, la libertad de expresión y el derecho a la información”, pidieron dirigentes gremiales, periodistas y trabajadores y trabajadoras de prensa en la bandera que desplegaron en la puerta del Congreso Nacional. La acción de visibilización fue impulsada por el Sindicato de Prensa de Buenos Aires (SiPreBa) y la Federación Argentina de Trabajadores de Prensa (FATPREN).







Presentamos una solicitud formal a su presidenta, @carmenAlvarezR , y al resto de los legisladores para exigir que cumplan su compromiso y traten los proyectos de actualización y prórroga del Estatuto.




No vamos a permitir que el silencio parlamentario y los intereses de las empresas de medios destruyan nuestros derechos ante un contexto de ataques a la prensa y grave precarización laboral.




#SiPreBA2026




— SiPreBA – Sindicato de Prensa de Buenos Aires (@sipreba) 

October 30, 2026







En el marco de la protesta, se presentó una solicitud formal dirigida a la senadora Carmen Álvarez Rivero, presidenta de la Comisión de Trabajo y Previsión Social del Senado, y a los legisladores que la integran. El documento exige la inmediata convocatoria a reunión de comisión para evitar que la inacción parlamentaria decante en un vacío legal, que termine exponiendo al periodismo en una situación de vulnerabilidad mayor a las presiones políticas, económicas y judiciales.







La nota convoca a todos los miembros de la comisión a tratar los proyectos, pero puntualmente a los legisladores que se comprometieron a discutir una actualización de la Ley 12.908 en el marco de la prórroga, como los senadores Carolina Losada, Eduardo Vischi, Sonia Rojas Decut, José Carambia, Flavia Gabriela Royón y Carolina Moises, entre otros.




“Desde la sanción de la reforma laboral, la Comisión de Legislación del Trabajo del Senado no se volvió a reunir ni una sola vez. Las y los senadores que muchas veces hablan de la regulación laboral no están haciendo su laburo”, sostuvo Agustín Lecchi, secretario general de SiPreBA.




“En un contexto de gran ataque a la libertad de expresión, donde el Presidente de la Nación dice que nos quiere quemar en la hoguera, los empresarios de medios aprovechan la política laboral de este gobierno para derogar una ley que nos protege y resguarda la libertad de expresión”, agregó Lecchi.







 NI UN DÍA SIN ESTATUTO DEL PERIODISTA




Mariano Recalde @marianorecalde , senador de Unión por la Patria, realizó un pedido de preferencia para que se trate de manera urgente los proyectos para sostener la vigencia y actualización del Estatuto del Periodista Profesional. 




Exigimos a la senadora @carmenAlvarezR que sesione la Comisión de Trabajo y Previsión. Denunciamos que desde la Reforma Laboral no se juntó ni una sola vez, bloqueando cualquier tipo de debate democrático.




— SiPreBA – Sindicato de Prensa de Buenos Aires (@sipreba) 

October 30, 2026







Durante el acto expresaron su apoyo los senadores Mariano Recalde, Marcelo Lewandowski, Jimena López, Ana Inés Marks y María Teresa González, junto al diputado Esteban Paulon y el legislador porteño Gabriel Solano.







Los senadores no están haciendo su trabajo y tienen que tratar el Estatuto del Periodista.




Nuestro secretario general, @AguLecchi estuvo en @radioconvos899 en el programa de @aleberco donde comentó que desde la sanción de la reforma laboral, la Comisión de Legislación del Trabajo del Senado no se volvió a reunir ni una sola vez y convocó mañana a las 12 frente al Senado para exigir a la comisión laboral que trate el proyecto de actualización del Estatuto del Periodista Profesional y del Personal Administrativo presentado en junio pasado.




Convocamos junto a muchos sindicatos de prensa del país nucleados en la @PrensaFATPREN , la @FIP_AL , @aRGra_ , @Fadeccos , @REDCOMargentina , el @CELS_Argentina , @comuUBA , @PeriodistasdArg




— SiPreBA – Sindicato de Prensa de Buenos Aires (@sipreba) 

October 28, 2026







Entre las organizaciones que acompañan el pedido al Congreso se encuentran la Federación Internacional de Periodistas (FIP), el Centro de Estudios Legales y Sociales (CELS), la Asociación de Reporteros Gráficos de la República Argentina (ARGRA), la Federación Argentina de Carreras de Comunicación Social (FADECCOS), Periodistas Argentinas, la Red de Carreras de Comunicación Social (REDCOM) y la Carrera de Comunicación de la Universidad de Buenos Aires (UBA).

author: Ahmed Ismat Ahmed
title: El Fasher, a year later
content:
Nasr City, October 26, 2026

Today is the anniversary, and I still don’t know what that word is supposed to do for anyone.

I was in Cairo when the city fell. I disappeared there — not in any way a person standing outside me could have seen — and I am not leaving that out, as if the one doing the remembering were a pane of glass. But El Fasher sits on an older arithmetic, and the arithmetic is where I have to start.

The old arithmetic

I was in the street in Omdurman on International Women’s Day in 2019, a month before they finally put Omar al-Bashir out of the palace he had occupied for 30 years. Three out of every four people in that crowd were women. The proportion mattered because NISS — the National Intelligence and Security Service, Sudan’s secret police, who have spent decades learning exactly where a society keeps its weight — knew where to look. They find it. Then they go after it.

So they started arresting the women.

There was nothing accidental in this, and nothing hidden. They were not ashamed, because shame requires believing someone is watching who matters, and they did not believe that. If the police took a man that day, it cost almost nothing to get him back: a friend, a cousin, anyone his age from his own street could walk into that station the same afternoon and walk him out again, because a man’s word, in that system, was still worth something on its own. A woman could not do this. A woman arrested had to produce a man — a father, a brother, a husband, some uncle twice removed — because the state had built itself, brick by brick, on the conviction that a woman’s name, standing alone, was not collateral enough to release a woman’s body.

I watched it work. I watched women I knew go quiet in the weeks after, not because they themselves had been taken, but because they understood, suddenly and completely, that the price had changed shape under their feet. It was no longer only her own body in the cell. It was her family’s name, dragged into a police station because she had been standing in a square where the government had decided women should not stand.

That is the oldest trick this state has ever run. I have come to call the thing that runs it a machine — not a government with occasional failures, but an arrangement built to find whatever a population has left, and take it. The war now being fought in Darfur did not invent the trick. The Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the paramilitary formed from the Janjaweed — the militias the state itself armed in Darfur two decades ago — inherited it, and scaled it, until a tactic became the way a siege was built.

The city

The siege had an address. Most people who will read this have only ever met it as a dateline, and a dateline doesn’t let you feel what was emptied.

Darfur is the west of Sudan. It is about the size of Spain, pressed up against Chad, Libya, and the Central African Republic, far enough from the Nile and from Khartoum that the center has always been able to treat the distance as a kind of ownership. Farmers and herders live there — Fur, Zaghawa, Masalit, Berti, Borgo, Rizeigat, and more peoples than a briefing ever bothers to list — Arab and non-Arab, in categories the last century hardened and this one found useful. They have shared land, and they have fought over land, and since 2003 they have done both inside a counterinsurgency. The rebellion started the way rebellions in that region usually start. The center took men for its wars and sent almost nothing back. Bashir’s government answered by arming militias, the ones the world learned to call the Janjaweed, and aiming them at the communities the rebels came from. Hundreds of thousands died. The world said genocide, and then largely changed the channel. The militias were not disbanded. They were paid, given rank, and renamed. The Rapid Support Forces are that renaming. Their commander is Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, Hemedti, and he is at war with the army that made the renaming official. El Fasher is where that arrangement came back to the ground it was built on.

The city is older than any of these men. It was the capital of the Fur sultanate, the place Darfur governed itself from, until that was broken from the outside in 1874. Ali Dinar put a sultanate back together in what was left and held it until 1916, when the British killed him and took Darfur into Sudan. After that El Fasher was no longer a capital in the old sense. It was the town where the new state proved it could still reach the west: an administrative post, and the home of the army’s 6th Infantry Division. As long as that division was standing there, Khartoum could still say the west was inside the country.

By the second year of this war, it was the last place in Darfur where that was still true. Nyala had gone. El Geneina had gone, and with it a campaign against the Masalit that anyone willing to look already knew how to name. Zalingei had gone. What was left was a headquarters, an airport, a city swollen with people displaced by the wars before this one and then by this one, and the roads.

Whoever held those roads held the last lock on a corridor running from Khalifa Haftar’s eastern Libya down through North Darfur toward Nyala, with branches toward Chad. Gold moves on them. Weapons move. Fighters move. The army needed the headquarters, because a flag on the 6th Division was the last way to say that west of Kordofan this was still one country. The RSF needed the corridor. They also needed something the army did not. A garrison can change hands in a day. A population that still believes it can come back and call a place its own takes longer, and the siege was how they worked on that.

The siege

What the RSF has done to women across Darfur is the old arithmetic, taken all the way to its end: that you can control a population by making its women afraid. Afraid to flee, afraid to stay, afraid of the simple fact of being visible in daylight.

I have tried, more than once, to sit with the numbers long enough that they stop being numbers, and I am not sure I have ever once succeeded. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) 

documented 3,396 survivors

 of sexual violence who reached the organization’s own clinics in North and South Darfur between January 2024 and November 2025. Survivors, they are careful to say, not incidents, and only the ones who could get as far as a door. Of them, 97 percent were women and girls. Armed men carried out more than 95 percent of the assaults recorded in North Darfur. The report takes its title from a survivor — “There is something I want to tell you. . . . ” After the city fell, those clinics treated more than 140 people who had reached Tawila in November alone. Almost all of them had been attacked by armed men. Many of them on the road.

The UN’s own investigators have verified patterns of gang rape and sexual slavery, part of a campaign they later concluded 

bore the hallmarks of genocide

. Most of what they verified traces back to the RSF and the militias riding with it.

The number is the edge. The point of the siege is what the edge is for. A woman who cannot cross her own neighborhood without calculating what waits past the checkpoint has already been removed — from the market, from the clinic, from the street, from every place I have ever believed a republic has to live, if it is going to live anywhere at all. I do not use that word lightly, or as a figure of speech. I mean the kettle, the stall, the gate where people fed each other without being asked. The world people build underneath the one that is trying to kill them. A siege’s first target is always that world, because that world is the only proof a population has that it does not need anyone’s permission to survive.

And the siege did not begin with a massacre. It began the way these things begin, with hunger, and with a word withheld.

In February 2024, MSF estimated that around 13 children were dying each day in Zamzam camp, just south of the city — at least one every two hours — and said the severely malnourished who had not yet died would die within weeks if they could not reach treatment. 

Famine was not declared there until August

. It was the first place in this entire war where the word was finally permitted to be official. The children had not been waiting on the paperwork. The paperwork had been waiting on them.

In April 2025, six months before El Fasher fell, the RSF stormed the camp. The UN Human Rights Office 

later documented more than 1,000 civilians killed

. Hundreds of them were summarily executed. People were killed in the market. A market is where a besieged population keeps the last thread of an ordinary life, and the logic of a siege is to find every thread a people have left and cut it. More than 400,000 people were driven out within days, toward Tawila and into El Fasher — a city that was already starving, and that would fall with them still inside it.

The UN would later say that what was done in the city mirrored what had been done in the camp. I do not think Zamzam was a prelude. I think Zamzam was El Fasher, rehearsed first on people the world had already quietly decided it could afford to lose.

The fall

By the last week of October 2025, what remained of El Fasher had gone 18 months without reliable food, without medicine, cut off from the rest of the country the way you cut a limb off and tell yourself the body will manage. They had pushed earth up around it, and people who tried to leave were shot along that earth. The final offensive ran from October 24 to 30. The killing crested on October 26. The army’s retreat is dated to October 27. I am writing on the second of those days, a year on, and I still do not know what an anniversary is supposed to accomplish for the dead, except to force the living to do the arithmetic again, out loud, on a date.

When the garrison left, the plan reached the end it had been built for.

A city is rooms, with people inside them who had, until recently, every reason to believe the rooms would hold.

On October 26, RSF fighters turned heavy weapons on 

about 1,000 people sheltering in Al-Rashid dormitory

 at El Fasher University. Witnesses, independent of each other, put the dead in that room at around 500. The UN’s report records another mass killing at the university the same day: around 600 people executed where they had taken shelter, about 50 of them children.

Two days later, fighters went into 

the Saudi Maternity Hospital

 — the last hospital in the city still working, in a place whose clinics had already been hit again and again since the siege began. The World Health Organization’s count is no fewer than 460 people — patients, and those who had stayed to care for them instead of fleeing. A hospital is where a person goes because some part of them still believes, against everything, that there is one room left that will not be turned into this. El Fasher did not have that room left. Not one.

Then the numbers, which are not one number.

Everyone wants a figure that can be defended. That is what a fact-check wants. It is, God forgive me, what my own training as a journalist wants. In February 2026, the UN Human Rights Office 

published

 what it could document from more than 140 survivors and witnesses: at least 4,400 people killed inside the city between October 25 and 27, and more than 1,600 killed on the roads as they tried to leave. In the same breath, in the same finding, it said the real toll of that week was undoubtedly higher. The hospital is not inside those three days. October 28 sits outside them. So does everything the interviews could not reach, which is most of what happened.

Yale’s Humanitarian Research Lab

, reading the ground from orbit because no one could walk it and live, identified at least 150 clusters of objects consistent with human remains between October 26 and November 28. The same report said the images could not be turned into a count. It assessed that the RSF had likely killed tens of thousands — burning, burying, moving bodies until piles visible one week were gone the next.

The Guardian

, on December 5, 

reported

 a closed briefing to British MPs. Sarah Champion, who chairs the House of Commons International Development Committee, said an academic there had called 60,000 killed in three weeks a low estimate. Not a figure Parliament adopted. Not Yale’s figure. Not the UN’s. One is a documented minimum for three days, and it distrusts itself. One is a month of disposal, and it refuses to be a toll. One is an estimate offered in private, for a different stretch of days. Defend any of them as the number and you have given it work it cannot do.

I used to want the distance between them to prove a last stage of the operation: an arithmetic made impossible on purpose, so the argument would never close. I cannot show that order. I won’t invent it. There was a systematic effort, visible from space, to manage the dead. There is, a year later, a quarrel about which figure may be said out loud. A massacre everyone can settle on a number for is a massacre someone has lost control of. That sentence is mine. The record’s sentence is the gap, and the gap needs a different word than killing.

Mustafa Hijazi, the Lebanese psychologist whose work on the psychology of oppression is widely read across the Arab world, spent a career trying to build a vocabulary for what long oppression does to a person, and English has no clean twin for the word he eventually chose. He did not use it in the book that made his name. That book was about 

qahr

: oppression, subjugation, a pressure that at least still recognizes you enough to require your submission. Decades later he decided 

qahr

 was not a wide enough net, and he reached for 

hadr

. He meant something beyond subjugation: the withdrawal of recognition altogether. A life converted, as he put it, into a discarded number. He was writing about poverty, and dictatorship, and what the long afterlife of colonization does to a person’s sense of being worth counting at all. He was not writing about mass graves. I do not know a better word for a human being caught between 4,400 and an estimate of 60,000 that no office will sign. 

Qahr

 killed them. 

Hadr

 is what the rest of us do to them afterward, every time we let the counting stand in for the reckoning.

A year on, 

Amnesty International

 — from testimony gathered in August and September 2026 — cites figures from humanitarian organizations working in the city: fewer than 70,000 people still there, against a pre-war population of more than a million. I am not going to subtract one from the other and call the result the missing. “Pre-war” and the day the siege closed were not the same city. People had already fled into El Fasher from the rest of Darfur and stayed. The dead, the fled, and the remaining do not resolve. Neither confirmed dead nor confirmed living, they remain an absence where a population stood, without even the dignity of a number.

Disappearing

Hadr

 was not only done to the dead. Some of it was done to me, and I am done leaving that implied.

I disappeared the way I have disappeared before. Not with any ceremony. A thread slipping loose somewhere behind the sternum, so quietly that you only notice it afterward, the way you only notice you were holding your breath once you have already let it out. I stopped answering messages. I let the phone ring itself out. I told people I was working, and some days that was even true, in the way that keeping your hands busy can be true while the rest of you has already left the room. Mostly I was just gone. A street can look fully occupied from the outside while every house on it has quietly, completely emptied.

I am Sudanese, and I have watched enough other Sudanese people do this exact thing by now to know it is not a personal failing. It is what happens when a body finally runs out of the part of itself that knows how to grieve in public, in real time, on a schedule, while the people around you expect you to produce an explanation for numbers that should never have required an explanation from anyone.

I only found a name for it years after I had already lived it. Not in the later book, the one about 

hadr

, but in the earlier one, which Hijazi wrote on what it does to the inside of a person to live under someone else’s boot. He called it escape — one of exactly two moves left open to anyone who has run entirely out of room to fight back. The other, he wrote, is identification: borrowing the logic of whoever is crushing you, because at least their logic still has power running through it, and yours, by that point, has none. I took the first. I have spent this year looking, longer than I wanted to, at men who took the second.

He had another name, from that same book, for the month I had after the city fell. A disturbance of continuity. The past stops leading anywhere, and the future stops being a place you are still allowed to arrive at. You live inside a fog with no before and no after, an unbearable present you survive one hour at a time, and nothing more ambitious than that. He did not write it about me. I do not know a more exact description of the month I had.

We keep calling this resilience. I have come to hate that word. It gets handed to us like a compliment, by the same hand that keeps doing the breaking. Nobody told me, when El Fasher fell, that it was allowed — that it was all right — to simply stop. So if you are the kind of person who disappears the way I do: it was all right. It still is.

What brought me back was not a decision, because I do not think I had one left to make. It was smaller than that. A friend who kept texting me without once asking for anything back. Someone who called and stayed on the line while I said almost nothing at all, for as long as I needed to say nothing. I have come to believe that is the only cure there actually is for this particular kind of disappearing. Not time. Never time. Someone who simply refuses to let your silence mean that you are gone. It is the same republic: people who decide, without being asked, that you still count.

I am writing this because the people who died in that dormitory, and in that hospital, and the women this war has tried to silence by the oldest means it has, do not get to wait until I feel ready. The only thing I have left to offer them, from this distance, in this language, is a record. This happened. Here. To people who had names. Somebody’s son. Somebody’s patient. Somebody’s entire reason for getting up that morning. The record does not stop at the rooms. It has to say what the land had been prepared, for years, to allow inside them.

What the land was for

The dead in El Fasher were mostly Zaghawa. The dead in El Geneina, in 2023, were mostly Masalit. Both are non-Arab peoples of Darfur, and the men with the rifles treated that fact as the whole explanation. I have never found a history that lets it be.

Witnesses say the fighters moving through the city had already decided, before they arrived, that no one left inside counted as a civilian. Everyone who remained was a soldier, in their language. That sentence is not a description of a battlefield. It is a permission slip — the same permission slip Khartoum wrote for Darfur in 2003, the campaign the world eventually agreed to call genocide, back when it needed men willing to burn a village all the way down so its people could never come back and call it theirs again.

The British, once Ali Dinar was dead, did not see a plantation, the way they saw the cotton at Gezira. They saw a buffer: men recruited cheaply, a population run through chiefs — 

nazir

, 

omda

, 

sheikh

 — paid a salary and told the office was tradition. It was administration, with a tribal face. Mahmood Mamdani, in 

Citizen and Subject

, calls the result a bifurcated state. Citizens at the center, who can reach a court. Subjects at the edge, who can reach a chief set over them and nobody else. Birth decided whether a grievance would ever arrive somewhere built to hear it. The arrangement outlived the British by 60 years. Darfur is where it still tests what it can get away with.

Land and water were real grievances, and so was a Sahara moving south. Hunger is not a metaphor. For decades they passed through a system that could see a person only as a tribe. Khartoum armed the men who held the grievance, gave them a story about which neighbors were properly Sudanese, and called that a policy. Not an ancient hatred of herders and farmers, turning itself on. A state, burning the cheapest fuel it had.

In the man with the rifle, Hijazi’s second move is what the fuel feels like. Identification: you adopt the logic that broke you, because no other logic has looked like power, and you aim it sideways — at whoever has less cover than you — rather than up, at the room that armed you. Recognition, the first move, is a resistance committee, the kind that organized neighborhoods in 2019, or a kettle at a gate no ministry appointed. What was done to you was built, and built things can be unmade. Both moves come from the same neglect. They live on the same streets.

Abu Lulu

In the last week of October, one of those streets had a man on it with a camera.

Abu Lulu’s name is Al-Fateh Abdullah Idris. He filmed himself executing civilians in El Fasher. 

Reuters has verified

 four videos of him, on October 27, shooting at least 15 unarmed captives. All of them were in civilian clothes.

He had been filming for months before that. In August, inside the city, he questioned a trader who owned a restaurant and asked the man’s tribe. The man said he did not know where the army’s commander was. He said he had a restaurant. 

Sudans Post

 and 

Al Jazeera

 do not fully agree on the name he gave when the question came. They agree on the kind of answer the question was built to pull out of him — a non-Arab person of Darfur — and they agree on what happened next. Abu Lulu shot him at close range. He told the camera that since the Rapid Support Forces had existed, he had never spared a prisoner. Not one.

He kept filming as the city fell. On a livestream he said he had killed more than 2,000 people, lost count, and would begin again at zero. 

BBC Verify

 recorded what he said to a man who was begging, and a fighter beside him who tried to step in. The captive had pleaded that they knew each other, that he had called out to him days before. Abu Lulu waved the fighter off. “I will never have mercy,” he said. “Our job is only killing.”

I keep coming back to the word job. Not grief, which would have had a dead person of his own somewhere behind it. Not a feud a family could tell you the beginning of. Not an order he could later say he hated and followed anyway. The job.

In the hours before there was an arrest or a statement, I watched accounts loyal to the RSF celebrate him. They called him 

faris

, knight, and turned him into generated images, copper, a figure for a monument rather than a charge sheet. On the livestream where he boasted of the 2,000, men attached to the force called him a hero. Where there was anger, the anger was that he kept filming, not that he kept shooting. They were saying what he did was all right.

He had already done this in public in August. The handcuffs didn’t appear until the end of October, after the videos from the fall had gone around the world and the force needed to be seen taking account of something. A spokesman said Abu Lulu had never been inside the RSF’s command. An allied militia leader, in their telling, who had borrowed the name. There was an arrest, and handcuffs for the cameras, and a promised investigation.

Gedo Hamdan Abu Nashuk, the RSF’s commander for North Darfur, was walking with Abu Lulu on the morning of October 27. Reuters put him within 40 meters of two of the executions, in the same two-hour window. That same day the 

Centre for Information Resilience

 placed Abdelrahim Dagalo — Hemedti’s brother, and the force’s deputy — inside the headquarters of the 6th Infantry Division while the city was being taken.

The Security Council 

sanctioned Abu Lulu in February 2026

, together with Dagalo and two other commanders.

In May 2026, 

Reuters reported

 that he was out and fighting. Nine sources described a release and a return to the front in Kordofan. Three of them — an RSF commander, an officer close to the leadership, and a researcher in contact with the committee charged with investigating him — said Abdelrahim Dagalo gave the order. Separately, another commander and a relative said he was released on the condition that he not film and not be filmed. Reuters did not establish that those were Dagalo’s words. The RSF called the report of a release completely false: he had remained in custody since the arrest, the force said, and he would face a special court with the others accused of violations in El Fasher.

They are arguing about where he is being kept. They are not arguing about the man who said he had a restaurant.

I used to think the worst of what this does to a man was his honest belief that he had done nothing wrong. The belief is real. I watched people mean it. What I no longer think is that the institution needs the belief. It can let fighters call a man a knight, and let a spokesman say the man was never theirs. If the sources are right and the denial is not, it can have the deputy commander free him and then tell the public he is still in the cell. He did not arrive over El Fasher out of nowhere. He is what a long series of reasonable decisions, each of them made in a room, leaves standing in a street.

I understood the rooms differently after I heard him. Not as what happens when fighters lose their heads on the day a garrison falls. The garrison was what the army was holding. The 18 months before it fell were pointed at something else — a population that would not be able to stay, or come back, or keep a market, or trust a hospital that still believed it was a hospital. They attacked Zamzam’s market in April. They shot the roads in October. The ward was two days after the dormitory. At the end of that, the roads are still there, and the gold is still there, and there are fewer people left who can stand on either of them and say the place is theirs.

That is 

hadr

 worked from the other direction. A government can spend generations deciding which of its people are citizens and which are only fuel, and some of the fuel will do the violence and experience it as the way the world has always been. Nothing in that sentence defends a dormitory or a hospital. It refuses the easier account, in which the evil of those rooms needs no past.

Abu Aqla Keikal commanded RSF forces in Gezira until he defected to the army in October 2024. Fighters under him are accused of mass rape in the towns they held. He is not a clean witness. In May 2025, in a closed meeting with journalists in Port Sudan, he said Hemedti ran the war himself — the calls, the ammunition, the uniforms — and that when the rapes were put in front of him, the tears came and the words did not. He said he had not commented on the silence. His office, the same day, called the published account excerpted and fabricated, and promised a tape. I have not seen the tape. I will not build a commander’s knowledge on a story his own office disowned. I will not pretend the story was never told.

The pay does not depend on it.

The RSF lacks the things that matter in an army here: wages that arrive whether or not you steal, and a court that can overrule your commander. Men who have worn the uniform describe being paid late, or in money the war has already destroyed, or not paid, and sent to take the rest from the battlefield — ransom, gold, whatever a town still contains. That is the wage, not a problem the wage is waiting out. Try Abu Lulu honestly, all the way down, and the tribunal has to ask his whole rank the question the videos already asked in public. There is not enough rope in Darfur for that answer. You would not be disciplining a fighter. You would be indicting the pay that keeps him facing your direction. That is the old meaning of militia, whatever it is wearing: it answers to whoever pays it this week, and both of the things it exists to do — fight, and extract — require that nobody above the fighter can tell him no and be obeyed. Darfur had not been given the courts the center was given. The RSF did not invent the absence. It enlarged it, from a province stripped without an accounting to a force that strips without one. The design held. The uniform changed.

One floor higher, the failure is different, and I won’t write it as if it were. Since 2005 the International Criminal Court has had jurisdiction over Darfur, on a referral from the Security Council. On October 6, 2025, three weeks before El Fasher fell — not during the week of the offensive — it 

convicted Ali Kushayb

, a Janjaweed commander, for killings and other crimes committed in 2003 and 2004. The sentence came in December. It is the only conviction that mandate has produced. In January 2026 the deputy prosecutor told the Council that her office assessed war crimes and crimes against humanity in the capture of the city, and was working toward individual responsibility. The lag is shameful on its own: a verdict about the previous war, delivered while this one was still starving a city, and a briefing months later still at the work of naming commanders. It is not the same act as killing people and then denying the count. The two acts land on the same dead. That is the charge. Coordination is a different allegation, and I don’t have it.

El Fasher was the last ground the army held in Darfur. Whoever held it held the gold there, and the roads out to Chad and Libya, and the buyers who have not needed to ask where the metal came from. The RSF inherited that use of the land. A buffer you can take from is worth more, to whoever controls it, than a buffer left in peace. I cannot make every line of that inheritance neat. I can say what stood at the end of the line. A city starved for a year and a half. A camp next to it where, months before famine was a word anyone official would use, the children were already being counted by the hour.

The women who absorb it

What I know about the cost of a closed room, I did not learn from a report.

My mother was pregnant with me, and still finishing her degree, when a government she had no hand whatsoever in choosing decided what the next decade of her life was going to cost her. Nobody consulted her in the room where that decision was made. Nobody ever does. She carried both of us through everything that came after, the pregnancy and the degree both, because someone in that room had decided she only got to keep one of the two, and she declined to agree. I have no more complicated word for it than that.

I did not understand, until much later, that this was not only her story. It is the only story I have ever actually learned how to tell about Sudanese women, and it has been true, without a single exception, of every one I have met since this war began. A decision is made in a room none of them were in. A militia is outsourced instead of disbanded. A shipment of weapons clears a port where nobody asks the hard question. An arms embargo is debated for another month, because another month of debating it costs the people in the room nothing. Far from that room, a woman absorbs what was decided. Not as a symbol of anything. With her body, and her time, and the work she had been studying toward before the decision arrived and insisted on coming first.

This is the part of 

hadr

 that does not need a massacre to operate. It is what gets done, every day, more quietly, to the living women left holding what the dead left behind. The labor doubles, because a closed room created it. Then the doubled labor is praised as strength, and nobody asks who gave the room the right to decide any of it without her sitting there.

Rape as a weapon of siege is not new. The RSF has found a crueler practice of an argument Sudanese women have already been winning, slowly, for longer than this force has existed in any uniform. Absorbing a decision made in your absence is not the same thing as agreeing to it. It is never the same thing.

I am not interested, tonight, in performing a hope I do not feel. I am angry, and I intend to go on being angry. Anger is the only thing still standing upright in me, after everything else that was supposed to carry me through this year has given out underneath me. I still don’t know what the word anniversary is supposed to do. I know what she did.

She did not wait for anyone’s permission to decide when she was finished absorbing what other people had signed. If 

hadr

 is what was done to El Fasher — a people reduced to a disputed figure, an absence the world still cannot agree how to count — then refusing it is not a speech. It is her, decades on, still finishing what she started. Still here. A woman insisting, against every room that ever tried to decide otherwise, on being counted as a person, and not as an outcome.

author: Marina Amaral
title: É o momento de aprofundar a democracia e agir pelo país que queremos
content:
Quer receber os textos desta coluna em primeira mão no seu e-mail? Assine a Newsletter da Pública, enviada sempre às sextas-feiras, 8h. Para receber as próximas edições, 

inscreva-se aqui

.







Não sei se todos vocês sabem, mas a 

Pública 

tem um podcast sobre a emergência climática que chama “

Bom Dia, Fim do Mundo

”. Somos três em volta da mesa — o escritor Ricardo Terto, a jornalista Isabel Seta e eu — dirigidos por Sofia Amaral, nossa coordenadora de audiovisual, e com uma coluna em áudio de uma economista do NoVe — Novas Vozes Econômicas, um grupo que busca abrir e qualificar o debate sobre o tema na imprensa.




Conversamos durante 30 minutos, todas as semanas, com realismo e bom humor, sobre os fatos relevantes para o futuro do país e do mundo, em momento em que a própria existência da humanidade depende da possibilidade de criar uma nova maneira de viver. Como disse o sociólogo Miguel Lago na Piauí: “o clima tornou-se a condição a partir da qual todas as demais questões devem ser pensadas”.




Por isso a gravação do último episódio foi tão emocionante. Depois de alertas e denúncias durante toda a campanha, 

celebramos a democracia, o diálogo, o debate e o engajamento público

 que decolaram na reta final da campanha e afastaram a extrema direita do poder. Comemoramos o resgate de nossa identidade e soberania, ameaçadas por gente que ostenta a bandeira — e o míssil — dos Estados Unidos e de Israel em manifestação de rua.




Não há como engajar os governos e as sociedades para cumprir uma tarefa global, a luta pela emergência climática, sem respeito à autodeterminação dos povos e à soberania das nações, sem espaço para o diálogo e o debate, atravancados pela guerra, pela miséria, por governos autoritários, e atravessados por pensamentos mórbidos de quem considera o fim do mundo inevitável (o que está por trás do negacionismo propositalmente fomentado por aqueles que pensam estar acima do sofrimento global).




Por isso, o mundo comemorou a vitória brasileira contra a extrema direita, forjada por gente que aprendeu a força que detém valores como a vida, a liberdade, a fraternidade, a luta para que todos vivam melhor. Sem ingenuidade, mas com sinceridade, fé no diálogo, e na capacidade de persuasão ancorada em fatos e inspirada por afetos.




Das redes às ruas, as lições do Exército de Lula são agora armas para resistir, junto com o governo democraticamente eleito pelo povo de um país soberano, mas também para ir além, exigindo transparência e urgência em ações e decisões e cobrando a abertura de canais para a participação política. Não há como imaginar possibilidades e agir na direção da mudança, sem entender o significado, a forma e a intensidade que tomou a mobilização eleitoral que levou à vitória da democracia em condições inéditas.




A imagem de Lula com a Constituição de 1988 nas mãos, cercado da multidão com o verde-amarelo da nação e o vermelho da resistência, é para mim um símbolo dessas eleições, e um guia para a construção coletiva desse futuro. Começando pelo presente, com ações eficazes para cumprir o que está determinado na Constituição Cidadã, o que tem sido tarefa sobretudo de organizações e movimentos sociais, indígenas, negros, pessoas trans e mulheres que frequentemente são alvo da violação de direitos fundamentais.




O “povo da luta” pode contar agora também com a mobilização de todos que se aliaram pela democracia, pela soberania e pela defesa das conquistas sociais nas eleições e forçar a implementação dos princípios e garantias determinados pela Constituição, incluindo o direito à informação e à participação política, para construir um futuro mais justo e inovador.




Neste 

episódio

 do Bom Dia, Fim do Mundo, em que também falamos dos desafios internos e externos que temos pela frente, lembramos de um artigo da Constituição, pouco utilizado, que traz grandes possibilidades para os que desejam uma nova forma de governar, como disse o presidente Lula no discurso da vitória.




“A soberania popular será exercida pelo sufrágio universal e pelo voto direto e secreto, com valor igual para todos, e, nos termos da lei, mediante: I- plebiscito, II – referendo; III – iniciativa popular”, enuncia o artigo 14. Até hoje tivemos um único plebiscito (em 1993, para decidir sobre sistema e forma de governo) e um referendo (em 2005, para decidir se a comercialização de armas continuaria a ser permitida).




O terceiro instrumento, a iniciativa popular, é ainda menos lembrado, embora crucial para o aprofundamento da democracia. Ele permite a proposição direta feita pelo cidadão de um projeto de lei ao Congresso, desde que subscrito por 1% do eleitorado, o que favorece a mobilização da sociedade perante o parlamento, assim como outros instrumentos permitem a representação popular na Justiça. Foi assim que foi criada a Lei da Ficha Limpa, em 2010, com a assinatura de 1,6 milhão de eleitores.




Imagine as possibilidades que temos pela frente para utilizar esses mecanismos da democracia direta com todas as lições que aprendemos nessa campanha que uniu sociedade e imprensa independente para qualificar o debate público. Também é a oportunidade de renovar instrumentos como os conselhos populares, as audiências públicas e intervenções de movimentos sociais junto ao STF para cobrar a aplicação das leis, o que é especialmente importante para manter o Senado dentro do campo delimitado por elas.




Com a Constituição nas mãos e as informações na cabeça, podemos ampliar as vozes e a intensidade da participação política no governo nestes quatro anos decisivos para o planeta e para o futuro da democracia. O ano-marco de 2030, que vai definir se conseguimos ou não conter o aquecimento global a 1,5 grau, está logo ali e “a gente combinamos de não morrer”, lembram? O jornalismo independente está à disposição da sociedade.




PS. Estarei em férias pós-eleitorais na próxima semana, volto a encontrá-los no dia 13 de novembro.

author: Shan Kenshin Ecaldre
title: Hegseth visit exposes deepening US military intervention in the Philippines
content:
For ILPS Philippines, these agreements are not merely defense arrangements. They further integrate the country into Washington’s military operations and its First Island Chain strategy against China.







The arrival of US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth in Cebu on October 28 has drawn condemnation from progressive groups, which warned that the Philippines is increasingly being drawn into Washington’s military and economic agenda at the expense of national sovereignty.




The International League of Peoples’ Struggle (ILPS) Philippines said Hegseth’s visit for the ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting comes amid the Trump administration’s aggressive expansion of US military power in the Asia-Pacific and its preparations for greater confrontation with China.




The group described Hegseth as a key enforcer of Washington’s war agenda, criticizing Ferdinand Marcos Jr. administration for facilitating the growing US military presence in the country.




Under the Marcos administration, military cooperation between Manila and Washington has expanded through weapons deployments, joint military exercises, intelligence-sharing arrangements, and the increased use of Philippine military facilities.




Read: 

Missiles, markets, and massacres: Balikatan, ASEAN, and the war logic of US imperial decline*




During Hegseth’s March 2025 visit, the two governments agreed to deploy advanced US weapons, including the Navy Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (NMESIS), expand high-end military exercises, strengthen defense-industrial cooperation, and launch joint cyber operations.




In October 2025, Hegseth and Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. announced a Task Force-Philippines to strengthen joint military planning and operational coordination. This was followed by a 15-year Communications Interoperability and Security Memorandum of Agreement (CISMOA) in May 2026, further institutionalizing secure military communications and information-sharing between the two countries.




These arrangements build on the General Security of Military Information Agreement (GSOMIA) and the nine Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA) sites across the Philippines.




For ILPS Philippines, these agreements are not merely defense arrangements. They further integrate the country into Washington’s military operations and its First Island Chain strategy against China.




The consequences, the group warned, extend beyond military installations. With US forces increasingly capable of operating advanced weapons from Philippine territory, Filipino communities could become vulnerable to retaliation in the event of a regional conflict.




Read: 

Tacloban fishers slam Balikatan exercises




During the May 2026 Balikatan exercises, the US military reportedly 

launched a Tomahawk 

cruise missile from Tacloban Airport, demonstrating its capacity to conduct long-range missile strikes from Philippine soil.




“Our country is being transformed into a forward operating platform for US wars, exposing millions of Filipinos to the grave danger of retaliation, devastation, and death in a regional conflict,” ILPS Philippines said.




The group accused the Marcos administration of sacrificing national independence through its cooperation with Washington, using tensions with China to justify the expanding US military footprint.




While opposing China’s coercion and violations of Philippine sovereign rights, ILPS Philippines stressed that the country cannot defend its sovereignty by allowing another foreign power to use its territory for military operations and war preparations.




Beyond military intervention




Progressive groups also warned that US intervention is not confined to military installations. They said Washington’s economic initiatives are tied to its strategic interests in the Philippines, particularly its access to critical resources and supply chains.




The Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP) condemned Hegseth’s visit, saying the US is pursuing both military access and greater control over resources through initiatives such as Pax Silica.




A US-led initiative seeking to secure supply chains for critical minerals, semiconductors, and other strategic technologies, Pax Silica could further open Philippine resources to foreign corporate interests, the farmers’ group warned.




KMP Chairperson Danilo Ramos said the Marcos administration is surrendering the country’s sovereignty on both military and economic fronts.




“Washington wants access not only to our territory for its war machine but also to our resources. Farmers and rural communities will bear the cost through land grabbing, resource extraction and displacement,” Ramos said.




The group linked these concerns to the 

Luzon Economic Corridor

, which includes infrastructure and industrial projects that could support US strategic and commercial interests.




Among the developments cited were shipyard expansion in Subic for US military warships, an ammunition hub, and a proposed advanced manufacturing park in Capas, Tarlac, intended to support artificial intelligence supply chains.




KMP warned that these projects could intensify pressure on agricultural and ancestral lands, further threatening farmers already struggling with landlessness, agricultural imports, and the encroachment of mining and large-scale energy projects.




For rural communities, the group said, the consequences could mean displacement, loss of livelihood, and greater foreign corporate control over the country’s natural resources.




“Marcos is selling out our sovereignty on both military and economic fronts,” Ramos said.




US military assistance?




Meanwhile, the Makabayan coalition demanded transparency over the latest military arrangements, including their financial implications, operational scope, and consequences for national security.




The growing US military presence has also raised questions about Washington’s own record of military operations and accountability.




Hegseth has faced scrutiny from US lawmakers over strikes on suspected drug-trafficking vessels in the Caribbean, including reports of a follow-up strike that killed survivors. Lawmakers have likewise raised concerns over alleged violations of the laws of armed conflict involving civilian casualties in Iran, including the bombing of a girls’ school in Minab.




Ramos said such incidents must be investigated and those responsible held accountable.




“Deliberately killing defenseless survivors and unlawfully attacking civilians are grave violations of international humanitarian law. US officials like Hegseth must be held accountable, not shielded by their political and military power,” he said.




For progressive groups, the issue goes beyond Hegseth’s visit. It reflects the continuing struggle against foreign intervention and the country’s dependence on a military power whose geopolitical interests do not necessarily serve the Filipino people.




ILPS Philippines stressed that opposing US intervention does not mean tolerating aggression by China or any other foreign power. Rather, genuine sovereignty means refusing to surrender Philippine territory, resources, and military facilities to foreign strategic ambitions.




“The region needs genuine peace, not more American missiles, military bases, and troops,” the group said.




KMP called on Filipinos to oppose US intervention and demand the termination of unequal military agreements that facilitate Washington’s military presence and operations in the country.




“We must fight for genuine independence, national sovereignty and freedom,” Ramos said. 

(AMU, RVO)

Hegseth visit exposes deepening US military intervention in the Philippines

author: Dulce Amor Rodriguez
title: 9 years later, parents still seek answers over son’s killing amid ‘drug war’
content:
Nine years later, the family still has no definitive answers about who killed their son, why the gunmen targeted him, and whether authorities thoroughly investigated the shooting.







Trigger warning: details of violence and death




Nine years after their son was killed in former president Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Nanette and Bong Castillo stepped forward to the Truth Commission’s fifth Public Truth-Telling Session on October 23 to recount what they believe happened to Aldrin Castillo and seek answers on his death.




They believe that the case of their son may have been a case of mistaken-identity, while the police and medical records reviewed by forensic pathologist Raquel Fortun exposed significant gaps in the original documentation of Aldrin’s death.




Aldrin was 32 when gunmen shot him in Tondo, Manila, on October 2, 2017. He was visiting his sister to help repair her air conditioner.




His parents believe the gunmen were looking for another man and killed Aldrin because they mistook him for their intended target.




Nine years later, the family still has no definitive answers about who killed their son, why the gunmen targeted him, and whether authorities thoroughly investigated the shooting.




Son with a future




Nanette came to the Truth Commission determined to tell people who Aldrin was beyond the circumstances of his death.




“I want everyone to know how good Aldrin was as a son,” she said in Filipino.




Aldrin was her firstborn, whom she remembered as affectionate, hardworking, and attentive to the needs of others.




In elementary school, he was recognized for keeping himself neat and clean, and he ranked first in his class in Grade 4.




Nanette recalled that he would ask her to share food with friends who had nothing to eat, even when their own family had little money.




When Aldrin began earning, he gave his mother part of his salary and made sure they ate together before she went home.




Bong also brought his son to catering jobs so he could learn to work and earn money.




Aldrin later learned welding through his partner’s family and dreamed of working abroad to give his parents a better life.




Nanette remembered his promise to take her to Saudi Arabia and build her a house when he found work there.




“Gagawin kitang doña,” 

(I will make you rich.) Aldrin would tell her.




For Nanette, the promise represented a future her son wanted to build for their family, a future cut short when he was killed.




The night of killing




On October 2, 2017, Aldrin visited his sister in Tondo to help repair her air conditioner.




Nanette hesitated before allowing him to leave because she had heard reports of killings in the area. She thought the checkpoints and the election gun ban in effect at the time might help keep him safe.




She gave him money for transportation and watched him leave.




Bong was away in Quezon City for work when the family learned that Aldrin had been shot.




According to the police incident report presented by Fortun, Aldrin was with friends in Tondo when armed men arrived on motorcycles and shot him before fleeing.




Nanette recalled reaching the scene and finding her son lying motionless on the street, his eyes open.




She called for a doctor and an ambulance, still hoping someone could save him.




She held his hand and pressed her ear against his chest, trying to feel a pulse or hear a heartbeat.




“Umaasa ako. Umaasa ako. Umaasa ako,”

 she recalled, repeating how she kept hoping that her son might still be alive.




Nanette also recounted how police officers initially prevented her from approaching Aldrin, saying she might disturb the crime scene. She pleaded to stay beside him, promising not to move anything.




The shock of that night has remained with her.




She still remembers the ordinary details of life with Aldrin, including the meals he loved and the way he would come home and ask what they would eat.




Those memories now coexist with the questions that followed his death.




Mistaken identity




During the session, Nanette recalled hearing that the gunmen had been looking for someone wearing a white sleeveless shirt. It was her nephew who mentioned this detail.




Bong also recounted that a man later approached him and said he was the person the gunmen had been looking for that night.




The parents presented these accounts as the basis for their belief that Aldrin was killed by mistake.




Their account has not, in the material presented during the session, established the identity of the intended target or the people responsible for the shooting.




The possibility of mistaken identity has nevertheless shaped the family’s search for answers. If the gunmen were looking for someone else, the family wants to know why Aldrin was killed and who was behind the attack.




Nanette continues to ask people in the area, including tricycle drivers, whether they know anything about the killing.




She said she returns to the place where Aldrin fell to light candles and ask questions, hoping someone might share information that could help clarify what happened.




“Parang hanggang ngayon nga po ako’y nag-iimbestiga,”

 she said, describing how she still finds herself investigating her son’s death.




Her words underscored a central concern raised by the case: the burden of seeking answers has continued to fall on the family, even years after the killing.




Gaps in forensic record




Raquel Fortun reviewed Aldrin’s death certificate, police autopsy report, incident report, and crime-scene photographs. She also examined his remains after they were exhumed on September 24, 2026, with the family’s consent.




Her presentation identified significant shortcomings in the documentation of Aldrin’s death and the subsequent investigation.




Fortun first questioned the death certificate’s incomplete manner-of-death field. She said it should have identified the death as homicide rather than leaving the field blank.




She also criticized the record’s reference to “death by legal intervention,” questioning the terminology used.




The police autopsy report, conducted on October 3, 2017, the day after Aldrin was shot, stated that he had sustained five through-and-through gunshot wounds. Fortun noted that the body had already been embalmed before the examination.




She said the report was only about one and a half pages long and lacked the detail needed to document the injuries adequately.




The report described gunshot wounds to the head, neck, and trunk, including injuries involving the spinal cord, a major blood vessel, the lungs, heart, liver, and intestines.




But Fortun questioned whether the report sufficiently documented the injuries and their trajectories. Without a detailed account of the entry and exit wounds, she said, it was difficult to determine which wounds corresponded to one another.




The limitations of the original autopsy became particularly important years later, when Fortun examined the preserved remains.




During the September exhumation, she examined the bones and conducted X-rays. Her preliminary findings identified fractures consistent with gunfire to the head and neck region and the trunk, including damage to the first cervical vertebra and ribs.




However, the remains could not answer every question. The soft tissue had decomposed, and the passage of years limited what could be determined from the bones alone.




Fortun said she could only assess the evidence available to her. She also expressed hope that additional records and materials could be obtained to clarify the case.




Her presentation did not identify the gunmen or establish who ordered the killing. Instead, it highlighted the limitations of the original medical documentation and the questions that remain because the available evidence does not provide a complete reconstruction of the shooting.




Questions about the police investigation




Raquel Fortun’s concerns extended beyond the autopsy to the police investigation at the crime scene.




The police incident report described men arriving on motorcycles before shooting Aldrin and fleeing. Investigators recovered five spent cartridge casings, according to the records Fortun presented: two .45-caliber casings and three .40-caliber casings.




But the available documentation did not provide a complete account of the shooting or establish what further investigative steps had been taken.




Fortun questioned the handling and documentation of evidence at the scene, pointing to photographs that raised concerns about crime-scene control, lighting, and the way evidence was marked.




She also raised questions about whether investigators had adequately documented physical evidence and followed up on potential leads.




The gaps in the records left Fortun unable to reconstruct the attack with greater certainty. She said the original investigators should have gathered and documented evidence more thoroughly.




“The people who should have done the investigation, the gathering of evidence, the documentation should have done their job,” she said.




Fortun acknowledged the limits of what the Truth Commission could establish from the available material. Without more evidence, she said, the Commission could not confidently determine what further action the case might warrant.




The shortcomings she identified do not establish who killed Aldrin or prove the family’s mistaken-identity theory. They do, however, raise questions about the completeness of the investigation and whether authorities did enough to establish the circumstances of his death.




Grief beyond killing




Aldrin’s death fractured the Castillo family in ways that extended far beyond the funeral.




Nanette said she blamed herself for allowing him to go to Tondo and later blamed her daughter for asking her brother to visit.




She stopped speaking to her daughter for more than a year because she could not understand why the family had lost Aldrin.




Bong described trying to support his wife while dealing with his own grief and anger.




He said he sometimes withdrew or drank to cope, while Nanette struggled with the emptiness of returning home without her son.




Their pain also followed them online, where strangers mocked Aldrin and told the family that he deserved to die because they believed he was involved with drugs.




Nanette said she initially fought back against such comments, but she later learned to ignore people who did not know her son or understand what the family had endured.




“Kung hindi niyo kami kayang damayan, huwag niyo kaming bastusin,”

 she said, asking people not to insult the family if they could not offer support.




She told the commission that even if people accused someone of a crime, they should not celebrate that person’s death.




The family’s account challenged narratives that reduce people killed during the drug war to labels that make their deaths appear acceptable.




Nanette said she wanted the public to know Aldrin as a son, brother, worker, and person with plans for his future.




Demand for accountability




The Castillo family wants those responsible for Aldrin’s killing to be identified and held accountable.




Bong thanked the Truth Commission for giving them an opportunity to tell their story. Nanette said she hoped the Commission would help establish what happened to her son.




She called on those responsible for the killing, whether police officers or people paid to carry out the drug war, to confront the harm they had caused.




Nanette said she would not seek revenge. She wanted those responsible to face due process, the protection that Aldrin did not receive before gunmen shot him.




For the family, accountability would not bring Aldrin back. But establishing the truth could help them understand his death and prevent other families from experiencing the same loss.




Fortun’s presentation showed how incomplete records and unanswered investigative questions can constrain efforts to establish the circumstances of a killing years later.




The Commission’s next steps will depend in part on whether additional records and evidence can be obtained to clarify the gaps Fortun identified.




At the end of the session, participants took part in a ritual for loved ones who had died, represented by an empty chair and a lit candle.




Nanette read a poem she had written for Aldrin, recalling the difficulty of saying goodbye to a son whose absence continues to shape her life.




She remembered his familiar questions about dinner and the sound of his voice at home.




“Walang hanggang pagmamahal, Aldrin ko, hanggang sa muli nating pagkikita, anak,” 

she said, ending the poem with a promise of enduring love.




Nine years after Aldrin’s killing, his parents gave their account before the Truth Commission and renewed their call for answers.




Their testimony has brought the case back into public view, while Fortun’s review has highlighted the limitations of the records left behind. Who killed Aldrin, whether he was mistaken for someone else, and whether the remaining evidence can help establish accountability are questions that still await answers. 

(RTS, RVO)

9 years later, parents still seek answers over son’s killing amid ‘drug war’
