author: Crystal Greene, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: In Manitoba, community protests legislation that would fast-track resource projects: ‘Have we not lost enough?’
content:
About 100 people attended a demonstration outside the Manitoba legislature on Saturday, ahead of Monday’s First Nations – First Ministers’ meeting where Bill C-39 was on the agenda in Ottawa. Photo by Crystal Greene




Indigenous people in Manitoba are protesting against proposed federal legislation that aims to fast-track resource development — saying it undermines their rights and sovereignty over their lands.




Activists point to several pieces of legislation that they worry would cause more harm to their territories, which are already impacted by climate change and the biodiversity crisis. They also have safety concerns over “man camps” created by industry and potential harms to vulnerable Indigenous women and girls.




Both 

Bill C-5

 and 

Bill C-39

 are set to fast-track major infrastructure projects in “Canada,” by designating them to be of “national interest.” C-5 was passed in 2025, and C-39 is in its third reading. Meanwhile, the proposed 

Bill C-37

 — under review after a second reading — has heightened concerns over First Nations water rights. 




One such 

project of “national interest”

 is 

Churchill Plus

. It would see a pipeline and terminal built to internationally export LNG through the Port of Churchill on Hudson Bay. The arctic deepwater seaport would also handle increased mining exports out of Manitoba, eventually including the 

Ring of Fire

.




About 20 people gathered outside of the Manitoba Legislature on Monday rallying against the legislation and in response to the First Nations-first ministers meeting in Ottawa, which was part of similar solidarity events that happened across “Canada.”




It was one of a few protests in Manitoba in late October against the bills and the extractive projects being pushed through by colonial governments despite opposition. 




People who once stood together in the same spot – the Manitoba legislature – during Idle No More, are standing together again to oppose the fast tracking of major infrastructure projects. Photo by Crystal Greene




Alex Wilson

 of Opaskwayak Cree Nation, a professor in the Faculty of Education at the University of Winnipeg, and an organizer with Idle No More, was at Monday’s rally outside the legislature




Wilson read 

a collective statement from Idle No More

 founders that said “the conditions that gave rise to Idle No More in 2012 are confronting us again.”




Wilson said that includes “sweeping legislative changes, threats to environmental protections, and government decisions affecting Indigenous territories without respecting the authority of the people who belong to those lands.”




Wilson told IndigiNews that there’s been “a constant erosion of treaty rights of Indigenous sovereignty and legislation that protects land, water and the sky.”




“The bills that are proposed are kind of galvanising our understanding that this is an agenda that is continually harming First Nations, Indigenous peoples and our environment.”




At another earlier rally at the Manitoba legislature, on Saturday, Indigenous activists and allies spoke against Bills C-39 and C-37.  It was a finale of the 

Arctic Crossroads Tour

 in Manitoba that visited Churchill, Nisichawayasihk, Thompson, Brandon, and Winnipeg.




Anishinaabe water protector Taylor Galvin who works closely with Manitoba First Nations that are impacted by hydro projects on their lands, attended the event.




Taylor Galvin spoke during Saturday’s event to oppose Bills C-37 and C-39 outside the Manitoba legislature. Photo by Crystal Greene 




“Have we not lost enough? We are living in a ticket time bomb, and our lands and our waters don’t have time, and in Manitoba, our sturgeon relatives don’t have time,” said Galvin, who is from Baaskaandibewi-ziibiing (Brokenhead Ojibway Nation).




“Our fish and our waters are already sick, traces of life-threatening metals like mercury, lead, arsenic, and cadmium are being found in those fish and in those waters.”




Galvin spoke of political greed and “a broken system” that has harmed the environment and continues to extract from it.




“We have a broken system and yet they want more, Bill C-39, removing Indigenous rights, and trying to move forward at a very quick pace for projects of ‘national interest,’” Galvin said.




“Why aren’t the people considered national interests? What aren’t the animals considered national interests? Why are they talking about these things without protecting anything?”




Environmental activists and land defenders came together to oppose Bills C-39, C-37 and C-5, outside the Manitoba legislature on Saturday, Oct. 26. Photo by Crystal Greene




‘We are deeply concerned’




IndigiNews spoke to provincial minister of environment and climate change Mike Moyes on Monday outside the legislature.




Moyes said he recognizes Indigenous Manitobans have concerns about Bill C-39, and the province will continue to hear them out despite their lack of jurisdiction on the proposed federal legislation.




“I would advocate that they speak with their MPs and with the federal government,” Moyes said.




“We’re going to continue to talk to lots of nations because we know that relationship is important and we want to make sure that we are hearing directly from them.”




Pimicikamak Elder Jack Osborne questions Mike Moyes, Manitoba’s environment and climate minister on Monday. Photo by Crystal Greene




During an Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs’ 

press conference in Ottawa

 on Saturday, David Monias, chief of Pimicikimak Cree Nation north of Winnipeg, called for the withdrawal of Bill C-39. 




“We are deeply concerned that this legislation could accelerate major project approvals, allow construction to begin before assessments and consultations are complete, especially, the free prior, and informed consent,” he said.




“It creates regions where important safeguards could be weakened and permit changes to conditions to previously approved agreements like the Northern Flood Agreement.” 




Monias’s community was part of the 1977 agreement made with Manitoba Hydro that was supposed to compensate hydro-affected communities for the damage caused by hydro dams and diversions of waterways.




“You cannot call it a true partnership if the most important decisions that are to be made for our nations are not meaningfully heard,” he said.




“You cannot call it reconciliation if governments continue to recognize in principle, while their answers undermine those rights in practice.”




A Government of Canada press release about the introduction of Bill-39 

said the legislation

 “will reshape the regulatory approvals process.”




“Our government is bringing speed, certainty, and predictability to how we build,” said prime minister Mark Carney in the press release. “So investors know that when Canada says it wants something built, Canadians will get it built.”




A First Nations – First Ministers’ meeting was held in Ottawa on Monday, bringing together federal, provincial and First Nations leadership to talk about Indigenous priorities. Afterwards, Carney told reporters the government was “open to suggestions on amendments to C-39.”




“The core of C-39 is to organize the federal government to be more effective,” he said. “It puts a timeline on what the federal government’s response needs to be, to certain things, but it’s not a timeline on Section 35 consultations.” 




Carney also said Monday that he would “instruct” his minister of finance to work with the Assembly of First Nations and First Nations financial institutions to co-develop new revenue sharing mechanisms, including a “potential” 

First Nations Sovereign Wealth Fund

.




He also said the First Nations Fiscal Management Act would be amended to enable First Nations to invest in major infrastructure projects, which includes mining, pipelines and LNG.




“In major projects we’re also working together to recruit, train and hire, First Nation workers will actually build them,” Carney said.




“Informed by the insights of this meeting, the government of Canada will act with new measures, both today, new investments today, and in our upcoming federal budget.”




Prime Minister Mark Carney holds a combined First Ministers’ Meeting and Assembly of First Nations meeting in the Diefenbaker building, in Ottawa. 26 October 2026. Photo by Daniel Pereira, Office of the Prime Minister of Canada




Concerns about ‘man camps,’ violence




Kakeká ThunderSky, the northern and rural co-ordinator for Climate Action Team Manitoba, joined Saturday’s rally outside the Manitoba legislature.




“We came together on this tour to build solidarity and to tell our stories because our rights and our territories, our lands, our waters and skies are under attack by these pieces of legislation that so-called Canada is trying to fast-track,” ThunderSky said.




ThunderSky is of the thunder bird clan, with family roots in Poplar First Nation, an Anishinaabe community north east of Winnipeg. 




“They’re trying to put our livelihoods, our territories, our lands, our water, our sky, our women, our girls, our Two-Spirit relatives’ lives on the line for national profit, whose interests are they keeping in mind?” ThunderSky asked.




“We are here on this tour to say ‘that’s not right’ and that ‘enough is enough.”




ThunderSky added that fast-tracking resource extraction projects wouldn’t only accelerate the climate crisis, but warned that it would accelerate social implications for Indigenous communities, as “man camps” are known to bring violence to Indigenous women and girls.




“When will we be brought into consideration when implementing these pieces of legislation and these projects?”




Lisa Hart Currier of Nisichawayasihk Cree Nation traveled with ThunderSky and other panelists on the Arctic tour as an “auntie.”




“We’ve already seen what Manitoba Hydro has done to our communities, We’ve already experienced the violence,” she said. “We don’t want to deal with pipeline man camps, we don’t want RCMP militarized police in northern Manitoba, protecting a pipeline.”




Pictured are members of the Arctic Crossroads Tour, (left to right): Drew Harris, Ramon Kataquapit, Kakeká ThunderSky, and Lisa Hart Currier. Photo by Crystal Greene




Maxwell Burke,

 spoke at the Arctic Crossroads Tour stop in Churchill, a town of 800, on the southwestern shore of Hudson Bay. Burke, a lifelong Churchill resident, works as a guide, who gives beluga tours and takes people out to spot polar bears. 




The federal and provincial governments want to expand the Port of Churchill with its proposed Churchill Plus project. It would include a Liquid Natural Gas (LNG) terminal, receiving LNG from a pipeline going across the north, and destined for international markets via the Hudson Bay.




The Bay is where a beluga whale sanctuary sits and polar bears live, their habitats are already under threat from climate change. 




Burke recalled being in the same room last year where Manitoba premier Wab Kinew had proposed the 

Port of Churchill Plus project

, as part of a broader plan, the 

Western Energy Corridor

.  




“He came to us, dressed as a leader, talking like a leader, but what came out of his mouth was a sales pitch.” Burke said.




“What I saw was a buyer, a desperate buyer, because he wasn’t offering to sell us something, he was offering to buy something from us, what he was offering to buy from us, was everything, and he didn’t name a price.




“He is asking for us to sell our community. He is asking for us to sell our land, our water, our bears, our belugas.”




Burke said pushing back against development, however, is “not a hopeless pursuit.”




“I’ve met with people who’ve successfully negotiated with power, I’ve met people who’ve managed to, at every step of the process, from the beginning to all the way to the end, cancel these things,” Burke said.




“There is always a way to say ‘no.’ And Wab Kinew is actually right, because when he looked at me when I asked him how to say ‘no,’ he said, ‘it’s up to you,’ and unfortunately, it is up to us. “




A policy analyst questions the decision-making




In Ottawa on Monday, people gathered outside the First Nations – First Ministers’ meeting, including Mohawk policy analyst Russell Diabo, Idle No More, a delegation from Onion Lake Cree Nation in Treaty 6, and land defenders who came from near and far to have their say with the government. 




“Our people need to be involved in all of the decisions now, especially, since they’re trying to bring in this legislation Bill C-37, which we call the ‘the denial of water rights act,’ or Bill C-39, what we call the ‘building Canada wrong act,’ they’re going to continue pushing that legislation,” said Diabo in a 

Facebook live video

   




“I think we’ve made our point here today, if we weren’t here, the media would’ve said the First Nations are agreeing with the Carney approach and the premiers.” 




Diabo said Indigenous leaders had the chance to explain to government representatives that they oppose Bill C-39 and “we oppose the fact that as rights holders, we’re not included in decisions.”




“We know they don’t have a right to sign on our behalf, they’re going to do it anyway, and we have to react to it and then figure out what our next steps are,” Diabo said. 




”I hope we continue on and build this movement to something bigger.” 







The post 

In Manitoba, community protests legislation that would fast-track resource projects: ‘Have we not lost enough?’

 appeared first on 

Indiginews

.

author: Wini Omer
title: It’s not the refugees, it’s the austerity measures!
content:
A Sudanese journalist, with whom I worked for two years at the same newspaper, told me when I contacted him to check on his situation after the last wave of attacks against refugees in Libya: “We are trapped in our homes. We can’t leave. I didn’t send my kids to school since the beginning of this wave of violence. The situation is difficult beyond imagination.”

The Sudanese who left Sudan seeking refuge in Libya, amid very violent clashes that started in April 2023 and continue to this moment, are facing violence, danger, and hatred in what was supposed to be a safe refuge. But this reality is not exclusive to Sudanese refugees, and the violence is indifferent to other nationalities who are fleeing conflicts, war, and instability at home: Ethiopians, Eritreans, and refugees from the Central African Republic.

In Libya, African refugees faced waves of violence, the latest in June this year. Despite competing for power, Libya’s rival authorities in the east and west have united in stoking anti-migrant rhetoric and launching a violent campaign of mass detention and expulsions against migrants and refugees, as a recent 

Human Rights Watch report

 has indicated.

In Egypt, a 

crackdown campaign

 led by security forces, accompanied by social media hate speech against Sudanese and Syrian refugees, intensified on the ground, blaming them for the rise in living costs, mainly rents, groceries, and basic life needs. As a result of systematic brutality, between January and June 2026, 

12 Sudanese passed away in Egyptian detention centers

 and police cells, including a child of 17. Refugees processed for deportation are forced to sign voluntary return declarations.

Sudan hosts one of the largest refugee and asylum-seeker populations in Africa, mainly South Sudanese, Ethiopians, and Eritreans, who currently face detention and 

forced deportation

 from the capital, Khartoum, to refugee camps close to the borders with their countries of origin, after the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) regained control of the capital. This step was taken following a growing political rhetoric that profiled them as criminals and blamed them for the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) controlling Khartoum. Accordingly, they were deported to refugee camps in White Nile State, Al-Gadarif State, and Kassala State, camps that lack all basic human needs and restrict freedom of movement and the right to work. Many South Sudanese mothers were deported while their children were not allowed to accompany them, leaving them in limbo.

Such rhetoric, mainly produced and shared by pro-SAF individuals and platforms, provides the military establishment with a popular cover to reproduce its symbolic authority. It is also used by some actors within the army as a tool to bolster its legitimacy against the Rapid Support Forces, portraying it as the guardian of national sovereignty and the representative of the “authentic Sudanese” against the “foreign threat.” This reflects a deeper attempt to regain control over the state and society at a moment of total collapse of political and legal frameworks.

For many of these refugees, especially the Eritreans, returning is not an option, considering the human rights situation in Eritrea. But according to media reports, both Eritrea and Sudan are 

complicit in the repatriation of civilians from Sudan

 back to Eritrea.

Whether it is the systematic violence against Sudanese refugees on the continent, or the deliberate violence against African refugees in Sudan, these incidents reflect one broader reality in which violence is used and reproduced either by state actors or by the citizens of the host countries to whom the refugees sought safety within the African continent. This reality raises a critical question about how to understand such incidents, the politics behind them, and why we are seeing them now.

Shifting the blame

Have the refugees led to the economic crises in Egypt, Libya, or Tunisia? Or are these crises a direct result of the state’s social and economic policies?

In Egypt, the last ten years have witnessed a high level of dependence on debt; Egypt has become one of the IMF’s largest borrowers, while social expenditure, including social protection, health, and education, has shrunk, accompanied by political oppression. Those debts have been invested in projects lacking a developmental dimension, such as 

the new administrative capital

 project, which is expected to cost up to $300 billion by the time it’s finalized. The new capital is home to Africa’s tallest 

tower

, the world’s longest 

monorail

, and a new presidential palace commissioned by President Sisi. This tells the story of the political crisis through spatial isolation: Government ministries and parliament have been moved kilometers away from the historic urban spaces where demonstrations and revolutions were shaped. It is also heavily securitized through surveillance and the military, shifting budgets away from serving the people toward strict monitoring. State resources and national debt constrain the broader economy and exacerbate poverty and social inequalities.

Higher external debt interest payments, in addition to the 

cost of arms imports

, which increased by 215 percent in 2013–2017 compared to 2008–2012, led to an economic crisis. Debt has also been a tool for maintaining a grip on citizens, while the military’s economic empire has expanded. It’s also worth noting that 1,365 conditions were imposed by the IMF and World Bank on MENA nations over the last 15 years, enforcing austerity, privatization, and deregulation. Conditionality has shaped the social and economic realities in many countries across the globe.

The state has slowly 

moved away from the bread subsidy system

 over the past ten years of International Monetary Fund–guided policy adjustments. This economic crisis has also contributed to the 

rise in immigration rates

 among Egyptians to Gulf countries and beyond.

This pattern aligns with Samir Amin’s critique: Peripheral states are integrated into global capitalism in ways that prioritize capital accumulation and elite prestige over popular welfare.

In Libya, the political and economic crises have intersected, creating a hostile environment for refugees. The cash-flow crisis stemming from multiple changes to national currency notes, high unemployment rates, deterioration of social services, electricity instability, and a health-care system that is not adequately accessible to the population have compounded the situation. All of these crises are a direct result of years of conflict and political instability.

It’s also a direct consequence of imperialist intervention in Libya. NATO and US military operations in Libya, the sanctions, and the border-engineering policies financed by the EU have all resulted in building a racist architecture. Resources received from the EU were used to establish influential militias, including the Libyan Coast Guard, now running smuggling and human trafficking economies that are 

sanctioned by the UN

, even as they continue to receive EU 

funding and training

.

Similarly, Tunisia has been 

trapped in debt

. The social justice demands that ignited the 2010 revolution were not addressed; instead, an oppressive system is maintaining itself.

Such crises have led to high unemployment rates and rising poverty, fueling both the desire among young people to emigrate and scapegoating narratives against refugees promoted by those who stayed.

The South African case provides a clear example of this shift in blame. In a country with an unemployment rate of over 43.7 percent, protests against migrants have intensified in recent months, primarily led by the 

March and March

 movement, blaming African migrants for unemployment, poverty, crime, and lack of public services like education and health care. They called on the government to deal with the influx of migrants and protect opportunities. While it’s understandable that material despair and fear drive these protests, the root causes of this compounded crisis cannot be ignored. That includes the legacy of apartheid and the lack of economic justice post-independence. The white population, which constitutes 8 percent of the whole South African population, controls around 80 percent of the land, leaving the majority of the population, Black and coloured, with no ownership of land or means of production. With little being done to implement the social justice agenda in the post-apartheid state, wealth has remained concentrated among the same elite class, while the majority remain impoverished.

Adopting social and economic policies that impoverish people and limit their access to social services and basic needs is a key feature of the approaches in Egypt, Tunisia, Libya, and South Africa, among many other countries. This strategy is universal and aims to collectively punish populations to protect the systems that exploit them.

Refugees are being blamed for the difficult material conditions of citizens in crisis-affected countries, even though these conditions have their own political and historical structural causes and are closely linked to the political economies of states that are often highly dependent on the profiteering monetary and financial policies of international financial institutions.

Politics of hate and fear

But how are the political and economic crises entangled with hatred or fear of refugees?

Sara Ahmed’s 

The Cultural Politics of Emotion

 sheds light on how an anti-refugee sentiment is built, encouraged, and used to justify violence against them, and how building a national identity comes at the cost of the safety of refugees.

Fear is employed as a tool of political economy and as a technique of governance. In the Egyptian case, fear of refugees burdening the state’s budget is used to justify current social and economic crises and to trap people into relying on the political elite, represented by those in government, to resolve the refugee dilemma. Sudanese, Palestinian, and Syrian refugees have been labeled as such, and Sudanese refugees have lost their lives due to the security policies and interventions that forcibly deport them. A recent anti-refugee narrative relates to fear of what is called the “Afrocentrism discourse,” as many social media accounts share concerns over deliberate efforts by Black refugees to change the culture and demography of Egypt.

Fear of demographic change is echoed more loudly in official political speeches in Tunisia. President Kais Saied 

reflected on

 this specific issue during an official speech, while the crackdown on human rights activists continues, and voices that criticized the economic situation in Tunisia are silenced. Additionally, a 

Tunisian MP used racist language to deny reports

 on female refugees being sexually assaulted in Tunisia.

In Libya as well, such discourse spreads on social media, provoked by politicians seeking to build constituencies based on this fear.

On the other hand, Egyptian media portray refugees as the 

main cause of the crisis

 and as a burden on the social infrastructure, such as health and housing. On social media, these campaigns were led by 

pro-regime influencers

, as some fact-checking platforms have indicated.

Syrian refugees and immigrants in Egypt also suffer from this manufactured fear through campaigns, including calls to boycott their businesses, accusing them of hijacking market opportunities.

Similarly, in Sudan, long before April’s war, refugees have faced accusations of immorality and been labeled as a danger to the Sudanese community’s values and social cohesion. Burdening refugees with the responsibility of security and treating them as a threat to national security are also narratives used, especially by the Sudanese army, to justify the forcible deportation of refugees to camps.

Such narratives act as a political strategy: Fear is engineered to elicit collective emotions and utilized in political discourse to mask the flaws of political regimes.

Fanon’s critique of postcolonial elites is relevant in the contexts above; he argued that elites turn the people against imaginary enemies. In this case, refugees are those imaginary enemies.

The failures of neoliberal policy

The shared economic model of these states centers on austerity and privatization policies that aim to limit state spending on social infrastructure and services, while using securitization and violence to suppress any attempts to protest against these policies. This explains why Egyptian arms deals increase as the economy deteriorates.

Refugees are usually forcibly displaced by economic collapse, structural adjustment, climate harm, and governance failure. They are then governed through restrictive asylum regimes, border controls, and humanitarian management. So neoliberal policies help produce displacement and then shape how displaced people are subsequently controlled.

In other cases, we have seen the externalization of borders as a strategy that has allowed states to avoid direct responsibility for violating refugees’ rights. The EU is infamous for leading such strategies. Such policies often come with loans and financial support to the targeted origin and transit countries.

Tunisia has also received such support, leading to a refugee crisis, as thousands are 

trapped in Tunisia

, most of them from sub-Saharan Africa, in a very dire situation, while some have been dumped into the Algerian desert to face their fate.

Previously, the Rapid Support Forces received EU support to control borders in eastern and western Sudan. The Khartoum Process, which evolved into a regional agreement, brokered this deal and provided funding for border externalization.

The European Union Horn of Africa Migration Route Initiative (the 

Khartoum Process

) is a political cooperation platform launched on November 28, 2014, in Rome. It connects countries along the migration route from the Horn of Africa to Europe.

Libya’s decision to ban the entry of citizens from four African nationalities — Sudan, Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Somalia — is also understood as part of these broader policies. Libya was actually among the first countries to receive EU funds to control the influx of refugees at its borders. Meanwhile, 

Greece is recruiting mercenaries

 to push back refugees. Alongside these trends, 

the EU Parliament’s recent law

 reveals a similar stance, with members shouting “send them back” as a law to return refugees was adopted.

From Europe, to Africa, to Southeast Asia, refugees are facing violence, exclusion, and impoverishment. These are the direct social damages of neoliberal policies, generating economic exploitation and social exclusion, and stripping refugees of their dignity and their lives, as is happening right now in Egypt, in Libya, and on the coasts of the Mediterranean Sea.

The Sudanese refugee crisis was ignited by the ongoing war in Sudan; it’s rooted in a long history of conflicts that have driven thousands to leave their homes in search of refuge and dignity. The crises in Sudan that have led to conflict can’t be understood without tracing the histories of austerity, uneven development, and state violence.

Sudanese refugees deserve safety and protection, just like refugees on the African continent and beyond.

Political rhetoric centered on anti-Blackness and blame-shifting must be dismantled to center critiques on the role of capitalism and neoliberal policies. Systems that exploit refugees as cheap labor and as bodies that should produce surplus value must be exposed.

Instead of considering refugees as the problem, we should view them and their vulnerabilities as manifestations of social and economic crises manufactured by neoliberalism, and as direct products of political decisions that fail to center care, justice, and economic sovereignty. The nation-state survives by dividing people, provoking hatred and fear, and stoking competition. We, the oppressed people, must resist.

author: Daniel Avalos
title: Zapatazo en Plaza de Mayo: mil pares de calzado frente a la crisis de la industria nacional
content:
Convocados por Zapateros Unidos, pequeños productores y comerciantes del sector, entregaron mil pares de calzado en Plaza de Mayo, con el acompañamiento de la Cámara del Calzado y la Unión de Trabajadores de la Industria del Calzado. Desde las 11 de la mañana, una larga fila reunió a personas de distintos sectores sociales que coincidieron en una misma dificultad: comprar un par de zapatos. Desde el sector denuncian el cierre de más de 200 empresas y la pérdida de 10.000 puestos de trabajo, desde la asunción de Javier Milei. Una larga fila comenzó a formarse desde las 11 de la mañana en Plaza de Mayo. 

Fotos y texto de Daniel Ávalos (ANRed).







La concentración fue muy variada. Hubo personas en situación de calle, familias con niños y niñas, trabajadores de aplicaciones y personas de distintos sectores sociales. Todxs esperaban lo mismo: recibir calzados nuevos que, en otras circunstancias, podrían haber adquirido por sus propios. La jornada terminó con la entrega de mil pares de calzado.




La escena dejó al descubierto una realidad que atraviesa a más y más personas: afrontar los gastos básicos se vuelve cada vez más difícil. Quienes se acercaban coincidían en que comprar calzado resulta un esfuerzo que muchas veces no pueden sostener. Para muchxs, la entrega gratuita era una oportunidad que no podían dejar pasar. La convocatoria de Zapateros Unidos contó con el acompañamiento de la Cámara del Calzado y la Unión de Trabajadores de la Industria del Calzado. Pero detrás de los pares entregados había otra preocupación: el futuro de quienes producen y comercializan calzado en el país. Desde la asunción de Javier Milei, más de 200 empresas del sector cerraron sus puertas, según denuncian representantes de la actividad. A esa cifra se suma la estimación sindical de 10.000 puestos de trabajo perdidos durante el mismo período. Los números expresan la dimensión de una crisis que golpea a fabricantes, comerciantes, talleres y proveedores, y que amenaza con desarticular una cadena productiva construida durante décadas.




Desde el sector apuntan contra la apertura de las importaciones sin medidas que protejan la producción nacional. A la caída del consumo se suman las dificultades para competir con productos importados y sostener la actividad. Para los pequeños productores y comerciantes, la continuidad de esta política puede significar el cierre de sus emprendimientos y la pérdida de sus fuentes de ingreso. Pero la preocupación no se limita al impacto económico.







Quienes participaron del reclamo señalaron la falta de respuestas y de señales concretas por parte del Gobierno para encontrar una salida a la crisis. Mientras la actividad se deteriora, aseguran que no hay propuestas que les permitan proyectar un futuro.




El zapatazo puso en contacto dos realidades que suelen presentarse por separado. De un lado, personas que tienen dificultades para afrontar el costo de un producto indispensable. Del otro, quienes lo fabrican y comercializan y ven amenazada su fuente de ingresos. En Plaza de Mayo, el calzado pasó de ser una mercancía a convertirse en el centro de una denuncia. La fila expresó la necesidad de quienes se acercaron a buscarlo; el reclamo de productores, comerciantes y trabajadores, el temor a perder el empleo. La jornada dejó planteada una pregunta que excede al sector: ¿qué futuro tiene la industria nacional cuando una parte de la población no puede acceder a sus productos y quienes los producen temen quedarse sin trabajo?

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Giorgio Agamben: The countless people
content:
One of the fundamental political problems — if not the most urgent — is how to conceive of an uncountable multiplicity (or multitude). As a political concept, the people only makes sense on condition that it is uncountable; if it can be counted, then what is decisive is no longer the people as such, but a numerical quantity — the so-called majority — into which the people dissolves according to the perverse mechanism of elections or plebiscites. The people—like the human race—are not a collection of countable singularities: the “popular” or “generic” character—that is to say, the political character—must belong entirely to the singular as such. This is what Marx sought to articulate through the concept of 

Gattungswesen

 (“generic being”), which defines each individual and not a countable quantity. Insofar as each individual “refers to himself as the present and living genus”, the people cannot be a numerical sum of individuals, but is an essential reality fully present in each one. If the people, as the generic being, are counted, they are divided not only into a majority and a minority, but also into factions, amongst which a civil war is inevitably waged. Hobbes, in 

Leviathan

, attempted to resolve this aporia by hypothesising a countable multitude—which he calls the 

multitudo disunita

—that is constituted as a unity within the body of the sovereign; but this implies that the people possess no unity unless they abolish themselves in the artificial person of the sovereign. How, then, might one conceive of an uncountable multitude? Popularity and political agency are not definable properties which, like racial unity for the Nazis, can be attributed to each individual. Rather, they arise from the absence of a common identifying element that would determine one’s belonging to this or that group, to this or that class, and thereby render it countable as such. Like the proletariat according to Marx, the people cannot coincide with itself; it is constitutively not-all. If one attempts to grasp it as a whole, it resists all definition, and this resistance, this innumerable remainder, is the people; it is the genuine political element.




Quodlibet

, 23/10/2026

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Intifada and fascism. Resisting humans, affirming monsters
content:
by Rodrigo Karmy Bolton




from 

Ficción de la razón

, 27/10/2026







It has become fashionable, thanks to sociological bureaucracy, to claim that the danger of any uprising is that it leads to fascism. That fascism can capitalise on it, turn it into an electoral and political enterprise, and triumph by harnessing its power and transforming it into a force. They used to say that revolt expresses “anomie” – that is, a normative mismatch with social dynamics – and that it was “violent” and “senseless” in that it involved burning things, looting shops and disrupting the “normal” flow of events. Now they say it leads to fascism and that, for that reason, it must be avoided at all costs. That if Le Pen wins at the French polls, it will have been due to the undeniable revolt; for if 

Kast

 won in Chile, his victory would have been due precisely to that. The revolt would be anomic, violent and, moreover, reactionary. Nothing could be more of a threat to progressivism than the people taking to the streets; nothing could torment its pedagogical mindset more than a crowd on a war footing.







But there are certain things here—too long-standing, too antiquated—which, nevertheless, must be recalled: first and foremost, the argument that revolt leads to fascism (however complex it may be) obscures the question of why fascism exists, why it arose, if not from decades of violent neoliberal reforms which have literally left people on the streets, landless, 

with no place in the world

. How are we to interpret the case of 87-year-old 

Maricarmen

, who was evicted from the house she was renting because she could not pay the rent? Evicted from their homes and left out in the open, the people today are all Palestinians; they are all Maricarmen: they live landless, homeless, with a longing to return. Neoliberal reforms that have been imposed across the globe and which have now entered a new phase in their process of intensification, where they have had to resort to “so-called primitive accumulation” to escape the stagnation that their own model – their own “civilisation” – has produced.




In its various forms, neo-fascism—steeped in melancholic passions and capitalising on public panic—has been the means by which the model has chosen to realise itself, accelerating its processes of accumulation. To this end, it needs to bury any form of state-legal framework capable of curbing or containing its momentum, thereby hastening the fulfilment of a sort of “

parousia

” of capital in which, at last, capital encounters no restraints whatsoever and is definitively consolidated upon the earth. A new process of plunder, dispossession and conquest of the earth has begun to consolidate the new machine of death: the artificial intelligence corporations that have made war the leap through which they seek to break free from their own stagnation. Led by the super-rich, the violent process of acceleration through which they set out to appropriate new lands is meeting with resistance.




The global intifada—which is nothing other than a field of multiple interdependencies—becomes the disruption of worlds rising up against the levelling imposed by capital. Whilst the latter strips peoples of their lands, their landscapes and their places, the intifadas disrupt this levelling to reweave interdependencies between worlds precisely where capital and its globalisation seek to triumph: without distance, without fissures, without chasms—merely bodies pressed together. Capitalism reveals itself today in a completely transparent manner. There is no need to dream of a “behind-the-scenes” force manipulating history; it is enough to experience what happens every day: psychological disasters, the proliferation of genocides, the frantic efforts to work in the informal sector, widespread precariousness, and the systematic exclusion from our cultural, social and political rights. The repeated discourses of the old fogies who thought they were lecturing us after the October uprising—claiming that the uprising was lawless, violent and, moreover, that it would lead to fascism—believed themselves to be effective, but strictly speaking, they have been nothing but empty words, like all pedagogy today.




Young people have taken to the streets. Uninterrupted, for years now: today in France, Spain and Albania; previously in Chile, Iraq and the United States. The old fogies tell young people that they are “apolitical”, that they admire Spider-Man rather than Lenin, and they resort to the same old rhetoric about order: what applies to the uprising applies to “young people” – lawless, violent and, ultimately, “fascists”. Young people, too, are supposedly “fascists”. Not only should they go to the psychiatrist to manage their ADHD, depression or panic attacks, but they should also listen to the old fogies so they can lecture them on what democracy is and why it should be respected. And then comes the “left”: who really cares about that discussion at the very moment of our mass murder? Who could possibly care when it comes to the destruction of our life force? The bureaucrats will be satisfied, but always unhappy. For they believe that unhappiness is the norm. The sheer scale of the intifadas, their spill over at regional and global levels – spill over which, in turn, has been channelled into mapping new flows of insurrection across the globe, flows that remain invisible to the canons of representation – has flooded the Earth and has continued to do so for some time now. The intifadas lay bare the transparent corruption of public power, the war inherent in private power, the ecological disaster into which we have been plunged, and the massive devastation that has become an everyday reality.




Well, it is not the intifadas that lead to fascism. It is the violence of the state-capital, implemented over decades of neoliberalism, that underpins its stage and provides its space. The super-rich are its director; the apparatus of control and security, its stage. The intifada becomes their threat, the monstrosity that looms before the upright “humans” who besiege and devour the masses. For it is not a question of establishing a “civilisation” to make us “human”; rather, it is that the “humans” have waged an endless war against any form of life that transcends their models. The Palestinians, the poor, the migrants 

are not human

. They become monsters. And this is precisely the war between humans and monsters. We – like every living being – are nothing more than monsters inhabiting the interface between worlds. For centuries, the “humans” have sought to assert their dominance over the monsters. And when they have wiped them out, they have annihilated themselves. Our happiness on earth lies in inhabiting our monstrosity, travelling ceaselessly between worlds; and so, like 

Gabriela Mistral

 in “

Poem of Chile

“, we sing of the journey, we sing of our inhabiting the interface—that place no satellite can locate, yet which smoulders within us like the eternal fire through which the voices of the dead never cease to mingle with those of the living.




The bureaucrats will try to convince us – yet again – that life is meant for ruling and not for inhabiting; that play is useless, that stupidity serves only the master and the boors who accompany him, and that “success” and “profit” are the only things that matter. The literature of our bodies is good for nothing more than being sanitised by the “experts” in monsters, those who, at the slightest hesitation, declare us terrorists. That is what is at stake in the European uprisings, because it is what has been at stake in the various uprisings that have erupted over recent decades: not a programme, not a political project, not an electoral machine, but something far less significant yet perhaps far more threatening: a vital passion that yearns desperately to inhabit, a literature of bodies intertwined at the interface of worlds. A literature of monsters, the misfits who belong nowhere, who have been cast out for being too old, perhaps ugly, for being useless or simply for being poor. The intifada is against the “humans”, now that they have cloaked themselves in Zionism, now that, once again, they believe themselves to be “chosen” to occupy the Earth.




In any case, the plan is clear: just as in Palestine, to expel us, annihilate us, lock us away. Fascism only comes about thanks to the bureaucrats who concoct the fiction that revolt leads to fascism, thanks to that left which wants nothing to do with insurrection, which turns a blind eye to street violence, thereby leaving the dirty work to the police. Returning to the Earth means populating the interworlds, at the interface where they intersect, in the resonances that each carries of the other, where each is a mixture and their plurality is variegated rather than individualised. Fascism is not merely a friend of bureaucracy but rather 

bureaucracy itself, at its most efficient

, whose ultimate form crystallises in AI and its imperialist corporations.




Nothing can renew our spirits without embracing our monstrosity: the interregnum is our place, monstrosity our way of existing on Earth. If “humans” – monsters devoid of affection, devoid of eroticism—have denied their monstrous condition by repeating “resentment” as the condition by which they tame their passions to play a part in a highly technological machine of mass murder, precisely so as not to be “affected” by the very efficiency of the task they carry out, we must affirm it: we are the monsters who declare war on the “humans” and their arrogant civilisation. Neither animals nor humans. Monsters: creatures of the interface who dance amongst the multiplicity of worlds and their interdependencies.




October 2026

author: Augusta Lunardi
title: Um ano após chacina, as crianças da Penha precisam voltar a ser crianças
content:
A Praça São Lucas, na Vila Cruzeiro, no Complexo da Penha, amanheceu mais alegre do que de costume. Era 12 de outubro deste ano, Dia de Nossa Senhora Aparecida e também das Crianças. A rua foi tomada por balões, brinquedos infláveis, pula-pulas e até show de mágica.




No meio dela, acontecia uma batalha de barbeiros, uma competição para ver quem fazia os cortes de cabelo mais perfeitos e o melhor “loiro pivete”, estilo descolorido popular entre os jovens das favelas cariocas. A criançada fazia fila para ganhar bolo, pipoca, cachorro-quente e refrigerante. Por toda parte, gritos de alegria e clima de festa.





































Comemoração do Dia das Crianças, na Praça São Lucas, na Vila Cruzeiro, no Complexo da Penha




Em outubro do ano passado, o cenário na mesma praça era bem diferente. “Fazia um ano que eu não pisava aqui”, disse Tauã Brito, de 37 anos, com os olhos cheios de lágrimas. “Quando pintaram a praça na Copa do Mundo, eu queria muito ter vindo, porque foi um amigo meu que fez as pinturas. Mas não consegui. Toda vez que eu via as filmagens do drone, eu dizia: ‘Está lindo o chão, mas eu só consigo olhar e ver o corpo do meu filho estirado nele.’”




Seu filho, Wellington Brito, de 20 anos, foi uma das vítimas da chacina da Penha, chamada oficialmente de “Operação Contenção” pela Polícia Civil. 

A megaoperação contra o Comando Vermelho foi realizada há um ano, em 28 de outubro de 2025 nos complexos da Penha e do Alemão, na Zona Norte do Rio. Ação do então governador Cláudio Castro (PL), executada pelas polícias Civil e Militar, tornou-se a operação policial mais letal da história do Brasil: 122 mortos, entre eles cinco policiais.




Foi ali, na Praça São Lucas, que os próprios moradores enfileiraram os corpos recolhidos por eles numa área de mata usada como rota de fuga, no dia seguinte ao massacre. Caminhonetes não paravam de chegar com as vítimas empilhadas, mutiladas e com sinais claros de execução. O cheiro de morte impregnava o ar. O silêncio sepulcral só era cortado pelo choro desesperado de mães, esposas e irmãs das vítimas. As imagens dos corpos estendidos no chão rodaram o mundo.





































Tauã Brito, de 37 anos, segura foto do filho, Wellington Brito, de 20, uma das vítimas da chacina do ano passado




Desde então, os moradores da Penha se mobilizam para tentar superar a tragédia.

 “Estar aqui hoje é quebrar um tabu, tentar mudar na minha mente um cenário de muita dor. Você não vai ver quase nenhuma mãe das vítimas aqui, porque esse local ficou marcado por muita tristeza”, afirma Brito.




A escolha da Praça São Lucas para o evento do Dia das Crianças, organizada pela associação de moradores, não foi por acaso. Nascida e criada no bairro, Brito precisou deixar a Vila Cruzeiro depois de receber ameaças de policiais nos meses que se seguiram ao massacre. Mesmo assim, fez questão de participar como voluntária naquele dia, e até fez um bolo para colaborar com a festa.




“A gente está fazendo isso para tentar olhar a praça com outros olhos. A favela é vida, é alegria, e a gente quer mostrar isso para o mundo”, disse. 

“Muitas das nossas crianças viram aquelas cenas de morte. Nós, mães das vítimas, vamos carregar essa dor dentro de nós para sempre. Mas a comunidade precisa seguir a vida aqui dentro de forma mais leve.”




Andressa Ignácio, de 29 anos, moradora da Vila Cruzeiro, também voltava à Praça São Lucas naquele dia pela primeira vez desde a chacina. Veio à festa acompanhada dos dois filhos. “Fico muito feliz, porque as crianças hoje estão vendo um lugar colorido e animado, e não aquela cena de corpo jogado no chão”, disse. Até então, Ignácio evitava passar pelo local. “Para gente que mora aqui, a lembrança ainda é muito recente e dolorosa. O brilho da comunidade se apagou por causa do que aconteceu.”




Um ano depois, moradores dizem que pouco mudou na presença do Estado no bairro. “Não chegou nada de importante na área social, na saúde, na educação”, afirma Gilberto Santiago, advogado criminalista e morador da Vila Cruzeiro. “Quando o Estado entra, só entra pra matar.”
















No ano passado, fotos de corpos empilhados e enfileirados após a chacina chocaram o mundo




Chacina é usada eleitoralmente por Flávio Bolsonaro e apoiadores




Logo após a chacina, em 2025, a operação foi fortemente aplaudida por políticos de direita e de extrema direita. Castro a definiu como “um sucesso” e afirmou que as únicas vítimas eram os policiais mortos.

 Dois dias depois, recebeu no Palácio Guanabara governadores de oposição ao presidente Lula e anunciou a criação de um “Consórcio da Paz” para ações conjuntas contra o crime organizado.




Na época, a 

Agência Pública

 

mostrou

 como a maioria dos governadores que integram o consórcio teve um aumento nas mortes causadas por policiais nos respectivos estados durante a sua gestão.




O governador de São Paulo, Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos), disse que a ação havia sido realizada “com muita excelência”. A operação também teve respaldo da maioria da população: segundo o 

Datafolha

, 57% dos moradores da capital e da região metropolitana do Rio a avaliaram como um sucesso.




Para a pesquisadora Carolina Grillo, coordenadora do Grupo de Estudos dos Novos Ilegalismos da Universidade Federal Fluminense (GENI/UFF), a operação teve um efeito político imediato, mudando os termos do debate sobre segurança pública no Brasil. Na época, o Planalto defendia a PEC da Segurança Pública e apostava em investigações para asfixiar financeiramente as facções. “O governo federal vinha com propostas de ataque inteligente, de desmantelamento de redes, de seguir o dinheiro”, diz Grillo. “E, naquele momento, a partir do Rio de Janeiro, conseguiu-se deslocar a discussão para ser contra ou a favor do massacre.”




O senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), derrotado nas eleições de 2026, já falava em guerra às facções antes mesmo da operação.

 Cinco dias antes da chacina, ao compartilhar uma publicação do secretário de Defesa dos Estados Unidos, Pete Hegseth, sobre o ataque a uma embarcação no Pacífico, 

escreveu em inglês

, no X: “Que inveja! Ouvi dizer que há barcos como este aqui no Rio de Janeiro, na Baía de Guanabara, inundando o Brasil com drogas. Você não gostaria de passar alguns meses aqui nos ajudando a combater essas organizações terroristas?”. No dia seguinte, o líder do PT na Câmara, Lindbergh Farias, protocolou no Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) uma representação criminal contra o senador por afronta à soberania nacional.
















Print da conta de Flávio Bolsonaro em que ele sugere ação contra barcos na Baía de Guanabara, em referência à chacina na Penha e no Alemão




Em maio deste ano, depois de um encontro com Donald Trump no Salão Oval da Casa Branca, Flávio disse ter pedido ao presidente norte-americano que o Comando Vermelho e o PCC fossem classificados como organizações terroristas.

 Disse que, enquanto Lula pedia a Trump que não adotasse a medida, ele fazia “o contrário”. No início daquele mês, Lula havia se reunido com Trump e apresentado argumentos contra a designação: o governo temia que ela abrisse caminho para sanções ou até para uma ação militar dos Estados Unidos em território brasileiro.




Dois dias após o encontro com Flávio, o Departamento de Estado, chefiado por Marco Rubio, 

designou

 as duas facções como “terroristas globais especialmente designados” e anunciou sua inclusão na lista de organizações terroristas estrangeiras a partir de 5 de junho. Nos bastidores, aliados da oposição viram a decisão como uma vitória política do senador.




Para Grillo, a classificação foi política, não técnica. “Os Estados Unidos não se basearam na realidade, mas usaram um artifício político”, afirma.

 Segundo ela, as facções brasileiras não têm projeto ideológico, religioso ou de mudança de regime, características que definem o terrorismo. “São grupos do crime organizado que, como cartéis e máfias, buscam apenas o lucro. É simples assim.”




A pesquisadora não vê risco de intervenção militar norte-americana no curto ou no médio prazo, embora reconheça que a medida cria “uma abertura jurídica” para isso. O impacto mais imediato, diz, seria econômico. “Os Estados Unidos se autorizam a confiscar todos os ativos de qualquer empresa que tenha alguma forma de vínculo com organizações terroristas, mesmo que a empresa não saiba disso. Isso cria insegurança jurídica para todas as empresas que atuam aqui.”




Santiago, que mora no Complexo da Penha há 45 anos, inverte o argumento. 

“Terrorismo é o que o Estado pratica nas comunidades”, afirma o advogado. “Praticar terrorismo é fechar escolas, creches, aterrorizar crianças, mulheres grávidas, moradores, matar pessoas inocentes, executar pessoas rendidas.

 Isso é terrorismo.”




Em agosto deste ano, já candidato à Presidência, Flávio levou o tema para o centro da campanha. No lançamento da candidatura de Douglas Ruas (PL) ao governo do Rio, no Maracanãzinho, declarou “guerra aos narcoterroristas” e prometeu que, se eleito, também classificaria o Comando Vermelho e o PCC como organizações terroristas no Brasil.




Mortes viram trampolim eleitoral no Rio de Janeiro




A chacina também serviu de trampolim eleitoral para quem a comandou.

 O ex-secretário da Polícia Civil Felipe Curi foi eleito deputado federal pelo Progressistas (PP), com mais de 133 mil votos. Ainda à frente da Polícia Civil, dias depois da chacina, Curi defendeu que as facções recebessem “tratamento à altura de terroristas”.




Segundo 

reportagens

, aliados e integrantes da área de segurança associaram, durante a campanha, o número de urna de Curi, 1122, ao total de mortos na operação. O ex-secretário da Polícia Militar Marcelo de Menezes (PL) conquistou uma cadeira na Assembleia Legislativa do Rio (Alerj), com mais de 46 mil votos. O delegado Bernardo Leal, que também participou da ação, foi eleito deputado estadual com mais de 57 mil votos.




Para Grillo, 

o termo “narcoterrorismo” dá voto justamente por traduzir uma sensação cada vez mais presente entre os brasileiros: o medo. “É uma forma de mobilizar o medo da população por meio de uma categoria exagerada”

, explica. A pesquisadora também afirma que megaoperações como a da Penha não reduzem o poder das facções. “No segundo em que a polícia saiu, aquele território continuou sob controle do Comando Vermelho”, diz.




“Todas as pessoas que foram mortas são insubstituíveis do ponto de vista dos seus familiares, mas perfeitamente substituíveis do ponto de vista das facções.” Operações como esta, segundo ela, não passam de “um método ineficaz e populista. E todo populismo, de alguma forma, mira as eleições”, conclui.




Curi e Menezes chegam ao Legislativo enquanto a operação que comandaram segue sob investigação. Familiares relataram ter sido impedidos de reconhecer os corpos das vítimas. 

A Polícia Federal (PF) e o Ministério Público do Rio de Janeiro (MPRJ) abriram investigações, e o MPRJ já denunciou 17 policiais por condutas como invasão de domicílios, apropriação de bens e armamentos, constrangimento de moradores e tentativas de impedir ou prejudicar o registro das câmeras corporais.




A ONG Human Rights Watch apontou

 que a Polícia Civil não preservou os locais das mortes, comprometendo as perícias. Em abril deste ano, a PF informou ao STF que ainda não havia recebido as imagens das câmeras corporais dos policiais militares que participaram da ação.




Castro tentou surfar a mesma onda. 

Após a operação, recebeu o aval da cúpula nacional do PL para disputar o Senado, e seu perfil no Instagram ganhou cerca de 1,5 milhão de seguidores.

 Mas, em março de 2026, um dia depois de renunciar ao governo para concorrer, foi declarado inelegível por oito anos pelo Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), por abuso de poder político e econômico na eleição de 2022.




Coube a Ruas, seu aliado e ex-secretário estadual das Cidades, levar a bandeira adiante. Durante a campanha, Ruas buscou se afastar de Castro e do ex-presidente da Alerj Rodrigo Bacellar, ambos investigados, mas não abandonou a defesa da Operação Contenção em suas falas públicas.




O discurso parece ter colado: em 10 de outubro, depois que o TSE anulou os votos de Anthony Garotinho (Republicanos) e o Tribunal Regional Eleitoral do Rio (TRE-RJ) refez a totalização, Ruas foi declarado eleito em primeiro turno, com 50,88% dos votos válidos, contra 44,16% de Eduardo Paes (PSD).




Depois das eleições, o medo de operações ainda mais letais




Em sua primeira entrevista como governador eleito, à TV Globo, Ruas afirmou que a segurança pública será o foco central de sua gestão. Prometeu convocar logo no início do mandato os aprovados em concursos das forças de segurança e retomar territórios dominados pelo tráfico e pela milícia com operações planejadas, seguidas da ocupação permanente das áreas.

 Questionado sobre quais comunidades seriam as primeiras, respondeu: “Não vou fazer assessoria para bandidos”.




Na Penha, a promessa é recebida com desconfiança. “Vão entrar para matar mais”, afirma Tauã Brito. “Muita gente aplaudiu o que aconteceu aqui. Então eles entenderam que morte, de certa forma, dá voto.” Para Andressa Ignácio, a eleição de Ruas repete a de Castro. “As próprias pessoas elegeram um segundo Cláudio Castro. Eles são farinha do mesmo saco”, afirmou, antes do segundo turno.




O temor cresceu com a disputa eleitoral. Em 9 de outubro, ao lado de Ruas, na Barra da Tijuca, Flávio, que disputou o segundo turno contra Lula em 25 de outubro, disse que os dois estão alinhados para “declarar guerra” ao crime organizado

 e mandou um recado “aos narcoterroristas de Comando Vermelho, PCC e milícias”. Nas urnas, Lula foi reeleito com 51,79% dos votos válidos, contra 48,21% de Flávio, segundo o TSE. A designação das facções como terroristas pelos Estados Unidos, decidida em maio, não depende do resultado eleitoral brasileiro.




Nesta quarta-feira, 28 de outubro, dia em que a chacina completa um ano, os familiares das vítimas organizam um grande ato pacífico na Praça São Lucas. O evento acontece três dias depois do segundo turno, com Ruas eleito no estado e Lula reconduzido ao Planalto.




Perguntada sobre o que pediria a quem vencesse a corrida pela presidência, a mãe de Wellington respondeu: “Eu só peço que olhem para a Penha não como um cenário para tirar vidas, mas de uma forma mais humana. Que lembrem que existem pessoas aqui dentro que precisam ser respeitadas, crianças que precisam crescer num ambiente de paz. 

As crianças da favela precisam voltar a ser crianças”

.

author: Unknown
title: Argentine Human Rights League calls for freedom for Öcalan
content:
The Argentine Human Rights League (Liga Argentina por los Derechos Humanos, LADH) has sent a letter to the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), calling for stronger international efforts to secure the release of Abdullah Öcalan. The organization, itself a member of the federation, also proposes that the FIDH assume a guarantor role in the ongoing peace and democratic society process.




In its letter, the human rights organization, founded in 1937, pointed to the Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan’s 27 years of imprisonment on the Turkish prison island of Imrali. It said that Öcalan has spent most of this time in solitary confinement and was sentenced to aggravated life imprisonment without any ordinary prospect of release. Even the so-called right to hope—the possibility of having his detention reviewed with a realistic prospect of release—continues to be denied to the Kurdish leader, now 77-year-old, it stated.




“These demands are of crucial importance today”




In its letter, the Human Rights League acknowledges that the FIDH has already addressed Öcalan’s situation on several occasions, recognized him as a political prisoner, and called for his release. However, in light of current political developments, these efforts must be intensified, it noted.




“We believe that these demands are of crucial importance, especially now,” the letter said. “The changing political circumstances offer the possibility of peace that could benefit both the Kurdish people and other peoples of the region. At the same time, they could pave the way for the release of Öcalan and thousands of other political prisoners in Turkey.”




The organization therefore believes that international human rights institutions bear a particular responsibility. “We consider it necessary to maintain solidarity and persist in our demands for freedom,” the Human Rights League declared. Given its international standing, the FIDH could make an important contribution to a just peace and “assume a role as guarantor in potential negotiations.”




Decades of international solidarity work




In its letter, the Argentine Human Rights League also highlighted its own history. Since its founding in 1937, it has campaigned for political prisoners and against state repression. Numerous members have been killed because of their commitment to human rights.




Among its international activities, the organization cites solidarity with the resistance against the Franco dictatorship in Spain, opposition to the Vietnam War, support for the Cuban Revolution, and efforts to pursue legal accountability for crimes committed during Argentina’s military dictatorship. It also expresses solidarity with the Palestinian people and the struggle for self-determination in Western Sahara.




According to the League, it has maintained ties with the Kurdish movement for many years. On behalf of the organization, Nora Podesta, Hector Trajtemberg, and Alejandro Avots conveyed their greetings to the Kurdish people and reaffirmed their support for Abdullah Öcalan’s freedom and a political solution to the Kurdish question.

author: Unknown
title: Students in Dêrik demand constitutional recognition of Kurdish
content:
In the city of Dêrik in Rojava, students have once again protested against the education policies of the Syrian transitional government. They are demanding that Kurdish be officially recognized in the Syrian constitution and that the right to education in their mother tongue be guaranteed.




The demonstrators initially gathered outside the school administration building in Dêrik. They then marched to the headquarters of the regional administration, where they met with regional director Şero Şero and presented their demands.




Şero stated that he supported the students’ rights within the framework of a new, democratic Syria. He said the regional administration would forward their demands to the relevant authorities.




The protest concluded with slogans calling for the right to education in the mother tongue and the official recognition of the Kurdish language.

author: Unknown
title: Nazan Üstündağ: Democratic integration does not mean being absorbed into the state
content:
According to sociologist Nazan Üstündağ, the democratic integration of Kurdish society must not be confused with adapting to existing state structures. Rather, she says, it involves legally recognizing Kurdish life in its entirety while strengthening society’s independent capacity for political action. Speaking to ANF, Üstündağ emphasized that the development of a democratic society must not wait for state reforms.




The academic made these remarks on the sidelines of a conference on democratic integration organized by Akademî Kurd in Zurich. The concept is one of the central topics of discussion in the ongoing peace and democratic society process. It is closely linked to Abdullah Öcalan’s concept of a democratic society and the question of how relations between the Kurdish population and the Turkish state should be shaped in the future.










https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/90c73c27_20261025134559_2026-10-25-zurih-nazan-ustundag-sosyolog-demokratik-entegrasyon-devletle-butunlesme-degildir-1.mp4













Bringing Kurdish life out of illegality




Üstündağ defined democratic integration as both a legal and a social process. The decades-long exclusion of the Kurds, she said, extends far beyond political prohibitions or state repression. “Rather, everyday aspects of life have also been marked by the denial of rights and criminalization. The Kurds have repeatedly been pushed into illegality in various ways. I do not mean this only in political terms, but also in relation to social life: access to healthcare, electricity, employment, and income. One could say that they have been pushed into a kind of illegality in their everyday social lives.”




Üstündağ pointed out that: “Democratic integration therefore also means ensuring that Kurdish life receives legal recognition in all its dimensions. Interactions with state institutions must no longer be characterized by criminalization but must instead be based on rights and equal access to social resources. However, this legal equality is only one aspect of the process. Equally important is that Kurdish society itself defines the forms of exclusion it experiences and determines how they can be overcome.”




A democratic society emerges through self-organization




In Üstündağ’s view, democratic integration cannot be achieved solely through legislative reforms or political negotiations: “It must also emerge from social discussions, collective organization, and the development of independent alternatives. This will happen through social organization, by engaging in discussions within society, sharing experiences, and developing demands based on them. Sometimes, these processes will give rise to alternative forms of production, alternative ways of life, and alternative spaces.”




Üstündağ identifies two interconnected dimensions of the current process: the democratization of state structures on the one hand, and the independent development of a democratic society on the other. For this very reason, she says, social development must not be made dependent on the pace of state decisions. “The fact that the process of democratizing the state is progressing slowly must not mean that the development of a democratic society should also proceed slowly. This is the most important issue.”




“Democratic integration never means becoming one with the state”




Üstündağ draws a fundamental distinction between democratic integration and the notion of a harmonious unity between state and society, free of contradictions. “Even under changing political conditions social interests and the state’s claims to power will continue to come into conflict. Democratic integration can never mean merging with the state to become a single entity. For we know that fundamental contradictions exist between the state and society, and that there will always be tensions between them.




The crucial task, therefore, is not to eliminate these contradictions but to develop new ways of addressing them through democratic means. While the conflict in the past was largely shaped by armed struggle, society itself must increasingly emerge as an active political force in the future.




Of course, society has always been active. But we must make it even more active, enable it to become a stronger actor in this struggle, and mobilize society at every level. That is what I understand by democratic integration. This also means beginning now to consider how social conflicts can be organized and addressed through civilian means. People must develop new ways of representing their own interests and exerting democratic pressure.”




Alliances must emerge from below




Üstündağ also emphasizes that the social dimension of democratic integration must not be limited to the Kurdish population: “Other population groups in Turkey also experience exclusion and are pushed into legally precarious living conditions by existing political and economic circumstances. This could give rise to shared interests and new forms of solidarity-based organization. What matters, however, is that such alliances are not formed exclusively at the level of political leadership.




Of course, we must forge alliances and build relationships, but above all, these must be alliances from below, not from above. In Turkey, it is not only the Kurds who have been pushed into illegality. This affects many people and social groups. This can also create common ground.”




As an example, the sociologist points to people who, because of their living conditions, are forced to rely on informal or criminalized means of making a living. She states that the common struggle for legal recognition and social participation must bring different population groups together. According to Üstündağ, such alliances are among the indispensable foundations of democratic integration.




Social transformation even in the face of state resistance




Asked whether democratic integration could also be developed against the will of the state, Üstündağ rejects a rigid opposition between social resistance and state transformation. The two processes, she argues, can influence one another. “Against the state and at the same time with the state. I do not believe these two things necessarily exclude each other. After all, we have seen over many years that, through our actions against the state’s will, we have also been able to bring the state to a certain point.”




Üstündağ continued: “The past five decades of Kurdish resistance have demonstrated that social movements can bring about change even when their achievements do not initially receive formal legal recognition. Political terminology, social representation, and public debate can be transformed through sustained resistance, eventually putting pressure on state institutions to adapt.”




“Legal reforms and independent social organization must therefore be considered together. However, the political starting point must not be the expectation of concessions from the state. Our goal must be to understand ourselves, represent ourselves, and develop our own voice through democratic means,” Üstündağ concluded.

title: Comunicado de familiares y la Coordinadora Arauco Malleco, denuncian discriminación y persecución política al Lonko Daniel Canio Tralcal
content:
«Comunicado




A nuestro Pueblo Nación Mapuche, comunidades en resistencia y a la opinión pública en general , los familiares del PPM Daniel Canio Tralcal y la CAM declaramos lo siguiente;




Kiñe: Nuestro peñi Daniel Canio fue detenido el año 2018, condenado posteriormente a más de 16 años de prisión, por hechos que dicen relación a una digna acción de sabotaje contra la industria forestal que depreda nuestros territorios.




Epu: Que dicha acción de justicia, valiente y consecuente fue en contra de Forestal Arauco en pleno territorio wenteche y tras un enfrentamiento con carabineros del comando jungla. Nuestro peñi fue herido de bala y posteriormente torturado quedando con secuelas producto de las fracturas sufridas tras su detención.




Kvla: Nuestro peñi pertenece al lof Yeupeco – Catrileo y es un weichafe histórico de la CAM. Hablante del mapudungun, apegado toda su vida al mapuche monguen, al rakiduam ka kimun ha dedicado gran parte de su vida al resguardo de nuestra cultura y los elementos políticos e idearios de la cosmovisión mapuche desde el weichan. Acorde a este actuar, en la cárcel ha llevado adelante una digna prisión política, coherente, en todo momento, a su calidad de weichafe, manteniendo una impronta de integridad que nos honra como organización y familiares. Jamás a renegando ni se ha arrepentido del weichan asumido. Por lo cual no se ha sometido al trato de gendarmería, manteniendo una conducta irreprochable cómo preso político mapuche. Por todo lo anterior es que valoramos su autoridad moral y política, y se le reconoce como LONKO de los presos y de la organización.




Meli; El peñi actualmente lleva más de 8 años en prisión, sumado un abono de 3 años y 7 meses por una causa anterior. Es decir, de la condena actual ha cumplido 11 años y 7 meses superando de sobremanera los tiempos que la ley winka establece para obtener beneficios tanto intra penitenciarios así como de la libertad condicional por parte del poder judicial. Sin embargo días atrás, la Corte de Apelaciones de Temuco, sin argumentos de derecho, ha vuelto a negar el beneficio de la libertad condicional a nuestro peñi. A lo anterior se suma las negativas de gendarmería, bajo el actual gobierno, de otorgar los beneficios intra penitenciarios que le corresponden ya que cumple con todos los requisitos que se establecen para el efecto.




Kechu: La negativa de otorgar beneficios por parte de la institucionalidad chilena a un comunero mapuche es a nuestro juicio una acción racista y de castigo a la dignidad y coherencia de nuestro peñi, a su pertenencia a un lof en resistencia y a su calidad de lonko de nuestra organización. Ello porque nuestro lonko no demuestra arrepentimiento ni sometimiento ante el sistema winka representado por gendarmería y sus trabas burocráticas.

KAYU: Denunciamos, a su vez, que aquí hay una decisión arbitraria y colonial, por la posición política en contra de los dignos representantes de nuestra lucha mapuche, ya que, mientras se entregan beneficios en contra de violadores y abusadores de niños, así como de violadores de DDHH, asesinos y torturadores, se castiga a íntegros luchadores, en este caso a un Weichafe, a un lonko del movimiento autonomista mapuche.




REGLE: Por último hacemos el llamado a nuestra gente, a las comunidades en resistencia y a todos aquellos que acompañan al consecuente weichan de nuestro pueblo, a estar atentos a este injusto caso judicial y a futuras movilizaciones de acompañamiento. El llamado es a continuar en el control territorial y la disputa en contra de los intereses capitalistas para la reconstrucción nacional de nuestro pueblo.




Por territorio y autonomía para la Nación Mapuche




Libertad al lonko Daniel Canio, pu ppm cam y todos los PPM !!




Fuera forestales y milicos del wallmapu.




Weuwain – Marrichiweu»
