author: Jeff Rickertt
title: Phil Monsour’s ‘Time of Monsters’ is a call to action against Israel’s genocide
content:
Time of Monsters Phil Monsour October 2026 Pre-order the album and lyric book at: pozible.com/profile/phil-monsour. Listen now on Bandcamp.

In the mythical Anglo-Saxon poem Beowulf, an entire population is subjugated by a bloodthirsty and seemingly invincible monster, Grendel. He “ruled in defiance of right, one against all”. “Malignant by nature, he never showed remorse.” (Seamus Heaney, Beowulf: A New Verse Translation, New York, WW Norton & Co, 2000, p11.)

With the genocide in Gaza now into its fourth year, and with Israel extending its military savagery to Lebanon, Syria and Iran, and tightening its bloody grip on the West Bank and East Jerusalem, it is clear the peoples of the Middle East are also living under the sway of a monster, malignant by nature, never showing remorse.

Unable to resolve the crisis of legitimacy generated by its founding act of land theft and dispossession, unable to quell the desire of the land’s indigenous people for liberation, the Israeli state, like Grendel, lashes out in rage, resorting to ever-increasing violence to sustain its power.

Halfway across the planet, in Magan-djin/Brisbane, Australia, a new album by Phil Monsour foregrounds the trauma, resilience, courage, fears and hopes of those resisting this evil; first and foremost the Palestinians themselves, but also the millions who have mobilised globally in solidarity with them over the past three years.

This album, Time of Monsters, adds to Monsour’s already impressive body of music about colonisation and war in the Middle East. It comprises 12 songs written over the past three years, each a response to Israel’s latest genocidal escalation of its never-ending war of subjugation.

One track is a rousing cover of Macklemore’s “Hind’s Hall 2”, the only song on the album not by Monsour. Another track, “Song for Fatima Hassouna”, honours the Palestinian photojournalist murdered by the Israel Defense Forces, alongside six members of her family, in April last year. The other songs respond to the genocide and Western complicity thematically. They invoke the visceral monstrousness of it, framing their narratives around recurring motifs: barbarism, loss, grief, survival, love and hope. The style is acoustic rock, although closer to Bruce Springsteen than Billy Bragg.

Monsour’s music is inscribed with activism. He is a founder and coordinator of Justice for Palestine Magan-djin, the Palestinian solidarity organisation that, since October 2023, has spearheaded the movement in Magan-djin, organising hundreds of rallies, pickets, vigils and public meetings. The size and intensity of this mobilisation has surpassed anything before it in the city’s history, including the struggle against the United States war in Vietnam.

Monsour composes and sings as a partisan of this uprising, a musician-activist, rather than a musician-ally. Without ever assuming to speak for Palestinians, some of his songs on Time of Monsters adopt a Palestinian first-person perspective. “Free Me from the Dust”, for example, addresses the horror in Gaza from the viewpoint of a Palestinian survivor: “In this shroud I bury soon something inside of me, flesh that binds me.” In “One Day in the Sun”, Monsour describes a Gazan’s daily struggle for survival: “All I can do is breathe, all I can do is wait, wait for tomorrow, and one day in the sun.” In another track, “I Am Not a Number”, the narrator tells us, “I live beyond your pictures; this land and I, we are the same.”

The Palestinian persona of these songs, however, is not ubiquitous across the album. The lens of the title song cuts away to an ally watching the genocide in livestream: “I am staring at something, can’t look away, the past the future is haunting me this day, crimes that echo on a million screens.”

The effect of this shifting perspective from song to song is a reframing of the Palestinian “I” as a “we” of the global liberation movement, positioning the Palestinians as a universal subject and Monsour himself (and us) as part of that multitude. “Our world is in pieces,” he declares in “Long List of Lost Things”, speaking for all of us. Monsour’s own place in the struggle — his own authorial “I” — is never far from the surface: “I can’t say if I’m broken, I can’t say if I’m whole, I just keep walking, nowhere else to go.”

This positioning gives the lyrical content of Time of Monsters urgency and emotional immediacy that sets Monsour’s songwriting apart in the genre of protest music. Woody Guthrie, Pete Seeger and Joan Baez, to name just three of the luminaries in the political folk tradition, sang about the resistance of the oppressed, often joining them in song at picket lines and rallies.

Even Bob Dylan, in his early years, occasionally engaged directly with the subjects of his protest tunes. Today, the likes of Macklemore, Roger Waters and Irish rappers Kneecap sing in solidarity with the Palestinians, using their profiles to mainstream the cause and call out the complicity of so-called non-alignment.

Monsour occupies a different place in this tradition. His songs not only articulate the demands for liberation, they are infused with the temper of the liberation movement itself. They do not constitute — to invoke an old cliché — the “soundtrack” of a movement. They are not an appendage. They are the resistance talking to itself and the world at large in verse and chorus, guitar in hand, amp turned up. They register the intensity of the rally, the march, the picket. They stridently declaim justice, urging everyone to keep showing up, to fight the despair with active solidarity, to believe that the monsters of our time can be vanquished by our collective efforts.

And as these monsters keep going about their awful business, these songs also speak to our grief and doubt. “Can we repair what is broken, rebuild what is left?”, we are asked.

The pedigree of such resistance art can be found in the activist songs of the Industrial Workers of the World, in “Bella Ciao” and the European anti-fascists, in the African American spirituals transformed into anthems of perseverance by the underground, and of course in the poetry of Palestinians themselves.

It is a tradition with a deeply personal dimension. Monsour enacts resistance through his music, and that resistance is psychological as much as political. Confronting monstrous evil, this work of songwriting and performing serves as a metaphorical call to arms and an outlet for anguish.

This is art as politics and catharsis. And in both realms it lifts us up, prepares us to struggle another day, one step closer to liberation. “Revolution love will see us through,” Monsour assures us. In the end, Grendel was defeated by the warrior Beowulf. In Time of Monsters, Beowulf is all of us.

author: Cas Smith
title: Students, staff rally against proposed ‘mega university’ merger plan
content:
About 500 people, including students, academics and concerned members of the community, rallied at Western Australian Parliament in Boorloo/Perth on October 21 to oppose the shock proposal by the state Labor government to merge three major universities.

Organised by the National Union of Students (NUS) and student guilds of Curtin University, Murdoch University and the University of Western Australia (UWA), the rally came only a week after WA education minister Tony Buti unveiled details of the merger plan, which he said would allow the state’s tertiary education sector to remain “highly competitive, accessible and relevant”.

But, speaking to the crowd gathered outside Parliament, Curtin Guild President Dylan Storer said students and faculty had not been consulted. “We are not going to let you decide the future of our universities without us,” he said.

“Our universities do not belong to the government, they belong to the people of Western Australia, and we deserve a say in their future.”

The proposed merger is set to cost upwards of $1 billion. Storer said the money could be better spent addressing WA’s cost-of-living crisis, which is also having a profound impact on university students.

“New research has revealed that more than 456,000 West Australians are living in poverty: around one in six people in one of the wealthiest places on the planet,” he said.

“Students are skipping meals to afford rent and working multiple jobs just to stay at university.

“The state government has the opportunity to shelve this merger and instead invest in our students, our staff and our universities. To invest in affordable student housing, to invest in better teaching, better facilities and better student support.”

Instead of better, more-accessible education institutions, Labor has presented “a billion-dollar corporate restructure”. Storer said the state government-commissioned feasibility study is riddled with errors, likely introduced by the use of artificial intelligence.

UWA guild councillor Rojin Didari argued that the focus on corporate interests, rather than student needs, was obvious, given the language of the feasibility study, which used the words “competition” and “business” more than 100 times.

She said the plan was “about subordinating our future to the interests of the mining industry, the defence sector, militarism and AUKUS”.

National Tertiary Education Union Curtin branch president Barbara Whelan said if WA Labor was serious about addressing problems in higher education, it would call for a Senate inquiry into university governance, as has been done in NSW, or develop a statewide strategy, as the feasibility study itself had recommended.

WA Greens MLC Sophie McNeill told the rally the plan was an attempt to “erode academic independence, reduce choices in universities and entrench further the corporatisation of your education”.

She said that students and staff could not trust Buti when he said the final decision on the plan was yet to be made, because he had handpicked a steering committee full of people who support it.

An enthusiastic sentiment prevailed for much of the gathering, including chants of “the students, united, will never be defeated” and “our degrees, our say, no merger in WA”.

Liam Staltari, Liberal MP for Carine and shadow education minister, said his party also opposes the merger. He was met with anger from the crowd over the Liberals’ history of education funding cuts.

NUS WA branch president Rama Sugiartha said the NUS had also invited Labor to speak at the rally, but they refused.

“Students are asking, ‘Will my course still exist?’, ‘Will my campus still be there?’, ‘Will my lecturer still have a job next year?’, ‘Will my tutorial go from 20 people to 40?’,” Sugiartha said.

“These are not hysterical questions. And this Labor government cannot answer a single one.

“They paid their consultants to study this merger, and the consultants were told in black and white not to look at staffing, not to look at redundancies. They studied the buildings and ignored the people inside them.”

He said the “mega university” that would result from the merger would have more students per academic than any of Australia’s Group of Eight universities.

University of Western Australia

National Tertiary Education Union (NTEU)

National Union of Students (NUS)

author: Kodao Productions
title: The risks journalists face (2)
content:
The “secret” complainant in the cyberlibel case against tabloid columnist Philip Lustre Jr. — who was arrested on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, right at the venue of the Saturday News Forum at Dapo Restaurant in Quezon City – turned out to be Atty. Mans Carpio, the once-proud stockholder of Cale88 Food, which was exporting banana chips to Hong Kong, China and other countries. Atty. Carpio was apparently erased from the ownership structure of Cale88 in July 2026, just as the impeachment trial of his wife, Sara Zimmerman Duterte Carpio, commenced at the Senate.




Based on the court documents, the complaint stemmed from Lustre’s March 6, 2026 Facebook post which alleged that Carpio “spent” P300-million to finance the operation of the 18 Marines who claimed to have delivered billions of pesos from flood control projects to lawmakers. The post read: 

“SUMUKA si Mans Carpio ng P300-M sa operasyon ng Marines: P150-M kay Mike; P50-M kay Levi; at P5-M sa bawat isa sa 18 Marines?”

 (Did Mans Carpio cough up P300 million for the Marines’ operation: P150 million to Mike, P50 million to Levi, and P5 million each to the 18 Marines?) 

[Mike probably referred to former Congressman and Secretary Michael Defensor and Levi to Atty. Levi Baligod—ed.]




Since what Lustre posted was a question to which Carpio could respond on Facebook, it is doubtful whether the Davao City prosecutor considered the difference between a categorical statement accusing Carpio of bribery and a question that seeks corroboration or denial. Thus, Lustre’s counsel, Atty. Dino de Leon, might as well question why he or she gave short shrift to the respondent. However, based on the Davao City prosecutor’s reading, the written online statement “taken in its plain, natural, and ordinary meaning, directly imputes upon Atty. Manases R. Carpio.”




De Leon noted that Lustre was never informed about the complaint that was given due course in March 2026. In eight months, the Davao City prosecutors failed to know Lustre’s residence and thus could not serve him with subpoenae to compel him to contest Carpio’s allegations. Too convenient for Mans to have all the chances to pursue a case against Lustre without the benefit of a reply. Everything was ex parte and such proceedings would normally warrant dismissal in other jurisdictions. Miffed by the tactics of the other party, de Leon said: “We will confront this case properly and we reserve our client’s right to file the appropriate counter-charges.”




For posing a question, Davao City prosecutors now want Lustre to be on the dock to answer charges that he had willfully and maliciously imputed a criminal act on Carpio in violation of Sec. (4C) 4 of the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012, also known as Republic Act No. 10175. Lustre was in the dark about the identity of the complainant, telling reporters that he suspected it was either Mans or Rep. Pulong Duterte. It was only a copy of the information was sent to de Leon that they finally pinpointed Mans, who is still grieving after his father, Atty. Lucas Carpio, died.




Journalists are mourning, too, over the conduct of the Lustre arrest and the dubious process that led to the Oct. 24, 2026 apprehension at a Quezon City news forum. With the information kept in some black hole, there was no way for the accused to reply and demolish the allegations lodged against him. Such puerile tactics as “failing” to determine the address of Lustre and merely listing his “residence” as the editorial offices of a Makati-based newspaper, are part of the scheme to make it hard for him to prepare his defense.




Moreover, Judge Retrina Espe Fuentes of Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 10 in Davao City, who signed the arrest warrant for Lustre, was the same judge who issued the arrest warrant for Davao Death Squad (DDS) whistleblower Arturo Lascañas in 2017 after he turned his back on Rodrigo Duterte, who was sitting as president then. Lascañas tagged Duterte as the architect of the “tokhang” murders. Eventually, Lascañas fled the country and revealed everything he knew about the slaughter of 30,000 people during the anti-drug war as well as the murders of the enemies of the Duterte political dynasty. In 2022, Fuentes also signed the arrest warrant for Walden Bello for the cyberlibel case filed against him by Sara Duterte’s cherished staff member Jefry Tupas.




Legal experts said that from the looks of it, the case may have to pass through the eye of a needle before it earns a tad of gravitas. From the outset, it appears that justice will elude Lustre in the Duterte fiefdom and the logical option is to seek its transfer to another venue but expect a bitter fight from Mans, who naturally wants the trial to be held in Davao City. At any rate, this case is a significant one for libel laws, from print, broadcast to social media. Times have changed so much, indeed, that fair comment and simple questions now make a commentator liable for Facebook libel. It is a frightening prospect that asking questions may yet become a prohibited act in Davao City. #

The risks journalists face (2)

Kodao Productions

author: Unknown
title: Ephéméride des luttes : 28 octobre
content:
L'éphéméride des luttes du 28 octobre abhorre les fascistes, comme toujours, ainsi que les armées et les patrons. Elle se méfie toujours autant des faux alliés autoritaires et pose de nouvelles bases pour un mouvement féministe, tout en ne reniant pas sa culture émeutière.




1791 :

 Olympe de Gouges, militante "proto-féministe", présente la 

Déclaration des Droits de la Femme et de la Citoyenne

 à l'Assemblée nationale.




1893 :

 A Chicago (Etats-Unis), "

un individu qu'on dit être un anarchiste pénétra dans la résidence du maire de Chicago Mr. Carter Harrison et le tua de plusieurs coups de révolver. Mr. Harrison avait été plusieurs fois menacé par les anarchistes et un attentat avait été commis contre lui, sans succès, quelques semaines auparavant

".




Repris de l'éphéméride anarchiste.




1904 :

 La police apprend à utiliser les dépôts gras laissés par les doigts : c'est le début de l'utilisation des empreintes digitales à des fins policières.




1919 :

 Au Japon, sortie du premier numéro du journal "Rôdô Undô - The Labor Movement" (Le Mouvement Ouvrier), d'inspiration anarchiste.




1922 :

 En Italie, les fasciste commencent leur marche sur Rome. C'est de lébut de 22 ans de dictature.




1937 :

 Au cours de la guerre d'Espagne, le gouvernement républicain est transféré à Barcelone.




1938 :

 En Espagne, les Brigades Internationales sont démobilisées du front.




1938 :

 A Marseille, pendant un congrès radical-socialiste, un incendie accidentel ravage les Nouvelles Galeries sur la Canebière, gagnant l'hôtel de Noailles, le Grand-Hôtel et l'hôtel Astoria. Plusieurs dizaines de personnes y ont trouvé la mort. Le Grand-Hôtel abrite aujourd'hui le commissariat de Noailles.




 

 

 

 




1956 :

 A Budapest, on est toujours en plein dans l'insurrection Hongroise.




1968 :

 A Paris, des militants maoïstes et anarchistes attaquent au molotov le bar Relais-Odéon, qui accueille les meetings de l'organisation néofasciste Occident.




1974 :

 A Ballynkilar en Irlande du Nord, l'IRA fait sauter des explosifs contre une caserne de l'armée Britannique. Deux soldats trouvent la mort dans l'explosion.




1979 :

 - En Irlande du Nord, deux soldats sont abattus par l'IRA près de Belfast.




 Aux Etats-Unis, les Hopis et Big Mountain Dine déclarent leur indépendance vis-à-vis des gouvernements tribaux et du pays.




1986 :

 A Berlin, les Cellules Révolutionnaires (RZ) tirent dans les jambes du chef de la police des étrangers.




1988 :

 A Las Queñes, dans la cordillère chilienne, deux commandants du FPMR-Autonome, Cecilia Magni ("comandante Tamara") et Raúl Pellegrín ("comandante Rodrigo") sont abattus par les carabiniers de Pinochet après une attaque à l'explosif et à la mitrailleuse contre la caserne du village. Rodrigo et Tamara faisaient partie des principaux responsables de cette organisation de lutte armée contre la dictature.




 

 

 

 




1998 :

 A Vitrolles, destruction à l'explosif du transformateur du stade qui devait accueillir un concert de Rock Identitaire organisé par la mairie FN.




2001 :

 De grosses émeutes ont lieu à Belfast, des bombes artisanales sont lancées sur les officers du Royal Ulster Constabulary par les émeutiers. De nombreuses voitures sont incendiées et deux autres charges explosifs dans d'autres zones de la ville.




2011 :

 A Thessalonique, des manifestant-e-s parviennent à faire annuler un défilé militaire en bloquant les voies de chemin de fer et en attaquant la tribune officielle.




2013 :

 A Berlin, un véhicule de l'entreprise Sodexo est incendié pour protester contre la cogestion des prisons et des centres de rétention par l'entreprise d'alimentation de masse.




Voir aussi 

l'éphéméride anarchiste

 du 28 octobre.

title: Political Prisoner updates October 27, 2026
content:
Here is the latest compilation of every-other-week updates:

https://nycabc.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/27-oct-2026.pdf

author: none
title: Censorship in the Education Department at FCI Allenwood Medium
content:
Casey Goonan

10/26/26




Casey offers here their reflections on the recent book drive they organized for the prison library, its popularity with everyone locked up, as well as how it has since been blocked and how Casey subsequently was fired from their library job.

Please share and repost.

– Casey Support Committee







AFFIRMATION

Thank you to everyone out in the so-called “free world” for contributing to our Summer Book Drive. On behalf of the Support Committee and every convict at FCI Allenwood Medium involved in this autonomous initiative, we send our revolutionary love and profound gratitude. From this self-organized prisoner initiative, we introduced a wide range of new, interesting, and relevant books into the prison’s official library collection. During my time as a library worker, many significant changes were made to the form and content of the library here at Allenwood Medium. Unfortunately, because of the Book Drive’s budding success and overwhelming popularity among the captives, i was fired from my job as librarian last week.

TERMINATION

On Thursday, October 1, i was fired as a library worker at FCI Allenwood Medium prison for no reason other than “ordering too many books” and “donating them directly into the library catalog” without the approval of the Education Department Supervisor, Mr. Williams. Although my boss, Ms. Ashton, knew about the plans for a mass donation and granted permission to do so, i was thrown under the bus once she learned her boss found out, and especially once she learned i was adding certain books into the catalog without her approval. There is nothing against policy within the books that were donated, even the ones i donated without Ms. Ashton’s knowledge. The Book Drive was successful in adding around one hundred brand new books to the library catalog, which transformed the library space from a realm of entertainment and distraction into one of pedagogy and critical study. By the first week of September, around seventy more books were delivered to the mailroom, yet staff deliberately let them pile up, before complaining to admin about the quantity of donations and returning them all back to sender. A few days later i learned of my termination.

It’s the overwhelming pettiness of the reaction that bothers me. There is no BOP policy that states we as prisoners cannot donate books into the library collection. There is an official process to do so however and i bypassed some of the red tape. Yet the only violation of policy i am “guilty” of is not showing my boss, Ms. Ashton, every single book that i was donating. My decision to not report donations wasn’t at all due to any intentional plot of deception. It was simply because whenever i gave my donations to Ms. Ashton, she would “never get around” to adding them into the catalog. They would just sit around and often disappear. I was frustrated by Ashton’s lack of enthusiasm regarding this rare opportunity to enhance the library collection, so i decided to just start marking, labeling, and cataloging the books myself. Basic direct action.

ACTION/REACTION

All who were involved in the Summer Book Drive (not only me as an individual) took direct action both to remedy the negligence of the correctional officers who oversee “education” operations at Allenwood Medium and to counter fascist anti-intellectualism, of which the official indifference to our depraved learning conditions is symptomatic. I am not exactly sure how the process occurred behind the scenes, but apparently a mailroom officer (who does not like me) contacted S.I.S. (the surveillance and investigative wing of the prison administration), who then contacted Mr. Williams, who in turn emailed Ms. Ashton ordering my termination as a library employee. I believe that the primary reason i was fired was politically motivated censorship, coupled with the fact that some of the COs already had an issue with me working in the library.

My termination as a library worker demonstrates how the administration at FCI Allenwood Medium will attempt to stifle any act of autonomous sufficiency and self-organization among us convicts, especially if activities aim to improve the conditions of life. The Summer Book Drive initiative was not only an attempt to counter the dehumanizing conditions of a neglectful Education Department but a demonstration of collective action to provide and (re)distribute resources in the face of (or rather in spite of) organized abandonment. Inadvertently, the initiative also illuminated a potential collective capacity that exists between concrete people across prison walls. Within a matter of weeks around 200 books were donated through a public wishlist. What other outcomes might result from a similar constellation of autonomous, informal organization? The purpose of this reportback, however, is not to address this question in particular. That must be the topic of discussion elsewhere. For now, i just want to catch everyone up to speed and explain just how the Summer Book Drive unfolded, and how our work in the library was demonstrably changing the atmosphere of learning in this prison.

REPORTBACK

When i arrived at FCI Allenwood Medium back in February, i was appalled by the lack of resources provided by the Education Department’s “library.” Barely any of the books were visible on the shelves. The shelves themselves were behind a desk, so no patrons could walk up and pull a book on their own. The content of the library catalog was almost entirely fiction, and none of the scarce non-fiction texts were visible at all. In fact, i was told by my boss Ms. Ashton that “this bunch are more of the fiction, fantasy kind of guys” — an assumption proven completely false once i conducted a survey and began offering fellow prisoners non-fiction books with social, cultural, and historical relevance. From what i’ve gathered, the library at Allenwood Medium is by far one of the worst libraries in the Federal BOP. The more time i spent in the library, i became intimately attentive to the inadequacies and intricacies of why this alleged library earned the reputation of “worst of the worst.”

In June 2026, when i was hired as a librarian, i began conducting a survey of each “car” in my unit and then across the entire compound, researching what the most popular books are among prisoners at Allenwood Medium. (For those who don’t know, “cars” are how we are collectively organized, prisoner-to-prisoner throughout the BOP; i.e. the Midwest Car, White Car, Gang Cars, Pennsylvania Car, and so on.) I made sure that all races and religious affiliations were considered in this survey, and i consolidated the results to a list of around 100 specific books, as well as dozens of authors, publishers, and topics of books that prisoners desired to read at this facility. From there my support committee and i created a wishlist derived from the survey findings and circulated the wishlist publicly using the incredible www dot bookshop dot org. The idea was to use the social platform that my support committee has worked so hard to maintain over the past two and a half years to organize a SUMMER BOOK DRIVE, where people on the outside can purchase the requested books from the public wishlist. The books then were to be delivered to me, which i would donate directly into the library collection.

As the Book Drive began, i was already involved in the process of rearranging the library stacks by subject and genre and had the support of Ms. Ashton to do this. In fact, she initially welcomed my consistency and enthusiasm. For FICTION i divided up the shelves to hold (with visible labels) ‘Fantasy’, ‘Western’, ‘Science Fiction’, ‘Thriller & Suspense’; ‘Mystery & Crime Drama’, ‘Deep State Fiction & Political Drama’, ‘Military Fiction’, ‘Historical Fiction (Modern)’, ‘Historical Fiction (Pre-Modern)’, ‘Historical Fiction (20th Century)’. As time went on my plan was to also create an section of the library for ‘Urban Novels’ and ‘African American Classics’. For NON-FICTION, i made the existing books in the library visible to patrons for the FIRST TIME EVER and then created various subject categories such as ‘US History (Pre-20th Century)’, ‘US History (20th-21st Century)’, ‘World History’, ‘Social Studies’, ‘Native Studies’, ‘Science & Nature’, ‘Geography’, ‘Music, Film, & Pop Culture’, ‘Sports’, ‘Health & Fitness’, ‘Business & Marketing’, ‘Self-Help’, ‘Survival & Uplift’, and ‘Resume & Job Search Resources’.

As i described above, around 100 books were successfully delivered to me. After receiving what books the mailroom *did* allow, i added those books into the library catalog. By “adding into the catalog,” i mean that my coworkers and i stamped, stickered, added check-out cards in the books, and shelved them. The feedback from fellow convicts regarding the Book Drive was wildly supportive and positive without a doubt. As the library collection progressed, regular patrons who entered the library would comment on how much better the selections were; how much easier it was to find books; how they felt more interested in going to the library; and most of all, i noticed a substantial interest in the non-fiction sections, especially Social Studies, US History, and Native Studies. The number of nonfiction books that patrons checked out increased markedly. Most importantly, in the days leading up to my termination, a new spirit of critical study and discussion seemed to be permeating the library and its users.

I have to remind myself that there is only so much you can do without greater organization of opposition to the prison regime from within and without. I am chalking this up as another experience, or maybe, rather, the marking of a new chapter in the Campaign Against Prison Censorship and Book Banning

[ see 

https://trueleappress.wordpress.com/2023/04/13/new-zine-campaign-against-prison-censorship-and-book-banning/

 ].

I’m not sure what my next moves will be, but one thing is for certain: There’s a growing number of convicts in this prison who desire a deeper grasp of the world beyond the false sense of “participation” shoved upon us by the TV screens, corporate newspapers, radio shows, remedial programs, and commercial-distraction novels sanctioned by the Federal Bureau of Prisons. The Book Drive could be blocked but the information that such literature instills in our convict class is something that fascists can never return to sender. One idea that my celly had was to simply order books on anti-prison activism, abolition, and prisoner movement history for every prisoner at FCI Allenwood Medium. All of our information is public access on the BOP website. Just pick a name on the BOP “Inmate Locator” and order a book. Brilliant!

Ever more obvious is the substantial mass of people beyond the wall in the so-called “free world” who are impacted by the regime and continue to express a desire to participate in collective anti-prison resistance. These are people actively searching for opportunities to support their own loved ones and others in captivity.  As Ruth Wilson Gilmore writes in her 1999 article ‘You Have Dislodged a Boulder’, by “organizing surplus labor into cages,” the state pulls our loved ones, especially mothers and other caregivers, into its “spheres of operation.” The regime’s gravitational pull on our families and communities creates opportunities where our people can find each other and cooperate together *against* the state’s interests. Gilmore writes, “The magnitude of imprisonment suggests the magnitude of possibility”; and that magnitude “starts small, over and over again.” The scale and dynamic capacity of formal and informal prisoner-support structures put on display by the Summer Book Drive suggests the embryo of such possibility. I know if i were on the outside right now, i would be dreaming and scheming of where to take this collectivity next. I send my blessing for anyone reading this to do the same. After all, it’s one struggle at base.




To write Casey:

Casey Goonan #24611-511

FCI Allenwood Medium

PO BOX 2000

White Deer, PA 17887




Casey Support Committee

email: 

cscommittee@proton.me

instagram: @freecaseynow

donations: 

https://chuffed.org/project/supportcasey

author: Maria Martha Bruno
title: Bolsonaristas fogem da Justiça e se espalham por ao menos quatro países
content:
Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) pode ser o mais novo integrante da lista de bolsonaristas que deixaram o Brasil. Caso confirmada a chegada aos Estados Unidos, o candidato derrotado nas eleições de 2026 se somará a parentes, influenciadores e ex-membros do governo de Jair Bolsonaro, que deixaram o país por condenações ou investigações. Sempre sob o argumento de perseguição política. 




A denúncia partiu do veículo argentino 

Infobae

, que publicou hoje, 27 de outubro, que Flávio estaria na cidade de Puerto Iguazú, que faz fronteira com o Brasil, pronto para tomar um voo rumo aos EUA. Ainda não se sabe como o senador teria saído do Brasil para o país vizinho. Em 26 de outubro, dia seguinte à derrota nas urnas, o ministro Alexandre de Moraes determinou que Flávio entregasse o passaporte à Justiça.




Um dos fundamentos da decisão de Moraes foi uma entrevista do irmão de Flávio, Eduardo Bolsonaro, dada dois dias antes do segundo turno, afirmando que o então candidato deveria deixar o país se perdesse o pleito. Também nesta terça, o blogueiro Paulo Figueiredo disse em sua live que, na noite de domingo, após confirmada a derrota, havia aconselhado o senador a ir para os EUA.




Flávio Bolsonaro é investigado em duas frentes pelo Supremo Tribunal Federal, mas, terminado seu mandato como senador, em 31 de janeiro de 2027, perderá o foro privilegiado. Sob relatoria do ministro André Mendonça, ele é investigado pela suspeita de evasão de divisas e de lavagem de dinheiro por conta do financiamento da produção do filme “Dark Horse”, sobre a trajetória de Jair Bolsonaro. A investigação mira repasses de Daniel Vorcaro, ex-dono do Banco Master, à produção do longa. 




Em outra frente, sob relatoria do ministro Alexandre de Moraes, Flávio é investigado pela suspeita de lavagem de dinheiro por meio de uma casa de apostas. A Polícia Federal (PF) quebrou o sigilo telemático do 

advogado Willer Tomaz

, amigo de Flávio, e encontrou e-mails que apontariam que o senador foi cadastrado como “usuário master” de uma conta bancária da empresa Alcazar Holdings, de propriedade de Tomaz.




Segundo a PF, há indícios de “vínculo de controle ou propriedade de fato de Willer Tomaz sobre a Rede Loto”, a primeira a obter autorização estadual da Loterj, no Rio de Janeiro, para explorar bets no estado.
















O senador Flávio Bolsonaro afirmou em seu Instagram ter sido intimado pela Polícia Federal (PF), nesta segunda-feira (26), a entregar seus passaportes.




Bolsonaristas nos EUA de Trump




Eduardo Bolsonaro mora no Texas (EUA) desde março de 2025. Ele foi condenado pelo STF em junho de 2026 por sua atuação para obter sanções americanas contra autoridades brasileiras. O ex-deputado teve a prisão decretada em outubro, entre o primeiro e o segundo turno das eleições.




Eduardo tem passaporte italiano e também 

conseguiu

 o 

green card

, documento que garante a residência permanente nos EUA. Desde que fugiu do Brasil, ele fez diversas viagens ao Oriente Médio e chegou a 

abrir uma empresa

 no Bahrein, conforme a 

Pública

 revelou.




Seu braço direito nos EUA, Paulo Figueiredo, mora na Flórida há dez anos. 

Ele

 é investigado no Inquérito das 

fake news

 e foi denunciado pela Procuradoria-Geral da República pela tentativa de golpe em 8 de janeiro de 2023. Seu caso nunca foi julgado porque o neto do ex-ditador João Figueiredo 

nunca foi intimado

, mas ele é considerado 

foragido

.
















Eduardo, Allan dos Santos e Alexandre Ramagem juntos, em 2026, em encontro nos EUA




Outro foragido que vive na Flórida é o blogueiro Allan dos Santos. Ele teve mandado de prisão preventiva decretado pelo STF em outubro de 2021 e 

reforçado

 em 2024, bem como o bloqueio de suas contas bancárias e perfis digitais no Brasil. O criador do extinto “Terça Livre” também é investigado no Inquérito das 

fake news

 e das milícias digitais por disseminação de conteúdo falso e ataques a autoridades.




Ainda na Flórida mora Alexandre Ramagem, ex-diretor da Agência Brasileira de Inteligência (Abin) e ex-deputado federal pelo PL. Ele foi alvo de pedido de extradição após ser condenado pelo STF a 16 anos de prisão pela trama golpista.




A fuga, em setembro de 2025, contou com a ajuda de Rodrigo Cataratas, condenado por liderar o garimpo ilegal na Terra Yanomami, conforme 

revelou

 a 

Pública

. O empresário do garimpo 

também está foragido

 por ter ajudado na fuga de Ramagem.




Em abril de 2026, Ramagem chegou a ser detido pelo serviço de imigração dos EUA (ICE), mas foi liberado dois dias depois. Hoje, ele é um imigrante ilegal no país, segundo o Departamento de Segurança Interna (DHS, na sigla em inglês) e está sujeito a detenção e deportação, como a Pública também 

mostrou

.




Bolsonaristas na Argentina, Itália e Espanha




Na Itália, a ex-deputada federal Carla Zambelli chegou a ser presa em junho de 2025. Em maio de 2026, ela foi solta pela Corte de Cassação de Roma, última instância da Justiça do país. Ela havia sido 

condenada

 pelo STF a dez anos de prisão por contratar um hacker para inserir um mandado de prisão falso contra o ministro Alexandre de Moraes, do STF, no sistema do Conselho Nacional de Justiça (CNJ).




Ainda na Europa, mas na Espanha, mora o blogueiro Oswaldo Eustáquio, considerado foragido da Justiça brasileira desde 2023. Em outubro de 2026, ele se tornou 

réu

 por associação criminosa no âmbito do inquérito que investiga a tentativa de golpe de 8 de janeiro. Em junho de 2025, o governo espanhol rejeitou o pedido de extradição do governo brasileiro por considerar que houve motivação política.




Leonardo Rodrigues de Jesus, o Leo Índio, é primo de Flávio, Eduardo e Carlos Bolsonaro. 

Ele

 é investigado no inquérito do golpe de Estado em 2023 e teve a prisão decretada em 2025. Ele mora na cidade de Puerto Iguazú, do lado argentino da tríplice fronteira, por onde Flávio Bolsonaro teria passado para tomar um voo para os EUA. A 

Pública

 mostrou que Leo é um dos investigados por desinformação e tentativa de golpe que 

seguem ativos

 nas redes em 2026.




Também na Argentina, estão cinco brasileiros condenados pelos ataques golpistas de 8 de janeiro de 2023 foram extraditados em dezembro de 2025: Joelton Gusmão de Oliveira, Joel Borges Correa, Rodrigo de Freitas Moro, Wellington Firmino e Ana Paula de Souza, segundo 

apuração

 da BBC Brasil.

title: Gane quien gane el sionismo seguirá: Israel votó entre dos bloques que coinciden en perpetuar la ocupación palestina
content:
Con una elección ajustada y una fuerte participación de la población árabe, pese a las trabas y las denuncias de intimidación, Israel define su próximo gobierno. Al momento, Netanyahu estaría conservando una gran cantidad de votos pero menos que la oposición.  Pero advertimos que las principales fuerzas que disputan el poder comparten el rechazo a la creación de un Estado palestino soberano y retirarse de Gaza y Cisjordania. Las diferencias pasan por la conducción política, la estrategia militar y los métodos para sostener el dominio israelí. Por ANRed




Las elecciones legislativas de Israel se desarrollan este martes 27 de octubre en un escenario de fuerte polarización, con Benjamin Netanyahu buscando conservar el poder y el exjefe del Estado Mayor Gadi Eisenkot encabezando la principal alternativa. Pero detrás de la disputa por el gobierno hay un consenso que atraviesa a buena parte del arco político israelí: la negativa a reconocer la autodeterminación palestina y a poner fin a la ocupación de los territorios palestinos.




La participación de la población árabe israelí, mayoritariamente de origen palestino, adquirió un peso central en la jornada hasta el momento con un incremento del 80%, las mas altas desde 1965. Las largas filas en localidades árabes contrastaron con la campaña de Netanyahu, que presentó la concurrencia a las urnas como una amenaza política y advirtió sobre la posibilidad de que los partidos árabes adquirieran influencia en el próximo gobierno. Estas declaraciones fueron denunciadas como racistas e intimidatorias. También hubo controversias por los intentos de excluir a representantes políticos árabes, mientras referentes de la ultraderecha pudieron competir pese a sus declaraciones contra la población palestina.




La participación árabe podría incidir en la distribución de escaños y en las negociaciones para formar una coalición, aunque el bloque opositor también mantiene límites explícitos a una alianza con los partidos árabes. La disputa electoral, por lo tanto, no equivale necesariamente a una disputa sobre el fin de la ocupación.




Dos bloques, un mismo rechazo a la soberanía palestina




Benjamin Netanyahu, líder del Likud, representa la continuidad de un proyecto nacionalista y religioso que profundizó la expansión de los asentamientos en Cisjordania, reforzó el control militar sobre los territorios ocupados y rechazó abiertamente la creación de un Estado palestino. Durante la invasión contra Gaza, su gobierno sostuvo una ofensiva que provocó una destrucción masiva, desplazamientos de población y decenas de miles de muertes palestinas. Una comisión de investigación de Naciones Unidas concluyó que Israel había cometido 

genocidio

 en Gaza, una calificación que el gobierno israelí rechaza.




La alternativa encabezada por Gadi Eisenkot, exjefe del Estado Mayor de las Fuerzas de Defensa de Israel, cuestiona aspectos de la conducción de Netanyahu, pero no plantea una ruptura con los pilares de la política hacia Palestina. Eisenkot también rechazó la solución de dos Estados y cuestionó la idea de un Estado palestino. Su discurso pone mayor énfasis en la seguridad, la capacidad militar y la necesidad de una conducción política y estratégica diferente.




Las coincidencias no son menores. Ninguno de los dos principales referentes propone una retirada integral de los territorios ocupados, el desmantelamiento general de los asentamientos o un acuerdo que garantice la soberanía palestina. Tampoco existe, en el centro de sus propuestas, un compromiso claro con la reparación de la destrucción causada en Gaza y con el reconocimiento de los derechos nacionales palestinos.




En Gaza, la diferencia entre ambos sectores se expresa principalmente en cómo administrar la guerra, qué hacer con Hamás y cómo garantizar el control territorial y la seguridad de Israel. En Cisjordania, el rechazo compartido a la creación de un Estado palestino deja abierta la continuidad de la ocupación militar, la expansión de los asentamientos y las restricciones a la población palestina.




Esto no significa que ambos bloques sean idénticos. Netanyahu depende de una coalición que incluye fuerzas religiosas y ultranacionalistas que promueven la anexión, la expansión territorial y, en algunos casos, el desplazamiento de la población palestina. Eisenkot representa una alternativa con otra composición política y mayores diferencias respecto de la gestión del gobierno, la institucionalidad y la conducción militar. Pero esas diferencias no se traducen, por ahora, en una propuesta de descolonización ni en el reconocimiento efectivo de la soberanía palestina.




El sionismo como proyecto político colonial




Para comprender estas coincidencias es necesario analizar el sionismo no solamente como un movimiento histórico vinculado a la búsqueda de seguridad y autodeterminación del pueblo judío, sino también como una corriente política expansionista y colonizadora que, en su vertiente dominante dentro del Estado israelí, ha impulsado un proyecto de control territorial y de limpieza etnica sobre Palestina. El sionismo no es una corriente homogénea: existen tradiciones judías y sionistas con posiciones diferentes, incluso críticas de la ocupación. Sin embargo, la crítica anticolonial apunta a las consecuencias concretas del sionismo estatal y de sus expresiones nacionalistas y expansionistas, aunque su expresión es muy minoritaria.




Desde esta perspectiva, el carácter colonial del proyecto se expresa en la apropiación de tierras, la colonización mediante asentamientos, el desplazamiento de la población palestina y la construcción de un sistema que otorga derechos y posibilidades diferentes según la pertenencia nacional. La Nakba de 1948, cuando cientos de miles de palestinos fueron expulsados de sus hogares durante la creación de Israel, constituye un antecedente central de esta historia. La negativa al retorno de los refugiados y la continuidad de la expansión territorial muestran que el conflicto no puede reducirse a una disputa religiosa ni a una sucesión de enfrentamientos militares.




En Cisjordania, los asentamientos israelíes y las restricciones a la circulación fragmentan el territorio palestino. En Jerusalén Este, las políticas de ocupación y desplazamiento constante amenazan la permanencia de comunidades palestinas. En Gaza, la destrucción de viviendas e infraestructura y los desplazamientos masivos han profundizado una catástrofe humanitaria que sin dudas es un genocidio. La continuidad de estas políticas, bajo gobiernos de distintas orientaciones, permite analizar la ocupación como una estructura de dominación que excede a un solo primer ministro.




Criticar el sionismo como proyecto político colonial no significa responsabilizar colectivamente a las personas judías ni cuestionar sus derechos como pueblo. Significa discutir un orden estatal y territorial que subordina los derechos nacionales palestinos, incluso su supervivencia.




Un arco político desplazado hacia la derecha




El mapa electoral israelí muestra un desplazamiento sostenido hacia posiciones nacionalistas y militaristas. La ultraderecha que integra el gobierno de Netanyahu, con figuras como Itamar Ben-Gvir y Bezalel Smotrich, defiende abiertamente la expansión de los asentamientos, la anexión de territorios y distintas formas de desplazamiento de la población palestina. Sus posiciones no son marginales: participan del gobierno, influyen en las políticas públicas y condicionan el debate electoral.




Pero el problema no se agota en esa ultraderecha. El rechazo a la soberanía palestina atraviesa también a sectores que se presentan como centristas o como una alternativa institucional a Netanyahu. La negativa de Eisenkot a la solución de dos Estados constituye una expresión concreta de ese consenso. Mientras la disputa interna se concentra en la gestión de la guerra, la seguridad, la justicia y la formación de coaliciones, los derechos nacionales palestinos quedan relegados.




El espectro político israelí como ultraderechista es  hegemonico pero sería preciso mencionar la existencia de fuerzas árabes, judías y de izquierda que cuestionan la ocupación, la discriminación y la guerra. Pero el centro de gravedad parlamentario se ha desplazado hacia la derecha y las principales alternativas con posibilidades de gobernar no ofrecen, hasta ahora, una salida que garantice la autodeterminación palestina.




La continuidad del respaldo político y militar a la ofensiva contra Gaza, así como la persistencia de la ocupación y la expansión de los asentamientos, permite señalar que el consenso dominante ha sostenido políticas denunciadas internacionalmente como crímenes de guerra y, en el caso de Gaza, como genocidio. La responsabilidad política y jurídica debe establecerse a partir de las decisiones, los actos y las pruebas correspondientes, pero la discusión electoral no puede ocultar sus consecuencias para la población palestina.




Una elección sin voto para millones de palestinos




La participación de la ciudadanía árabe israelí puede modificar el equilibrio parlamentario e incluso resultar decisiva para la formación de un gobierno. Sin embargo, la mayoría de los palestinos que viven en Gaza y en los territorios ocupados de Cisjordania y Jerusalén Este no pueden votar en estas elecciones, pese a que las decisiones del Estado israelí determinan aspectos centrales de sus vidas: las fronteras, la circulación, la seguridad, el acceso a los recursos y la posibilidad de permanecer en sus hogares. Un verdadero 

Apartheid.




Esa desigualdad política es uno de los puntos centrales del conflicto. Mientras los partidos israelíes discuten quién debe conducir el Estado y cómo garantizar su seguridad, millones de palestinos siguen sin poder decidir sobre el poder que controla buena parte de su territorio y sus condiciones de existencia. En esta situación convive el estado sionista.




El resultado electoral puede cambiar la composición del gobierno, el peso de la ultraderecha y la forma de conducir las operaciones militares. También puede abrir disputas institucionales y modificar la relación de Israel con sus aliados internacionales. Pero, si no cambia la política de ocupación, la expansión territorial y la negación de la soberanía palestina, una alternancia en el poder no significará, por lo menos, un cambio sustantivo en la ocupación.

title: İranlı yönetmen Cafer Penahi'ye 5 yıl 1 ay hapis kararı
content:
Fotoğraf: Kacy Bao/Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 4.0

İranlı yönetmen ve senarist Cafer Penahi, Tahran Devrim Mahkemesi’nin 26. Şubesi tarafından görülen davada 5 yıl 1 ay hapis cezasına çarptırıldı. Mahkeme, Penahi’nin taşınır ve taşınmaz tüm mal varlığına el konulmasına, 2 yıl sanal medya faaliyetlerinden men edilmesine ve yurt dışına çıkışının yasaklanmasına karar verdi.

HRANA’nın Emtedad’a dayandırdığı habere göre, Penahi’nin avukatı Mostafa Nili, kararın müvekkilinin yokluğunda verildiğini açıkladı. Nili, Penahi’nin banka hesaplarının dondurulmasının ardından karardan haberdar olduğunu belirtti. Avukat Nili, müvekkilinin 30 Mart 2026’da İran’a dönmesine rağmen dava dosyasında ülke dışında olduğunun belirtildiğini ve duruşma tarihinin kendisine bildirilmediğini söyledi. Penahi hakkında 20 Mayıs 2026’da yakalama kararı çıkarıldığını da aktaran Nili, yönetmenin şu anda üç ayrı hukuki dosyasının bulunduğunu ifade etti.

Penahi, daha önce “rejime karşı propaganda” suçlamasıyla ayrı bir davada 1 yıl hapis cezasına çarptırılmış, 2 yıl yurt dışına çıkış ve siyasi ve toplumsal örgütlere üyelik yasağı almıştı. Yönetmenin yeniden yargılanma talebi Haziran 2026’da reddedilmişti.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Karyn Pugliese
title: Nearly 200 First Nations leaders, the prime minister and premiers gathered for a historic meeting about almost everything. Now what?
content:
The John G. Diefenbaker Building on Sussex Drive was perhaps, in its own imperfect way, a fitting place for nearly 200 First Nations leaders, most of the country’s premiers and a prime minister to hold a meeting First Nations have wanted for more than a century.




It’s actually two buildings mashed together: a modern glass construction, like a church nave, that lets light pour in from above and gives the hallways a sense of something sacred, while behind it, the old city hall rises as a plain grey slab, a maze of stairs leading to small, dark meeting rooms. 




Outside, the chief set up teepees that strangely echo the building’s peaks.




Three very different structures, sharing the same address.




“This is the first time in 119 years of Crown-First Nations relations that a first ministers meeting has focused solely on First Nations,” Cindy Woodhouse-Nepinak, the national chief of the Assembly of First Nations, has said many times leading up to the meeting and it’s a line she would repeat at the gathering.




Of course, a hundred-year wait puts a lot of pressure on a meeting.




After an opening prayer by Algonquin Elder Claudette Commanda, the mic went to Algonquin Grand Chief Verna Polson, who reminded everyone that Ottawa sits on unceded Algonquin territory, that the Algonquin have shared the land, been welcoming and “expect respect in return.”




 ”We are ready to work with you. That work must begin with respect for our land, our rights, and our responsibilities. Today, I welcome you as our people had welcomed others before you. Respect our land you’re on, listen to the people who have cared for it for generations, and carry the respect into the decision you make today and the years that go by,” said Polson.




The national chief’s opening statement covered the hundred-year list of asks: sovereignty, treaty rights, the environment, land, water, natural resource rights, closing the gaps in health, racism in the health system, Jordan’s Principle, Joyce’s Principle, infrastructure, education, jobs, and income.




Ultimately, the meeting seemed to be about everything, which made it hard even for those who had spent months preparing position papers, trying to compress a philosophy of survival worked out over generations, into the three minutes most were allotted to speak.




“ Of course, three minutes is not nearly enough time,” said Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs Grand Chief Kyra Wilson. “And having one representative speak on a number of different issues, it’s very difficult to ensure that we’re getting everything forward in terms of what our needs are as First Nations and our respective regions.”




Space was also limited, she added, “I’m somewhat disappointed that some of our leadership who should have definitely been in the room were not able to be in the room.”




Chiefs crammed so much into each three-minute burst.




In his opening remarks, Chief Sheldon  Sunshine of the Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation, speaking on behalf of Treaty No. 6, Treaty Number 7, Treaty Number 8, and the Blackfoot Confederacy delegation, said the meeting must be about changing the relationship.




“ I’ve heard people describe this meeting as historic. It certainly has the potential to be. But history will not remember us for gathering in a room, taking photographs, making speeches,” said Sunshine. “History will judge us by what we change. 




“Prime Minister, premiers, we need your commitment for a different way forward, one that is grounded in treaty, demonstrates the respect for treaty nations, and a shared responsibility and results.”







Inside the room at the First Ministers Meeting Photo: Raven Brascoupe/APTN.







Matthew Coon Come was back in the room, this time as a consultant on natural resource rights. He is a former AFN national chief who served from 2000 to 2003, and a former grand chief of the Cree in Quebec, credited with helping stop Hydro-Québec’s Great Whale project, which threatened to flood Cree and Inuit lands. 




“You’re right, I’ve been in a few meetings,” Coon Come joked when reporters asked for his insights on what would make this meeting a success. “One of the challenges of meetings of this nature is that you’re tempted to rehash history, repeat injustices, talk about unfulfilled obligations of the federal government. 




“If this First Ministers’ meeting is to succeed, it must come up with concrete measures for next steps. If they don’t do that, this is another meeting of just talks — ‘we’re going to do this, we’re going to do that’ — but nothing concrete,”  he said. 




After opening remarks, the doors closed to the public, including the media, as is tradition for the non-Indigenous governments at the table.




 ”You know, we wish that the media could have been there for the entire day to see all the deliberations,” said Woodhouse Neepinak.




So in a closed-door meeting about almost everything, how do you know if the thing that gets picked to work on is the thing that matters most and who did the picking?




Chiefs came out with very different perspectives and pieced together the day’s key themes. 




The public statements and announcements from PMO




After the Elder spoke Monday morning, Prime Minister Mark Carney made a public statement that set the context for the talks as he saw them: the economy, a nod to the outside threats to Canada’s sovereignty from the United States. 




The answer, he said, was to pull together. 




Then he reminded the room of what Canada has already committed to First Nations as measured in dollars: $3.5 billion more a year for education on reserve, more than $4 billion for housing, $4.5 billion for water and $6 billion for health. 




More, he promised, would come later in the day and in the budget. 




His job now, as he saw it, was to make that money work better and ensure First Nations share in the wealth from Canada’s projects.




At the end of the day, after keeping the press and the national chief waiting more than an hour for a scheduled news conference, Carney arrived with pre-packaged  announcements.




There was $260 million to connect Indigenous (not First Nation-specified) workers with jobs tied to his economic vision for Canada through “major projects,” more than $2.5 billion for emergency preparedness and wildfire response, more than $630 million for policing, and a promise of changes to expand First Nations lending. 




Some of the funding announcements were high on a list of priorities.




Chief Kirby Constant of James Smith Cree Nation, safety and policing are an issue.




In September 2022, his community lived through a mass stabbing that killed 11 people and injured 17. This fall, it marked four years since the tragedy.




“First Nation policing is big on our agenda in Saskatchewan, because we feel like without First Nation policing, the RCMP is not fulfilling their requirements to keep our community safe, so the public safety aspect of that is really big on our forefront,” he said. 




For others, the First Nations-led agenda still seemed to revolve around what the prime minister wanted.




“The structure, format and agenda of this meeting were solely reflective of federal and provincial interest,” B.C. Regional Chief Terry Teegee said in a news release. “The limits placed upon First Nations to participate in this meeting are unacceptable. The Prime Minister and the Premiers have an obligation to meet directly with First Nations to engage in reciprocal dialogue on issues of shared importance, not simply those items which align with this government’s priorities.”




Still others said program money wasn’t the point.  They had come to change the relationship. 




“ Our nations are not obstacles to Canada’s future. We’re treaty partners. Our knowledge, laws, and solutions must be respected,”  said Sunshine.




“The question is not whether we can build a stronger Canada. The question is whether you are prepared to build a future that honours our treaties and includes our treaty First Nations.”




What they came for: AFN




AFN National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Neepinak addresses the First Minster’s meeting. Photo: Keelan Jacobs/APTN.







In the days before the meeting, the Woodhouse Nepinak repeatedly told reporters she hoped it would not be “one and done,” and hoped for a follow-up in 2027, a sentiment Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew echoed on his way in. 




By the end of the day, the prime minister made it clear that was unlikely, saying success isn’t measured by how often they meet and that timing might be right again in two years, depending on progress.




For Chief Jeff Copenance of Onigaming First Nation, the idea of ongoing talks at any table is hopeful. He advised former prime minister Paul Martin on the 2005 Kelowna Accord, which was never implemented after the government fell. 




“Paul Martin’s government held 18 months of talks, and then held a meeting; the Carney government seems to want to do the opposite, hold the First Minister’s meeting then hold 18 months of talks. I’m keeping my mind open,” said Copenance.




The AFN also floated the idea of a sovereign wealth fund during one of their meetings, pooling money so communities can own part of projects built on their land. 




The idea started with Chippewas of the Thames First Nation and the Anishinabek Nation. The AFN brought it to the table as a national project proposal, though details on how it would work, if it ever comes to fruition, remain up in the air.




The prime minister said he was open to exploring the idea.




Then Carney committed to a process that moves Canada beyond the Indian Act, after Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew flashed his status card at the press mic during the midday break, and, as the prime minister put it, “other participants in the meeting” raised it too, though “not everybody.” 




How did the Indian Act come into it?




With so much of the day spent on the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, or UNDRIP, and on First Nations rights, it was a strange turn to start talking about the trappings of a Canadian law.




Abolishing or somehow fishing the Indian Act, is a commitment made before. More than one prime minister has regretted tinkering with the Act. 




Jean Chrétien tried it in 1969 with the White Paper. At the time, Canada’s constitution didn’t recognize land and treaty rights, and the courts barely did, having heard very few cases because a longstanding clause of the Indian Act made it illegal for First Nations to hire lawyers to pursue claims. Wiping out the Act then would have wiped out reserves without leaving land title or treaty rights in their place.




In more recent attempts, after many court cases, constitutional amendments, and UNDRIP, the question was no longer whether to get rid of the outdated Act, but how.




In 2012, Stephen Harper’s government backed a private member’s bill to repeal it. Justin Trudeau tried it in 2018 with his rights framework. Each time, the Indian Act has outlived the promise.




Even the Carney government’s latest attempt at a narrow fix to Indian status, through Bill S-2, has sparked controversy. 




Many First Nations openly support a Senate amendment that would end the second-generation cut-off. 




Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty has been consulting instead on band membership, which is separate from legal status. 




Natural resource ownership




For many chiefs, economic reconciliation came down to land, and who owns what lies beneath it.




Signed in 1930, the 

Natural Resource Transfer Agreement

 (NRTA) hand

ed control of Crown lands and resources from Ottawa to Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. 




First Nations were not part of those talks. The agreements also narrowed hunting, fishing, and trapping rights to hunting for food, cutting off the commercial rights First Nations understood the treaties to protect.




“ Right now, the province has full control and authority over the lands and resources within each province of Manitoba, Alberta, Saskatchewan,” said Grand Chief Kyra Wilson.  “And of course, we know that’s not something that was identified in the treaties. It was all about sharing the lands, the resources, and the wealth, and First Nations have not seen that, and we continue to see decisions imposed on First Nations when it comes to lands, resources, and water.”




Inside the meeting, Okimaw Vernon Watchmaker, chief of Kehewin Cree Nation and foremer grand chief of the Confederacy of Treaty 6 First Nations, raised the issue. 




Matthew Coon Come was in the room, this time as a consultant on natural resource rights and the architect of the proposal. 




“The NRTA remains an unfinished matter that Canada must be prepared to address,” Coon Come said. “The question is not simply who controls the resources; it is whether the transfer of resource jurisdiction in 1930 properly accounted for the rights, interests and constitutional relationship of First Nations.




“Today we are asking to establish a formal negotiating table,” he added. “We are not asking for every question to be resolved today. We are asking governments to agree that these questions deserve a fair, structured and good-faith process.” 




What chiefs want, he said, is “constructive constitutional negotiations.”




According to Coon Come, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said in the meeting that he was willing to set up a table for discussion, and the prime minister said he would comment later.




Questioning if the transfer of natural resources to the provinces is even legal was a difficult topic to raise in a room where the prime minister had spent the morning talking about fast-tracking major projects, many of them on First Nations land.  







Read More:




Carney open to conversations around ‘moving beyond’ the Indian Act




Protest outside First Nations–First Ministers Meeting decry closed doors and ‘economic coercion’




Diplomats and disruptors: First Nations get set for a meeting with Canada’s leaders with ceremony







For Chief Christine Longjohn of Sturgeon Lake First Nation in Saskatchewan, it came back to the treaties.




“Our land is important to us. We know that when the treaties were signed… our Elders tell us that when we signed the treaties, we agreed to share the land to the depth of a plough. I have travelled all over the world, all over Canada, and I have seen what has been built over the depth of a plough throughout our country,” she said. 




Modern Treaty Chiefs




Nisga’a Lisims Government President Eva Clayton, co-chair of the Land Claims Agreements Coalition, spoke for 29 nations with modern treaties and self-government agreements. 




She said they came to help. Canada has ambitious nation-building projects underway, she said, “and the modern treaties are ready for that.” 




For her, participation means being “involved right from day one.” 




When asked by reporters, she also said she was not worried about Bill C-39.




Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act, is almost certain to pass in the Liberal majority government; it would let Ottawa fast-track major projects, exempt some from environmental laws, and set a one-year timeline for decisions. 




Several regional First Nations organizations have rejected it, saying it overrides their rights and squeezes consultation into federal timelines. The prime minister says it only speeds up Ottawa’s own work, “not a timeline on section 35 consultations.” 




But Clayton pointed to what sets First Nations with modern treaties apart. 




“We are constitutionally protected and we have rights that differ from the other First Nations because of that.” 




Her message to First Nations worried about the bill was to look at “how they can benefit and how they can glean from the opportunities that arise out of Bill C-39.” 




Bread and butter issues

 




Chief Kelsey Jacko holds up his speech, which he says he never got to read: Photo: Karyn Pugliese/APTN.







For Nishnawbe Aski Nation Grand Chief Alvin Fiddler, none of it could be separated.




In a press statement, Fiddler said several communities are being pressured to open their territories to resource development while trying to address the impacts of climate change, dealing with boil water advisories and losing young people to addictions and suicide. 




Marten Falls First Nation, a partner in the proposed road into the Ring of Fire, is a case in point.




“How can you expect a community like Marten Falls to effectively negotiate a meaningful agreement while trying to access clean water for themselves? They have been on the boil water advisory list since 2004. The same as my community,” he said.




“My message to you, Prime Minister, and to the Premiers, is this: our Treaties should not be seen as obstacles to your economic agenda. They should be viewed as the foundation of our relationship. That is the only way we can make meaningful progress — if there is respect on both sides.”




Chief Kelsey Jacko of Cold Lake First Nations said he felt snubbed when he was told he could not close out the meeting because the prime minister had to leave to host a state dinner for the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. 




Jacko took a red-eye to the meeting because of two funerals at home, and he wanted to share that story in the speech. But, in the end, he never got to read it. 




“Do you know some of our families still dig the graves by hand? Lots of reserves don’t have the equipment to do that for them. For all the colonial leaders in this room, when we talk about intergenerational trauma, we aren’t always talking about the stuff in the past,” he said. 




Jacko has been an outspoken leader on treaty rights, and his community is challenging Ottawa’s decision to designate the Pacific Link pipeline as a project in the national interest, but most of his speech was conciliatory. 




“We need each other now more than ever and I hope we can count on Canada and the provinces to be there for us the same way First Nations were for them,” he said. 







Chief Kelsey Cold Lake







Everything Else




With so much on the table, from economic reconciliation to treaty rights to the bread-and-butter issues that keep too many First Nations in poverty, it was hard to know what the prime minister would carry out of the room. 




“Over these two days, we saw Canada as its best,” said National Chief Woodhouse Nepinak. 




“I think he knew that 39 was going to be a problem. He understands the sovereign wealth aspect and what that can mean. I think the prime minister also understands the social issues affecting our communities, which are very real and have been made clear to me by my leadership. But what that understanding will translate into is still unknown at this point,”

 said Ontario Regional Chief 

Abram Benedict. 




So what to make of it all? 




This was a First Nations-led meeting, but it happened in the prime minister’s context: one project, one year, everything faster, to save Canada’s sovereignty.




For First Nations still waiting on their rights and on the most basic bread-and-butter issues, the problems a century of being left out created may not be solvable on a one-year clock. If it’s possible, they’re up for it. But is it possible?




It’s a hard message for a prime minister in a hurry.







Correction: This story was updated to say that Chief Watchmakers is the former grand chief of the Confederacy of Treaty No. 6 First Nations. The current Grand Chief is Joey Pete, who was not in attendance. We regret the error.

title: İsrail ordusunun Gazze'ye düzenlediği saldırılarda 4 Filistinli hayatını kaybetti
content:
Filistin sağlık kaynaklarından alınan bilgiye göre, Gazze Şeridi'nin kuzeyindeki Cibaliya Mülteci Kampı'nda bulunan El-Hoca Caddesi'nde İsrail askerlerinin açtığı ateş sonucu 28 yaşındaki Filistinli Mahmud Semih el-Herş hayatını kaybetti.

Refah kentinin batısında yer alan Mevasi bölgesindeki El-Alem Kavşağı'nı hedef alan İsrail saldırısında kimliği belirlenemeyen bir Filistinlinin de cenazesine ulaşıldığı aktarıldı.

Önceki saldırılarda yaralanan 2 Filistinli öldü

İsrail ordusunun açtığı ateş sonucu Mevasi bölgesinde yaralanan 6 yaşındaki Tehani Muhammed Said Şelalife, müdahaleye rağmen kurtarılamadı.

Gazze kent merkezindeki Es-Sevra Caddesi'ne birkaç gün önce düzenlenen İsrail saldırısında yaralanan Ahmed Yasin Buseyso da tedavi gördüğü hastanede hayatını kaybetti.

Gazze'nin çeşitli bölgelerinde birisi çocuk yaşta olmak üzere 5 Filistinlinin de İsrail saldırılarında yaralandığı aktarıldı.

İsrail'in Ekim 2023'ten bu yana Gazze Şeridi'ne düzenlediği saldırılarda en az 74 bin 561 Filistinli hayatını kaybederken, yaralı sayısı 175 bin 759'a ulaştı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

title: Eğitim-İş'ten beslenme çantası tepkisi: "Bir ayda yüzde 6,20 zamlandı, maliyeti 2 bin 147 liraya çıktı"
content:
Eğitim-İş, beslenme çantasının maliyetinin yüzde 6,20 artarak 2 bin 147 liraya yükseldiğini açıkladı.

Eğitim-İş'in sosyal medya hesabından yapılan açıklamada, şu ifadelere yer verildi:

"Okulların açılmasından yalnızca bir ay sonra beslenme çantasının maliyeti yüzde 6,20 artarak 2 bin 147 TL’ye yükseldi. Bu tutar, asgari ücretin yüzde 7,65’ine, emekli gelirinin yüzde 9,12’sine, yeni başlayan öğretmenin maaşının ise yüzde 3’üne karşılık geliyor. Emekçilerin gelirleri temel ihtiyaçları karşılamaya yetmezken çocuklar okula boş beslenme çantalarıyla gidiyor. Aileleri yoksullaştıran ekonomik politikaların sorumlusu siyasi iktidar, çocukların beslenme sorununu görmezden gelerek kamusal sorumluluğu ailelerin omuzlarına yüklüyor. 15 Ekim 2026’da açıklanan bütçe gerçekleşmelerine göre Türkiye Maarif Vakfı’na yalnızca eylülde 2 milyar TL, yılın ilk dokuz ayında ise 4 milyar 58 milyon TL aktarıldı. Eylül ayında vakfa aktarılan kaynakla 931 bin 150 öğrencinin bir aylık beslenme ihtiyacı karşılanabilirdi. Çocukların beslenmesi kamusal bir sorumluluktur. Ücretsiz bir öğün yemek haktır."

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.
