author: Unknown
title: "Women, Justice and Memory" vigil in Amed: “Rojda is not alone”
content:
Women’s organizations have once again protested against patriarchal violence, femicides, and impunity for perpetrators outside the courthouse in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır). The “Women, Justice and Memory,” organized by the Network Against Violence, entered its fourth week on Tuesday. Alongside representatives of political parties and civil society organizations, Rojda Odabaşı also took part in today’s demonstration. She had survived an attack in late August when a neighbor shot at her with a shotgun in her apartment.




The participants carried photographs of murdered women and a banner reading “Women hold vigil for justice and memory,” chanting “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî,” “Femicide is political,” and “Long live women’s struggle.”




ÖHD: Rojda’s safety must be ensured immediately




The demonstration focused on demands for protection and justice for Rojda Odabaşı. The suspect had been released late last week following the armed attack on her. Aycan Diril, from the Women’s Commission of the Association of Lawyers for Freedom (ÖHD), criticized the decision and called for a thorough investigation into the case. “We demand that Rojda’s safety be ensured immediately, that the decision to release the suspect be subjected to effective judicial review, and that every aspect of the attack, including possible intent to kill, be investigated. We will continue to follow this case. Rojda is not alone,” Diril declared.




The lawyer emphasized that the vigil was intended not only to commemorate women who had been killed but also to highlight the responsibility of state institutions. This week, the focus was on seven women who were killed or died under unclear circumstances between October 18 and 26. Representatives of the participating organizations shared their stories.
















Killed despite protection orders




Criticism of the state’s failure to protect women from violence was particularly evident in the cases of Sevda Dinler and Perihan Akbulut. Both women were killed despite having already obtained protection orders against the suspected or eventual perpetrators. Sevda Dinler, a 22-year-old graduate of a vocational school of health sciences, was shot dead with a hunting rifle on October 21 in the Kozan district of Adana. According to media reports, she had rejected Gamber Fidan’s advances and had subsequently been threatened and stalked by him. A protection order had been issued against the man. Following the killing, he was arrested and placed in pretrial detention.




Perihan Akbulut, a 61-year-old mother of five, was stabbed to death in the street the following day in Yeşilyurt, in Malatya. She sustained eight stab wounds. A protection order had also been issued against her husband, Hasan Akbulut. The perpetrator died in hospital after attempting suicide while being pursued by police.




“Femicide is not an unforeseeable event. Previous violence, threats, persistent stalking, and applications for protection orders are often warning signs. When a woman is killed despite a known risk to her life, it must also be investigated whether state authorities fulfilled their duty to protect her,” the statement said. The activists linked this criticism to the economic conditions that can prevent women from leaving abusive relationships. They opposed political attacks on alimony rights and highlighted the lack of security regarding housing, income, and caregiving responsibilities.




Femicides and unexplained deaths




The vigil also commemorated Melek Altınboğa and Aliye Aker. Melek Altınboğa, a 30-year-old mother of one, was killed with a hunting rifle by her husband, Murat Altınboğa, on October 18 in the Akören district of Konya. The couple had been married for just four months. The perpetrator subsequently injured himself with the same weapon. Women’s organizations criticized media reports that reduced the murder to a domestic dispute, thereby downplaying the patriarchal violence involved.













Aliye Aker, 27, was shot dead on October 21 in Osmaniye by Salih Aker, whom she had married just 20 days earlier. The man subsequently took his own life. The activists emphasized that a perpetrator’s death following a femicide did not absolve the authorities of their duty to investigate possible failures to protect the victim and the circumstances surrounding the crime.




Particular attention was also paid to 26-year-old lawyer Özge Penbegül, who was shot dead on October 22 in her apartment in Menemen, near Izmir, by her fiancé, Aykut Erol. The man, who worked as a police officer in Hakkari, subsequently took his own life. The network emphasized the particular responsibility of state institutions when armed public officials commit violence against women. They underlined that wearing a uniform must not shield anyone from scrutiny or accountability for such acts.




Alongside these femicides, the women highlighted two unexplained deaths. Remziye Damar, 61, was found dead in her apartment on October 20 in Kızıltepe district of Mardin. The activists warned against prematurely classifying her death as suicide. They demanded that possible circumstances involving violence and coercion also be investigated.




Kazakh national Aisulu Bekmakhanova (26) died after falling from a great height in Istanbul’s Şişli district. The exact circumstances remain unclear. The network called for a thorough investigation and emphasized that women’s protection and access to justice must not depend on their nationality or residence status. In this context, the activists once again criticized Turkey’s withdrawal from the Istanbul Convention.




Bucak: Rojda demands justice for herself and other women




Following the commemoration of the seven women, Rojda Odabaşı herself addressed the gathering. She demanded justice and appealed to the media and women’s organizations to support her struggle. Amed co-mayor Serra Bucak praised Odabaşı’s courage: “Rojda has stated with great courage and clarity that she wants justice. She is demanding this justice not only for herself but also for other women.”




Bucak called on the women of the city to join the vigil and maintain pressure on the judiciary. “I appeal to all women in Amed: Come here every Tuesday, to stand before the institution that fails to hold the perpetrators accountable.”




The fourth vigil ended with a minute of silence in memory of the women who had been killed.

title: Trial begins in Leipzig over knife attack on Kurdish woman
content:
Proceedings began today, 27 October, at the Leipzig Regional Court in a case concerning the stabbing and serious injury of a 31-year-old Kurdish woman on a tram on 26 January 2026. The 21-year-old Syrian defendant, Ahmed A., faces charges including aggravated assault, threats, robbery and insult.




According to the indictment, the defendant, Ahmad A., and another person who is being investigated separately insulted and attacked the Kurdish woman aboard tram line 16. The attackers reportedly threatened Kurds, saying, “We will kill all Kurds.”




During the incident, the woman was injured by knife blows and her thumb was severed. It was later surgically reattached at a hospital. She reportedly sustained permanent restrictions in movement and loss of sensation in her hands and fingers, and continues to receive psychological treatment.




Defendant denies anti-Kurdish motive




Speaking in court, the defendant, Ahmed A., admitted to attacking and robbing the victim but claimed that he had no personal issue with Kurds or with the woman he attacked. He said he had consumed alcohol on the night of the incident and had become involved in a knife fight on the tram.




The victim previously told the German newspaper 

Taz

 that she believed she had been attacked because of her Kurdish identity. “Their problem was that I was Kurdish. They didn’t need my money,” she said.




Defendant faces up to eight years in prison




Ahmed A. has been held in pretrial detention since May. He is also facing charges relating to another robbery that took place in Leipzig in February and resisting police officers.




The presiding judge stated that, under certain circumstances, the defendant could face up to eight years in prison for the attack on the tram. The trial is scheduled to continue with four further hearings through 24 November.

title: I’m fine with anyone using ‘dead naming’ for themselves. People have many reasons to have a painful…
content:
runicdesk

:

Trans sensitivity question!

Is the term ‘dead naming’ reserved for trans people, or can it be used for people who changed their name for other reasons? Thank you in advance.




I’m fine with anyone using 'dead naming’ for themselves. People have many reasons to have a painful association with their past name and if having a term that says ’

do not fucking use this name

’ is convenient for you: go for it. 

But also, I may be an outlier, as I am trans and I hate the term 'dead naming’ and would never use it for myself. 

I’m not dead. Nothing about me died. My past name isn’t a horrible memory that must never be uttered, it’s just a name I once used. It’s as mundane as my pre-transition pictures, which are still on my wall because my transness is not a dirty secret to be hidden. 

Someone who uses my past name for me deliberately is being a transphobic asshole, but they don’t hold any power over me. I will not cry myself to sleep because they used the secret spell of trans pain. I’ll just think they’re a transphobic asshole and I’ll move on.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Prohíben alojar detenidos en un jaulón de la Comisaría 1a de Bahía Blanca
content:
La Sala 1 de la Cámara de Apelación y Garantías del departamento judicial Bahía Blanca revocó, con el voto de los jueces Christian Alberto Yesari y Gustavo Ángel Barbieri, el fallo del Tribunal Oral Criminal 2 departamental que había rechazado un habeas corpus colectivo presentado por la Comisión Provincial por la Memoria (CPM), en su carácter de Mecanismo Local de Prevención de la Tortura (MLPT). En ese sentido, la Cámara prohibió el alojamiento de personas en el sector denominado comúnmente “jaulón” de la Comisaría 1

a

 de la Policía Bonaerense, por el agravamiento de las condiciones de detención. Se trata de un pequeño espacio enrejado y sin techo, y las personas pasan la noche a la intemperie en camastros de cemento, sin poder ducharse y sin elementos de limpieza. En su apelación, la CPM había cuestionado la contradicción del tribunal de origen que reconoció la inhabitabilidad del sector pero evitó dictar la prohibición total de alojar personas.







El habeas corpus colectivo en favor de los detenidos en la Comisaría 1

a

 de Bahía Blanca había sido interpuesto el 30 de enero pasado, tras una jornada de monitoreo en la que se habían constatado gravosas condiciones de alojamiento y del régimen de vida en los calabozos, y principalmente en un pequeño espacio cerrado llamado “jaulón”: sin techo, módulos sanitarios, colchón, agua corriente y otros elementos mínimos de habitabilidad. De las 9 personas detenidas en esa dependencia, una había pasado toda la noche en el jaulón y los demás permanecían amontonados en los calabozos.




Tres días después, el 2 de febrero, se realizó una jornada de constatación judicial a instancias del Tribunal Oral Criminal 2 de Bahía Blanca; las magistradas que asistieron al lugar pudieron observar lo mismo que lo denunciado por la CPM en el habeas corpus colectivo. En efecto, los testimonios recogidos indicaron la falta de colchones, asistencia médica y de elementos de higiene personal y limpieza de los calabozos, escasa cantidad de comida provista por la dependencia policial, poca variedad y de mala calidad, entre otros agravantes.




Sin embargo, en su resolución del 4 de febrero, el mismo tribunal rechazó la acción de habeas corpus colectivo y se limitó a dictar “la prohibición estricta de alojar personas en el sector denominado normalmente como ‘jaulón’ por más de 12 horas, toda vez que no reúne las condiciones mínimas para recibirlos dignamente (…) Ordenar la entrega de colchones a todas las personas alojadas en la dependencia, ya que la autoridad ha admitido que existen suficientes pero se desconoce por qué razón hay quienes duermen en el piso”.




Es por ese motivo que la CPM presentó un recurso de apelación por considerar que se produjo una deficiente valoración de la prueba, teniendo en cuenta que todos los actores intervinientes en el proceso -incluso las autoridades policiales de la Comisaría- reconocieron que el ‘jaulón’ se utilizó y se sigue utilizando de forma constante y habitual.




Para el organismo de derechos humanos no resulta razonable ni legítima la resolución del tribunal, para el que aparece como jurídicamente válido que se alojen personas en un espacio “a la intemperie” que no cuenta con baño, suministro de agua corriente ni calefacción.




Al decir en su fallo que “…estamos en condiciones de concluir que tal agravamiento al día de hoy no existe, y que la acción de habeas corpus como tal no puede prosperar”, el tribunal cae en la contradicción lógica sobre sus propios razonamientos y concluye en una arbitrariedad, debido a que tanto en la jornada de constatación judicial como en sus propia resolución admite las características de inhabitabilidad de ese espacio.




El 19 de octubre, finalmente, se conoció el fallo de la Sala 1 de la Cámara de Apelación y Garantías, firmado por los jueces Christian Alberto Yesari y Gustavo Ángel Barbieri, que revocó el fallo del TOC 2 de Bahía Blanca y dispuso la prohibición de alojar personas en el sector denominado comúnmente “jaulón” de la Comisaría 1

a

 por los argumentos denunciados originalmente por la CPM y verificados en distintas ocasiones durante la tramitación de la causa.




Las comisarías bonaerenses continúan siendo lugares inhabitables donde se reproducen graves violaciones de derechos humanos. Si bien la población alojada en ellas descendió hasta 1.386 personas en 2025, en el mes de septiembre del 2026 trepó a 1.733 detenidos en 1.159 lugares informados por el Ministerio de Seguridad. Esos cupos no cumplen con los estándares dispuestos por los organismos internacionales de derechos humanos y el Comité Nacional de Prevención de la Tortura. Un ejemplo es el lugar finalmente clausurado de la Comisaria 1ª. Para más información sobre el estado de las comisarias bonaerenses, consultar en  

https://www.comisionporlamemoria.org/datosabiertos/comisarias-datos/







Fuente: 

https://www.andaragencia.org/prohiben-alojar-detenidos-en-un-jaulon-de-la-comisaria-1a-de-bahia-blanca/

Prohíben alojar detenidos en un jaulón de la Comisaría 1a de Bahía Blanca

Indymedia Argentina Centro de Medios Independientes (( i ))

author: Breza Race Maksimovic
title: How Serbian students toppled a dictator
content:
This article 

How Serbian students toppled a dictator

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







On Oct. 25, Serbia voted and the Student List won. Late that evening, President Aleksandar Vučić — the man who has dominated the country’s politics since 2012, steadily hollowing out its courts, media and elections along the way — went on television and admitted that his Serbian Progressive Party and its allies had lost. The final count isn’t in yet, but the result is not in doubt. Candidates selected by the Students List protest movement have more than half the vote and a majority in the 250-seat parliament.




For more than 20 years, our team at the Belgrade-based Center for Applied NonViolent Actions and Strategies, or CANVAS, has worked with activists from dozens of countries on one question: How do ordinary people defeat a government that looks unbeatable? This time the answer came from our own streets, again. We want to explain what happened, because movements elsewhere will try to learn from it, and we’d like them to learn the right lessons.










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










You can’t understand Sunday without understanding the 14 years before it, since Vučić first came to power.




Most people in Serbia learned to live with a low, constant fear. You assumed your phone wasn’t really yours. Amnesty International later 

confirmed

 what many suspected: Spyware was being installed on the phones of activists and journalists, sometimes while they sat in a police station. If you spoke up, a tabloid might put your face on the front page the next morning with a story about who was 

supposedly

 bankrolling you. People lost jobs and contracts for being on the wrong side. Plenty stopped saying what they thought, even at the kitchen table.




We see this pattern in almost every country we work in. That kind of power doesn’t have to arrest everyone. It only needs everyone to believe they could be next.




How it started




On Nov. 1, 2024, the concrete canopy at the Novi Sad railway station fell and killed 16 people. The station had just been renovated. Everyone understood immediately what that meant: The money meant to keep people safe had gone into someone’s pocket. Within days, “Corruption kills” was written on walls across the country.




Students shut down their colleges and refused to go back to class. Many observers abroad missed how important this was. A march lasts an afternoon. The blockade of the universities lasted for months and took a whole part of society out of normal life. In our field we call that noncooperation, and it is far more powerful than protest alone. Every regime depends on people showing up and doing what is expected of them. The students stopped.




For two years the students were arrested, followed, slandered and called foreign agents. Cars drove into crowds. People were beaten. The government gave them every excuse to respond with violence, and they didn’t.




A protest marshal at the front of a crowd during the largest march in Serbia’s history on March 15, 2025 in Belgrade. (Gavrilo Andrić / protesti.pics)




At the largest protest in Serbia’s history, in Belgrade on March 15, 2025 — with between 275,000 and 325,000 people, according to the independent Archive of Public Gatherings — student marshals in yellow vests kept the crowd calm and blue flares showed people the way out if things went wrong. None of that was improvised. The students organized themselves. The assembly of each fakultet (a specialized college within a university) chose its marshals. Before every big action they went over the same things again and again: how to spot provocateurs, how to calm a tense moment, how to move a crowd out safely. At CANVAS, we teach this in every training we run: Nonviolent discipline doesn’t happen by itself. It is planned, practiced and repeated until it’s second nature. The students did exactly that.




Here is why it mattered so much. Violence was the one thing the regime wanted from them. A single burning car would have given the government its “terrorists” and sent the cautious middle class back indoors. 




Because the students stayed nonviolent, everyone could join. Grandmothers did. Farmers did. People who had never been to a protest in their lives did.




What it cost




People sometimes talk about nonviolent action as if it were the soft option. Anyone who watched these students over the past two years knows better.




They walked across Serbia. They arrived with bloody socks and taped-up blisters, slept wherever someone offered a floor, and set off again in the morning. In village after village people stood by the road with bread, hot tea and blankets, and a lot of them were crying. Those marches reached places that no rally in Belgrade ever could, places the government thought it owned.




Wherever they stopped, they talked with people. In town squares, school yards and village halls, they explained why they were marching and listened to what local people were angry about. They also urged residents to set up their own citizens’ assemblies, and in many towns people did, often for the first time in their lives.




Their professors paid a price, too. When fakultets sided with their students, the government cut university salaries to a small fraction of what they had been. Some professors received nothing at all for months. The president went on television and said that instead of salaries, they would get potatoes. Schoolteachers who backed the protests were punished the same way. These are people with children, mortgages and parents to look after, and they stayed with their students anyway.




A list with no politicians on it




Then the students did something we had not seen done quite like this anywhere.




They didn’t hand their momentum over to the opposition parties, and they didn’t run for office themselves. They wrote their own rules for the slate of candidates that they would support. No students could be on the list. Nobody from the ruling coalition. No officials from the opposition parties. No extremists.




For more than a year, over 80 student assemblies in six university cities proposed names, argued about them, interviewed people and vetoed the ones they didn’t trust. It was slow, messy and deeply democratic. We think that is exactly why it worked. Nobody could say it was cooked up in a back room.




What came out was a list of 250 people, one name for every seat in parliament, who were respected long before politics: professors, teachers, doctors, actors, artists and athletes. 




Serbia doesn’t have local districts. The whole country votes as one constituency for party lists, seats are shared out by each list’s share of the vote, and they are filled in the order the names appear. So the order matters, and the first name on the list was a cardiologist from Novi Sad. A former governor of the National Bank shared the list with one of the best basketball players this country has ever produced. Several opposition parties pulled their own lists and backed the students instead, which could not have been easy for them.




Tens of thousands gathered at Slavija Square in Belgrade on Oct. 22 ahead of the general election. (Gavrilo Andrić / protesti.pics)




The people on that list don’t agree about much. Some are on the left, some on the right, and some have never thought of themselves as political at all. State-owned media called that chaos.




We see it the other way around. Movements win by bringing huge numbers of people on board, and huge numbers of people never share one ideology. If the list had looked like one camp, it would have attracted one camp. Because it looked like Serbia, almost anyone could find someone on it they trusted.




What held it together was simple. Nobody wants another leader the whole country has to obey and adore. Nobody wants to live again in a place where a handful of people get rich off everyone else. The students put it on their posters in three words: “Serbia or Mafia.”




Healing from a cancer




The best way we can describe where Serbia is today is this: we’ve had the diagnosis, and treatment has just started.




For years the country lived with a cancer — with 

captured courts

, captured media, public money flowing into private pockets, and fear as the normal background of life. It spread slowly into 

nearly every

 institution.




Sunday’s defeat of Vučić didn’t cure it. Sunday made treatment possible.
















Support Us




Waging Nonviolence depends on reader support. Make a donation today!




Donate













Anyone who has sat next to someone they love during chemotherapy knows what comes next. It takes a long time. It hurts. Some weeks the treatment feels worse than the illness. There will be setbacks and bad results, and people saying things were better before. The old networks won’t leave quietly, and some reforms will fail the first time they are tried.




But this cancer can be beaten. And the whole body has to heal, including the neighbors, relatives and colleagues who voted for the other side on Sunday. They aren’t the disease. They’re part of the country that has to get well.




What we ask of each of us




No government can do this healing by itself. Here is what we think it will take, and from whom.




1. The new governing majority:

 Start with institutions, not with settling scores. Establish courts that are actually independent, a public broadcaster that tells the truth, and clean elections — all of which will outlast any government. And open a full, public investigation into the surveillance of citizens, so no one is tempted to do it again.




2.

 

The movement:

 Don’t let the assemblies fade away. They built this list, and they are the best protection Serbia has against the next strongman, including one who might come from inside the movement itself.




3. Friends abroad:

 Support Serbian institutions and citizens rather than personalities. In practice, that means long-term funding for independent media, watchdog groups and local citizens’ assemblies; sending judges, auditors and prosecutors from your own countries who can work alongside Serbian colleagues rebuilding theirs; and support tied to concrete rule-of-law results rather than to warm words for whoever is in office. And please stay for the whole treatment, not only the first week.




4. Activists in other countries:

 Don’t copy the slogan. Copy the method. Go beyond marching to real noncooperation, train for discipline instead of hoping for it, and build unity out of your differences.




Serbia has just shown that nonviolent action still works when it’s planned, patient and carried by many hands. Now it has to show that a country can heal. We intend to be part of that work: training the next generation of organizers, writing down honestly what worked and what didn’t, and holding the new government to the same standard the students held the old one.




A version of this article first appeared on

 

CANVAS’ newsletter

.







This article 

How Serbian students toppled a dictator

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.

author: David Swanson
title: The Coup This Time
content:
Asia, East and Southeast Asia, Nonviolent Activism, North America, World

By David Swanson, World BEYOND War, October 27, 2026

When the South Korean President declared martial law in December 2024, protesters immediately assembled, the National Assembly voted down the decree, and the protests grew to include a million people following through until impeachment, arrest, and a change of power were achieved. The Nation had an article last week called How to Stop Trump’s Coup. It brought lessons to the United States from South Korea and was written by Jungmin Choi and by Paul Loeb who had made Choi’s earlier article into the first chapter of his book.

The lessons are key, but I think we should be careful to apply them fully. The version in The Nation has been made timely by claiming to offer “lessons for how Americans can counter Donald Trump and his allies if they disrupt or defy the results of November’s midterms,” while the version in the book has been made timeless by being stripped of explicit reference to any application. But the original article in Waging Nonviolence got it right, I think, in suggesting that the emergency was already upon us, that in fact there was no need to wait for a moment of even worse government malfeasance.

A man who campaigned for the presidency the first time instigating violence at his rallies and promising to strip the public treasury for his personal profit while disregarding laws as he saw fit has been put into office twice, has scorned the rule of law, has used wars and all variety of lesser crimes to fill his own bank account, and has intentionally damaged our health and environment, all while promoting fascistic hatred. Every day has been an appropriate moment for an impeachment, a prosecution, and a nonviolent public uprising — but the U.S. Congress and public have mostly been otherwise occupied. And the attempted coup of January 2021 was halted by the Capitol Police of all things without most members of the public needing to trouble themselves to leave their homes. One might draw the lesson that, while the rest of the world needs to rise up against its tyrannical threats, we in the United States are all right sticking with football and shopping. This would be a dangerously erroneous lesson.

A particularly outrageous moment can be used as a catalyst for action, but there is no reason to wait to plan actions until a worse moment than the current one arrives. In recent months, the people of Bolivia have shut down their capital, not because of a military coup but because of an elected government not keeping its promises. I don’t know which is harder to imagine, the people of the United States nonviolently shutting down Washington or a U.S. government keeping its promises. Last year in Peru, protesters forced out a brutal and illegitimate president as part of an ongoing years-long struggle. Two years ago, in Bangladesh, a student-led movement replaced an oppressive government without “resorting to war.” Equally useful, perhaps, for our learning, in recent years in Colombia, a community has claimed its land and largely removed itself from war. (See here, here, and here.) In Mexico, a community has done the same. (See here, here, and here.) In Canada, indigenous people have used nonviolent action to prevent the armed installation of pipelines on their lands. These are nonviolent actions taken against heavily armed powers because the corruption and cruelty have grown too horrible to any longer withstand. Just like real-world frogs, and unlike the libel we tell about them, humans can jump out of a heating pot.

It’s tempting to lament how enormous and spread-out the land of the United States is, as if demographics completely prevent behaving like Koreans or Bolivians (or as if the much larger Russia has never had a revolution). Bolivia has only 12.7 million people, of whom 2 million are in or very near a capital of only 182 square miles, and the rest of whom are within 700 miles of there. South Korea has only 51 million people of whom 26 million are in or very near a capital of only 234 square miles, and the rest of whom, on the mainland, are within 230 miles of there, with lots of trains available. The United States has 342 million people of whom only 5 million are in or very near a capital of 68 square miles, the rest of whom are within 2,400 miles of there, not counting Alaska, Hawaii, or other territories. But look closely. Washington is not too large. Five million people are not disastrously fewer than 2 million. Even the 26 million at and around Seoul are readily available within the train-and-highway corridor from Washington to New York. A democracy should include everyone, but a nonviolent movement of a few million people is as capable of representing 342 million as is a violence-prone, campaign-funded government of 500 Congress Members.

Of course, not all Congress Members are created equal, and the better ones — as well as the Capitol Police — and many other groups are critically needed. This is one of the lessons from South Korea. Here are the lessons in the various versions of the article linked to above:

Take action commensurate with the threat and move quickly. / Act quickly to confront attempted seizures of power.

Encourage defections from security forces. / Encourage security forces to stay loyal to the Constitution.

Beware of the next martial law. / Prevent the coup’s initiators from consolidating power.

Create festive, diverse forms of resistance.

Elections matter all the more under a would-be dictator.

If there’s anything we’ve got down it’s how much elections matter. Half the people don’t vote, but that’s due to the absence of inspiring candidates, the gerrymandering of districts, and the second-class status of immigrants, not the failure of millions of people to spend months telling everyone else how dearly elections matter.

We’re also pretty darn good at festive, diverse forms of resistance. We’ve got the props, costumes, music, and rally cries down.

Mainly we need the showing up part, the larger numbers, which depends on the underlying premise: belief that anything can be done. We’ve so excelled at learning helplessness that the main thing we need to learn from the world and the past is that we have the power to change things if we choose to use it.

The midterm elections could nudge things in a better direction. I imagine there will be people who voted for Trump as a supposed “peace candidate” who will now vote against anyone in his party as the “war party” while others will deem the effort useless and stay home. The good news is that openness to a new approach may result in an unprecedented number of much better new representatives and senators being elected, perhaps a dozen or so, and — at least in theory — a block of progressive lawmakers could exercise influence in the new year, or even sooner.

They would be up against the so-called leadership of their own party as well as the party of Trump. Read what happened in Korea and then just try to imagine Hakeem Jeffries or Chuck Schumer filling the role of the courageous opposition! Even as Republicans are viewed as the war party and the War on Iran party, many Democrats are misreading the room and aggressively advertising themselves as the party for escalating the war in Ukraine, as though the problem in the public mind is not the wars and other outrages but rather whatever Trump does, whether warlike or peaceful.

A Trumpian refusal to accept election results could nudge things in an even better direction, if we refuse to accept his refusal. We should be looking for such opportunities. Not to have larger weekend marches with cleverer signs, but to combine massive nonviolent action that actually disrupts and prevents government action with public persuasion and legal and legislative efforts to redirect the U.S. government away from the path of disaster and destruction.

A Trumpian acceptance of election results could likewise provide the needed encouragement.

It’s up to us to seize the moment. Fortunately, a nonviolent uprising against warmongering, money-stealing criminality is already being planned for November 10-12 in Washington, D.C. Be there.

author: Simon Ramapuputla
title: Cosatu to campaign for ANC and SACP
content:
Cosatu has pledged to campaign for both the African National Congress (ANC) and the South African Communist Party (SACP) in the upcoming local government elections, warning that its political support will not prevent it from confronting either party if workers’ interests are undermined.




SACP candidates will be contesting the local government polls on 4 November, independently of the ANC for the first time since 1994. 




The position emerged from the federation’s 15

th

 national congress, which was held from 12 to 14 October after its 

first attempt in September collapsed

. In her first formal press statement as the newly elected general secretary, Zingiswa Losi said the congress reaffirmed Cosatu’s historic mission to organise and mobilise the working class, defend workers’ rights and advance a programme of democratic transformation towards socialism.




The federation’s decision to support both the ANC and SACP followed consultations among affiliates. Losi explained that the unions had adopted positions intended to influence the national congress, which ultimately passed what the leadership called a “super resolution” to support both parties.




The motion to back the SACP was championed by one of Cosatu’s largest affiliates, the National Health and Allied Workers’ Union (Nehawu). Losi defended Nehawu and the right of affiliates to consult their constituencies and bring their positions to the congress. She maintained that they had not acted improperly and that the decisive outcome was the congress’s collective resolution supporting both the ANC and SACP. Cosatu’s demands regarding local government, labour rights and public services would apply to both parties. she said. 




Congress resolutions




The agenda of Cosatu’s congress involved discussions on the future of organised labour amid mass unemployment, poverty, inequality and rising living costs. The congress acknowledged the need to rebuild Cosatu’s organisational strength and reverse the trend of declining membership in parts of the private sector. 




Cosatu’s declared priority is to rebuild workplace structures, organise un-unionised and precariously employed workers, strengthen collective bargaining and to improve accountability among affiliates.




One of the federation’s key proposals is a workers’ cost-of-living index to inform wage negotiations and government policy. Losi argued that economic progress should not be measured simply by declining inflation or headline growth, but by whether workers and their families could afford to live with dignity. “What it costs for workers to live must inform the bargaining strategy,” she said.




The proposed index would assess the weight of food, transport, electricity and healthcare costs on household budgets. Cosatu wants wage negotiations to take into account what money workers have left after meeting essential expenses, particularly when salary increases fail to keep pace with inflation.




The federation is also calling for an expanded basket of zero-rated goods, affordable basic services and the implementation of National Health Insurance to ease the cost of medical care.




Cosatu urged consumers and government to support locally produced goods, arguing that stronger domestic production can help protect manufacturing jobs. The federation maintains that economic growth must translate into employment and improved living standards rather than leave workers trapped in poverty.




Cosatu’s general secretary, Zingiswa Losi campaigning for the ANC in Khayelitsha recently. Photo from Zingiswa Losi’s Facebook page




Cosatu criticises the composition of GNU




While continuing to support the ANC, Cosatu still criticised the composition of the government of national unity, particularly the inclusion of the Democratic Alliance, citing differences over policies such as national health insurance and the national minimum wage. The federation argued that rebuilding the tri-partite alliance with the ANC and SACP must not require workers to accept policies that undermine their interests.




Newly elected president, Mike Shingange stressed that Cosatu’s electoral support was not unconditional. “It doesn’t mean when we campaign and vote for you, and you undermine the interests of the workers, that we’re not going to come for you. We will,” he said.




Shingange said Cosatu would not remain silent if either political partner failed to honour commitments to workers. He warned that their conduct in government could influence the federation’s future political support, although he did not specify what concrete political sanction would follow.




He said the federation would continue defending workers through collective bargaining, workplace representation, legal processes and public mobilisation.

author: Greta Zarro
title: MEDIA RELEASE: Cross Country Coalition Demands Canada Halt Fast-Tracked Trade Deal With the UAE
content:
***MEDIA RELEASE***




October 27, 2026




CANADA TAKES GENOCIDAL PROFITS IN TRADE DEAL WITH UAE




Cross Country Coalition Demands Canada Halt Fast-Tracked Trade Deal With the UAE, Impose Arms Embargo To End Canadian Complicity in Sudan Atrocities 




Civil society organizations condemn Canada’s new defence cooperation pact with the UAE as the Emirates continues to fuel Sudan’s genocide.







MEDIA CONTACT:

 Gur Tsabar, 

movementmediahub@gmail.com




OPEN LETTER DENOUNCING CEPA: 

Available 

here

. Campaign 

webpage

.




CANADA

 — Following the initial signing of a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) between Canada and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), a broad coalition of human rights, international solidarity, and civil society organizations is demanding an immediate halt to the deal – it must not be ratified. The 

coalition cites

 Abu Dhabi’s direct role in 

fueling mass atrocities

 and genocide in Sudan through its consistent material, financial, and logistical support for the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the militia currently engaged in committing widespread arson, systematic sexual violence, and targeted mass killings across Sudan.




“The Canadian government cannot escape the reality that continuing to deepen economic and military ties with the UAE means deepening complicity in one of the most 

devastating conflicts

 and 

genocides

 of the twenty-first century. The Canadian state proves again and again its commitment to capitalism is stronger than its commitment to international human rights,” the coalition stated in an open letter signed by groups including the Sudan Solidarity Collective, Inter Pares, Canadians for Justice and Peace in the Middle East (CJPME), World BEYOND War, Palestinian Youth Movement, Independent Jewish Voices, and the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives.




“CEPA constitutes the largest trade deal between Canada and the UAE and it was signed on the one year anniversary of the UAE-funded RSF militia committing genocidal massacres in El Fashir, North Darfur. Pools of blood were visible via satellite images from space,” explains the Sudan Solidarity Collective. “This is how genocides are legitimized and how perpetrators are gifted impunity.”




Yesterday, on the one-year anniversary of the RSF’s full-scale genocidal invasion of El Fashir, Global Affairs Canada put out a 

statement

 recognizing the role of the RSF and declaring that states must “use their influence to protect civilians, prevent further atrocities and help bring this devastating conflict to an end, including by ceasing to arm, finance and otherwise enable the war in Sudan.”




“Yesterday the Canadian government announced they would ‘pursue accountability for those responsible’ for the horrific violence in Sudan. Today they signed a trade and military cooperation deal with those directly enabling it,” a representative from the Sudan Solidarity Collective explained. “This free trade deal and defense MOU is bookended by atrocity, complicity, and blatant hypocrisy. Expanding free trade with the UAE makes it clear that securing foreign investment and the buy-up of Canadian resources by UAE investors trumps any supposed concern Canada insists it has about the genocide in Sudan.”




“The Canadian government’s decision today to sign a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on Defence Cooperation with the UAE is shameful and unjustifiable,” said Rachel Small with World BEYOND War. “The UAE military has played a well documented and horrific role in supporting war crimes in Sudan and Yemen. It’s completely unacceptable for Canada to be rewarding this military with increased cooperation and support instead of holding them to account.”




Instead of entering military partnerships with the UAE, the coalition calls on Canada to impose an Arms Embargo on the UAE. Open-source investigations by groups like the CBC Visual Investigations team and War Noir have repeatedly verified B.C.-made 

Sterling Cross

 sniper rifles and 

Streit Group

 light armoured vehicles in the hands of RSF fighters.




“Canadian military hardware is already making it into Sudan for use in genocide today,” continues Small. “If Global Affairs Canada cannot prevent the UAE from allowing Canadian weapons to be used by the RSF, locking in CEPA or new military partnerships will completely collapse any illusion that Canada is trying to control the flow of weapons into Sudan through the UAE. Sudanese lives cannot be exchanged for Emirati blood money.”




Critics have also called out the UAE’s well-documented position as one of the worst perpetrators of 

modern slavery

 globally, noting that it is in contradiction with the Canadian government’s forced labour commitment to sign a free trade deal without any enforceable standards in the agreement, with a country with despicable  labour standards.




The coalition is calling on Members of Parliament to intervene ahead of the planned ratification of CEPA and prevent the implementation of today’s announced Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on Defence Cooperation.




###

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Rogers Solicits Funds to “Protect Elon” — the Biggest Political Donor in History
content:
The Republican’s campaign made the plea to help Musk avoid congressional inquiry into his DOGE work.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

The world’s first trillionaire, Elon Musk, recently took another record: He is now the largest single political donor in modern American history, according to an analysis by The Washington Post, after pouring nearly half a billion dollars into backing Republicans in this year’s midterm elections.

This has contributed to an enormous gap between Republican and Democratic political spending this cycle, with Republicans outspending Democrats by over $300 million as of last week. Musk’s spending in particular could be the edge in several tight races across the nation, like the race for Senate in Texas.

And at least one Republican candidate is seeking to return the favor. Michigan’s Democratic Party posted a leaked fundraising email on Monday from U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers that calls on supporters to back his campaign in order to “protect Elon.”

“When you stand with my Senate campaign today, you are directly shielding Elon Musk, protecting the movement to audit the federal government, and stopping this socialist retaliation plot dead in its tracks,” the email reportedly says.

“Please, make an immediate, urgent contribution right now to protect Elon and save America,” concludes the message, signed by Rogers.

The Democrats did not specify when this email was sent, but the Detroit Metro Times reported on an appeal with the same wording sent in July.

According to that report, the email is referring to a call by Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) for Musk to be subpoenaed and for there to be “accountability” for his sweeping “Department of Government Efficiency” (DOGE) actions that he took as a “special” government official early in Donald Trump’s second term. Khanna said that, among other things, Musk must answer for “the 4.5 million children around the world who he possibly sentenced to death by dismantling” the U.S. Agency for International Development.

Numerous court cases have found that Musk and DOGE’s gutting of the federal government broke the law, but Musk has faced little consequence or even congressional oversight of his actions, despite the vast impacts on the American public and the 14 million people abroad that his cuts are projected to kill by 2030. Though the sweeping cuts spurred by DOGE affected everything from Social Security to veterans’ care to cancer treatments, little is known by the public about Musk’s role in leading the illegal purge.

Still, Rogers’s fundraising email paints the call for accountability as a “socialist retaliation plot” in the style of “Soviet Russia and communist Cuba” that seeks to “destroy him.”

Rogers’s pledge to protect Musk comes as his campaign has benefited from Musk’s massive spending spree this election cycle.

Musk’s America PAC, of which he is the primary donor, has contributed $8.6 million to the Michigan Senate race. Roughly $5.2 million of that has been spent opposing Abdul El-Sayed, while $3.4 million has gone toward backing Rogers.

Musk also gave $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, Republicans’ super PAC for Senate races, this summer, representing one of the largest political donations in U.S. history. That PAC has been the biggest outside contributor in the Michigan Senate race, according to Detroit News, pouring $43.3 million into the race, the vast majority of which has been put toward opposing El-Sayed.

author: Chris Walker
title: Trump Says He’ll Accept Midterm Results If He Deems Them “Honest”
content:
Trump has repeatedly — and baselessly — suggested that widespread voter fraud may play a role in this year’s races.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

On Tuesday, President Donald Trump told reporters that he would only accept the results of the 2026 midterm elections if he felt they were “honest” — echoing statements he’s made in the past while peddling baseless claims of widespread voter fraud.

When asked by journalists if he would “respect” the results of the midterms, Trump indicated his response may depend on the elections’ outcome.

“I will, if they’re honest elections, yeah,” Trump said. He then walked away, seemingly to avoid follow-up questions.

Q: You'll respect the election results whatever happens?TRUMP: If they're honest elections(That's a no!)

Trump’s recent remarks echo other statements he’s made regarding election integrity.

In February, for example, he said that he would only accept the results of the midterms if he deemed them “honest.” If not, Trump added, then “something else has to happen.” The president didn’t elaborate on what he meant.

In the spring of 2024, Trump similarly said he’d only accept the 2024 election results “if everything’s honest,” saying that, if it wasn’t, he would “have to fight for the right of the country.” Trump ended up winning that race, but afterward made grandiose claims that he had won with a mandate, despite not winning a majority of the vote and having one of the narrowest Electoral College victories in U.S. history.

Trump has peddled baseless claims that widespread fraud has affected election results over the past decade, particularly in the 2020 election, which he lost to Joe Biden. In that year’s race, Trump repeatedly indicated a reluctance to accept the pending results, stating in July of that year that he would “have to see” the results before accepting them.

Months later, when Biden won over Trump, the latter refused to accept the outcome, filing dozens of lawsuits and ranting online about supposed fraud he could never prove. He eventually invited his loyalists to Washington, D.C. on January 6, 2021, the day the Electoral College was set to be certified. Following Trump’s incendiary speech that morning, a mob of his followers attacked the Capitol building with Congress inside, delaying the certification of the election.

Trump has continued to sow doubts about elections, including the upcoming 2026 midterms, with his administration publishing questionable reports suggesting that tens of thousands of voters are registered illegally. He has pressured states to remove these residents from voter rolls, and has called for Republicans to “nationalize” elections based on his claims, despite constitutional restraints that place control of elections in the hands of states.

Trump’s most brazen attempt to interfere with this year’s elections took place in Alaska last week, when he ordered the Department of Justice (DOJ) to preemptively sue to block the state from certifying a U.S. Senate election if the incumbent Republican, a loyalist to the president, lost the race.

These and other actions and statements from Trump have sparked doubt among voters that he will accept the midterm results, especially if Democrats win one or both houses of Congress, which they are currently favored to do. A recent Washington Post/ABC News/Ipsos poll found that 7 in 10 voters are not confident that Trump will respect the election outcomes.

Some observers have posited that Trump could be attempting to create just enough distrust among his base for Republicans to justify refusing to certify the midterm results. In one such scenario, GOP Speaker of the House Mike Johnson could replace the House Clerk, or pressure the current one, telling whoever is in that position that they must refuse to seat election winners due to supposed voter irregularities.

Election experts say that such a move would likely be illegal and blocked by the courts. But given Trump’s history — and Johnson’s willingness to block election winners from assuming office before — many are worried that partisan maneuvers by Republicans are within the realm of possibility.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: NTI commits $40.8M in federal funding toward health initiatives
content:
Over the next five years, Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. is committing $40.8 million in federal funding to support health and wellness programs.




The organization made the announcement Oct. 21 in a news release.




The funding covers April 1, 2027 to March 31, 2032, and is intended to close the “gap in health outcomes between Inuit and other Canadians,” according to the release.




Nunatsiaq News has requested a copy of the full five-year spending plan from NTI but has not received a response.




In Iqaluit, the Umingmak child and youth advocacy centre and the Piruqatigiit Resource Centre, which provides support to those with fetal alcohol spectrum disorders and other conditions, are among those that will receive an unspecified amount of money.




As well, an unspecified portion of money is earmarked for Qaujigiartiit Health Research Centre’s Inunnguiniq childrearing and parenting training program, as well as its Makimautiksat Youth Camp, which aims to promote wellness by getting those aged nine to 12 out on the land.




NTI’s board of directors approved three other spending plans earlier this month aimed at strengthening Inuktut language training and advancing the elimination of tuberculosis.

author: Julia Conley
title: Mike Rogers Receives Last-Minute Donation From Anti-Abortion PAC
content:
While in office, he was a sponsor of four fetal “personhood” bills that aimed to ban nearly all abortions nationwide.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Michigan voters were clear in 2022 when they voted by a 13-point margin to codify the right to abortion care in the state constitution, and the state’s Republican US Senate candidate, former Rep. Mike Rogers, claimed two years ago that he had no interest in “going back to Washington, DC to undo what the people of Michigan decided to do.”

But a recent campaign contribution from the National Pro-Life Alliance political action committee (PAC) left reproductive rights advocates warning that Rogers has shown throughout his political career that he will fight to stop Michiganders from accessing abortion care — and that extremist groups are counting on him to win the Senate race to ensure abortion is banned nationwide.

Recent filings from the Federal Election Commission show that on October 23, just before Michigan residents began voting early ahead of the November 3 midterms, the National Pro-Life Alliance PAC donated $5,000 to the Rogers for Senate campaign.

The group has lobbied for the passage of the Life at Conception Act, which would ban all abortions with no exceptions for rape, incest, or health risks for the pregnant patient, and previously donated $1,700 to Rogers between 2000-10.

In 2010, when the then-congressman received $1,000 from the group, the National Pro-Life Alliance stipulated that candidates they supported must support the Life at Conception Act.

Shanay Watson-Whittaker, director of Michigan campaigns at Reproductive Freedom for All, told Common Dreams on Tuesday that the “last-minute donation shows how desperate anti-abortion groups are to buy this election — and they’re counting on Mike Rogers to deliver for them.”

“His record gives them every reason to believe he will,” she added.

Despite Rogers’ earlier claims that should he win the Senate seat, he would respect Michiganders’ support for the right to abortion care, he spent his 14 years in office backing a constitutional amendment to enshrine “personhood” in the US Constitution, aiming to ban all abortions from the moment of conception, and supporting a national 20-week ban — “still very much a national ban that could carry disparate harm for people experiencing medical emergencies and fetal conditions,” wrote Kylie Cheung at Jezebel in 2024.

“I oppose abortion at any time except to save the live [sic] of the mother,” Rogers wrote in a candidate questionnaire distributed by the Michigan Catholic Conference, affirming that he supported the Human Life Amendment. He added that he opposed the use of “taxpayer funds for any abortions.”

Rogers was also a sponsor of four fetal “personhood” bills that aimed to ban nearly all abortions nationwide.

Watson-Whittaker urged Michigan voters to keep Rogers’ donation from the National Pro-Life Alliance and his record in mind as they go to the polls in the coming week.

“Michigan voters fought hard to protect reproductive freedom, and these extremist groups want a senator who will help them undermine it in Washington,” said Watson-Whittaker. “We need someone who will fight for our rights, and Rogers has spent his entire career showing us he won’t.”

author: Amy Goodman
title: Egypt Shutters Independent News Site Mada Masr and Detains Its Editor-in-Chief
content:
This “severe blow” to independent media is an “unprecedented escalation,” says a journalist who previously worked there.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

A court in Cairo has ordered the closure of the independent Egyptian news site Mada Masr. The court also ordered the site’s editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, to be detained until she pays a fine of over $50,000. She was convicted on charges of managing an unlicensed website. Mada Masr is “the flagship independent media outlet in Egypt and a pillar of independent media in the region,” says Sharif Abdel Kouddous of Drop Site News, who previously worked at Mada Masr. The independent outlet was founded in 2013 “in the midst of Egypt’s revolution and counterrevolution” and has “managed to survive all of those years in one of the most hostile media environments” in the world. Still, “what happened today is an unprecedented escalation” because Attalah and Mada Masr had never before been referred to trial.

Kouddous adds that the attack on Mada Masr comes less than a month after Egyptian authorities arrested an entire newsroom at the independent fact-checking outlet Matsadaash. They remain behind bars.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman, broadcasting from Colorado State University in Fort Collins, with Nermeen Shaikh in New York.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: [We end] today’s show with breaking news from Egypt. A court in Cairo has ordered the closing of the independent news site Mada Masr. The court also ordered the site’s editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, to be detained until she pays a fine of over $50,000. She was convicted on charges of managing an unlicensed website. After the court’s ruling, Attalah was taken into custody.

AMY GOODMAN: We’re joined right now by Sharif Abdel Kouddous, the Middle East editor at Drop Site News, previously worked at Mada Masr in Egypt for four years as a journalist and editor.

Sharif, talk about the significance of this breaking news.

SHARIF ABDEL KOUDDOUS: Well, Amy, this is a dark day for journalism, not just in Egypt, but in the entire Arab world. Mada Masr is one of the last remaining independent media outlets reporting the news in Egypt. It’s really the flagship independent media outlet in Egypt and a pillar of independent media in the region.

It was founded in 2013 in the midst of Egypt’s revolution and counterrevolution. It’s managed to survive all of these years in one of the most hostile media environments for the media in the world. It’s had its journalists jailed, foreign staff deported. Its website has been blocked for nearly a decade. Their offices were raided by security forces. There are various forms of intimidation, and the threat of imprisonment is always there. Lina herself has been hauled before interrogation in numerous cases over the years.

But what happened today is an unprecedented escalation. This has never happened before. Lina Attalah or Mada Masr have never been referred to trial before. Then, barely a week, you know, after their being referred to trial, they hold a court session today, where Mada Masr’s defense lawyers are denied a request to even review the case file, that’s given to them in the moment. They’re supposed to review it right there on the spot and present their defense. The court then calls for a recess to deliberate the request, comes back into session, clears the entire courtroom of everyone except for Lina and her lawyer, and then fills it with plainclothes security guards and security officers. And then the court announces it’s rejected all the requests by the defense, including to submit any documentation or hear any witnesses. And the judge then appoints a lawyer for Lina, despite objections, of course. And then, after that, he just summarily reads out the conviction.

And the conviction is fining Lina Attalah herself, as editor-in-chief and co-founder of Mada Masr, to the maximum possible penalty, which is a fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds, which translates to about $50,000, the closure — and the closure of Mada Masr, of the website, and the confiscation of its property. And then security personnel physically surrounded Lina, physically lifted her off the ground and took her out of the courtroom. And she remains in custody now. Her lawyers and her colleagues are scrambling to gather the money to pay the 3 million pounds before the courthouse closes in just a few minutes from the time of this broadcast, so she doesn’t have to spend the night in custody.

But really, you know, the future of Mada and of independent media in Egypt has suffered a very severe blow today. And if there is not a lot of noise made about this by journalists around the world, her colleagues and by the power brokers that this authoritarian Egyptian government relies on to survive, including, of course, the United States — you know, Egypt’s the second-biggest recipient of U.S. foreign aid in the world — if there isn’t an uproar, then we may lose this crucial media outlet in Egypt and in the region.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: Sharif, as you mentioned, of course, Mada Masr has come under attack by the state many, many times and in various ways, but this, as you said, is an unprecedented escalation. Why do you think this is happening now?

SHARIF ABDEL KOUDDOUS: It’s difficult to say why now. Let’s remember this is coming less than a month after Egypt authorities arrested an entire newsroom of Matsadaash, six people from — arrested the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, which is six journalists, threw them into prison, interrogated them, abused them and tortured them and forced them to record false confessions, and they remain behind bars. And that was allowed to happen. So, that was also an escalation.

It’s coming after Sisi, the president of Egypt, announced a bombshell last week, where he said, for the first time in Egyptian modern history, that he is not going to — he’s going to step down at the end of his term. Whether that happens in 2030, whether that happens or not, we don’t know. Not that it will be a democratic transition, but the fact that he will hand over power in some way.

It’s also coming as Egypt has, controversially, agreed to send its military to Saudi Arabia to, what they said was, defend against attacks by Ansar Allah and the Houthis in Yemen. It’s coming as Egypt held this big conference, you know, lauding its achievements over the past few years.

But it’s also coming as the world is on fire, and, you know, no one may be paying attention to what’s happening in Egypt and what’s happening to Mada Masr. You have elections around the world that are consequential, that have happened in Brazil and Serbia. You have an election today in Israel. You have the U.S. midterms next week. You have the genocide continuing in Gaza. You have a war raging between Ansar Allah and Saudi Arabia and all across the region.

And so, it’s also coming at a time, I think, when the authorities — they’ve been trying to close Mada for many years. When I was working there, they raided our offices and hauled Lina away in front of us, and the managing editor and Rana Mamdouh, a senior reporter, and tried to imprison them. And they had the case ready and everything. And it was only pressure from foreign governments that had them released, and from solidarity within Egypt, as well. But this may be the moment where they can close it down and get away with it.

AMY GOODMAN: Sharif, we have to leave it there, but we’ll continue to follow this. Sharif Abdel Kouddous, Middle East editor at Drop Site News, previously worked at Mada Masr in Egypt for four years as journalist and editor. To see our interviews with Lina Attalah, go to democracynow.org.

We have to end right now, and I want to thank the amazing student team here at Fort Collins, Colorado State University, at Rocky Mountain Student Media, CTV: Michael Urbaniak and Laila Duran and Hazel Canner and Calvin Masten and Devon Allen and, as well, Josh Middleton and Hana Shiro and Beth Ryan.

I’ll be appearing tonight at Colorado State University’s Democracy Summit with a screening of Steal This Story, Please! at 6:30 at the Lory Student Center Theatre, and it will be followed by a Q&A with the film’s director, Tia Lessin, as well as the moderator with us, Colorado State University President Amy Parsons. That does it for our show. I’m Amy Goodman, with Nermeen Shaikh.

author: Perseus
title: Εξάρχεια: Πορεία αλληλεγγύης στην επιζώσα που έσπασε τη σιωπή της (Βίντεο – 24 Οκτώβρη 2026)
content:
Εξάρχεια: Πορεία αλληλεγγύης στην επιζώσα που έσπασε τη σιωπή της (Βίντεο – 24 Οκτώβρη 2026)




Στις 24 Οκτωβρίου 2026 πραγματοποιήθηκε στα 

Εξάρχεια

 συγκέντρωση και πορεία αλληλεγγύης στην επιζώσα που έσπασε τη σιωπή της, καταγγέλλοντας την κακοποιητική μεταχείριση και τους πολλαπλούς βιασμούς που υπέστη από τον Μ. Με δυναμικό παλμό, η πορεία ξεκίνησε γύρω στις 

7:30

 μ.μ. με ένα συγκροτημένο σώμα περίπου 250 ατόμων. Η κινητοποίηση καλέστηκε από την Ανοιχτή Συνέλευση Αλληλεγγύης στην Επιζώσα τον Βιασμό και στηρίχθηκε από αναρχικές συλλογικότητες και ατομικότητες, το αντιθεσμικό τρανς κίνημα και κουήρ υποκείμενα, φεμινιστικές ομάδες και συνελεύσεις αναρχικών καταλήψεων. Στους δρόμους στάθηκαν αλληλέγγυα ο κόσμος της γειτονιάς και εργαζόμενα άτομα

.







Διαβάστε επίσης: Οι τακτικές της κακοποίησης και η απάντηση των θυμάτων




The post 

Εξάρχεια: Πορεία αλληλεγγύης στην επιζώσα που έσπασε τη σιωπή της (Βίντεο – 24 Οκτώβρη 2026)

 appeared first on 

Alerta.gr

.

author: Matthew Guariglia
title: New Records Obtained by EFF Expose More Problems with Medicare’s AI Experiment
content:
New records obtained by EFF expose additional issues with Medicare’s AI-driven prior authorization program and show why we need stronger legal limits around government use of 

automated decision-making

. 




EFF 

sued

 the government back in March for information about the 

Wasteful and Inappropriate Service Reduction (WISeR) model

, a new Medicare program that uses AI to evaluate prior authorization requests for certain medical services. We 

previously released records

 showing that WISeR has resulted in delays and denials of care, operational chaos, and reports of patient harm. Today, we’re publishing over 800 new pages of records, including:







Requests for information (RFIs) or requests for corrective action plans (CAPs) sent from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) to four of the six WISeR vendors, along with the vendors’ responses.




Applications of 66 companies to the WISeR model, including those of the 6 selected companies. 




Task orders and contracts for the evaluation, implementation, and monitoring of the WISeR model.







Documents obtained through EFF’s lawsuit are available 

here

.




These newly released documents show that the WISeR rollout was rushed and rocky from the start, highlighting the dangers that arise when governments 

treat AI like a silver bullet

 for complex problems. The documents also highlight the need for more transparency about safeguards against inappropriate, AI-driven denials. The public still lacks the information needed to assess whether clinician review is providing meaningful oversight of AI systems and whether appropriate data is being used to evaluate prior authorization requests. 




EFF has 

long argued

 that AI has no place in consequential government decisions about peoples’ rights or access to benefits, such as 

immigration enforcement

 and 

policing

 decisions. That’s because using automated decision-making in these contexts risks decisions that violate people’s rights or deprive them of benefits they’re entitled to based on biased or inappropriate considerations and without proper due process or accountability if there is an error. 




By outsourcing decision-making to private AI companies without sufficient transparency, testing, or legal limits, WISeR jeopardizes seniors’ access to medical care. Congress should step in to place greater legal limits on the use of automated decision-making in Medicare. 




WISeR’s Rollout Was Rushed and Rocky 




CMS launched the WISeR program just six months after 

announcing

 it, ignoring calls from 

medical providers

 to delay its rollout. In records previously released by EFF, CMS acknowledged this “

extremely condensed timeline

.” 




New records suggest that WISeR’s unusually rapid rollout contributed to widespread problems in the first few months of the program. CMS did not disclose the extent of these issues to the public, even as agency employees privately contacted vendors about potential noncompliance with program requirements. 




In the first three months of the program, CMS sent RFIs or requests for CAPs to at least four of the six WISeR vendors. These requests, which describe delays, technical failures, and a lack of communication with providers, suggest that widespread problems during the program’s rollout were not limited to one vendor or state. 




These letters underscore the severity of the problems with the program. For example, CMS requested information from one vendor, Virtix, about numerous reported issues, including “

determination turnaround times that exceed established guidelines

,” “

denials that appear inaccurate or inconsistent with applicable criteria

,” and “

inadequate customer service

.” CMS’s RFI to Zyter–a vendor that 

uses Palantir software infrastructure

–observed that the agency had received reports that “

Zyter is not issuing determination letters in a timely manner

” and communications indicating that it “

may lack adequate processes for responding to and escalating provider/supplier concerns

.” The vendor Innovaccer received two CAP requests and a “Performance Notice of Non-Compliance” over its failure to implement a fully functional portal for WISeR providers and suppliers.




Excerpts from CMS’ letters to vendors describe problems during WISeR’s rollout:




Excerpt from the 

RFI for Virtix

, March 17, 2026




Excerpt from the 

RFI for Zyter

, February 27, 2026




Excerpt from the 

Performance Notice of Non-Compliance for Innovaccer

, February 20, 2026




Vendors’ responses to CMS provide further evidence that WISeR’s rushed rollout contributed to its problems. 

Innovaccer claimed

 it warned CMS months in advance that it might not be ready to provide full portal functionality by the launch date, even before signing a Participation Agreement. Another vendor claimed that “technical and workflow stabilization challenges were encountered due to the compressed implementation timeframe” it faced after joining the WISeR program a month after the other vendors. 




Excerpt from 

Innovaccer’s Proposed CAP

, January 16, 2026




The issues reflected in CMS’s letters to vendors, and the vendors’ responses, illustrate the risks of deploying automated decision-making systems without proper testing or safeguards. While 

vendors’

 

responses

 

describe

 

fixes

 for the problems CMS identified, after-the-fact remedies cannot undo the 

harms

 that patients and providers already experienced during WISeR’s rushed rollout. 




More Transparency Needed About AI Safeguards




The public still knows far too little about any safeguards that WISeR vendors may have adopted—in part because the government chose to conceal some of this information. Transparency about these safeguards is critical to protecting patients, especially because WISeR’s 

payment structure

 gives vendors, as the government put it, “

an incentive to deny as many claims as possible

.” 




 Information provided by a vendor about safeguards that it says "ensure the responsible and clinically appropriate application of automation” appears to have been redacted from 

records released to EFF




The public has limited means to evaluate the effectiveness of even the safeguards that 

weren’t

 redacted from records released to EFF. For example, one vendor’s application touts safeguards like “

Human-in-the-loop (HITL) workflows

,” “

Continuous model monitoring

,” and “

Transparent audit trails

.” Yet it remains unclear whether these measures effectively prevent improper prior authorization denials. Some evidence suggests they may not: the company 

denied more requests than it approved

 in the first few months of the program, and CMS inquired about “

denials that appear inaccurate or inconsistent with applicable criteria

.”




Ultimately, the records obtained by EFF raise more questions than they answer about the safeguards used by WISeR vendors. 




Having a Human in the Loop Is Probably Not Enough




CMS has emphasized having a human in the loop as a key safeguard against inappropriate, AI-driven denials. The 

WISeR FAQ page

 on the CMS website states that “Non-affirmations will require the review of a human clinician and cannot be performed solely by technology.” But whether human review provides any meaningful protection depends on the 

details of its implementation

, such as whether human reviewers have enough time to evaluate requests and practical authority to override AI recommendations. We still lack many of those details for WISeR vendors. 




A 

growing

 

body

 of 

scholarship

 points to the substantial limitations of “human in the loop” policies as guardrails for AI systems. AI-generated recommendations can unduly influence human decisions, leading reviewers to over-rely on automated judgements and rubber stamp them as correct. Even worse, at least one health insurance company actively 

pressured clinical reviewers

 to accept its AI systems’ recommendations. 

Another company

 built a system that allowed clinical reviewers to reject claims without opening patient files; clinical reviewers using this system spent an average of just 1.2 seconds on each case.




Is the Right Kind of Data Informing Companies’ Decisions?




Some WISeR vendors’ applications offer general descriptions of the types of data informing their decisions. But far more details are needed to allow medical professionals to assess whether the data inputs to these AI systems are appropriate for evaluating prior authorization requests. 




Inappropriate training data or input data can lead to biased, unfair, or inaccurate decisions. 

CMS guidance

 for Medicare Advantage organizations using AI to make coverage decisions emphasizes the importance of basing decisions on individual patients’ circumstances. It cautions against using “an algorithm that determines coverage based on a larger data set instead of the individual patient's medical history, the physician’s recommendations, or clinical notes.” 




WISeR vendors’ applications reference data sources like “

provider behavior

,” “

patient demographics

,” “

utilization management datasets

,” “

provider and payer performance metrics

,” and “

historical claims data

.” Whether these sources could introduce bias or give too much weight to population-level patterns depends on how vendors use them to inform individual decisions. But we don’t yet have these important details about vendors’ data and algorithms. By outsourcing decision-making to private companies’ AI systems, the government has made it harder for the public to evaluate whether decisions are being made fairly.




Next Steps




As the government expands its use of automated decision-making, the potential for consequential mistakes increases rapidly. The records we’ve obtained so far raise questions about the rushed rollout and lack of guardrails for automated decision-making by the U.S. government. EFF urges transparency, oversight, and 

legal limits

 to protect people from the harms of automated decision-making in high risk systems.  




Related Cases: 

EFF v. CMS
