author: Chan Tsz Yung Frederick
title: Laying on Thin Water: The Looming Danger of Sub-Saharan Africa’s Subsea Repair Vessel Deficit
content:
Submarine fibre-optic cables (subsea telecommunications cables) handle up to 

99%

 of our global internet traffic and communications, underlining the operations of numerous businesses and institutions across the world. Their continued proliferation will bring higher network speeds and connect more people and regions to digital communications. Yet, whilst the world is on a roll in laying down more of this critical infrastructure, it is severely underequipped in properly maintaining them. Sub-Saharan Africa is no exception. As the region with the 

fastest-growing population

 and a 

large gap

 to fill in terms of internet connectivity, Sub-Saharan Africa is occupying an increasingly important position in the world’s network of submarine fibre-optic cables.




Sub-Saharan Africa in the growing demand for Subsea telecommunications cables repairs




Once a subsea telecommunications cable is laid, many potential costs are incurred: the future need for repairs due to factors such as human activity, natural disasters, and mechanical failure. Filling this role is the 

registered

 fleet of 63 ships that has subsea telecommunications cable repair capabilities, 

60% of which are not solely dedicated to repairs but are also cable-laying ships.

 For Sub-Saharan Africa, it is serviced by the 

44-year-old 

Léon Thévenin

, the sole permanent subsea telecommunications cable repair vessel stationed at Cape Town to care for the cables connected to this massive region.







Figure 1. 

Photo of the 

Léon Thévenin

 by Vessel Finder




It is true that many cables are soon to be retired, with 

forecasts

 predicting the decommissioning of roughly 450,000 kilometers of cable over the course of 2026–2035. This means there will be legacy cables that no longer require constant maintenance or fault servicing. Yet, the laying of new cables far outpaces this retirement trend, with an expected 1,010,000 kilometers of new cable laid during that same time period. New cables carry higher technical resilience, but they remain just as vulnerable to external physical force, which 

accounts for the vast majority

 of subsea telecommunications cable faults. Consequently, overall demand for repairs will likely increase rather than shrink. Following the global trend, a net increase of subsea telecommunications cables and subsequent faults is 

expected

 for Sub-Saharan Africa. Major new subsea telecommunications cables are planned for Sub-Saharan Africa – such as 

Via Africa

 and the 

ReuNION Cable,

 with multiple landing sites in the region. It is imperative that regional repair capacity increases to match growing infrastructural needs.




Existing deficiencies in repair capacity




According to industry reports, Sub-Saharan Africa’s current situation seems to be fine on paper. In fact, it was 

forecasted

 that only around one vessel is needed to cover not just the region but the whole continent’s repair demands. It makes sense if we are only looking at the amount of expected subsea telecommunications cable faults, but this is not the case as we take distance into consideration.




To illustrate how this relying on a single permanently stationed repair vessel is insufficient in answering potential demands in Sub-Saharan Africa, 

a report by the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) in July 2026

 highlighted how vulnerable this one-ship baseline really is through a hypothetical scenario where subsea telecommunications cable faults occur simultaneously near Mombasa and Dakar. One vessel clearly couldn’t cover both faults at the same time, not to mention the long transit time needed for the vessel to travel from one side of the continent to the other. North Africa is comparatively more well covered, such as by the 

Mediterranean Cable Maintenance Agreement (MECMA)

, which provides two repair vessels based in nearby European ports to answer maintenance demands. And it should be noted that even so, the Mediterranean region itself is currently suffering from a repair vessel shortage.




Even though Sub-Saharan Africa is technically supplemented by several vessels that are based in other regions, the overall repair readiness has proven to be insufficient. Recalling the high profile case of the 

2024 underwater landslide in the Trou Sans Fond Canyon off the coast of Cote d’Ivoire

, damaging four cables – MainOne, West Africa Cable System (WACS), Africa Coast to Europe (ACE), South Atlantic-3 (SAT-3). Under the ACMA (Atlantic Cable Maintenance Agreement), the C.S Sovereign arrived from London to repair the MainOne, WACS and ACE. The remaining cable (SAT-3) was repaired by the 

Léon Thévenin

, which was directly responsible for the cable’s maintenance.

 It took the vessel 16 days to reach the fault area, and the repair operation by C.S 

Sovereign

 was even slower as it had to travel from London, taking more than a month since incident to fully repair the first cable (ACE). 

Distance matters as in another major incident the same year offshore of the Mtunzini Cable Landing Station, it only took the 

Léon Thévenin 

4 days in transit

 to reach the site, 

repairing both the SEACOM and Eastern Africa Submarine Cable System (EASSy) cables in 3 weeks

 and restoring full internet capacity to East Africa.




Fulfilling demands whilst balancing the books




It is clear that Sub-Saharan Africa requires new ships and new local bases of operations to fulfil subsea telecommunications cable repair demands. However, the situation is more complex than simply buying more vessels. The maintenance cost of subsea telecommunications cables is highly fragmented between various entities within regional maintenance agreements. Simply calling for adding more repair vessels and supporting port infrastructure is not nuanced enough to solve the repair shortage on its own. To start, we must first understand more about these maintenance consortia and their subsea telecommunications cable repair vessels.




Existing maintenance consortia (such as 2OCMA) are usually composed of private sector companies (e.g Orange) and state owned enterprises (e.g China Telecom). This includes telecom companies, technology corporations (e.g Meta). These consortia are also run on a non-profit basis (e.g 

ACMA

), with members pooling up resources to fund things such as repair vessel and remotely operated vehicle contracts. The mode of commission of repair vessels under these consortia varies. For instance, the 2OCMA has a long-term contract with Orange Marine (which is a subsidiary under Orange), to provide a permanent stationed vessel – the 

Léon Thévenin

. The ship is based in Cape Town, and the depot is owned by 

Telkom SA

. Other consortia hire external, third-party marine companies such as the 

Global Marine Group

 to fulfil their repair vessel needs.







Figure 2. 

Consortium agreement distribution map by Orange Marine




Hence, we must look toward expanding the contracted fleets of existing consortium agreements like 2OCMA and ACMA. For example, upscaling the 2OCMA from its one-ship configuration by contracting multiple vessels – which allows for simultaneous response to faults on different sides of the continent. If possible, to establish another contracted repair vessel base in either East or West Africa to provide quick, localised responses. ACMA may also set up a contracted forward base in West Africa, adding to the four existing bases in Europe, Bermuda and the Caribbean. Beyond consortia, 

private regional agreements such as APMA and E-marine

 technically cover parts of Sub-Saharan Africa, and should be considered and coordinated during these expansion efforts.




Notwithstanding the higher costs of maintaining an expanded repair fleet, expanding repair capacity still deserves serious consideration given the astronomical costs of unaddressed faults. The high-profile Cote d’Ivoire underwater landslides in 2024 demonstrated this reality, with Nigeria alone suffering an estimated 

593.6 million USD

 in economic losses from cable disruptions in the first four days. Even though it is unlikely that having more repair vessels can reduce this upfront loss, it can reduce the cascading systemic risks that are incurred as the cable remains unrepaired for weeks. On the other hand, the 

expected cost

 of maintaining a repair vessel goes up to 100,000 USD per day, with individual missions costing up to 3 million USD. These costs are undoubtedly heavy, yet this is to avoid the unquantifiable ripple effects from cascading systemic risks. And in the unlikely event that even the rerouted cables also suffered from damage, a delayed repair response could result in a prolonged internet blackout with insurmountable losses.




It is understandable that not all telecom companies operate on the scale of hyperscalers or can afford the high maintenance costs of an expanded fleet and infrastructure. Since cost is usually shared, governments and hyperscalers active in the region should actively close possible funding gaps – aligning financial contributions directly with their systemic exposure. Just as the 

ITU recommended the establishment of Public-Private Partnerships (PPP) for underserviced regions

, establishing PPPs for this purpose will likely help streamline the process by providing platforms for easier coordination.




Alternatives for consideration




It is also possible to consider improving the operational capacity of existing vessels. Similarly challenged by a deficit in repair capacity despite a growing network of subsea telecommunications cables, the European Commission announced on June 23, 2026, its efforts to fund adaptable modules that can be 

“rapidly installed and deployed by existing repair vessels”

. Tentatively costing 40 million Euros, this initiative aims to bolster Europe’s local cable repair capabilities. As peers facing a similar challenge, organisations such as the African Union can consider establishing similar, localized mechanisms to strengthen regional repair readiness. The positioning of such modules in Cape Town could allow the 

Léon Thévenin

 to respond to crises even faster. South Africa at the present already stands out globally as the country with the 

shortest “commencement time”

, only needing 1.95 days on average before the repair vessel disembarks. With the world’s 

median at 8 days

, South Africa’s system provides a powerful blueprint for future regional bases in Africa and the rest of the World. This would likely bolster the operational capacity of repair vessels in the region, yet, it does not fully remedy the dangers caused by the insufficient amount of repair vessels in Sub-Saharan Africa.




Governments in the region should also ensure the relative ease and convenience in acquiring repair permits in Exclusive Economic Zones, avoiding bureaucratic delays to minimize service disruption. This could be achieved through explicitly exempting cable repairs from cabotage laws, implementing fast track, single-window approval for repair vessels that have been previously registered. This would allow them to carry out repair work much faster than before, with minimal delays once arriving on site.




It is important to note that interventions surrounding repair vessels are not the sole answer to this problem. Increasing cable resilience through the use of tougher materials, optimized positioning of cables, and real-time monitoring can serve as vital, simultaneous interventions to alleviate strain on the repair network and protect the region’s network stability. Yet, it does not distract us from the centrality of repair needs. Expanding repair readiness is not merely about staying online — it is about ensuring that Sub-Saharan Africa remains a resilient and fast-growing region.




The post 

Laying on Thin Water: The Looming Danger of Sub-Saharan Africa’s Subsea Repair Vessel Deficit

 appeared first on 

African Arguments

.

author: labor4pal
title: Motown and the Making of Working-Class Revolutionaries: an Interview with Jerome Scott and Walda Katz-Fishman (UAWD Daily Struggle)
content:
Anthony Stoner October 26, 2026

Jerome Scott and Walda Katz-Fishman, authors of Motown and the Making of Working-Class Revolutionaries: The League of Revolutionary Black Workers, share their reflections on the UAW’s Black radical tradition, the tactic of the wildcat strike, and the importance of unions fighting for the working class as a whole.

In the 1960s, Chrysler—the only Big Three corporation whose operations remained largely in Detroit at the time—began to hire Black workers, many fresh from the U.S. South. They had the worst and most dangerous jobs, and Chrysler frequently fired them before they obtained UAW contract protections after a 90-day probation. In 1968, these conditions and the lack of representation by the white-dominated UAW—at that time led by Walter Reuther, whose “Administration Caucus” dominated the union then and for decades after his death led to a wildcat strike in the Dodge Main plant initiated by the Dodge Revolutionary Union Movement (DRUM) (A wildcat strike is a strike not officially authorized by a union). A number of other RUMs were then created around Detroit, and in 1969 the League of Revolutionary Black Workers (LRBW) was founded by Black militant labor organizers to help unite and aid struggles around the city. Among those organizers was Jerome Scott, who, along with Walda Katz-Fishman, has written an account of the LRBW, based on extensive interviews with surviving members of the League, their families and comrades. Their book, Motown and the Making of Working-Class Revolutionaries: The Story of the League of Revolutionary Black Workers, is available from University of Georgia Press.

—Anthony Stoner, UAW Local 4811

Anthony SToner: Why were wildcat strikes the tactic both DRUM and then the LRBW focused on? What’s the role of a wildcat strike for today?

Jerome scott: The wildcat strike became our principal tactic mainly because it was a two-edged sword. We could attack the company as well as struggle with the union. The company of course was and is the major enemy, but back in the day, and in some unions even today, the collaboration between the union and the corporation is not good for the workers themselves. And so we realized after the first wildcat strike (for us, and the first in the country for about fifty years) at Dodge Main that that wildcat strike really did attack both of our struggles. What we didn’t realize when we started it was that it was also a very offensive tactic. We were making the decisions; and the corporation and the union had to respond and defend against that, rather than the workers always being on the defensive. So the wildcat strike was a hell of a weapon.

AS: How did Doug Fraser [then head of UAW Chrysler Department] and the UAW International use the “flying squadron” during the 1973 wildcat?

JS: A little bit on the history of the flying squadron. It started with the United Mine Workers movement in Appalachia because of the rolling strikes that happened in the organizing of that union. It was an organized group of union members that they would take from strike event to strike event and try to make sure that nobody crossed the picket line. They were an apparatus that actually really backed up the picket lines in the strikes that were held in the heyday of organizing the UAW, the United Mine Workers, and so on. And the purpose was really to let the workers know that the International was part of this strike. So the concept of the flying squadron had a long tradition of respect from the union movement.

In our case, in our strike at Chrysler in 1973, we were able to shut down the entire Chrysler corporation for about a week; and that was because of the strategic nature of the Detroit Forge plant where I worked. There was only one other plant in the world that made the same parts that we made and it was a forging plant in [apartheid-era] South Africa. The corporation had done all it could do to try to break our strike, and try to break the picket line, but the picket line was going on 24/7.

What we learned later is that the corporation had called Solidarity House and said, “you have to do something about this strike.” And it was then that Fraser organized the historic flying squadron to come break our picket line rather than support it. And it was a pitched battle—it wasn’t like we saw them coming and laid down our picket signs—it was a big struggle. But eventually they were able to break our picket line and end our struggle after a week. Now the company decided that they would permanently fire three of us. But later on we learned that the company didn’t decide who to fire—the company left it up to the union to decide. They fired two Black workers and one white worker, two production workers and one skilled trades worker. The two Black workers were in the League of Revolutionary Black Workers leading up to that strike, and the skilled trades person was someone we had worked with in our plant over the previous two years. So not only did they bring out the flying squadron to break our strike, they also collaborated with the company to decide who would be permanently fired.

Now, that permanent fire for the three of us sort of backfired on them, because one of the skilled tradesmen who was out on the wildcat strike was also in the process of buying a bar across the street from the plant we had just shut down, and across the street from six other Chrysler plants up and down that block. So he hired the three of us as bartenders, and that became the best job we had ever had. Because once you shut down the corporation and people knew you were in this fight with the union and the company, they wanted to talk to us. So we had a constant flow of workers coming into the bar, having political discussions, trying to figure out how they could have a wildcat strike at their shop.

AS: Why do you think the International was acting this way—was it mostly racism, was it also their investments in the company?

JS: The 70s was a period when the unions were really trying to collaborate with corporations to have these “Joint Work Committees” on the shop floor with the foremen and the workers. They were promoting this whole idea that we could have peace in the working-class battle between the owners of the Chrysler corporation and the workers. So it was this notion, I think, that we could have this “peaceful” period, where they wouldn’t have to strike, they wouldn’t have to do the real fight for workers, but the corporation would somehow allow them to make advances.

I think there’s one other thing that played into this: early on in the 50s, unions made a decision that they would only represent their members, and not the working class as a whole, and so they saw this peaceful coexistence with the corporation as a way to support their members and separate themselves from the struggles of the working class as a whole and concentrate on just the relations between their members and the corporations as opposed to the struggles between the working class and the corporations.

WALDA katz-fishman: The workers also did some investigation, and they found out the union was actually invested in the corporation and was making more money from its investments than from the actual dues from its members. So it was not just a political collaboration, it was really an economic merging of the interests of the “union hierarchy” and the corporation. And that’s pretty extraordinary: Y’all should do some investigation today.

AS: Your book discusses the idea of union organizing for the working class as a whole rather than just representing the members of the union. Why is that important? What can we do with that today?

When you struggle for higher wages in a shop, that really does affect the whole community around it. And so if you fight and bring in the communities around the shops and bring in whatever motion around police brutality or the fight against poverty or any of those community-based fights, they’re all working-class fights.

JS: It’s more important today than it’s ever been. When the trade union movement was developing in this country, it developed on the basis of representing the working class. Back in the 30s and 40s, there were at least 9 or 10 international unions that demanded the end of capitalism as the way for workers to actually get and hold what they were fighting for. So the trade union movement has a revolutionary guts to it that they’ve been trying to stomp out ever since. I think it was during the McCarthy era in the early 50s, one of the demands that the ruling class made on the union movement—well of course, one of them was to rid itself of any communists that existed in the leadership and try to scorch its membership as well. But one of the other demands was that they had to stop trying to mobilize the working class as part of the union struggle and only concentrate on their members. And the corporations would then back off on the struggle around contracts and give them easier access to making contracts. So the leadership of the international trade union movement made that agreement. They agreed that they would concentrate on their membership.

The reason it’s so important is because when you struggle for higher wages in a shop, that really does affect the whole community around it. And so if you fight and bring in the communities around the shops and bring in whatever motion around police brutality or the fight against poverty or any of those community-based fights, they’re all working-class fights. And a trade union struggle in the middle of that can add a lot of power and prestige to those struggles as well as provide the trade union with support from the community that will also have an effect on their battle in the shop.

We have got to understand that we’re in a much more powerful position if we approach it from the standpoint of a broad-based front of struggle to organize a shop. Not just the workers in it, but their families, the community that it sits in, the drivers that service it, the whole shebang. And more or less a working-class strategy for organizing a union rather than a membership-based strategy for organizing a union.

WKF: Huge sections of the working class, the academy, professors and scientists and doctors and nurses and the whole tech industry that has not been historically unionized, are losing jobs. They’re losing jobs, job security, certainly benefits, and so we’re in a class war. And so to develop that class consciousness when the trade union movement is such a small percentage of the working class, it’s really important for us to think about the working class as a whole, and it’s really important for that section that is more highly organized to help broaden out the understanding of who we are, what our interests are in society, and how do we help lift up and help organize the working class as a whole. And I think some of the unions have played an important role—in May Day Strong, or in the call for a 2028 general strike—so we can see that they have a capacity to take some important “leadership roles,” because they do have resources and organization.

AS: How important was organizing around health and safety issues to expanding League contacts with the non-Black workers in the factory, the white workers, the skilled trade workers, and so on?

JS: Health and safety was a lot bigger than anybody thought, when you think back on it. There were two major things that were really the impetus for wildcat strikes. One of course was the way management treated workers. The whole question of white supremacy in the plants back in the 60s was just as bad as anyplace else. The foremen thought they could treat Black workers any way they wanted to, and treated us like, I’ll fire your ass in a second, if you don’t do as I tell you to do and not argue with me, not discuss with me whether or not it’s legal for me to treat you this way. The other reason was health and safety. Somebody was always getting hurt in the plant, every day. Once we began to reach out to white workers to try to figure out how to build those kinds of relationships, we realized the connecting factor was health and safety, and skilled trades workers were just as concerned that they might get injured on the job as we were as production workers.

WKF: As I recall, it was a white worker whose hand was cut off; that was the provocation for the ‘73 wildcat strike.

WKF: And what the white workers said to you all, the Black workers, we’re really glad you all have been carrying forward this fight. So once they were able to work together, it was better, the wildcat was more powerful when it was a multiracial wildcat.

There has always been multiracial struggle—there’s been Black working-class struggle but also multiracial struggle—in the South against the conditions of life there.

JS: The difference between the wildcats that happened prior to our ‘73 wildcat, which was mainly Black workers that went out and were able to shut down the process of that particular factory for a while. Our ability to shut Chrysler down for a whole week was the difference between having the vast majority of the workers in that shop support the strike versus only Black workers. So it meant all the difference in the world.

AS: Many of the League workers either themselves or their families had come from the South. Why is the South this important battleground in the class war?

WKF: What I think the League expresses is that there has always been multiracial struggle—there’s been Black working-class struggle but also multiracial struggle—in the South against the conditions of life there. There is union organizing in the South, despite Taft-Hartley, which said states can implement state-by-state right-to-work laws, which makes it almost impossible for unions to organize, so the South became the “solid South” of right-to-work. So both in terms of both working-class organizing and in terms of federal policy—economy, ecology, politics, and society, public institutions—the South is either a place where the working class breaks through or the capitalist class manages to control it and therefore the nation. And that’s why the South is such a battleground today, it’s emerging because the working class is in motion, and they know this is the place where it’s easiest for them to grab control back.

JS: The ruling class is once again relying on the fact that if they’re going to consolidate fascism in this country, they have to consolidate it in the South. And therefore they have to get rid of the Voting Rights Act, and they have to prevent unions from spreading across the South in this period where unions are really beginning to pick up again and beginning to organize.

AS: Tell me about the history of the League and its contacts with the PLO (Palestine Liberation Organization) and the Arab Workers Caucus (in the UAW in Dearborn, Michigan), especially given Israel’s genocide and the UAW’s divestment from Israel bonds.

JS: Over the last couple years, we’ve given a lot of thought to this too. We looked at ourselves as oppressed and exploited people—and Detroit and Dearborn was a special sort of area of the country. We had a bigger Middle Eastern population in Dearborn than any other place outside of the Middle East. And that was true because of the recruitment of international workers by the auto industry. They figured that cultural division might slow down the union process. But the fact was that we were working side by side with Middle Eastern folk who had migrated here to the United States and were part of our working-class brothers and sisters. When we learned that the UAW was buying Israeli bonds and that that was supporting the oppression of the Palestinian people, we reached out to our coworkers, and we even had delegations go to the Middle East and meet primarily with the PLO.

We realized it was our country, our government, that was sending all this money to Israel and soliciting our trade unions to use our pension funds, our money, to buy Israeli bonds. So not only did we develop good relations with them, but one of the wildcat strikes back in the day was a wildcat strike against the UAW continuing to buy those bonds. We didn’t appreciate our dues being used to support the oppression and exploitation of another set of oppressed and exploited people. That was the basis of our relationship, and we continued to have those kinds of relationships not only with the Palestinian people—we did the same thing with the Vietnamese people, and the Irish struggle against the British, the whole shebang of oppressed and exploited people—we tried to reach out to and let them know we were all fighting the same kind of fight, only on different fronts.

You have to return to the roots of the trade union movement and make your struggle […] a working-class issue, and any advancements, you want to be applied not only to the workers in that industry but also to the communities in which those workers live and to the section of society which those workers represent.

WKF: So internationalism was a big part of their working-class understanding of the world. It was Edna in our interviews who said what Jerome just said: We organized together because we lived side by side, in the same neighborhoods and worked together. So it was a very concrete unity, as well as an intellectual kind of unity, a political unity.

AS: What does the experience of the League contribute now to militant unionism?

JS: This is a war on the working class—it’s a war on the unions, so you’ve got to act like it’s a war—but it’s also a war on the working class as a whole. You have to return to the roots of the trade union movement and make your struggle, your contracts or whatever issue you’re fighting around, a working-class issue, and any advancements, you want to be applied not only to the workers in that industry but also to the communities in which those workers live and to the section of society which those workers represent. And so there has to be a working-class victory. And in order for there to be a working-class victory, you’ve got to mobilize and educate the working class as a whole.

That would be my message to the UAW. If they want this general strike in 2028 to actually happen and be a success, the mobilization for it has got to be a society, working-class-wide mobilization. When ‘28 comes, you might have those contracts that expire at the same time. But if you don’t have some secondary boycotts organized, if you don’t have some secondary supports mobilized around the logistics industry, then it will not be successful. So it has to be a community-wide effort if we’re going to make this general strike be an advancement for the working class in taking the offensive in this war.

WKF: The only other thing is that if it’s only about 10% of workers—and that’s workers who have jobs—who are unionized, then we’ve got to go back to our working-class roots. The trade union movement has an opportunity to really play a leadership role. But they’ve got to reach deep down to where the working class is, which is outside of the trade union movement, and figure out how to really play that role to build an organized hub of organizing.

author: Monthly Review Press
title: In Amsterdam in November? Join Chris dePloeg, Jason Hickel and more, LIVE, for “The Exterminating Empire”
content:
Pakuis de Zwijger

, Monday, November 23rd: :ive with Jason Hickel, 

Ghassan Abu-Sittah

, 

Harriët Bergman

, 

Chihiro Geuzebroek

, 

Max de Ploeg

 and the author!




In collaboration with In collaboration with Pijke ter Laak, join 

Pakuis de Zwijger

 for a conversation with author Chris de Ploeg about his new book, a radical and urgent indictment of the global capitalist system and the imperial violence it unleashes upon people and planet alike. At its core, the book argues that genocide and ecocide are not tragic byproducts of capitalism – they are its fundamental features. 




Together with renowned climate author Jason Hickel (in person), frontline Palestinian surgeon Ghassan Abu-Sittah (joining online) and our moderator, climate justice activist and researcher Harriët Bergman, we will dive deeper into the interconnections of the great challenges of our time–and more importantly, how to fight back. There will also be cultural performances from Chihiro Geuzebroek and brothers Chris and Max de Ploeg, tying their ancestral struggles in Bolivia and Armenia to the global struggle for liberation. 

REGISTER HERE!




REVIEWS:




Morning Star

:

 “How did such a horror come to pass?” by Alex Hall




“

The Exterminating Empire

 began life as a Master’s thesis, nurtured into book form by Jason Hickel — the degrowth economist and author of The Divide, who contributes the foreword. The mentorship was well placed and De Ploeg has produced an impressively searing panorama of our global predicament…”




Counterpunch

, “

Resisting Annihilation: Reviewing “The Exterminating Empire”

, by Seth Sandronsky




“…de Ploeg, who does far more than compile lists of atrocities, draws parallels between the American holocaust of the native inhabitants’ relations with buffaloes and Israel’s genocide against Palestinians and their farming of olive trees. Land theft and separating those living on the land from it are nothing new. The author has skin in the game, given his family survived the Armenian genocide and Nazi holocaust…”




Counterpunch

, “

Capitalism is Waging War on Palestine While Creating a Burning Planet

” by Daniel Falcone:




Daniel Falcone: 

What is the central argument of 

The Exterminating Empire

 and how is the book structured? It looks as though the book serves as an intervention as well as an addition to current scholarship.  




Chris Kaspar de Ploeg:

 I open the book with some jarring facts that seem paradoxical at first sight. We need about 30 percent of our productive capacity to 

give everyone on the planet a good life

. Not just the basics like housing, clothing and healthcare, but also modern appliances like refrigerators, laptops, access to the internet and more. At the same time, that standard of living is denied to about 

80 percent of the world population

. Green energy has been cheaper than fossil fuels for years, yet climate breakdown is only accelerating. We could 

solve world hunger

 with about 0.03 percent of global GDP, but hunger is only increasing.




That looks like an extraordinarily wasteful system, and it is. The point, however, is that under capitalism, these are not paradoxes at all. In fact, they are signs of capital’s success. Under our current economic system, the primary goal, ruthlessly pursued, is 

profit maximization

. That profit maximization is reached through pushing down costs–and we are those costs, our labour, our environments, our lives–and by conquering markets, often through a mix of military and economic warfare. That essentially puts 

capitalism on a warpath against life

. The system is working exactly as it is supposed to.




We see, for example, that profit rates are higher in the fossil fuel industry because it essentially 

functions through monopolies

, despite the higher costs. We see that the military-industrial complex is growing exponentially, targeting any vestiges of resistance against 

US-led global hegemony

, which globalized harsh budget cuts in social welfare, healthcare and education. These very conditions of 

structural impoverishment

 then create the conditions of desperation necessary for people and countries to accept their status as sources for cheap labour, resources and land for global corporations, mostly centered in the Global North.




In the book I write about a dialectic between slavery and genocide, and between structural genocide and active genocide. A good way to understand that relationship is by going back to the 

We Charge Genocide petition

, which was presented in 1951 at the United Nations by William L. Patterson, on behalf of the 

Civil Rights Congress

. He estimated that, since the abolition of slavery, some 10,000 black people had been lynched, often for something as small as looking a white woman in the eyes. These lynchings were not hidden affairs, but were a 

public spectacle

, for which neighbors came together, and pictures were spread on postcards across the country.




Patterson

 goes on to argue that this kind of active violence serves a deeper purpose. It was meant to intimidate the black masses to accept lower living standards, functioning as a dehumanized workforce for corporations. At the time, this led 32,000 excess deaths every year among Black Americans compared to white death rates. Patterson charges this as a ‘genocide for profit’, based on the article in the UN convention that lists “

deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction

.” Combining two studies that were done since that time, I show that between 1940 and 2020 the total excess death toll of African Americans is 6 million.




Nowadays, scholars tend to call this ‘

structural genocide

’. And I argue that this is a global phenomenon under capitalism. In a sense, the active genocide in Palestine is a lynching aimed at intimidating the Global South into accepting its role as devalued lives for Western profits. The blatant, live-streamed and openly announced nature of that genocide is exactly the point, just as the lynchings of the American South were broadcast widely. It is aimed to intimidate people, because the active genocide serves the broader, structural genocide.




The histories of 

genocide and slavery

 are deeply intertwined. In fact, almost every genocide in history also deployed slave labor–even in the archetypical death camp, Auschwitz – and chattel slavery also contained genocidal dynamics of cheapened lives and heightened death rates. In a sense, even in Gaza the exterminated are forced to labor as 

guinea pigs

for the global arms industry, whose weapons are then sold as ‘battle tested.’ But on a more structural level, the survival mode that is forced upon the global masses makes them accept conditions they normally never would. Generations of workers used to call this ‘

wage slavery

’, to emphasize the lack of freedom underlying these conditions. Indeed, the global peasantry first had to be robbed of their communal lands – where they could often provide for themselves – before they could be forced to work under the hierarchical system of capitalism. Essentially, then, the global architecture of capitalism promotes various modes and gradations of extermination and slavery.




The book marshals a lot of data and history to demonstrate how this system has functioned so consistently throughout the centuries. I also fuse 

ecology and climate breakdown

 deeply into this analysis, both theoretically and empirically, as any attack on human life tends to be equally fused with attacks on their environments. 

Ecocide and genocide

 go hand in hand, both on the active and structural level. The very idea that we can separate the humans from ecology is itself a colonial and capitalist phantasy. But the book is not only gloom and doom. I end with a long chapter on strategizing how to beat this system, learning both from the accomplishments and failures of 

resistance movements

 from the past and the present. Honestly, the pace of the book is quite high, so it is impossible to summarize everything in one interview.




Daniel Falcone:

 To what extent does the 

spirit of resistance

 become the prime target for annihilation? Also, how is 

cultural genocide

 related to capitalist alienation? You discuss the cogs in the hierarchical machine, but I am wondering how this idea explains your thesis and impacts collective identity.




Chris Kaspar de Ploeg:

 When the Polish-Jewish legal scholar 

Raphael Lemkin

 coined the term genocide in 1944 in his 

Axis Rule in Occupied Europe

, he was not thinking primarily about mass killings. Rather, he saw in Nazi rule an attempt to wipe out the collective coherence of peoples, their languages, their institutions, their intelligentsia, cultures, all of it. He defined genocide as imposing ‘

the national pattern of the oppressor’

, either on the people themselves or on their territory after their deportation or slaughter…..




Read more at 

Counterpunch




APPEARANCES:




Just hours after its release, the first interview with Chris De Ploeg immediately went live!




Adnan Husain

‘s Office Hours 39










Taking the ongoing genocide in Palestine as a point of departure, 

The Exterminating Empire

 traces capital’s centuries-long war against life itself. From the slave plantations and scorched-earth campaigns of early colonialism, to Vietnam, Haiti, Iraq, and today’s climate apartheid, Chris de Ploeg shows that, not only has exterminatory violence against peoples and ecosystems been central to the imperial project, but omnicidal tendencies—the drive to kill everything—have always been present. Operating at different scales, these tendencies possess the potential to annihilate even the imperial core itself, along with the rest of the planet. 

Read more….




Empire Watch










In episode 89 of Global Majority for Peace, Ileana Chan speaks with journalist, author, and grassroots organizer Chris de Ploeg, also the author of 

The Great Colonial Wars

 trilogy.













The post 

In Amsterdam in November? Join Chris dePloeg, Jason Hickel and more, live, for “The Exterminating Empire”

 appeared first on 

Monthly Review

title: Antalya'da hortum nedeniyle parçalanan konteynerlerde 4 işçi hayatını kaybetti
content:
Antalya'nın Kepez ilçesinde etkili olan hortumda parçalanan iki konteynerde bulunan 4 işçi hayatını kaybetti, 1 işçi yaralandı.

Meteoroloji Genel Müdürlüğünün sarı kodlu sağanak uyarısında bulunduğu kentte, Kepez ilçesi Fevzi Çakmak Mahallesi'ndeki bir inşaat alanında hortum oluştu.

Hortum, inşaat işçilerinin kaldığı iki konteyneri parçaladı. Konteynerlerde bulunan 5 işçi savruldu.

İhbar üzerine bölgeye 112 Acil Sağlık, polis ve itfaiye ekipleri sevk edildi.

İşçilerden 2'sinin olay yerinde, 2'sinin ise kaldırıldıkları hastanede hayatını kaybettiği belirlendi.

Yaralanan işçinin sağlık durumunun iyi olduğu öğrenildi.

Antalya Valisi Hulusi Şahin konu hakkında yaptığı açıklamada "Maalesef 2 işçimiz olay yerinde 2 işçimiz de kaldırıldıkları hastanede vefat ettiler. Bir işçimiz yaralı durumu hafif. Çok enteresan bir doğa olayı ile karşı karşıyayız. Çünkü şehrin herhangi başka bir yerinde fırtına, hortum ihbar edilmedi. Civarındaki binalarda bir şey yok ama sadece bu alanda iki konteyneri paramparça eden bir hortumla karşı karşıyayız."

Şantiye sahasındaki ölüm ve yaralanmaların vincin devrilmesi nedeniyle olmadığını söyleyen Şahin, bölgede incelemelerin devam ettiğini ve ekiplerin alanda yaralı veya ölü olup olmadığına dair çalışmalarını sürdürdüğünü kaydetti.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

title: Fransa'da ırkçılık ve İslamofobi karşıtı gösteriler düzenlendi
content:
Fransa'da farklı sendika, dernek ve kitle örgütü kuruluşlarının çağrısıyla Paris, Strazburg, Roubaix, Stains, Nanterre, La Courneuve dahil farklı kentlerde ırkçılık karşıtları bir araya geldi.

Ülkede artan ırkçılığa ve İslamofobiye tepki verilen gösterilerde, 23 Ekim'de Yvelines ilinde düzenlenen terör saldırısında hayatını kaybeden Kongo asıllı Fransız Pengo Bossio Wangi anıldı.

Gösterilerde, söz konusu ırkçı saldırıda yaralanan 1'i çocuk olmak üzere 5 kişiye yönelik destek mesajları da dile getirildi.

Başkent Paris'te Stalingrad Muharebesi Meydanı'nda yerel saatle 19.00'da başlayan gösteriye yüzlerce kişi katıldı.

Göstericiler, "Irkçılık bir görüş değil, hayatları paramparça eden bir suçtur", "Paramparça olan hayatlardan ziyade kırılan vitrinlere şefkat gösteriyorlar" ve "Irkçılık öldürür" yazılı pankartlar taşıdı.

Göstericiler, ırkçı söylemleri yaymakla suçlanan CNews kanalında çalışan bir gazetecinin gösteriye katılmasına "CNews dışarı" ve "CNews katil, (Cumhurbaşkanı Emmanuel) Macron suç ortağı" sloganları atarak tepki gösterdi.

Irkçılıkla mücadele derneği SOS Racisme'in Başkanı Dominique Sopo, burada yaptığı konuşmada, birkaç yıldır ülkede ırkçı saikli suçların yeniden işlenmeye başlandığını söyledi.

Sopo, bazı medya organlarının bünyelerinde ırkçı söylemlerin sarf edilmesine izin verdiğini belirterek, bu söylemin son derece "ciddi" olduğuna dikkati çekti.

Yvelines'e bağlı Trappes kentindeki saldırıyı yapan teröristin "siyahilere ve Araplara saldırarak 17 Ekim'deki gösterilerinde, dükkanı yağmalanan esnafın öcünü almak istediğini" dile getirdiğini aktaran Sopo, terör saldırısından birkaç gün önce Fransız televizyon kanallarında eylemlerdeki yağma olaylarıyla ilgili ırkçı bir çerçeve kullanıldığını belirtti.

Trappes Belediye Başkanı Ali Rabeh ise Ulusal Birlik (RN) Partisi Başkanı Jordan Bardella'nın daha önce Trappes kentini "Paris'e 30 dakika mesafedeki Kabil'e" benzettiğini hatırlattı.

Rabeh, Trappes'a yönelik damgalayıcı sözler kullananları terör saldırısının failine silah vermekle suçlayarak, "Kanallarda durmaksızın aktarılan yabancılara, göçmenlere, Müslümanlara karşı sarf edilen nefret söylemleri, Fransızların bir kısmının insanlıktan çıkarılmasına neden oldu." dedi.

Bu durumun, bu kişilerin "iç düşmanlar" gibi gösterilmesine sebebiyet verdiğini kaydeden Rabeh, ırkçılık zehrinin tüm ülkeye bulaştığını dile getirdi.

Irkçılık Karşıtı Koalisyon'dan yapılan açıklamaya göre, Paris'te Cumhuriyet Meydanı'nda düzenlenmesi planlanan bir diğer gösteri, Paris Emniyet Müdürlüğünce yasaklandı.

Sosyal medyaya yansıyan görüntülere göre, bazı göstericiler, yasağa rağmen Cumhuriyet Meydanı yakınlarında toplandı.

Sokakta yere oturan göstericiler, Fransa'nın ulusal marşı La Marseillaise'i okudu.

Polis, eylemi dağıtmak için kalkanlarıyla göstericileri iterek bölgeden uzaklaştırmaya çalıştı.

Yvelines ilinde 23 Ekim'de bir kişi, bulunduğu araçtan etraftakilere ateş açmıştı. Saldırıda 1 kişi hayatını kaybetmiş, 5 kişi ağır yaralanmıştı.

39 yaşındaki saldırgan Kevin T, olay yerinde gözaltına alınmıştı.

Fransa Cumhurbaşkanı Emmanuel Macron, saldırının ırkçı nitelikte bir terör saldırısı olduğunu duyurmuştu.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

content:
>Η νεολαία και οι λαοί της Ευρώπης μίλησαν – Η ομορφιά βρίσκεται στον αγώνα!, 19:00 Εκτός των Τειχών




>Προβολή ταινίας και συζήτηση για το κίνημα στη Γαλλία, 19:00 Πάντειο










Εκδήλωση: Η νεολαία και οι λαοί της Ευρώπης μίλησαν – Η ομορφιά βρίσκεται στον αγώνα!
















Προβολή ταινίας και συζήτηση για το κίνημα στη Γαλλία







Την Τρίτη 27/10, στις 19:00 στο αίθριο του Παντείου (αν ο καιρός δε μας το επιτρέψει θα μεταφερθούμε σε αίθουσα) θα προβάλουμε το ντοκιμαντέρ «Η ιστορία των κίτρινων γιλέκων από εμάς». Θα ακολουθήσει συζήτηση με καλεσμένο συντρόφι που μένει στη Γαλλία και συμμετέχει στις κινητοποιήσεις που λαμβάνουν χώρα την τελευταία περίοδο.




Οι εικόνες από τις μεγάλες διαδηλώσεις και συγκρούσεις στους δρόμους του Παρισιού μας γεμίζουν έμπνευση και ανασύρουν στη συλλογική μνήμη το δυναμικό φοιτητικό κίνημα του 23′ και τις τεράστιες απεργιακές κινητοποιήσεις και πορείες των Τεμπών. Ταυτόχρονα, τα αδιέξοδα που προώθησαν τη γαλλική εργατική τάξη σε έναν αγώνα που φαίνεται διαρκής και αμετάκλητος είναι τα ίδια με αυτά που αντιμετωπίζουμε όσο εξοντωνόμαστε στη δουλειά (μεταφορικά και κυριολεκτικά) για έναν μισθό που τελειώνει στα μέσα του μήνα αφού ξοδευτεί στο υπέρογκο και ολοένα αυξανόμενο κόστος ζωής και όσο η κρατική μέριμνα συρρικνώνεται και κάθε πτυχή της ζωής μας βυθίζεται στην επισφάλεια. Από τα ρημαγμένα σχολεία και τις επικίνδυνες κτιριακές υποδομές, στις ελλείψεις διδακτικού προσωπικού, από το διαλυμένο δημόσιο σύστημα υγείας, από την εκπαιδευτική αναδιάρθρωση που υποτάσσει τα πανεπιστήμια στους νόμους της αγοράς και πετάει εκτός χιλιάδες από εμάς που δεν έχουμε την άνεση να σπουδάσουμε με τους ασφυκτικούς όρους που επιβάλλει το υπουργείο.




Και όλα αυτά μας οδηγούν σε ένα ερώτημα και μια επιτακτική ανάγκη: πώς μπροστά σε αυτά τα αδιέξοδα θα ανοίξουμε δρόμους αντίστασης στην πραγματικότητα που μας συνθλίβει; Πώς η κατάσταση στη Γαλλία, αλλά και σε άλλες ευρωπαϊκές χώρες θα πάψει να είναι ειδησεογραφικό θέαμα και θα γειωθεί στο εδώ και τώρα, στο ελληνικό εργατικό, μαθητικό και φοιτητικό κίνημα, στις δικές μας διεκδικήσεις με όρους έμπνευσης; Η πρόσφατη πανεκπαιδευτική απεργία που έφερε χιλιάδες μαθητές, φοιτητές και εκπαιδευτικούς στον δρόμο αποτυπώνει ακριβώς αυτό το κλίμα: το ξεχείλισμα της οργής, το ότι δεν αντέχουμε άλλο και η μόνη μας διέξοδος είναι ο αγώνας και η ολομέτωπη σύγκρουση με το σύστημα που υποτιμά τις ζωές μας και τις καθιστά αναλώσιμες.




Εμείς θα πούμε ότι δεν έχουμε ακριβώς την απάντηση, αλλά ξέρουμε ότι τα κινήματα δε συνδέονται με reels, αλλά με πραγματικές σχέσεις αγώνα και ανταλλαγή εμπειριών στη βάση των κοινών μας αναγκών και επιθυμιών. Σας καλούμε όλους όλες και όλα λοιπόν στον κοινωνικό και πολιτικό μας χώρο, να ανταλλάξουμε σκεπτικά και να ζυμωθούμε γύρω από τους τρόπους και τα εργαλεία συνέχισης του αγώνα.




Αυτόνομη Πρωτοβουλία Παντείου

title: CNT denuncia la imposición de los servicios mínimos para la huelga general del 11N en Madrid
content:
Durante la jornada del viernes 23 de octubre, en que los sindicatos de la mesa sindical fuimos convocados para la supuesta negociación de los servicios mínimos por parte de la Comunidad de Madrid, lo que hemos presenciado es el autoritarismo que se ejerce desde esta administración y la constante falta de respeto a la clase trabajadora.




Esta convocatoria fue emplazada 7 días antes de la finalización del plazo de entrega de uno de los documentos necesarios para legalizar la huelga, la cual requiere de muchos pasos burocráticos para ser legalizada en su totalidad.




La costumbre es emplazar las negociaciones una vez finalizados todos los plazos para los sindicatos, sin embargo, quien moderaba comenzó la reunión poniendo en duda la capacidad negociadora de los sindicatos que aún no habían entregado la totalidad de los documentos.




Tras esto, en la reunión online, se enseñó un documento que había que leer en pantalla como supuesta propuesta, que se suele enviar días antes para su correcto estudio, con interrupciones, mostrándose los apartados sin sus títulos y con un continuo movimiento que dificultaba su correcta lectura.




No quedó un solo sindicato al que no faltasen al respeto por diferentes motivos, negándose continuamente a que pudiéramos tener una copia de la propuesta para poder analizarla y establecer una contrapropuesta con unos servicios mínimos que conciliasen las necesidades esenciales de la población con el derecho inalienable a la huelga de toda persona trabajadora.




Se comprometieron, tras dos horas y media de reunión, a enviar una copia a los sindicatos convocantes y emplazar una segunda reunión 3h después para que tuviéramos tiempo necesario para estudiar la propuesta.




La segunda parte de la reunión comenzó con la justificación de por qué nos habían tenido 3h esperando por un documento que nunca llegó, y es que, entre otras cuestiones, argumentaron que no tenían obligación de enviárnosla ni de negociar los servicios mínimos.




Los servicios esenciales no son algo baladí, la diferencia entre su fijación adecuada o abusiva implica la diferencia entre garantizar un servicio básico esencial o vulnerar el derecho fundamental a la huelga.




Esta actitud por parte de la administración regional de Madrid es otro caso más de su modus operandi a la hora de ningunear a los vecinos y vecinas de la Comunidad y a la clase trabajadora, como ya estamos comprobando con nuestras compañeras y compañeros de enseñanza, en plena huelga indefinida en la que, hasta la fecha, desde la Consejería de Educación no se han dignado a sentarse a negociar las reivindicaciones.




SUBAMOS LOS SALARIOS

BAJEMOS LOS ALQUILERES

¡HUELGA GENERAL!

title: Sözcü'nün Genel Yayın Yönetmeni Ercüment İşleyen gözaltına alındı
content:
Sözcü.com.tr Genel Yayın Yönetmeni Ercüment İşleyen, gözaltına alındı

Gözaltı gerekçesine dair bir bilgi verilmezken İşleyen'in Vatan Emniyet'e götürüldüğü öğrenildi.

2000 yılında milliyet.com.tr'nin yayın yönetmenliğini üstlenen İşleyen, daha sonra Demirören Medya Dijital Grup Başkanlığı ve İcra Kurulu Üyeliği görevlerinde bulundu. Bu görevini beş yıl sürdüren İşleyen, ardından Hürriyet'te Dijital İçerik Direktörü ve İcra Kurulu Üyesi olarak yaklaşık üç yıl çalıştı.

Daha sonra Halk TV'ye geçen İşleyen, halktv.com.tr'nin Genel Yayın Yönetmenliği görevini yürüttü. İşleyen, buradan ayrılmasının ardından Sözcü'ye transfer oldu ve Ağustos 2024'te sozcu.com.tr Genel Yayın Yönetmenliği görevine başladı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Alerta
title: Κοινή επιστολή 7 σωματείων για άμεσα μέτρα στήριξης στους εργαζόμενους της Pizza Fan
content:
Κοινή επιστολή 7 σωματείων για άμεσα μέτρα στήριξης στους εργαζόμενους της Pizza Fan.




ΠΡΟΣ: 1. Υπουργείο Εργασίας και Κοινωνικής Ασφάλισης


Γρ. κ. Κεραμέως




2. Κεντρική Διοίκηση Επιθεώρηση Εργασίας


Γρ. κ Τζιλιβάκη




ΘΕΜΑ: Κατεπείγον αίτημα για την άμεση οικονομική στήριξη και την πλήρη διασφάλιση των εργασιακών και μισθολογικών δικαιωμάτων των εργαζομένων στην Pizza Fan




Αποστέλλουμε την παρούσα επιστολή με κατεπείγοντα χαρακτήρα, λόγω των πρόσφατων εξελίξεων στα καταστήματα της Pizza Fan, οι οποίες δημιουργούν σοβαρή ανησυχία για την οικονομική επιβίωση και την εργασιακή ασφάλεια εκατοντάδων εργαζομένων. Τα σωματεία διανομέων, μαγείρων, λαντζιέρηδων ζητάμε την άμεση παρέμβαση του Υπουργείου Εργασίας και της Επιθεώρησης Εργασίας, προκειμένου να προστατευτούν οι εργαζόμενοι/ες και να διασφαλιστεί η καταβολή του συνόλου των νόμιμων αποδοχών και αποζημιώσεών τους.




1. Άμεση έκτακτη ειδική οικονομική ενίσχυση των εργαζομένων για έξι μήνες




Αιτούμαστε τη θέσπιση και την άμεση καταβολή έκτακτης ειδικής οικονομικής ενίσχυσης για όλους τους εργαζόμενους στα καταστήματα της Pizza Fan, είτε αυτά λειτουργούν με εταιρική μορφή είτε μέσω συστήματος δικαιόχρησης (franchise), στο ύψος των 880 ευρώ μηνιαίως για τους επόμενους έξι μήνες. Η ενίσχυση αυτή κρίνεται αναγκαία για την αντιμετώπιση των άμεσων οικονομικών συνεπειών που υφίστανται οι εργαζόμενοι/ες εξαιτίας των πρόσφατων εξελίξεων. Επισημαίνουμε ότι ακόμη και το ποσό των 880 ευρώ, υπό τις σημερινές συνθήκες ακρίβειας και αυξημένου κόστους διαβίωσης, καλύπτει μόλις στοιχειωδώς τις βασικές ανάγκες ενός εργαζομένου/ης. Για τον λόγο αυτό, η άμεση ενεργοποίηση ενός ειδικού μέτρου στήριξης αποτελεί επιτακτική ανάγκη.




2. Άμεση διασφάλιση των οφειλόμενων αποδοχών και έλεγχος ενδεχόμενης μεταβίβασης επιχειρήσεων




Ζητάμε να διερευνηθεί άμεσα κάθε περίπτωση μεταβίβασης ή συνέχισης της επιχειρηματικής δραστηριότητας με αλλαγή ΑΦΜ, εταιρικής επωνυμίας ή φορέα εκμετάλλευσης, εφόσον αυτή ενδέχεται να χρησιμοποιείται για την αποφυγή καταβολής οφειλών προς τους εργαζομένους. Η συνέχιση της ίδιας δραστηριότητας υπό διαφορετικό επιχειρηματικό σχήμα δεν πρέπει να οδηγεί στην απώλεια ή στην υπονόμευση των εργασιακών δικαιωμάτων. Στο πλαίσιο αυτό, ζητάμε την εφαρμογή των προβλεπόμενων διατάξεων του Π.Δ. 178/2002, καθώς και κάθε άλλου σχετικού μέτρου που απαιτείται.




3. Ειδικότερα, ζητούμε να παρέμβει άμεσα το Υπουργείο ώστε να διασφαλιστεί η εξόφληση όλων των οφειλόμενων δεδουλευμένων αποδοχών του τρέχοντος μήνα Οκτωβρίου, της αναλογίας του Δώρου Χριστουγέννων και του επιδόματος αδείας, καθώς και κάθε άλλης νόμιμης μισθολογικής υποχρέωσης που απορρέει από την εργασιακή σχέση. Παράλληλα, ζητάμε να εξεταστεί η ευθύνη κάθε εμπλεκόμενου, σύμφωνα με την ισχύουσα νομοθεσία, ώστε να μην καταλήξουν οι εργαζόμενοι απλήρωτοι και χωρίς ουσιαστική δυνατότητα διεκδίκησης των δικαιωμάτων τους.




Τέλος, ζητούμε τη διενέργεια ενδελεχών και άμεσων ελέγχων σε όλα τα καταστήματα της Pizza Fan, εταιρικά και franchise, για τις καταγγελλόμενες και δικαστικά διαπιστωμένες παραβάσεις που αφορούν την παράνομη υποδηλωμένη εργασία και την καταβολή μειωμένων αποδοχών σε σχέση με την πραγματική εργασία. Να αξιοποιηθούν οι σχετικές δικαστικές αποφάσεις, οι καταγγελίες και τα στοιχεία των Επιθεωρήσεων Εργασίας (ΣΕΠΕ), να καταλογιστούν οι προβλεπόμενες ευθύνες και να διασφαλιστεί η πλήρης αποκατάσταση και αναδρομική αποζημίωση των εργαζομένων για κάθε μισθολογική απώλεια.
