author: dev
title: Cinéastes de notre temps
content:
Le 17 octobre, on a vu refleurir des barricades sur les Champs-Elysées et des groupes d'insurgés portant le gilet fluo ont à nouveau envahi le pays. La France a été marqué par ce soulèvement légendaire et le mouvement en cours s'inspire de ces codes et de ces pratiques pour se renforcer. Les Gilets Jaunes, qui ont su faire trembler le pouvoir, hantent les consciences et les imaginaires de la jeunesse qui prend aujourd'hui la rue et la parole. Pour ce deuxième épisode de 

Cinéastes de notre temps

 nous passerons 

BoumBoum

 de Laurie Lassalle (2022).




Il est parfois difficile d'extraire ce qui mérite d'être vu parmi les milliers de productions cinématographiques dont nous sommes abreuvés. Les films sont jetables comme n'importe quelles autres marchandises. Le cinéma peut être une place forte contre le spectacle seulement si nous sommes en mesure de défendre une culture critique.







« Je voudrais que 

Cinéastes de notre temps

 soit une émission de laboratoire pour la création d'un nouveau langage ... Pour moi, cette émission poursuit un ensemble de réflexions sur le matériau filmique et sur la manière dont le sens peut ou non s'en emparer ».


(André S. Labarthe. 

Cinéma 69

, 140, novembre 1969.)







Régulièrement, nous proposerons sur 

lundimatin 

des films

 

gratuits et en streaming pendant une semaine,

 

accompagnés d'un entretien avec leurs cinéastes.







« L'idée était de mettre un réalisateur face à un autre réalisateur, qu'il soit mort ou vivant – même si on s'est vite aperçus que la rencontre avec les vivants présentait un plus vif intérêt. » (

Entretiens avec André S. Labarthe,

Thierry Lounas, 2011)







Notre époque est riche en soulèvements, en bouleversements, en évènements. Elle se caractérise par la mise en images et en sons, en cinéma, de ceux-ci. Nous irons à la rencontre des cinéastes qui ont été fidèles à un événement et qui ont fait du cinéma un lieu de son expression. Nous chercherons des films qui vont vers la rencontre et le dehors. Un cinéma dans lequel la vie se multiplie et qui invente de nouveaux désirs.




A rebours de la tyrannie de l'actualité et de la publicité, mais aussi contre toute nostalgie, nous essayerons de proposer ici une sélection de films « actuels » qui font l'épreuve du temps. C'est à dire que par leur puissance visionnaire, nous parions qu'ils ne s'useront pas.




Episode 2 : BoumBoum de Laurie Lassalle (2022) 




Pendant les Gilets Jaunes à Paris, Laurie et Pierrot tombent amoureux. Ils filment ensemble la révolte populaire et les personnes qui, comme eux, y sont engagés. « 

 

Nos corps se mêlent à des milliers d'autres qui expriment leur colère dans la rue tous les samedis, des mois durant. » Le film est fait de ce tissu-là : des inconnus fédérés autour d'un désir de l'autre, d'un désir des autres et autour d'un désir de changement, d'une ouverture des possibles. Le tout entremêlé et sous une pluie de grenades. Boum, Boum : comment vivre l'amour libre et comment faire la révolution ? Réinventer l'amour, changer le régime, surmonter les blessures aussi bien psychiques que physiques. Leur histoire va se construire au cœur d'un soulèvement, leur entente en suivre l'intensité et les remous. 

BoumBoum

 c'est l'histoire d'un amour et d'une insurrection.




Episode 1 : L'Époque, toujours en ligne 

A venir lundi prochain :




Entretien croisé - Matthieu Bareyre & Laurie Lassalle




Pour toutes propositions, écrire à 

dimanchepm@riseup.net

title: « Cher·es collègues, il va falloir cesser d'être respectables... »
content:
En attendant le « reprise des cours », des professeurs du secondaire ont réuni ces quelques réflexions quant à l'ambiguïté à laquelle les accule leur "statut" et au chantage exercé par l'institution qui les retourne 

de facto

 contre le mouvement.







« L'agent public doit se conformer aux instructions de son supérieur hiérarchique, sauf dans le cas où l'ordre donné est manifestement illégal et de nature à compromettre gravement un intérêt public. »




Code général de la fonction publique (article L121-10)







1. 

Non, ce n'est pas « leur » mouvement : le mouvement des lycéens, en ce qu'il concorde précisément avec nos revendications, est aussi le nôtre. Il faut donc s'en sentir partie intégrante et se demander : que nous faut-il faire pour contribuer à faire triompher notre mouvement ?




2.

 D'abord, reconnaitre une chose : les lycéen

·

nes ont réussi là où les professeur

·

es ont échoué. Notre profession, corporatiste et « bonne élève » est si soucieuse d'être constructive et respectable qu'il y a bien longtemps qu'elle n'est plus prise au sérieux. Après des années de mobilisations de personnels de l'éducation, qui se sont révélées pour la plupart perdantes, car elles cherchaient à rester crédibles aux yeux du gouvernement, le mouvement lycéen nous met face à nous-mêmes : allons-nous, cette fois encore, rester respectables ?




3. 

Rester « respectables », c'est persister à « remplir notre mission » comme si de rien n'était. Ne surtout pas déroger à nos « obligations légales » : la place d'un

·

e professeur

·

e est dans sa salle de classe, n'est-ce pas ? et puisque certain

·

es élèves veulent faire cours, quel

·

le professeur

·

e serais-je si je ne les prenais pas ? C'est se persuader que sa place n'est pas dehors, avec les élèves qui bloquent, mais bien dedans, derrière la vitre, derrière la grille – il ne s'agirait pas de cautionner, par notre présence, des tirs de mortier ou des poubelles brûlées. C'est recommencer à placer des évaluations dès que l'occasion se présente parce qu'il faut bien les évaluer, les élèves…




4.

 Si nous sommes autant à être tenté

·

es par la respectabilité, c'est que, au-delà de la position de supériorité morale qu'elle semble nous conférer, le chantage de l'institution est fort. Cette période révèle en effet avec cruauté ce que cette dernière attend réellement de nous, ce pour quoi nous sommes réellement payé

·

es : mettre des notes. Au-delà de nos envies si légitimes de retrouver nos élèves, de faire cours, de leur transmettre nos savoirs, telle est, in fine, notre crainte : ne pas pouvoir les évaluer. Même si nous savons qu'y procéder sans faire cours, sans passer du temps avec elleux, sans les préparer n'a pas de sens, nous persistons à vouloir le faire ; car l'absence de sens nous semble encore moins pire que le sentiment de les abandonner. Pris

·

es en tenaille par ces injonctions absurdes et culpabilisantes, dès lors que nous glissons dans un soutien marqué au mouvement, nous voilà réduit

·

es par les discours des proviseur

·

es, des médias des milliardaires, de certains parents et du gouvernement à la position intenable d'être des traîtres à la mission de l'école. Professeur

·

es soutenant les blocus, nous serions des opportunistes ou bien des fainéant

·

es, des gauchistes cherchant à « manipuler les élèves ». Tous les jours où nous déciderons de débrayer, de nous mettre en grève, de soutenir les élèves face à la police, quelque bon serviteur zélé de l'institution sera là pour nous rappeler quelle est notre place, sans se gêner de nous rendre moralement responsables des « débordements ».




5.

 Reconnaissons-le : l'institution, par le biais de ses directions d'établissement, exploite notre attachement à notre travail pour faire de nous, malgré nous, derrière la police, des agent

·

es de la casse du mouvement.




6.

 Mais la vérité, c'est que, si nous soulageons temporairement notre conscience professorale en programmant des évaluations ou en donnant du travail aux élèves pour « rattraper le temps perdu », ce même geste ne viendra jamais soulager notre conscience d'avoir vu nos élèves se faire gazer, matraquer, se faire mettre en joue, courser, charger, renverser, mutiler, interpeler, enfermer, insulter, brutaliser par la police de l'État. Il ne viendra pas effacer dans nos mémoires l'image des visages de nos élèves, de 14 ans, 15 ans, 16 ans, en pleurs, en rage, décontenancés, choqués, tout rouges et boursouflés du gaz, les bleus, les doigts, pieds, mains en sang, vides de pancartes confisquées sous l'œil bien affairé d'une direction complice. Il ne viendra pas annuler comme par magie les lignes rouges qui ont été franchies par un gouvernement qui ne reconnaît pas le traitement barbare qu'il réserve à ceux et celles qu'il prétend protéger contre toutes les violences : les enfants. La vérité, c'est que, dans ce moment si crucial, le sens que nous cherchons doit se construire ailleurs qu'en acceptant de courber l'échine face à une institution qui nous maltraite sans distinction.




7.

 Demandons-nous : est-il vraiment désirable de reprendre les cours quand aucune revendication du mouvement n'a véritablement été entendue ? (inutile ici de dénoncer la mascarade des 3000 professeur

·

es remplaçant

·

es) Souhaitons-nous vraiment reprendre nos élèves dans nos classes toujours surchargées, dans des salles gagnées par le froid, avec le même manque de personnels d'encadrement, professoral ou médico-social ? Quand ce gouvernement offre pour réponse au mouvement un énième simulacre de « dialogue social » (après le « grand débat », les cahiers de doléances des Gilets jaunes, la convention citoyenne pour le climat, encore 100 000 réponses à un formulaire qui vont rester au placard ?) auquel il fera mine de longuement méditer pour finir par répondre qu'il ne peut pas débloquer d'argent supplémentaire ? Quand ce même gouvernement, qui n'a plus aucune légitimité ni respectabilité, plonge, par le réflexe fasciste de préservation d'une bourgeoisie en crise, dans un autoritarisme assumé ? Avons-nous oublié qu'avant de voir les élèves réclamer eux-mêmes le minimum de décence pour leur éducation, nous avons passé des années à en faire autant ? Notre colère n'est-elle que de façade ? Au nom de quoi devrions-nous nous montrer respectables aux yeux de l'institution et faire notre travail quand cette dernière et le gouvernement ont à ce point failli ?




8.

 Envisageons alors ceci : devenir ingouvernables auprès de notre propre institution pour redevenir véritablement respectables aux yeux de nos élèves, celles et ceux pour qui nous enseignons, à qui nous faisons cours chaque jour et à qui nous tentons de transmettre des savoirs susceptibles de les émanciper d'une société qui cherche à éteindre leur voix.




9.

 Dès lors :


Refusons massivement de prendre nos élèves à la rentrée, en nous mettant en grève reconductible jusqu'au 5 novembre et au-delà ; acceptons mentalement de perdre des journées entières de cours, des semaines s'il le faut.


Accentuons la pression médiatique : faisons venir des médias devant nos établissements mobilisés, en lien avec les parents d'élèves ;


Érigeons-nous contre les discours et manœuvres coercitives ou culpabilisantes des directions, dont le but sera de chercher à tout prix un « retour au calme ».


Car là est le rapport de force.




Construisons et abondons dès maintenant des caisses de grève locales, qui peuvent être alimentées par des syndicats.


Car là est la sécurité du mouvement.




Protégeons et défendons nos élèves face la répression policière, judiciaire et administrative pour leur permettre de continuer à se mobiliser : faisons barrage avec nos corps, notre présence, fournissons-leur des masques, du sérum physiologique, transmettons-leur tous les conseils pour survivre en garde à vue, assurons-leur la présence d'un

·

e avocat

·

e par l'intermédiaire de legal team ou de collectifs d'avocat

·

es mobilisé

·

es, faisons le suivi des élèves interpelés, dénonçons les conseils de discipline qui toucheraient les élèves bloqueur-ses, récoltons des témoignages vidéos et écrits de nos élèves pour dénoncer avec les parents les violences policières ayant eu lieu aux abords de nos établissements en noyant le rectorat de rapports et en saisissant le défenseur des droits et le procureur de la République.


Car là est la solidarité.




10.

 Si l'école est assimilable à une usine, alors un blocus est un piquet de grève. Les élèves, les grévistes, la direction, le patron. Le patron voudra toujours rouvrir son usine au plus vite. Pour cela, il a deux options : 


1-fermer l'usine, c'est-à-dire fermer l'école (ce qu'il rechignera toujours à faire) ; 


2-mater la grève, c'est-à-dire briser le blocus (en faisant disperser les élèves par la police, quel qu'en soit le coût). Et nous, cher

·

es collègues, que ferons-nous ?




Des professeur-es en colère

author: Geoff Dembicki
title: As Midterms Loom, MAGA Lawyer Defends ‘Mild Amounts of Corruption’ in Governments
content:
Countries should be willing to overlook “mild amounts of corruption” in government if it serves the larger goal of political stability, according to a U.S. lawyer and political activist closely aligned with U.S. President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement.




“This may be the most provocative thing I say,” explained Will Chamberlain 

during a speech earlier this month

 at the National Conservatism Conference (NatCon) in Jerusalem, an event that 

brought together

 far-right figures from Europe and Israel along with MAGA leaders closely linked to the Trump administration.




Chamberlain is vice president for external affairs at the 

Edmund Burke Foundation

, which organizes NatCon, a conference that in previous years has been hosted in cities across the U.S. and Europe.




He is also senior counsel with the Article III Project, a MAGA group set up to fight against “lawfare,” which 

it describes as

 efforts by “Marxist” Democrats to weaponize the justice system against Trump and his political allies. The group has recently targeted what it calls “climate lawfare,” which refers to lawsuits that aim to hold oil and gas companies accountable for misleading the public about climate change




“Corruption is bad,” Chamberlain said during his Oct. 8 speech at NatCon. “But I think in general, countries should be willing to tolerate mild amounts of corruption in order to avoid lawfare.”




Chamberlain, through the Article III Project, works with the conservative political strategist and lawyer Mike Davis, who 

claims credit

 for helping win the nomination fights of conservative U.S. Supreme Court justices Neil Gorsuch and Brett Kavanaugh. Chamberlain’s comments come as the U.S. approaches midterm elections on Nov. 3 

where voters

 have identified government corruption as a defining issue.




He argued that efforts to impeach and prosecute politicians for corruption have driven up the stakes of elections to the point where candidates either win or risk going to jail, citing the example of Jair Bolsonaro, the former Brazilian president 

serving a jail sentence

 for planning a coup following his 2022 election loss.




He also cited Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is on trial for corruption charges including fraud and accepting bribes. Earlier this year, Trump said Netanyahu 

should be pardoned

. Chamberlain defended that position, arguing that pardons are a useful tool for reducing political tensions.




“People shouldn’t be afraid of them,” he said. “I think too many people are so obsessed with the idea that no one can ever be above the law that they’ll let their country tear itself apart.”




He added, “There’s another old maxim, ‘let justice be done though the heavens fall.’ I think that’s a bad impulse.”




Chamberlain didn’t respond to questions from DeSmog.




‘Climate Lawfare’




This year’s National Conservatism Conference in Israel featured speeches from senior White House official Sebastian Gorka, as well as Kevin Roberts, head of the 

Heritage Foundation

, which authored the Trump policy blueprint Project 2025.  




It took place as Chamberlain’s legal group, the Article III Project, turned its attention to the dozens of lawsuits filed by cities, counties and states across the U.S. against Big Oil.




In early October it 

co-hosted a Washington, D

.

C

.

, event

 where conservative legal experts argued that efforts to hold oil and gas companies legally liable for misleading the public about climate change is a form of “climate lawfare,” which one participant defined as “trying to basically drag these fossil fuel companies into court to get access to their documents and, of course, their pockets.”




The occasion for the event was the U.S. Supreme Court agreeing to hear oral arguments 

from the oil companies Suncor and Exxon

, which are trying to get the court to invalidate a lawsuit against them currently proceeding in Colorado state court.




That Colorado lawsuit alleges, based on extensive historical documentation, that these and other oil companies engaged in multi-decade campaigns to stave off climate regulation by running disinformation campaigns around their key role in global temperature rise.




Democratic Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse has framed this history of climate denial 

as large-scale deception

 meriting federal investigations and lawsuits. In 2024, Whitehouse 

described

 the Trump administration’s reported offering of political favors to the oil industry in exchange for $1 billion in campaign contributions as “the definition of corruption as the founding fathers would have used the term.”




From the perspective of MAGA legal activists such as Chamberlain, “lawfare is worse than corruption.”




“I mean, corruption’s bad. I kind of imagine it is like a slow-growing cancer that can undermine ultimately and eventually really hurt your country,” he said.




“But lawfare — and reciprocal, brutal lawfare against heads of state, especially — is kind of like having a gushing, gaping bullet wound in your chest,” he added.




‘Openly Corrupt’




That position appears out of step with many U.S. voters. A recent 

Fox News poll suggested that

 88 percent of voters are “extremely/very concerned” about “corruption in government,” making it the top issue ahead of cost of living, healthcare, and the Iran war.




That poll came out following 

reporting in the Wall Street Journal

 that Kimberly Guilfoyle, then U.S. ambassador to Greece, had asked a Trump donor for $100,000 to pay off her credit card bill in exchange for favorable access to the administration.




That seemed to cross a line even for Chamberlain and his colleagues.




After Guilfoyle resigned on Oct. 13, Chamberlain 

questioned on X

 whether her resignation message was written by AI, while another senior counsel at the Article III Project 

described her

 as “an absolutely stupid pick for U.S. Ambassador to Greece in the first place.”




Yet, Chamberlain argued at NatCon that civil and criminal efforts in recent years to hold Trump legally accountable for alleged financial fraud, defamation, his role in the Jan. 6 U.S. Capitol insurrection, and other legal violations have been “an enormous strain on the president’s time and resources, as well as everybody else.”




Chamberlain claimed that without unique features of the U.S. legal system, including the lack of an attorney general independent from the White House, “I think Trump would be in jail,” adding that “the Western world would be worse for it.”




Meanwhile Trump has reaped $2.2 billion in 2025 revenues alone from his cryptocurrency holdings and other personal business interests. This has led former general counsel at the Federal Election Commission Larry Noble 

to describe

 Trump’s second term as potentially “the most openly corrupt administration in our history.”







The post 

As Midterms Loom, MAGA Lawyer Defends ‘Mild Amounts of Corruption’ in Governments

 appeared first on 

DeSmog

author: Daron Letts
title: Horror writer Jamesie Fournier shares scares in print and on screen
content:
Horror author Jamesie Fournier says he enjoys scaring children almost as much as they enjoy being scared.




“It’s very entertaining to be terrified,” he said Saturday in an interview in his Inhabit Media office in Iqaluit. “That’s why we love horror.”




The Inuktitut and English writer had just launched his latest children’s book,

 Lemming’s First Halloween

, earlier that day at Nunatta Sunakkutaangit Museum.




Dozens of costumed children and their families dropped by the event to create creepy crafts and hear spooky stories.




The book is Fournier’s second in the series. He published 

Lemming’s First Christmas

 in English and Inuktitut in 2024. 

Lemming’s First Halloween 

marks Fournier’s first collaboration with Toronto-based Pakistani-Canadian illustrator Faiza Khan.




The tale follows Lemming and her pup as they cross paths with a qallupilluk, a monster known to drag children into the ocean.




Overcoming fear is an important life skill that Inuit horror stories tap into, Fournier said.
















“When you’re afraid you’re aware of your surroundings. You’re taking everything in. You’re being very cautious. Survivalism has kicked in,” he said. “To be brave we have to first know what scares us.”




Scary fiction help children remember life lessons that can help keep them safe, such as to stay away from sea ice when a trusted adult is not near.




“Once we’re afraid and we’re informed of how we can be safe, we are able to problem-solve,” Fournier said. “That skill translates to every facet of life.”




Children enjoy repeating memorable nightmarish narratives as well, Fournier has noticed.




“Whenever I read to children, they all want to tell me their stories, too,” he said.




Fournier added he can relate to that urge, as he was the same way as a child in Yellowknife.
















He would devour 

Batman

 comics and 

Tales From the Crypt 

magazines over breakfast with his dad. He also listened with keen attention at bedtime when his mom shared monstrous Inuit legends.




Throughout his career, Fournier has revisited those childhood frights in print and on the screen.




His work 

appeared

 in 

Taaqtumi 2:

 An Anthology of Arctic Horror Stories

, released by Inhabit Media in 2025.




This year, his award-winning 2022 

novel

 

The Other Ones

 was made into a 19-minute short film by Inhabit Media’s sister company, Taqqut Productions, in collaboration with Toronto-based Stop Motion Department.




That story follows a mother and daughter as they’re pursued by the wrath of an ancient terror, eerily animated by stop-motion and claymation puppets.
















An ancient terror stalks a mother and daughter in 

The Other Ones

, a new stop-motion short film written and co-directed by Jamesie Fournier. (Image courtesy of Taqqut Productions)




Fournier co-directed the film with Taqqut producer Danny Christopher.




It’s making the rounds of the Canadian film festival circuit this fall and winter after premièring at the Ottawa International Animation Festival last month.




The Other Ones

 is scheduled to screen at Iqaluit’s Astro Theatre at 7:30 p.m. Tuesday as part of Inhabit Media’s 

Alianaqtut: A Night of Inuit Horror

 film series, alongside five other Inuktitut films released by Taqqut.




Tickets are free on a first-come basis, and all ages are welcome.




— With files from Lilli Akpaleeapik

author: David Swanson
title: Madison for a World BEYOND War Takes Part in National Peace Walk
content:
Chapters, Madison Chapter, Nonviolent Activism, North America

By Madison for a World BEYOND War, October 26, 2026

Madison for a World BEYOND War welcomed the National Peace Walk to the Madison area.

World BEYOND War calls for war abolition: ending all wars. Governments should never engage in the organized mass murder that is war. Conflicts arise among humans and among countries. Negotiation and compromise are the solutions, not killing.

Supermajorities of Americans want Congress to end the Iran war, cut the Pentagon budget, and end forever wars. A new Fox News poll shows 75% of respondents were either “extremely” (42%) or “very” (33%) concerned about the war in Iran, and six in ten voters oppose U.S. military action against Iran. A poll from Rethink/ Brown Costs of War Project found that 59% of Americans believe the Pentagon budget is too high, with 40% saying it’s “much too high.” More details here.

This is a time of unprecedented opportunity to stop the Iran war and more generally US funding for wars. This year, Congress has successfully blocked the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). This is historic. For 64 consecutive years, Congress has approved the NDAA, but this summer it was halted. Congress is using the power of the purse to stop war and preparations for war. Also this year, both houses have introduced war powers legislation to stop the war on Iran.

Madison for a World BEYOND War calls on our government to stop the war on Iran; stop arming Ukraine, Israel and other countries; and close the more than 800 US military bases around the world.

The enemy is not the other side. The enemy is war.

author: CMI Argentina
title: “Defender el agua es defender la vida”
content:
Del 21 al 23 de noviembre se realizará en Traslasierra, Córdoba, la 7.ª Cumbre Plurinacional en Defensa del Agua para los Pueblos de Abya Yala, un encuentro que reunirá a asambleas, pueblos originarios y organizaciones de distintos territorios para compartir experiencias y fortalecer las luchas en defensa del agua y los bienes comunes.







Por Adrián Flores para Red Eco




En esta entrevista con Red Eco, Juan Manuel Izzo reconocido activista ambiental de la provincia y uno de los organizadores de la cumbre en Córdoba, analiza los conflictos socioambientales, cuestiona el avance del modelo extractivo y destaca la importancia de la organización colectiva. También convoca a quienes todavía no se han involucrado a acercarse y participar en la defensa de la vida y los territorios.







¿Por qué se eligió Córdoba y, particularmente, Traslasierra para realizar esta nueva cumbre?







La elección del territorio para la siguiente cumbre se realiza al cierre del encuentro anterior, entre quienes participan.




Córdoba forma parte de un territorio avasallado por el modelo extractivo. Aquí confluyen diversas problemáticas: el agronegocio y su contaminación, los desmontes y el desarraigo de las comunidades, el riesgo de que una minería presentada como de bajo impacto se transforme en una actividad de alto impacto cuando la demanda es excesiva, y un territorio castigado por grandes incendios, con los negociados que se esconden detrás.




También hay industrias que ponen en riesgo a la población de la propia capital, como el caso de Porta. A esto se suma la producción destinada a satisfacer la demanda de alimentos para ganado de mercados muy lejanos. Es el caso de Fondo Monte, que propicia una demanda de agua subterránea fuera de control y pone en riesgo los acuíferos.




Tenemos un gobierno que promociona la ecología en la publicidad, pero cuya práctica contradice ese discurso. Córdoba también forma parte del plan IIRSA y hay ciudadanos procesados judicialmente por defender la vida.




Estas y otras problemáticas son parte de los conflictos que se analizan y trabajan desde hace años en las cumbres. Por estos motivos se eligió Córdoba y, puntualmente, Traslasierra: porque estaban dadas las condiciones.







¿Cuáles son las principales problemáticas que tenemos con el agua en Córdoba y en el país? ¿Qué papel juegan los intereses económicos y los gobiernos?







El agua es un elemento fundamental, no solo para la vida, sino también para desarrollar cualquier actividad económica. Por eso está en disputa.




Córdoba está sofocada de conflictos. El negocio inmobiliario, por sí solo, está desbaratando ecosistemas y contaminando cauces y espejos de agua. El país atraviesa una realidad similar, aunque cada territorio tiene sus propios conflictos: minería, agronegocio, hidrocarburos, explotación offshore, litio y otras actividades que multiplican las zonas de sacrificio.




Desde la geopolítica internacional se nos asigna el papel de proveedores de materias primas, es decir, de bienes naturales. Toda la región de Abya Yala carga con ese estigma.




En cuanto a los gobiernos, considero que todos han sido funcionales a este modelo. Se pueden advertir diferencias en la contención social, el acceso al consumo y algunos esbozos de soberanía, pero estamos muy lejos de encontrar soluciones reales.




Frente a esta realidad, los pueblos se organizan y buscan soluciones de forma horizontal y participativa. La cumbre es un ejemplo de ello.







¿Por qué defender el agua es también defender nuestros territorios y los bienes comunes?







La lucha por la protección del agua es, simplemente, la defensa de la vida, de todas las vidas. Pensar el ambiente como algo lejano es un acto de ignorancia terrible. Siempre intentamos plantear que los conflictos no son solamente ambientales, sino socioambientales, porque tienen que ver con las acciones y omisiones de una sociedad.




El agua, además de ser dadora de vida, es necesaria para llevar adelante cualquier actividad productiva. Por eso, la propia demanda genera conflictos. Y si agregamos que el agua es un medio natural de transporte de sustancias, nos encontramos con que gran parte de nuestros espejos de agua están contaminados.




El cuidado del agua debería ser una de las prioridades de la agenda de las políticas públicas.







¿Qué importancia tiene encontrarse con otras asambleas, pueblos originarios y organizaciones para compartir experiencias y fortalecer las luchas?







Más que importante, es fundamental. Cuando en un mismo ámbito confluyen la diversidad étnica, teológica, cultural y geográfica con un propósito definido, como la protección del agua, se abre una posibilidad enorme.




Personalmente, estoy convencido de que la humanidad tiene esperanza. Entender la diversidad como una riqueza y no como un obstáculo es una instancia de maduración social.




En un territorio tan grande y diverso como Abya Yala, el desafío es dejar de lado las diferencias para construir colectivamente.







¿Qué se proponen con esta cumbre y qué esperan que surja de esos tres días de encuentro?







Los objetivos de la cumbre son diversos. En primer lugar, analizar la situación actual de las luchas que se llevan adelante en distintos territorios. También compartir experiencias, escuchar y aprender de ese abanico de vidas que se encuentran, se respetan y se reconocen.




Buscamos pensar estrategias para enfrentar una lucha tan desigual y generar contenidos que ayuden a despertar a un sector importante de la sociedad que todavía no comprende todo lo que está en riesgo en nuestra forma de habitar y relacionarnos con la Madre Naturaleza.




Y, en medio de esa tensión, encontrar espacios tan necesarios para compartir la alegría de estar vivos, activos y con un proyecto de futuro posible.







¿Qué les dirías a quienes todavía no están involucrados en estas luchas para que se acerquen y participen?







Ojalá estas palabras sean útiles. Volvamos a mirarnos a los ojos, dejemos de lado el individualismo y aprendamos a ser felices viendo al otro ser feliz. Es un trabajo interno necesario para dejar florecer las virtudes propias de nuestro ser. Una tarea difícil, pero no imposible.




A partir de ahí, el desafío es comunicarnos con los demás, intercambiar experiencias y abrirnos a los saberes ajenos. Que sean ajenos no significa que no puedan convertirse en propios: simplemente, se trata de aprender.




Actualmente delegamos nuestro bienestar en una democracia representativa que está socavando nuestra calidad de vida. Ante esta realidad, hay que tomar una decisión: dejar que otros decidan por nosotros y aceptar los abusos, o rebelarnos ante los responsables, organizarnos y aprender a construir una democracia participativa que tenga como objetivo crear una sociedad más equitativa.




De alguna manera, la cumbre transita ese camino.




Reflexión final: “Yo ya tomé mi decisión. ¿Vos qué vas a hacer?”


La situación socioambiental actual se encamina hacia el pináculo del modelo extractivo: un modelo ajeno, impuesto, que desde hace 530 años somete al continente.




Hoy, con este gobierno a la cabeza, se están destruyendo los cimientos de la soberanía argentina. Y lo peor de todo es que está teniendo éxito. Frente a esta situación, la rebeldía es un acto de coherencia.




También debemos reconocer a los sectores políticos que, desde distintos espacios, actúan como cómplices de esta entrega. Vivimos una realidad inadmisible y, por eso, es indispensable pasar de la preocupación a la acción.




No se trata solamente de Argentina: está en riesgo el continente, está en riesgo la humanidad.




Yo ya tomé mi decisión. ¿Vos qué vas a hacer?




La invitación de Juan Manuel Izzo es a no permanecer indiferentes: acercarse a las organizaciones, compartir experiencias, aprender de otros saberes y sumarse a la construcción colectiva de una sociedad que defienda el agua, los territorios y la vida.




Las inscripciones para la 7° Cumbre Plurinacional en Defensa del Agua para los pueblos del Abya-Yala están abiertas:




Nos encontramos para alzar la voz por nuestros territorios y proteger el ciclo vital de la vida.




Sumate llenando el formulario:




Enlace: 

https://forms.gle/9tof8EaQKCCUmarcA




Fecha: 21 al 23 de noviembre 2026


Lugar: Camping de Luyaba, Traslasierra, Córdoba. Argentina







Fuente: 

https://redeco.com.ar/nacional/ambiente/78062-defender-el-agua-es-defender-la-vida




La entrada 

“Defender el agua es defender la vida”

 se publicó primero en 

Indymedia Argentina Centro de Medios Independientes (( i ))

.

author: Monthly Review Press
title: Recently reissued: The Rainbow Challenge (Excerpt)
content:
From the Preface to the new edition of 

The Rainbow Challenge

:




“Jesse Jackson’s first presidential primary race in 1984 should have been a wakeup call for the Democratic Party. Without a large campaign chest, money for advertising, or seasoned political consultants he amassed 3.5 million votes (winning nearly the entire popular vote in the Deep South states of Mississippi and South Carolina, registering 2 million new voters, and winning 21 percent of the total votes cast). The press, the pundits, the pollsters, and the Democratic Party elites could not believe that the American people would vote for a Black man, let alone a man with such a progressive message, so they characterized him at first as a charlatan, then as a spoiler, and finally as a candidate who spoke only for African Americans. They had accepted the idea that Ronald Reagan’s election in 1980 meant that the New Deal reforms were over, that the growing polarization of the electorate could not be overcome, and that the Great Society had been defeated. Their marginalization of Jackson’s message of economic and social justice and international peace through cooperation, and their failure to imagine that anything else could be different, ceded the playing field to the Republican right. Walter Mondale’s tepid, neoliberal message could not compete with Reagan’s sunny, simplistic optimism; Reagan won by a landslide.

[i]




When Jackson ran again in 1988, laying out a coherent, progressive, populist agenda he was hailed for his soaring rhetoric, but his message was still dismissed as being too “radical” for him to win. It was a social democratic message with a moral underpinning and was consonant with most of the values and issues that public opinion polling showed Americans supported. Jackson drew the largest crowds of any of the candidates, but after he won the Michigan caucuses in March 1988, with the largest number of committed delegates, the media coverage turned toward alarm. Despite having apologized numerous times for having used the term “Hymietown” to characterize New York City in a private, overheard conversation during the 1984 election, that term was trotted out again to undermine his appeal to Jewish Americans. And although he was drawing white voters against all expectations, it is likely that the fear of the residual racism of the white population played a role in the belief held by Democratic elites that he was unelectable. This led to a “stop-Jackson” narrative in many mainstream editorial circles.




Thanks to Jackson’s race in 1984, Democrats had won back both the House and the Senate in the 1986 midterms and thus could have capitalized on their majorities by putting forward a progressive charismatic candidate like Jackson. Instead, after a crowded and messy primary fight, Massachusetts governor Michael Dukakis, a moderate, centrist technocrat, emerged as the Democratic Party’s choice. Dukakis’s lack of passion did not inspire the Democratic base, and it is likely that Jackson’s dismissal by the party convinced many African Americans to stay home. In at least twelve states the number of unregistered and non-voting African Americans exceeded the number of votes by which Dukakis lost.

[ii]

 Moreover, Dukakis was never able to overcome Republican accusations that he was weak on crime after a convicted murderer, Willie Horton, absconded from a weekend furlough program in Massachusetts and went on to commit kidnapping, rape and attempted murder in Maryland. On election day only half of those eligible to vote turned out. George H.W. Bush won with the votes of only 26 percent of all Americans of voting age.

[iii]




If Jesse Jackson was dismissed in 1984 and 1988, in death he finally received his due appreciation.  At the announcement of his passing on February 17, 2026, a blizzard of articles written with a whiff of nostalgia for lost opportunity appeared in the major media and all over the Internet, lauding his moral and political vision. The 

New York Times

 hailed his gospel of “seeking common ground, his pleas to ‘keep hope alive’ and his demands for respect for those seldom accorded it . . .”  Mr. Jackson, they said, enunciated in his 1984 and 1988 speeches at the Democratic conventions “a progressive vision that defined the soul of the Democratic Party, if not necessarily its political policies in the last decades of the 20

th

 century.”

[iv]

 “Quite simply,” Michael Eric Dyson wrote, “Jesse Jackson led one of the most consequential American lives. He was a genuine populist who stood in stark contrast to the ersatz populists of today.”

[v]

 Historians Clayborne Carson and Jon Meacham called Jackson the most significant political figure between Martin Luther King and Barack Obama. Said Carson, “Jesse Jackson played as central a role in his era as King did in his era. But it was not the kind of heroic struggle as in the 1960s. You’re not going to get a Nobel Prize for what Jesse Jackson did, but it took a lot of talent, initiative, energy, imagination and charisma, and he had those in full supply.”

[vi]

  Jackson’s campaigns, said another 

New York Times

 journalist, “created a path for scores of Black democrats to run for office while demonstrating for the first time that white Americans would vote for a Black presidential candidate.”

[vii]

 Without him Barack Obama could never have won.  

Read more










What accounts for this revisionist version of history? Perhaps the realization of what this failure to take Jackson seriously has finally dawned on at least a segment of the center left establishment. Perhaps Donald Trump’s blatantly racist, misogynistic, and antisemitic language and policies, perhaps the wrecking ball he has taken to all the institutions of democracy has finally led them to see the light. Perhaps the rise of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, affectionately known as AOC, and the stunning electoral victory of democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani to the mayoralty of New York City, or the courageous resistance of the people of Minneapolis to the fascist thuggery of ICE and Border Patrol agents has given these elites a picture of how far removed they have been from their core constituencies.  




It is far past time to reassess what we lost when the Democratic Party and even some of the left marginalized Jesse Jackson’s candidacies. In 1988, he increased his share to nearly 7 million votes, beating out future Vice President 

Al Gore

, future President 

Joe Biden

, and 

Dick Gephardt

, coming in second against Michael Dukakis, and forcing a change in the delegate selection process to enable more minorities to run and win. The failure to recognize what the two Jackson campaigns could have done for the country has led to the increasing polarization of the electorate, the neoliberal capture of the Democratic Party under Bill Clinton, and eventually to the election of Donald Trump. Even Barack Obama could not escape the racist backlash this rejection of the Rainbow Coalition portended nor the neoliberal pull of economic elites.




While many, in retrospect, have lauded Jackson’s charisma and his populist message, this book should be re-read for the specific lessons it can teach us about the nuts and bolts of running a progressive populist campaign. It contains positive lessons and points to some of the errors that were made. To be sure, we live in very different times. We are faced not with an encrusted political establishment that at least still played by rules established by the Constitution, but with a neo-fascist movement that has captured the presidency, the Republican Party, and the Supreme Court. Moreover, we face a media landscape dramatically altered by social media controlled by tech billionaires in which conspiracy theories run rampant; and we now have Artificial Intelligence beginning to zap our brains and eliminate our jobs, not to mention its potential for mass surveillance and for starting wars without the consent of humans. And Christian Nationalism, with its frightful messianic ideology, appears to have become the new public religion.




All of these new dangers will have to be addressed if we are to survive as a civilization. 




Thus, the stakes today are monumental and the time frame for action is both short and long term—short term because we have only a few months, in the face of Republican states imposing voter identification laws, making registration more difficult, aggressively purging voter rolls, and gerrymandering districts to mount a political campaign that can put a brake on the Trump administration’s worst impulses. The next two national elections are critical. The time frame is also long term because it will take decades of careful organizing to build the structures of a revised political system and economy that can work for all.




Some have lamented the lack of a visible charismatic leader like Dr. King or Reverend Jackson to mount a counteroffensive to the Trump administration. “The Black church isn’t as important as it was. It’s harder to have a figure come out of that tradition and command the power and respect that Jesse Jackson did,” Claflin University historian Robert Greene II said. “It’s hard to imagine someone today being able to enter the political realm already seen as a moral authority.” Institutional religion just doesn’t have the authority or power it once did in the in the United States, experts have said.

[ix]

  




But that may be changing. The moral clarity in the Minneapolis resistance movement was largely fueled by churches. Reverend William Barber’s Moral Monday and Repairers of the Breach movements have taken the ethical teachings of Jesus into the public square with multiracial marches, rallies and sermons. In his reverential post-mortem Substack on Jesse Jackson’s legacy, Reverend Barber vowed to carry on building the Rainbow Coalition for the new age. Jewish Voice for Peace seeks to apply the ethical teachings of the Prophets to matters of war, peace and social justice. In February 2026, 700 people of various faiths carrying signs that said, “Respect our Humanity” and “ICE Out “marched and sang as they surrounded the Federal building in lower Manhattan where immigrants are processed; and in that same month, over 2,000 United Methodists gathered in the nation’s capitol to witness on behalf of undocumented immigrants and make visits to their congressional representatives.  




Precisely because we are living in such fraught times, we may now have the constituency that is needed for this work. When he ran for president in 1984, Jackson had to build the Rainbow Coalition from the many identity movements that existed in those days (for example, the civil rights and Black nationalist movements, the Arab-American Anti-Discrimination Committee, the Latino movement, the Native American movement, the peace movement, the environmental movement, rank and file labor, the low-income tenants’ movement, the women’s movement, the LGBTQ movement, the disabled movement, and so on). In the intervening years, the right-wing assault on identity movements has left many of them weaker than they were in the 1980s. But Trump’s attacks on just about everything we hold dear, the blatant cruelty and immorality of his administration, have inadvertently created what amounts to a new Rainbow Coalition. When, in 1984, Jackson spoke for “the desperate, the damned, the disinherited, the disrespected, and the despised,”

[x]

 we knew whom he meant. It was the largely brown and Black underclass. In 1988, he had a related but somewhat different message.




“

We meet tonight at the crossroads, a point of decision. Shall we expand, be inclusive, find unity and power; or suffer division and impotence? . . . Tonight, there is a sense of celebration, because we are moved, fundamentally moved from racial battlegrounds by law, to economic common ground. Tomorrow we will challenge to move to higher ground. . . . Common ground! Think of Jerusalem, the intersection where many trails met. A small village that became the birthplace for three religions—Judaism, Christianity and Islam. Why was this village so blessed? Because it provided a crossroads where different people met, different cultures, different civilizations could meet and find common ground. When people come together, flowers always flourish – the air is rich with the aroma of a new spring. Take New York, the dynamic metropolis. What makes New York so special? It’s the invitation of the Statue of Liberty,” Give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses who yearn to breathe free.” Not restricted to English only. Many people, many cultures, many languages—with one thing in common, they yearn to breathe free. Common ground!

“




Tragically, that call for common ground was not heeded. The country became even more polarized and the calls for social and economic justice went unanswered. But today the great majority of us are the “desperate, the damned, the disinherited, the disrespected, the despised and the locked-out.” Think of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, executed by ICE; but think also of the Black and brown people who have routinely been killed by police. Think of the people who have lived and worked here for years, started families, and paid their taxes being dragged out of their cars and homes and sent to American style concentration camps awaiting deportation to countries from whose violence many of them had fled. Think of the single mothers who must decide whether to pay the rent or put food on their tables, or the young couples starting out in life who cannot afford to buy their own home. Think of the displaced industrial workers whose desperation leads them to fentanyl addiction or the professional federal government workers who have lost their jobs. Think of the young people just graduating from college whose once secure job prospects are being taken over by Artificial Intelligence, or the low-income families without Medicaid and the middle-class families who will be bankrupted by soaring health care costs. Think of the home care workers who are losing their livelihoods and their elderly and disabled patients who will lose their care. Think of the gay, lesbian, and trans community whose very identities are threatened. Think of all of us facing a rapidly warming climate.




Jesse Jackson’s concept of the Rainbow Coalition was not new, but he elevated it into a powerful symbol of unity. He made concrete the phrase imprinted on the Great Seal of the United States, 

e pluribus unum

. 




‘

Our flag is red, white and blue, but our nation is a rainbow —red, yellow, brown, black and white—and we’re all precious in God’s sight. America is not like a blanket—one piece of unbroken cloth, the same color, the same texture, the same size. America is more like a quilt—many patches, many pieces, many colors, many sizes, all woven and held together by a common thread.

‘….”










Read more – get the book!

Monthly Review
