author: Unknown
title: Democratic Integration Conference discusses equal and free coexistence
content:
The Kurdish Association for Social Research (Akademî Kurd) organized a conference titled “Democratic Integration” in Zurich, Switzerland. Held at the Kirchgemeindehaus in Zurich, the conference explored the concept of democratic integration from various perspectives within the framework of the Manifesto for a Democratic Communal Society put forward by Leader Apo. Following presentations by Kurdish politician Veysi Aktaş and sociologist Nazan Üstündağ, the conference moved on to its second session.







 







Political, sociological and cultural dimensions of democratic integration




The conference’s second session, titled “The Political, Sociological, and Cultural Dimensions of Democratic Integration,” addressed the role integration could play in a democratic resolution of the Kurdish question, along with issues such as the recognition of Kurdish identity, equal citizenship, and the construction of a democratic society.




Hasan Ali Muhammed of the Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria spoke in place of Mazlum Abdi, an adviser to the Syrian presidency, who was unable to attend due to a demanding schedule. Other speakers in the session included sociologist Engin Sustam of Paris 8 University, Zîlan Diyar, a member of the European Kurdish Women’s Movement (TJK-E), and Derya Arslan, a member of the Central Executive Board of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party).







Democratic integration does not mean subordinating yourself to a power




Hasan Ali Muhammed was the first to speak, evaluating the political, sociological, and cultural dimensions of democratic integration through the experience of Rojava. Muhammed stressed that democratic integration does not mean subordinating oneself to a particular political power or losing one’s identity within the existing system. Rather, he explained, it is based on the Kurdish people becoming an equal part of political and social life while retaining their own identity, will, and social values.




Muhammed stated that democratic integration requires the state in which the Kurdish people live to recognize them in the political, social, and cultural spheres. He emphasized that this process also entails building a democratic system.




Kurdish identitu must be recognized




Sociologist Engin Sustam of Paris 8 University then addressed the social and political dimensions of democratic integration. Sustam stated that the comprehensive recognition of Kurdish identity by the state must lie at the heart of democratic integration, emphasizing the importance of developing the process on the basis of equal citizenship. He pointed out that democratic integration should not be treated merely as a political arrangement, but as a transformation that enables Kurds to participate equally in social and political life while preserving their identity.







Women's role in democratic integration is crucial




Zîlan Diyar, a member of the European Kurdish Women’s Movement (TJK-E), and Derya Arslan, a member of the DEM Party’s Central Executive Board, also shared their assessments of the social and political dimensions of democratic integration.




They emphasized that democratic integration should not be limited to the recognition of the Kurdish people’s rights, but should also be based on the equal participation of all segments of society in democratic life. They highlighted the importance of women’s role in this process.




They stated that, for democratic integration to become a lasting solution, social organization must be strengthened, democratic politics must be allowed to flourish, and the equal and free coexistence of peoples must be guaranteed.




Legal dimension of democratic integration




The conference’s third session was held under the title “The Legal Dimension of Democratic Integration and a Solution for All Kurds.” Speakers included lawyer Özgür Erol, a member of the İmralı Delegation, and Hüsnü Yılmaz, a lawyer with the Lausanne Bar Association.




The session addressed the legal foundations of democratic integration, the recognition of the Kurdish people’s collective rights, equal citizenship, and the establishment of lasting legal guarantees for a democratic resolution of the Kurdish question. One of the central issues discussed was that democratic integration must not remain limited to political will, but must also be secured through legal arrangements.




The law has played a negative role for Kurds throughout history




Speaking first in the session, lawyer Özgür Erol of the İmralı Delegation assessed the legal dimension of democratic integration in the context of historical and social developments.




Drawing attention to the importance Leader Apo attaches to the legal recognition of the Kurds, Erol stated that the law must be examined and defined not only through legislation and constitutional arrangements, but also in its historical and social dimensions.




Erol said that the law had historically played a negative role for Kurds, emphasizing that the collective punishment of the Kurdish people had continued as a recurring historical pattern. He noted that Leader Apo had placed particular emphasis on the way the law treats Kurds and stated that the Kurdish question is not merely a political issue, but also a historical and legal one.




Erol argued that policies directed at the Kurdish question had played a decisive role in shaping Turkey’s legal system. He said that the political regime established around the Kurdish question had also obstructed the development of a democratic legal system in Turkey.




Referring to Turkey’s constitutional history, Erol noted that the period extending from the Constitutions of 1921 and 1924 through subsequent military coups had not followed a coherent path of democratic legal development. He explained that constitutions and laws had often been created in opposition to preceding arrangements, making it difficult to establish a stable and lasting legal system in Turkey.




Öcalan must be given a proper legal status




Erol also discussed the years-long struggle against the isolation imposed on Leader Apo, describing it as important in demonstrating the Kurdish people’s collective political will.




He stated that, at the current stage, it could not be said that the isolation had been completely ended. However, he said a new period had begun in which political and legal options for a solution were starting to be discussed.




Emphasizing the importance of legal guarantees in turning democratic integration into a lasting solution, Erol stressed that the legal and political status of Leader Apo, one of the central actors in the process, must be clarified.




He pointed out that the legal recognition of Öcalan’s status would be decisive in advancing the democratic integration process and establishing its legal foundations.




Obstacles to democratic integration must be overcome




Following Özgür Erol, lawyer Hüsnü Yılmaz of the Lausanne Bar Association discussed the historical development of Turkey’s political regime, the legal structure of the state, and the obstacles facing democratic integration.




Yılmaz stated that Turkish nationalism had been adopted as a fundamental ideological principle during the founding of the state, arguing that this outlook had historically obstructed the recognition of the Kurds’ collective rights. He examined discriminatory policies against Kurds through the concept of apartheid, which is recognized in international law as a crime against humanity.




Assessing Turkey’s state structure through the concept of the “dual state” (Doppelstaat), developed by German legal scholar Ernst Fraenkel, Yılmaz explained that a state governed by legal rules coexists with an administrative apparatus operating through extraordinary measures.




He argued that the continued use of emergency governance measures had weakened the principle of the rule of law. He also emphasized that the erosion of the separation of powers between the legislature, executive, and judiciary created serious obstacles to democratization.




Yılmaz stated that capitalism and the nation-state model had failed to produce solutions to humanity’s problems, drawing attention to the continued narrowing of democratic rights and freedoms.




Referring to French philosopher Jacques Derrida’s concept of “democracy to come,” he explained that democracy is not a completed system but an ongoing process of development.




Emphasizing that fundamental human rights, particularly the right to life, must be guaranteed by the state, Yılmaz stated that protecting these rights also requires social struggle.




He pointed out that the historical and legal obstacles to democratic integration could only be overcome through a struggle for democratization, adding that the struggle for democracy and freedom must continue without interruption.




The importance of democratic communal economy




In the conference’s final session, researcher and economist Ahmet Pelda and sociologist and anthropologist Neşe Özgen delivered a presentation on the economic dimension of democratic integration.




They focused on the importance of a democratic communal economy in promoting social equality and solidarity and in building a democratic society.

title: Gamze Çakan: Silence of guns is not enough
content:
Film critic Gamze Çakan highlighted the importance of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, stressing that bringing an end to a conflict that has lasted so long and exhausted both the people and the country is crucial. Çakan said, “If we genuinely want peace, we must also make room for stories we disagree with and those we have refused to listen to until now. An atmosphere of conflict suffocates not only ordinary people but also art.” She emphasised that silencing the guns was important, but that freedom was now essential: “We need to build a life in which people do not feel anxious about speaking their own language, expressing their identity or talking about the suffering they have experienced.”




ANF spoke to film critic Gamze Çakan, founder of the Independent Cinema platform, about the relationship between cinema and peace.




What can the relationship between cinema and confronting the past teach us about the current peace process?




I think the first thing cinema can teach us is how to look beyond our own stories. For years in this country, we have looked at the same events and seen completely different things. We have spoken without knowing what others have experienced, sometimes without even wanting to know. Cinema allows us to take a closer look at the life of someone we have judged from a distance. It can show us the life left behind by someone whose death appears merely as a number in the news, and how that loss changes everything within a home. Confronting the past begins, to some extent, at precisely that point: when we acknowledge that what we know is not the whole story.




That is also how I view the current process. Bringing an end to a conflict that has lasted so long and exhausted both the people and the country is extremely important. We cannot underestimate the significance of silencing the guns, but neither can we regard that alone as sufficient. The anger, fear and prejudices we harbour towards one another will not simply disappear. We need to build a life in which people can speak their own language, express their identity and talk about the suffering they have experienced without fear. Whether peace truly takes root in society depends, in part, on achieving this. Cinema's role here is not to persuade everyone to think alike. A good film can also make us uncomfortable and challenge the narratives we have grown accustomed to. I believe that is precisely what we need. But for this to happen, filmmakers must be able to create freely, and their films must be able to reach audiences. We cannot confront the past by making room only for stories we are prepared to hear. If we genuinely want peace, we must also make room for stories we dislike, disagree with or have refused to listen to until now.




Could progress in this process also create greater freedom for art?




I certainly believe it could, but it will not happen automatically. An atmosphere of conflict suffocates not only ordinary people but also art. The language of tension that has dominated for years has forced everyone to take sides. In such a climate, artists struggle with self-censorship, films are prevented from being screened at festivals, and even finding a cinema willing to show a film becomes a problem. This issue has drained so much of the country's energy that the space for thought and artistic expression has gradually narrowed. Removing the conflict from the equation could, at the very least, break this constant state of defensiveness.




However, there is something important we must recognise. Taking weapons out of the equation can create space for art, but that does not mean this space will automatically become free. If we cannot tolerate one another's views, if public attacks and campaigns of vilification begin as soon as a film is made, social pressure will continue even if official bans are lifted. Genuine freedom is only possible when everyone can tell their own truth without fear of punishment or exclusion.




In short, this process could provide an invaluable foundation for art. A society in which artists are no longer targeted because of their identities or the subjects they wish to explore, and where independent festivals can take place freely, is not an impossible dream. But this cannot be achieved through political measures alone. We must also accept that art does not always have to be agreeable or receive applause. Sometimes, it helps society heal precisely by asking questions that cause us pain.




Can cinema, then, help make peace a shared reality across society?




Cinema can help make peace a shared reality by breaking through the cold, distant language of politics and bringing a human dimension to the issue. Politics draws boundaries and negotiates conditions, but it cannot bridge the emotional distance between people. Unless we understand the suffering of others, peace will remain nothing more than an agreement on paper. A good film, on the other hand, can bring together people who have never met, perhaps even people who would hesitate to stand alongside one another, in a darkened cinema around a shared emotion. That collective experience can offer one of the most direct ways of overcoming the invisible walls that have been built between us over the years. People need more than grand slogans to become familiar with one another's languages, cultures and existence. They need stories that make room for different experiences. Bringing these stories to the screen honestly and without censorship can help peace take root throughout society.




How much impact do anti-war films have on audiences? Have you observed this yourself?




I think the impact of anti-war films depends directly on how they convey their message. If a film sets out with good intentions but does nothing more than condemn war, lecturing audiences and dictating what they should think, its impact may disappear as soon as they leave the cinema. Such an approach can alienate some viewers or reduce the film to a one-sided message. But if a film honestly examines the anger and fear that fuel war, along with the darker and more selfish aspects of human nature, it can have a genuinely profound impact on audiences. Rather than delivering a one-sided lecture, films that courageously explore all the contradictions of conflict can leave viewers alone with their own consciences.




That has consistently been my own observation. The films that truly transform audiences are not necessarily those that draw a clear distinction between who is right and who is wrong. The most powerful moments are those that force people to confront their own fears, their hidden prejudices and even their capacity for violence. A film leaves a lasting impression when it refuses to offer easy consolation and sends viewers out of the cinema with uncomfortable questions lingering in their minds. Films that convey the idea that opposing war is neither an easy nor a comfortable moral position, and that people must first confront the conflicts within themselves, can have a much deeper and more lasting impact.




When exploring conflict and peace, do documentaries or fictional films leave a more lasting impression on collective memory?




I do not think it is right to draw such rigid boundaries between the two. There is a quote by Éric Rohmer that I particularly like: he says that a good film is also a documentary. Even when telling a fictional story, you are, in some way, recording the relationships between people, the rhythms of everyday life and the feelings that characterise a particular period. Documentaries, too, are not simply collections of facts. They are shaped by the perspective and emotions of the filmmaker behind them.




Documentaries create powerful archives and preserve collective memory by presenting the unvarnished truth and concrete testimonies that official history seeks to erase. Fiction, meanwhile, can remove the invisible barriers to empathy, allowing us to experience that suffering or hope within ourselves. One records reality and makes it harder to deny. The other allows us to experience that reality through the eyes of someone who has lived it. Which leaves a more lasting impression depends on how honestly and directly a film brings us face to face with that truth.




How open are cinema audiences in Turkey to watching and understanding political or social narratives that are completely opposed to their own views?




It is difficult to give a single answer on behalf of cinema audiences in Turkey, but I think being open to different narratives is not easy in a climate where the distance between us has grown. Audiences may not show the same patience towards a story that challenges their views as they do towards one that reflects their own beliefs. I do not exclude myself from this. Nevertheless, I do not believe this distance is impossible to overcome. If a film makes us curious about the person behind an opinion we disagree with, we may be willing to stop and listen rather than immediately object. Understanding does not always mean agreeing. Sometimes, leaving a film without having changed our minds, but feeling that we can no longer judge the other person quite so easily, is significant in itself.




What stereotypes and Orientalist traps does Turkish cinema continue to fall into when portraying Kurds?




I think the most fundamental trap is seeing Kurds solely as representatives of a political or social issue, rather than as people with different experiences, identities and everyday lives. Constantly portraying the region through poverty, traditional customs and violence narrows our perspective, just as reducing people to victims of suffering or idealised heroes does. This can happen even in a film made with good intentions. There is a difference between recognising someone's suffering and defining them entirely by that suffering. Kurdish characters also have their own sense of humour, love lives, ordinary problems and contradictions. Making room for these aspects does not mean pushing the injustices they have experienced into the background. On the contrary, it allows us to see their lives more fully. What matters to me is not that filmmakers speak from a position of knowing everything, but that they allow the people whose stories they tell to surprise them.




What forms of censorship or self-censorship do films supporting social peace or portraying the other side of conflicts face in Turkey?




I do not think we should understand censorship solely in terms of a film being banned. Difficulty securing funding, a festival's reluctance to include a film in its programme, the cancellation of a screening at the last minute, or fears of being publicly targeted can all make it harder for a film to reach its audience. It would be wrong to attribute every obstacle to the same cause, but even the possibility of encountering such difficulties can influence the filmmaking process. Self-censorship sometimes begins at the screenplay stage, with questions such as, “If I tell this story, will I be able to make the film? Could I put the people I work with in a difficult position?” I do not think it is right to judge filmmakers who have these concerns. We cannot casually demand that people put their livelihoods or safety at risk. What we really need to examine is why telling a particular story might come at such a cost, and what we can do to reduce these fears.




Are there any films from world cinema dealing with post-conflict societies, such as Northern Ireland or South Africa, that you find inspiring for Turkey?




I mention these films not because I see them as models that can be directly applied to Turkey, but because they encourage us to think about what peace might look like in everyday life. As a film critic, what appeals to me is that these films approach the issue not through grand political agreements, but through small, tangible spaces where people come together.




One example from Northern Ireland is Good Vibrations. The film focuses on a new community that forms around a record shop opened in the midst of the conflict. Another example is Mickybo and Me. It tells the story of a Catholic boy and a Protestant boy from two divided neighbourhoods who come together through a shared adventure. In both films, people divided by politics find ways to coexist without the need for grand declarations. I would also like to mention a South Korean film, Welcome to Dongmakgol. During the Korean War, soldiers from opposing sides encounter one another in a mountain village whose inhabitants know nothing of the war. As they share everyday life with the villagers, the hostility between them gradually gives way to human connection. 




I find these stories inspiring because they show that peace can be built not only through official agreements, but also in places where people can come together and share their lives.




How successful has Turkish cinema been in developing a language of peace compared with these international examples?




We actually have some very valuable films that have managed to develop this language. For example, Iki Dil Bir Bavul (On the Way to School) managed to convey the complexities of education in the mother tongue without lecturing the audience, simply by following the everyday efforts of a teacher and children to communicate in a village school. Similarly, Büyük Adam Küçük Aşk (Hejar) showed how two people who seemingly have nothing in common gradually become accustomed to each other's language and presence while living under the same roof. Films such as Çoğunluk (Majority) have also sought a form of confrontation by holding up a mirror to the indifference and prejudices on the other side of the issue.




Compared with international examples, what Turkish cinema lacks is neither talent nor intention. The main difference is that, in those countries, such stories have gradually found their way into mainstream cinema. In Turkey, however, this language has largely survived through the individual efforts of independent filmmakers, often at considerable personal cost. The issue, therefore, is not so much what our cinema can or cannot achieve, but whether there is a public space where films that preserve and explore this collective memory can reach audiences freely and be openly discussed.




What kind of cinematic language should directors develop to help audiences from opposing political perspectives empathise with the same film?




It is certainly not my place to prescribe a method for filmmakers. But when I look at films that manage to bring people from opposing sides together through the same story, I notice that their characters are portrayed through their ordinary lives rather than primarily through their political identities. A parent's concern for their child, a silence around the dinner table, the struggle to earn a living or the fear of losing someone are universal experiences. They evoke the same sense of pain in people from all walks of life. When characters are presented through these human experiences rather than merely as representatives of grand political ideas, audiences begin to see them first and foremost as human beings. I think what makes empathy possible is recognising the shared concerns of everyday life that lie beneath the conflict.

title: Poverty deepens in Bağlar: ‘Many families eat only once a day’
content:
Deepening poverty, rising living costs and difficulties in accessing basic necessities are adversely affecting the living conditions of millions of people in Turkey. According to the Turkish Statistical Institute's (TÜİK) 2025 Poverty and Living Conditions Statistics, 27.9 percent of the population is at risk of poverty or social exclusion. Among children, this figure rises to 36.8 percent.




The same data shows that the material and social deprivation rate stands at 11.9 percent, while the persistent poverty rate is 13.6 percent.




A December 2025 survey by the Confederation of Turkish Trade Unions (TÜRK-İŞ) put the monthly hunger threshold for a family of four at 30,143 Turkish liras and the poverty threshold at 98,188 lira. The net minimum wage of 28,075 liras announced for 2026 falls below the hunger threshold, highlighting the increasingly difficult living conditions.







Deep economic divide between neighbourhoods




As the economic crisis and inflation worsen, millions of people are wondering how they will get through the approaching winter. Residents struggling to cover the costs of natural gas, electricity and firewood say the economic crisis is becoming increasingly severe.




The effects of the crisis are felt across every aspect of life in Diyarbakır (Amed), particularly in districts such as Bağlar and Sur, where residents face greater economic hardship. As the economic divide between districts and neighbourhoods widens, the recent rise in gang activity, individual gun ownership and violence in the city has also prompted debate about the social consequences of this situation. Residents of Bağlar who spoke to ANF about the causes and consequences of poverty said employment opportunities must be increased and a more equitable distribution of income ensured to address the problem.




The district is home to many people who were forced to migrate from villages burned down during the 1990s. Residents now struggle with illness and poverty in homes that receive little or no sunlight.




Characterised by narrow streets, detached houses and apartment buildings, the district also lacks natural gas infrastructure, making life even more difficult during the winter months. Poverty is particularly concentrated in the neighbourhoods of 5 Nisan, Muradiye, Şeyh Şamil and Kaynartepe. Its extent is reflected both in the records kept by neighbourhood headmen and in the credit ledgers of local grocery shops.




‘An average of 30 people seek assistance every day’







The headmen of Şeyh Şamil and Kaynartepe neighbourhoods, who spoke to ANF, drew attention to worsening poverty and the failure to address the problem. They said an average of 30 people approached their offices every day seeking assistance, with the number continuing to rise. Requests for stationery and school supplies had increased particularly since schools reopened.




The headmen also reported growing demand for food and firewood assistance and described the problems shared by their neighbourhoods: “We no longer even count the requests for assistance. There are people living in extremely difficult circumstances. We contact everyone we can to find support for them, and when we cannot secure any assistance, we try to do something with our own resources. People were already in a very difficult situation, but things have become even worse recently. Some receive no assistance at all, while others have no income because they cannot find work. There are families who cannot even find a single meal during the day. Some cannot afford a loaf of bread and have to buy even their bread on credit.




Charitable people provide support, but it is not enough. There are so many families without any income that we also struggle to meet their needs. Women living alone and families with children whose parents are unemployed face the greatest difficulties. Winter is approaching, and neither they nor we know what to do. There is no natural gas, so they will have to use electricity or coal for heating, but both are expensive. Things have reached a point where people can no longer afford even a second-hand wood-burning stove.




The causes of this unemployment and these problems must be investigated, and solutions must be found. In some neighbourhoods, people throw food away, while in others, people cannot even find bread to eat.”




GABB research also reveals the extent of poverty







A study conducted in Bağlar further confirms the situation described by the neighbourhood headmen. Based exclusively on interviews with women, the findings reveal the scale of poverty in the district. According to the 2026 Research Report on Women's Poverty in Diyarbakır, published by the Union of Municipalities of Southeastern Anatolia Region (GABB), poverty among women in Bağlar is deepening due to unemployment, unpaid care work and economic insecurity.




The study found that more than 90 percent of the women surveyed were not engaged in paid employment, while 46 percent had no personal income.




Childcare was the leading reason preventing women from working, cited by 58.2 percent of respondents. Some 77 percent said they struggled to pay their household bills, while 70 percent had difficulty covering their children's education expenses. The research also found that 48 percent of women were in debt, with approximately 52 percent of those in debt having borrowed money to meet basic needs such as food and clothing.




The study highlighted the barriers preventing women from achieving economic independence. Some 83 percent owned no property registered in their name, while 54 percent did not have a bank card in their own name.




The report highlighted demands for greater employment opportunities, more childcare centres, vocational training courses and stronger social support mechanisms to combat poverty among women.




‘Buying on credit is no longer even an option’




A local shopkeeper in Bağlar's 5 Nisan neighbourhood said he had burned his credit ledgers because customers could no longer repay their accumulated debts.







The shopkeeper explained that unemployment and financial hardship had forced people to buy even bread on credit and purchase cooking oil by the glass rather than by the bottle. He said his own income had fallen to almost nothing and that his business was on the verge of closing.




The shopkeeper, who wished to remain anonymous, described the economic difficulties they faced: “Women are struggling particularly badly. They are the ones looking after both the children and the household.




“In the past, when we allowed people to buy on credit, they would come and pay at the end of the month. But now buying on credit is no longer even an option.




“Sometimes people have no money to repay their debts or even buy a loaf of bread. We now give them what we can out of our own pockets. We can no longer make ends meet ourselves. Many shopkeepers have closed their businesses, and we continue opening our shop every day at a loss. We do not know how much longer this can go on.”




‘We only get sick in a house that receives no sunlight’




Residents said that despite the findings of the research and the hardships they had described, no lasting solutions had been introduced in their neighbourhoods. They stressed that poverty manifested itself not only through hunger but also through health problems.




Fatma, who lives in a single-storey detached house without a title deed in the Şeyh Şamil neighbourhood, said natural gas had not been connected to their home despite repeated requests, leaving them struggling with illness every winter. She explained that their house, surrounded by taller buildings, receives no sunlight throughout the day. Both she and her neighbours experience health problems throughout the year.







Fatma described their living conditions: “We pay our electricity and water bills, but when we ask for natural gas, they tell us, ‘You don't have a title deed.’ We have been facing the same problems for years. Buildings are being demolished, and people are being forced to move away. We stay here because we cannot afford to live anywhere else. I have a single-storey house, but it never gets warm. It is not just my home; my neighbours cannot heat their homes either. We no longer know what to do. Aid arrives, but it runs out before it reaches us.




If I had the means, I would not raise my children here, but I cannot afford to pay rent. Nobody can afford it. We just carry on living like this. My children go to school. Other people prepare packed lunches for their children, but I can only give mine the same things every day. If there were a job, I would take it. I would work. But there are no jobs, no childcare centres and no opportunities. There are no opportunities, only hardship.”

title: Sevda Karaca: War policies undermine unity and labour struggles - Part Two
content:
Sevda Karaca, Deputy Chair of the Labour Party (EMEP) and MP for Antep, answered ANF's questions about labour struggles and the struggle for peace. 




Part one of this interview can be read 

here

.




Do war, conflict and the resulting militarism push poverty, insecurity and workers' demands out of the public agenda? How exactly are labour struggles weakened during periods when security-driven policies intensify?




The past 40 years have shown us that the effects of war are not confined to areas of armed conflict. War permeates every aspect of social life. Workers' demands for higher wages, the right to strike, women's struggle for equality and people's democratic demands can suddenly be pushed into the background by debates over 'national security', 'the survival of the state' or the 'domestic front'. Rather than answering the questions working people raise about its policies, the government attempts to bring them into line by presenting them with another supposed threat.




This mechanism has very concrete consequences. Strikes are postponed on national security grounds. Trade union organising faces repression. Democratic protests are portrayed as security threats. The conflict of interests between workers and their employers is treated as a security threat, with employers' interests presented as though they were the common interests of society as a whole. Moreover, under conditions of war, those who voice objections can easily be accused of failing to care about their country or their nation. It is workers, working people and poorer sections of society who pay the heaviest price for war. People face both economic devastation and the social consequences of war. Yet they are still expected to make sacrifices. Their questions about why their wages are insufficient, where public resources are being spent and why their rights are being restricted are often drowned out by nationalist rhetoric and growing chauvinism.




Opposition to war and the labour struggle are not two separate areas of struggle. Opposing war cannot be separated from defending workers' livelihoods, their right to strike and their freedom to organise. The political climate created by war restricts working people's ability to defend their rights. At the same time, struggles to protect those rights can become a force against the social consequences of war policies. What matters is that opposition to war must not be confined to a separate sphere, disconnected from the everyday demands of working people.




Opposing war is not a separate task from defending workers' livelihoods, their right to strike and their freedom to organise. On the contrary, to understand why these rights are constantly under threat, we must recognise the social role played by war and militarism.




‘Racism and chauvinism prevent people from coming together’




How can we build a movement for social peace by connecting opposition to war with demands for a higher minimum wage, tax justice, trade union rights and women's right to life?




First of all, we must not reduce peace to politicians sitting around a negotiating table, the silencing of guns or the signing of an agreement. These are, of course, important. But those responsible for war have spent decades using propaganda to legitimise it, dividing peoples and forcing the working class into artificial divisions. Social peace cannot be achieved, nor can peace take root throughout society, simply by bringing the opposing forces to the negotiating table.




War is also a major obstacle to bringing class struggles and broader social movements together. The racism, nationalism and chauvinism being fuelled prevent people, women and young people from uniting around common demands. For example, a worker in the defence industry may be subjected to terrible exploitation, yet that exploitation can be dismissed as an issue because their work is presented as service to the nation.




We must also remember that an atmosphere of war and conflict makes it easier to promote false answers to the question of who is responsible for the poverty, insecurity, discrimination and violence people experience every day. The real causes lie in the existing system and its political and economic representatives. Yet the ruling classes can easily point the finger at migrants, women or an oppressed nation instead.




Another decisive aspect of the struggle to establish lasting peace on a social foundation is discussing what kind of lives people will lead, what rights they will have and whose needs society's resources will serve.




For a worker, peace also means no longer having to worry about their child's future, earning a wage sufficient for a dignified life and not being dismissed for joining a trade union. For a woman, it means having control over her own life, not being left alone in the face of violence, receiving equal pay for equal work and not having to shoulder the burden of care alone. For Kurdish workers, it means all these things, together with recognition of their identity, language and democratic will, and guarantees of equal citizenship rights. 




Simply listing these demands alongside one another is not enough. We must establish the connections between them. Consider tax policies. Wage earners hand over a significant proportion of their income to the state through indirect taxes, while big capital benefits from various advantages. Workers seeking to organise in trade unions face pressure from employers. Women are concentrated in insecure jobs and carry out unpaid care work. The suppression of democratic rights through policies of conflict has severe consequences for economic and social life. Each of these issues, in different ways, raises the same questions: Whose interests are society's resources serving? Who makes the decisions? And who pays the price?




This discussion is sometimes conducted through misleading assumptions that peace will automatically bring greater prosperity, economic growth and regional development. We, too, expect that an end to the conflict will lead to more rapid industrialisation in Kurdish provinces and changes in their economic structures and conditions. But we must emphasise that this does not automatically mean prosperity, development, growth or employment, and that the consequences for capital will be different from those experienced by working people.




The economic and social consequences of the conflict in Kurdish provinces, control over resources and decisions about the region's future must also form part of this discussion. The economic benefits of peace, increased investment or regional development do not, in themselves, tell us how working people will live. We must also ask who will control new investments, under what conditions workers will be employed and who will receive the wealth created.




A movement for social peace can be built through common struggles in which workers, women, young people, the Kurdish people and all oppressed groups participate with their own demands. We are not talking about unity that requires anyone to abandon their demands. On the contrary, we are talking about unity in which different demands reinforce one another and every section of society sees the struggle for others' rights and freedoms as part of its own struggle.




How do economic destruction, dispossession and ecological devastation in conflict zones affect workers in western Turkey? Has this connection been sufficiently established?




We cannot say that this connection has been sufficiently established. The consequences of war are often treated as a problem confined to the geographical areas where the conflict takes place. Yet the economic, social and ecological consequences of war do not recognise borders. Conflict forces people from their land, homes and sources of livelihood. Agricultural production suffers, while livestock farming and local economies are severely affected.




One of the historical dimensions of the policies of denial and assimilation directed against the Kurdish people has been the control of the region's resources, its economic underdevelopment, the destruction of livelihoods and the forced displacement of its population. We must also consider today's debates over mining projects, dams, power plants and the exploitation of natural resources against this historical background. Control over Kurdistan's resources is not simply a question of regional development. It is a question of ownership, labour and decision-making power.




Who decides how land, water and forests are used? Who receives the economic benefits? Can local people have a say in decisions affecting their own living environments? These questions are directly connected to the working class. People who lose their livelihoods may be forced to seek work in other cities, often taking insecure and low-paid jobs. As workers are turned against one another on the basis of differences in identity, the gains of the working class as a whole are rolled back in favour of capital. Workers in Kurdish provinces, employed in sectors ranging from agriculture and mining to textiles and other industries, also face harsh working conditions, low wages and a lack of organisation.




If people's livelihoods are destroyed in one place, they may be forced to enter the labour market elsewhere under even harsher conditions. This increases the pressure to drive down wages and working conditions for all workers. Of course, this is not the only factor determining wages, but it is an important mechanism through which working people's employment and livelihoods become increasingly insecure. 




Ecological destruction cannot be regarded as a problem affecting only a particular region. The destruction of land, water, forests and shared living environments for the sake of capital accumulation deprives people of their livelihoods and their future. The destruction of agricultural land for mining in a village and the conditions that force workers in an industrial city to live and work in unhealthy environments are, in different ways, consequences of the same relations of production and ownership.




That is why simply telling Turkish workers to be concerned about what is happening in Kurdish provinces is not enough. We must demonstrate together how that destruction is connected to their own lives through economic relations. We must make the common interests of Turkish and Kurdish workers visible through their working and living conditions, rather than leaving them as an abstract appeal for brotherhood.




‘War fuels the growth of capital groups’




Is war merely a tool of political rule, or is it also a model of capital accumulation? Who pays the price for the resources allocated to the defence industry?




War is more than a tool used by governments to control society and consolidate their political power. It is also a major area of capital accumulation. Arms production, military technology, security and logistics contracts, energy resources and reconstruction activities are all areas involving substantial economic interests. Prolonged wars, or the constant emphasis on security threats, can increase the profits of capital groups operating in these sectors.




We must also examine the rhetoric of national pride surrounding Turkey's defence industry from this perspective. Of course, a country's technological capacity, production capabilities and independence in defence can be discussed. But the fundamental question is this: Who controls this production, what needs does it serve, and at what social cost? Which companies receive public resources, and under what conditions? Do these investments serve the common good of society or the profits of particular capital groups? Are defence and armament policies being used to turn the country into an instrument of imperialist powers' wars in the region, or to provide a foundation for the peoples of the region to build an equal, democratic and free life? These are crucial distinctions. 




Amid rhetoric about national security and becoming a powerful country in the region, workers see their wages eroded by inflation, pensioners struggle to make ends meet, and young people cannot afford housing. Yet the government presents these hardships as necessary sacrifices under conditions of war, constantly calling on people and society to make sacrifices. But whether the same sacrifices are being demanded of capital is not questioned. Wage earners bear a significant proportion of the tax burden, while people have almost no oversight of how public resources are used. Capital benefits both from the economic resources created by the people and from conditions in which pressure on labour intensifies.




The issue, therefore, is not simply the amount spent on defence. It is about who controls production and resources, how social needs are determined and to whom those making economic decisions are accountable. The struggle for peace must also raise these questions.




Beyond saying that 'war budgets increase poverty', what other factors cause war to deepen poverty?




If we explain the increase in poverty caused by war solely in terms of the share of the budget allocated to military expenditure, we miss a significant part of the problem. War also changes how people work, where they live, which rights they can exercise and how they can build their futures.




First, war destroys economic life and sources of livelihood. Agriculture, livestock farming and local production suffer, while people may be forced from their land, homes and jobs. Second, forced displacement and growing insecurity push people into low-paid employment. Third, security-driven policies suppress the very means through which workers can improve their wages and working conditions, including trade union organising and the right to strike.




Fourth, the weakening of democratic oversight during wartime, together with the marginalisation of questions about how public resources are used, makes it harder to challenge economic privileges. Fifth, the fear and polarisation created by war make it more difficult for workers to unite around their common problems. Working people living under similar conditions can be turned against one another on the basis of identity and nationality. 




We must also consider the burden placed on women. As livelihoods shrink, public services become inadequate and care needs increase, much of the resulting burden is met through women's unpaid labour. Women are pushed into harsher conditions in paid employment while also being forced to shoulder responsibilities at home. Conditions of war also lead to the normalisation of all forms of violence, while those fighting against violence are marginalised and portrayed as terrorists.




War, therefore, does not merely consume society's resources. It also strengthens the relationships and mechanisms that perpetuate poverty. That is why opposition to war must also include a struggle against all these mechanisms that determine working people's living conditions.

title: Şerda Mazlum: The process requires women's self-defence networks - Part One
content:
Bêrîtan (Gülnaz Karataş), one of the symbolic figures of the Kurdish women's freedom struggle, made history on 25 October 1992 with her self-sacrificing resistance against betrayal and surrender in South Kurdistan. Choosing freedom at the edge of a cliff, Bêrîtan became a symbol not only of resistance but also of women's determination to achieve freedom and continue their struggle.




YJA Star commander Şerda Mazlum Gabar spoke about Bêrîtan's life, personality and resistance, stressing that her legacy of resistance continues to place responsibilities on women today.




Mazlum said discussions in the Peace and Democratic Society Process must give way to concrete steps, pointing out that the freedom of the Kurdish people and women remains under threat. “The greatest and most effective deterrent force is an organised and conscious society,” she said, emphasising the need for women to strengthen their self-defence networks and for society to develop its own forms of organisation.




What were the conditions facing the Kurdish people, Kurdish women and the freedom guerrillas at the time of martyr Bêrîtan's self-sacrificing action? How should her action be understood in the context of those conditions?




Throughout human history, the struggle for human existence has continued despite every hardship, suffering and massacre. It may have been inadequate or incomplete at times, but the struggle to be human and to live a dignified life has always existed. As long as human beings continue to dominate one another, nature and life itself, this struggle will continue. The struggle to reach into the depths of history and recreate love, freedom, justice and labour in their true essence has always faced brutal attacks and attempts to suppress and destroy it. The price of rebelling against slavery and domination in pursuit of freedom has been immense. Across different places and periods, freedom has repeatedly been redefined and given meaning through these sacrifices. The history of every oppressed people, class and gender contains countless extraordinary examples of this. Our own history of freedom also possesses a profound and magnificent legacy of resistance. Among those at the forefront of this legacy is our comrade Bêrîtan, the embodiment of our dignity and freedom. As we mark the 34th anniversary of her martyrdom and enter the 35th year since her death, I commemorate our courageous and brave-hearted commander, comrade Bêrîtan, and, through her, all martyrs of freedom with love and gratitude. I bow respectfully before their memory and renew my promise to fulfil their aspirations for freedom.




Our encounter with freedom as women and Kurds, and our journey towards it, have not been easy. They have been forged through boundless labour, effort and struggle. Comrade Bêrîtan's self-sacrificing action became a breath of life for the Kurdish people and Kurdish women at that time. It revealed the truth that a free life could only be achieved through great resistance. In this sense, her action constitutes one of the fundamental building blocks of the Kurdistan revolution and the morality of freedom that has developed in Kurdistan. 25 October 1992 was the day when the meaninglessness and disgrace of betrayal were answered with the magnificent meaning and sacredness of resistance. It was the will, voice and action of a free and dignified woman against every form of degradation and surrender imposed upon her. Comrade Bêrîtan Hêvî assumed responsibility for a people and their history, acting with an awareness of what it meant to be a pioneer. She reversed the course of surrender and betrayal, halted the downward spiral, rejected every form of degradation imposed upon her and recreated life out of death. She understood what the moment demanded, followed the teachings of freedom and acted in a manner that reflected the spirit of her time.




Historic actions acquire their significance because, at the time and place in which they occur, they address the most vital and pressing problems facing society or offer solutions to them. Not every action marks a turning point or represents a leap into a new stage. Historic actions are distinguished from ordinary actions by the convergence of the right time, the right place and the capacity to bring about meaningful social change. Through these qualities, they become a spirit and a guiding path.




Comrade Bêrîtan and her action embody precisely such a spirit and such a path. There is no one who has not been moved by the historic photograph that immortalised comrade Bêrîtan's powerful yet graceful bearing. Her beauty could not be contained within the frame, and the depth of her heart seemed to overflow beyond it, leaving an indelible impression on all of us. Guerrilla life suited Bêrîtan, and Bêrîtan suited guerrilla life. Every word and sentence she wrote in her diary was distilled from suffering, hardship and the most beautiful moments of solidarity, becoming refined and acquiring profound meaning. Her participation in the freedom struggle was not something superficial or added on from the outside. It was a process of complete integration, of becoming inseparable from the struggle itself. The more she became one with the freedom struggle, the more beautiful and meaningful she became, while also enriching the struggle with her own meaning. Bêrîtan walked the path of liberation with her head held high and with dignity, remaining true to her word. Embracing Bêrîtan's spirit and path gave our movement the character of resisting under all circumstances and sustaining that resistance without interruption. Kurdish women certainly had a tradition of resistance in earlier uprisings. However, those acts of resistance and rebellion had not developed into an ideological and organised struggle for freedom and equality. Comrade Bêrîtan's spirit and path of resistance brought about a development in the women's struggle based on organisation and continuity. Through this path, the women's struggle advanced step by step towards the formation of an organised women's guerrilla force.




What message did Bêrîtan convey to the Kurdish people and women through her stance and action? What are the fundamental values that define Bêrîtan's legacy today?




An ideology and a commitment to freedom embraced even at the cost of one's life have the power to leave indelible marks on history. Humanity's struggle for freedom, which has continued for thousands of years and passed through different stages, has been engraved in history and in the collective memory of peoples through the martyrs who sacrificed their lives and the sacred blood shed for this cause. No amount of oppression or persecution has ever been able to erase that memory. Countless freedom fighters, known and unknown, who rebelled against the slavery, oppression and indignity imposed on much of humanity, refusing to submit or accept a meaningless existence, constitute the driving forces and enduring values of historical progress. In our age, dominant powers have used science and technology to make their policies of alienation, erasure of memory and destruction of identity increasingly sophisticated and deeply entrenched. Yet humanity can still speak of freedom, dignity, beauty and justice. This is thanks to the efforts made in pursuit of these ideals and the values created by the martyrs of freedom. Otherwise, humanity would long ago have been reduced to a mass of robots.




In this sense, the most decisive forces standing in the way of the ruling powers' objectives are the unwavering commitment to freedom, embraced even at the cost of life, the struggle to create meaning, and the mountain-hearted martyrs who lived with dignity. In the history of our struggle, the legacy of martyrdom extending from Haki, Mazlum, Egîd, Zîlan and Bêrîtan to the present day has been created by heroes who refused to bow to any form of oppression and accepted nothing less than a free life. Each of them represents an example of heroism, overcoming the most difficult paths of struggle by leading from the front and illuminating the way with both their minds and their hearts.




Bêrîtan, the rebellious daughter of Dersim and the embodiment of our dignity and freedom, became a legend through both her life and her martyrdom. Bêrîtan's cry for freedom from the edge of the cliff echoed everywhere, from South Kurdistan to the major cities of Turkey, reaching countless people and inspiring hundreds of young women and men. Bêrîtan deepened our awareness of the need to oppose the nationalist-chauvinist line, while strengthening our commitment to freedom, rebellion and the refusal to surrender. She was among those who understood the Leadership (Abdulah Öcalan) most profoundly and who, with her determined and persistent character, sought to put that understanding into practice. She had joined the struggle inspired by the image of Besê, who threw herself from a cliff during the Dersim uprising. Bêrîtan carried a deep love of history and her homeland in her heart. Following Besê's path and footsteps, she became a free spirit and a powerful mind capable of spreading its wings over the cliffs. All our martyrs and all the values of resistance created throughout the history of our struggle formed the foundation upon which YJA Star was built. Comrade Bêrîtan's path of self-sacrifice, her determination to persevere in guerrilla life and the pursuit of freedom, and her identity as a dignified and free woman who devoted herself entirely to the cause of liberation embody the values upon which YJA Star is founded. Reorganising and developing the struggle along Bêrîtan's path will be a historic step towards achieving victory and shaping a new way of life, as well as women and men, capable of fulfilling the need for freedom.




How has the women's armed organisation developed along Bêrîtan's path changed over the past 33 years? How should we assess the progress YJA Star has made since its establishment?




Every living phenomenon in nature passes through stages of change while maintaining an internal consistency with its purpose and way of life. This dialectic also applies to human societies and the institutions and concepts they create. Something that can no longer change has lost its vitality and is either dead or approaching death. The women's armed organisation that emerged in Kurdistan around clearly defined ideological objectives has also undergone a process of transformation in keeping with this dialectic of nature and society. Our free women's units linked the development of their national identity directly to the pursuit of freedom from the very beginning. They maintained this principle throughout every stage of their development. For this reason, they have consistently struggled against reactionary, traditional and dominant ideologies. The question was never confined to the Kurdish national struggle. Instead, the emphasis was on developing the principles of freedom and justice for Kurdish and women's identities, both of which had been subjected to denial and destruction, within the framework of socialist ideology. Developing the women's freedom struggle around these principles made significant contributions to struggles around the world, including socialist movements, and created an entirely new experience.




The emergence of women's armed organisation as such a distinctive and original experience within the historical and cultural context of the Middle East was primarily made possible by Öcalan, his constant questioning and creative approach, and the martyrs who devoted themselves selflessly to the path he set out. Öcalan expressed this very powerfully when he said, “A new world is being born around women.” The importance of this organisation is undoubtedly multidimensional, both in overcoming the problems women face and in creating personalities and identities capable of serving as models for society.




No matter how much dominant historical narratives have attempted to erase women, their history and their culture from collective memory, the more we learn about our own history, the more clearly we see that women's history is a living history that has never been completely erased from language or memory. This search and rediscovery have emerged, and continue to develop, through difficult struggles, evolutionary and revolutionary processes, and tremendous sacrifices. Despite the oppressive, destructive and annihilating nature of patriarchal ideology, there has always been a tradition of women's resistance that has persisted with all its vitality and diversity, even when it was unnamed or excluded from official records. Our martyrs, who represent our historical roots and stand as monuments to life and resistance, are among the most important forces illuminating the darkness created by a system of domination that has turned the contradictions within life, between women and men, and in nature into seemingly impossible knots. The more we understand our history, the more deeply we understand the present, strengthen our love for women and humanity, and take firmer steps towards the future and freedom.




Our courageous commander, comrade Bêrîtan, embodied extraordinary simplicity, honesty, sensitivity, courage, intellectual depth and a profound search for meaning. Both the nature of her action and her diaries reveal remarkable courage in the way she approached and interpreted herself, society and the circumstances of her time. Comrade Bêrîtan's dignified stance against betrayal and surrender deepened the women's freedom struggle, both in terms of individual development and organisational progress. The women's freedom struggle grew through this tradition of resistance. This was not simply because of the forms of action undertaken, but also because of the passion for freedom, love of humanity and depth of consciousness embodied in the characters of our martyrs. This is a love of freedom. It is a love that transcends ordinary forms of love, centred on freedom, love for society, being oneself, living a meaningful life, becoming a dignified woman and developing the consciousness needed for victory. It represents a transformation from women whose will has been suppressed by the dominant patriarchal system, who have been alienated from themselves and confined to narrow worlds, into free women who possess their own identities and willpower. These women become capable of developing solutions to problems ranging from social issues to questions of gender, embracing the creative and life-giving universe within themselves with profound love. Like many pioneering women throughout history, the women martyrs of our struggle represent this lineage of free women driven by love. They are symbols of the rebirth of the goddess.




At the present stage of our women's freedom struggle, living, struggling and developing an identity in the spirit of Zîlan and Bêrîtan will bring success. The keys to victory and freedom are hidden in their characters. What matters is that we listen to their hearts with our own hearts and understand their minds with our intelligence. Only then can we make freedom and victory a lived reality.




What role does YJA Star play today, not only as a military force but also in women's organisation and self-defence? What are the most important achievements of its 33 years of experience?




The free women's units in Kurdistan were never organised solely as a military force. The very purpose of establishing women's armed organisation was defined as building a world without armies. A world without armies means a world without domination, inequality or injustice. The aim of free women's guerrilla organisation is to create a model of free life. Our women's defence forces in Kurdistan were organised, first and foremost, as a force safeguarding the values created through 33 years of struggle, as well as our Leadership, our martyrs and our people. A force organised on these foundations must, above all, understand and embrace the immense responsibilities, sacrifices and moral obligations that this entails.




It is equally essential to reflect deeply on how these responsibilities can best be fulfilled and what must be done to achieve this. For our women's defence forces, interpreting the political and military developments of the current process as effectively as possible and developing strong responses to them carries both historical and immediate significance. Our Leadership has always entrusted the women's defence forces of Kurdistan with major responsibilities. For this reason, achieving success is a debt we owe to life itself. A militant approach capable of responding appropriately to the expectations of our people, our Leadership and the current process is essential. Conscious struggle, carried out with a clear understanding of one's responsibilities and in the service of the democratic society paradigm, is the fundamental principle for fulfilling the tasks and responsibilities of this period. If the Peace and Democratic Society Process is approached in this way, success will leave its mark on the destiny of the Kurdish people and women, and no force will be able to prevent it.
