author: Unknown
title: Leonardo Caffo - The “enemy” isn’t in the streets. It’s what sends you there
content:
Author

: Leonardo Caffo

Title

: The “enemy” isn’t in the streets. It’s what sends you there




 From France to Albania, from Belgium to Turin, the protests of these days stage a clash between metaphors. Young people (the people) and police officers (the State), equally precarious, face each other as if the other were the enemy. But the enemy stopped living where we look for it long ago. And that is precisely where it organizes the anger, makes it visible and summons it into the street. 




 Let me say this right away, to leave no room for misunderstanding: the young people who have been filling the streets of Europe in recent weeks have every right to do so. This is not a rhetorical concession, one of those premises you write only to take back three lines later. They have reasons to spare: schools falling apart, overcrowded classrooms, a future shrinking like a room whose walls someone moves at night while we sleep. Anyone who dismisses them as vandals, as spoiled children of a prosperity they no longer know, or as puppets of some hidden director, has understood nothing. Or pretends not to understand, which is worse. But precisely because they are right, and precisely because their distress is real, it is worth asking the question nobody seems willing to ask these weeks. Not because it is difficult, but because it is uncomfortable for everyone: for governments, for movements, for newspapers, for commentators. The question is simple. Against whom are they protesting? In favor of what? 




 There is no point asking against 

what

. The what is clear, even too clear: the cuts, the cost of living, the decrees, the war that swallows resources, the idea that school should serve the labor market rather than people, impossible rents. But where does the power that produces all this live, if it lives anywhere at all? Because a protest without an addressee is not an absence of politics: it is a politics someone else is doing in your place, using your body, your time, your anger. 




I. The scene: a Europe that always ends up in the same frame




 Let us look at the images before interpreting them. In France the mobilization began in September in Brittany, in the schools, against staff shortages and the decay of public education, and spread across the whole country. On October 6, according to the Interior Ministry, more than 250,000 people were in the streets; according to the organizers, almost twice that. The toll of weeks of protest runs to thousands of arrests and hundreds injured, among students, teachers and officers. In Lens a fifteen-year-old boy lost a hand after coming into contact with a police grenade. In Brussels, on October 9, unions striking against budget cuts were joined by hundreds of students inspired by what was happening in France. A few dozen masked protesters threw stones at the police; the police responded with tear gas and water cannons; twenty-one people were detained, thirteen of them minors. In Albania, the student protest outside the Ministry of Education on October 13 turned within hours into a revolt against the Rama government: the Ministry of Justice in flames, attacks on public buildings, banks and businesses, 89 injured, 61 of them officers. 




 And then Italy. On October 16 thousands of students marched in every city against the school decree, the cap on foreign pupils in classrooms, the 4+2 model for technical institutes, the cost of living, military spending. In Milan, a river of second-generation young people, born here or arrived as children, forming a shield against those who would like to count them. In Rome, bottles and firecrackers outside the ministry. In Bologna, shields in front of the station. In Turin, stones against officers, water cannons against students, and in between some teachers who placed themselves between the two lines, as their French colleagues had done a few days earlier. You don’t need to be a sociologist to notice that the causes are different, and so are the contexts, and yet the final frame is always the same. A kid in a hood facing a kid in a helmet. The protest is born against something enormous and undefined, a social model, a stolen future, a politics that does not listen. And it ends, with almost mechanical regularity, in hand-to-hand combat between two people who have never met and have no personal reason to hate each other. 




 This frame is the real political subject under discussion today. Not because the clash is the heart of the matter: on the contrary, I argue that it is peripheral. But because that frame is a symptom, in the precise sense the word has in psychoanalysis: a compromise formation that shows and hides at the same time. It shows that there is a conflict. It hides who is really party to it. And the media, who love that frame because it brings in viewers, only amplify its function as a screen. Even the mayor of Turin said so, with unexpected lucidity: there are those who use those images to talk only about the clashes, leaving the problems the young people raise in the background. 




II. Two metaphors facing each other in a mirror




 Let us return to those two bodies. The student in the street is a metaphor: he stands for a generation whose future has been taken away, for a school turned into the antechamber of employment, for an existence that discovers itself precarious before it has even begun. But the police officer is a metaphor too. In fact, if you look closely, he embodies it even better. He is often young as well, almost always from the peripheries and the South, poorly paid for a hellish job that asks him to stand for hours under a hail of bottles to defend a ministry whose minister he will never meet. He too has watched his future shrink; he too is the product of a social model that offers a uniform as the only possible stability. The difference between the two is not one of class. It is one of position: one has been put in front, the other behind a shield.

title: Schplinky Donkanov - Infrastructure of Attack
content:
Author

: Schplinky Donkanov

Title

: Infrastructure of Attack

Subtitle

: To Kill and Sustain

Date

: May 2026







 Whatever is most enduring is ultimately overtaken in the ceaseless transformation of things. 




Roger Ames







 In the cycle of life and death,

 One third are the companions of life,

 One third are the companions of death,

 And one third again are people who, because of their preoccupation with staying alive,

 Move toward the execution ground with each and every step.

 Now why do they do this?

 Simply because of their preoccupation with staying alive. 




 I have heard it said that those who are good at holding on to life

 Do not steer clear of rhinos and tigers when travelling in the hills,

 And do not hide behind armor and shields when entering the fray.

 For the rhino finds nowhere to gore,

 The tiger nothing to sink its claws into,

 And the soldier nothing into which he can lodge his blade.

 How can this be so?

 Because there is not a whiff of the execution ground about them. 




Daodejing, Ch. 50




Coping With the Trouble




 I started writing this zine with one question in mind: “If the state is toppled, where the fuck am I getting my hormones?” Its stupid to think that making a stateless world would force me to detransition. As things currently stand, it’s also true. While there is some infrastructure in this country for drug production, according to the government “80% of the activities required to make the drugs sold in Canada are conducted in other countries”

[1]

. This means that even if the productive infrastructure we have was seized and operated correctly, being cut off from the global corporate-state apparatus would make acquiring the materials to manufacture many medicines difficult, if not impossible. 




 Technology is not neutral. This is as true of bio-tech as it is of tear gas and security cameras. The pathways through which we have developed modern medicine rely on resources found halfway across the globe, extracted through violence and exploitation. Getting beyond this state of affairs asks us to not only destroy what exists here and now, 

we also need to create technology that is aligned with our values and capable of meeting our needs

. Only we can create the structures to do that effectively. And while doing so will not free us, it can enable us to confront this world more effectively and expand what we are capable of as the global supply chain collapses. 




 When I started writing this zine, I wasn’t expecting to try and take a sober look at how climate change is likely to shape our world over the next 25 years. I’m not an expert, I don’t know the future, and frankly, thinking about it too much gives me the scaries. I, like most people, get all weird and wide-eyed and would much prefer to simply crawl into a hole, take a very long nap, and get on with living life as best as we can manage in this hellworld. Unfortunately for us, I don’t think we have that luxury. Continuing to stumble blind and unprepared towards an uncertain future is probably the wrong choice to make. That said, I think that the mind-boggling fear and uncertainty that arises in us when we look too closely is paralyzing and unhelpful. I think we should glance at it just long enough to properly inform our strategies, tactics, and actions, and then go dance and love and fuck and destroy until we come back to the presence of our bodies and can keep moving. My hope is that this zine encourages us to do just that. 




 It seems to me that we have about 25 years to invent answers to many difficult questions before the time and resources we need to create those answers becomes much more scarce. I don’t see this as reason to despair, I see this as fuel for joyous experimentation in living and destruction alongside those I love. I see this as an opportunity to train. An opportunity to cultivate the knowledge and skills that will give us an edge in a changing terrain, and to find pleasure in the novel ways we will find to take our freedom. The way ahead might be murky, but together we can find paths forward that this world has not yet seen. 




 A better world is possible. We choose to make it so. 




Principles for living and fighting




 The point of this zine is to argue that our struggle can develop a stronger offence if we put more energy into developing technologies that align with our values, and support us in adapting to the unpredictable effects of climate change. I believe that we not only need to be capable of hitting the state harder, we also need to be able to meet our needs without relying on state and corporate structures. 




 If technology isn’t neutral, then much of the technology we depend on has capitalist and authoritarian values embedded within them. The way we produce life-saving medicine for instance, depends on tightly controlled infrastructure made possible by fossil fuel extraction and global systems of exploitation. It also gives whoever controls that infrastructure immense power over those who depend on the medicine they produce. When power dynamics are created through the possession of essential material structures, power cannot be redistributed by simply taking control of that infrastructure. In my view, the clearest way to redistribute this power is by creating decentralized infrastructure, enabling people to create multiple lines of access to their medicine, or acquire what they need to make it themselves.

title: StudyCorgi - Anarchist Perspectives and the Sociological Imagination
content:
Author

: StudyCorgi

Title

: Anarchist Perspectives and the Sociological Imagination

Subtitle

: Exploring Complex Ideas

Date

: 15 January 2020

Notes

: Work Cited “Anarchist Perspectives and the Sociological Imagination: Exploring Complex Ideas.” StudyCorgi, 15 Jan. 2020, studycorgi.com/on-anarchist-squints-and-the-sociological-imagination/. Accessed 13 Oct. 2026. 

 This paper, “Anarchist Perspectives and the Sociological Imagination: Exploring Complex Ideas”, was written and voluntary submitted to our free essay database by a straight-A student. Please ensure you properly reference the paper if you’re using it to write your assignment. Before publication, the StudyCorgi editorial team proofread and checked the paper to make sure it meets the highest standards in terms of grammar, punctuation, style, fact accuracy, copyright issues, and inclusive language. Last updated: November 26, 2024.

Source

: https://studycorgi.com/




Introduction




 At first glance, it might seem that the two concepts – the anarchist squint and the sociological imagination – have almost nothing in common. 




 Although both concepts promise to drive humanity to a better future if implemented by people, there is a distinct difference in the main ideas: where sociological imagination aims to teach people to use their own experiences to address large social issues (Mills 5), the anarchist squint refers rather to the use of collective mind in solving global issues (Rathmann 232). 




 However, the fact that the two approaches address the importance of both the individual perspective and the community action allows finding the use for a combination of the two views. This essay aims to provide a broader definition of both the anarchist squint and the sociological imagination and to see the underlying similarities and differences that would allow for the employment of both concepts in ensuring a better future. 




Sociological Imagination




 The sociological imagination is an idea that was first introduced by C. Wright Mills, a prominent American sociologist, in 1959. In his book The Sociological Imagination, Mills describes the concept in depth while also suggesting the possible benefits that the implementation of sociological imagination would entail. 




 The author defines sociological imagination is the perspective that allows the person to view larger historical events and issues through the prism of his or her personal experiences and also to see his life and individual problems in the light of the current historical period (Mills 5). 




 According to Elwell, this was a significant drift from the approach used by the social science at the time, which targeted the development of society into an administratively approved form (par. 2), rather than the shape that would be beneficial for the development of humanity on a global scale. 




 Through the idea of sociological imagination, Mills addressed the structural and historical features of the community that significantly affect the views, values, actions, and motivations of the people who compose this community (Elwell par. 2). 




 According to Miller, sociological imagination involves a capacity to shift from one perspective to another across various religious, national, social, and cultural barriers (7), which makes it is an important tool to address the issues not just within one community, but across the world. 




Anarchist Squint




 Despite the fact that many people perceive anarchism as a socially destructive notion, which is chaotic and unreasonable in its aggressiveness, the anarchist squint, developed by Scott, is yet another viewpoint that could be adopted to improve people’s lives in general, especially in relation to the individual’s freedom of choice. 




 Scott admits that he adopted one of the main ideas that contributed to the development of this concept from a Russian philosopher Mikhail Bakunin’s statement “Freedom without socialism is privilege and injustice; socialism without freedom is slavery and brutality” (xi). 




 And, even though the Russian’s statement implies communistic ideas through the rejection of the “privilege,” Scott’s final concept goes beyond that, creating a framework of vision for the global community with the end goal of achieving a better, freer society. 




 As opposed to the more traditional anarchistic notions, Scott’s anarchist squint does not reject the state entirely: “While he occasionally expresses regret that the state’s elimination is probably impossible, more typically he denies any desire to get rid of the state” (Stone 8). 




 Scott insists that the state is not the only source of social problems and that other factors need to be addressed in the anarchist squint: “Nor do I believe that the state is the only institution that endangers freedom. To assert so would be to ignore a long and deep history of pre-state slavery, property in women, warfare, and bondage” (xiv). 




 Overall, anarchist squint implies looking at the history of various movements and states from the point of view of an anarchist. Scott believes that such an approach would promote “the ideas of mutuality, non-hierarchical cooperation and freedom to learn from one’s own mistakes” (King par. 8). 




Similarities and Differences




 Despite the fact that initially, the two concepts seem to have almost nothing in common, some similarities are indeed fundamental to them. 




 For instance, both the sociological imagination and the anarchist squint are based on adopting a certain viewpoint that emphasizes the connection between large issues and smaller ones, either focusing on an individual or the community. 




 By employing this technique, both concepts promote the empowerment of an individual and stress the influence of every person in society on the issues they intend to address. 




 Another similar idea that is present in both viewpoints is the idea of unity. Scott sees the community as one of the key contributors to freedom: “Forms of informal cooperation, coordination, and action that embody mutuality without hierarchy are the quotidian experience of most people” (Scott xxi). Mills, on the other hand, does not openly proclaim cooperation.

title: Wahono Karyadi & Matsutake - Anarchist Archives: Critique & Self-Critique #1.1
content:
Author

: Wahono Karyadi & Matsutake

Title

: Anarchist Archives: Critique & Self-Critique #1.1

Date

: 2026

Notes

: Anarchist Archives: Critique & Self-Critique—will be written and published periodically—is a space for those running the Archipelago Anarchist Archive to engage in critical reflection.

Source

: Retrieved on October 14, 2026 from https://archive.org/details/@archipelago-anti-authoritarian-archive




 Printed and published (or even unpublished) works—such as books, pamphlets, leaflets, and zines—hold a significant place among anarchists. This is because such media have proven capable of preserving the diverse experiences and thoughts of many individuals; in certain cases, even if there is an intervention targeting these printed materials, their existence will endure—if not be eternal—longer than the lifespans of the individuals who lived through those experiences and produced those ideas. And the individuals who have fully preserved these printed and published words will subsequently receive a benefit, such as having access to revisit past “practices for reaching emancipation” (movements and struggles). 




 That is why, according to Baker (2023) in his study of Spanish anarchist counterculture—or the process of evolutionary change—many anarchist libraries were established to provide access to a comprehensive collection of printed works that had long gone out of print. Unfortunately, the history of the growth of this counterculture—or the process of anarchist evolutionary change—did not proceed smoothly in Indonesia; in fact, it came to a standstill. This was because Indonesia endured a prolonged period of authoritarianism—in its harshest form. The anarchists of the 1920s were exiled to Digul following the 1926 uprising; meanwhile, individuals with (anarcho-)syndicalist leanings who emerged in the 1940s were forcibly removed by Sukarno’s Old Order regime from the factories they had self-managed and were gradually pushed out of the intellectual sphere by the PKI; their very existence became completely untraceable following the 1965 genocide and the rise of Suharto’s New Order regime to power (Bima, 2018). 




 However, this prolonged period of authoritarianism was not unique to anarchists in Indonesia. The prolonged period of harsh authoritarianism—namely, the Communist regimes of Gheorghe Gheorghiu-Dej (1948–1965; 17 years) and Nicolae Ceaușescu, meant that anarchists in Romania and Indonesia shared—without denying the differences in the impacts of the post-communist era in Romania versus the post-colonial and post-military-authoritarian eras in Indonesia, which created complex distinctions—a commonality in the historical development of their anarchist cultures. This is because when the communist regime came to power, anarchists were marginalized—ranging from having their movements suppressed to being killed—and those who survived had to go into exile abroad or, if they remained in Romania, chose to go completely underground (Anarhiva, 2021). This situation ultimately meant that the anarchists who emerged in Romania during the collapse of the communist regime in 1989 or afterward—the majority of whom were active in the anarcho-punk scene— had only a fragmentary understanding—or none at all—of the anarchists who existed before them, meaning they automatically lacked a collective experience to draw upon when practicing anarchist or anti-authoritarian principles (Tataran, 2026). 




 In line with Adrian Tataran, Ucok (2026) also made a nearly identical point during a discussion of the book Unfinished Nation held at the Bunga di Tembok Library. According to him, before Bima Satria Putra’s book Perang yang Tidak Akan Kita Menangkan was published—long after the Reformation—in 2018, the anarchists who emerged—and just like in Romania, many of whom were also active in the anarcho-punk scene—during the fall of Suharto and his New Order regime and the period that followed had no knowledge of earlier anarchist movements, so it briefly crossed their minds that they were the first generation of anarchists in Indonesia. Consequently, lacking the experience and collective memory passed down from earlier anarchists, these later-emerging anarchists had to start from scratch; in stark contrast, the authoritarian regime—though said to have collapsed—already possessed a bureaucracy, structures, and a military that had been built up over decades, were well-established, and ready to be handed down, making it no difficult task for them to return to the seat of power. 




 Drawing on that experience, Ucok said that it is important to launch an initiative to preserve collective memory, so that gaps in historical memory can be prevented and future generations can learn by looking back at history. This collective memory preservation initiative itself can take various forms, with shared responsibilities; for example—in the context of reading—some may collaborate to document and publish, while others discuss and put it into practice, only to have those insights documented and republished. In my view, in addition to the initiatives to publish, discuss, and put into practice—which many friends have already undertaken—archives efforts are essential for documentation and, furthermore, for the preservation of historical memory itself. 




 *** 




 Archives initiatives, particularly community-driven ones (community archives), have in fact been emerging in large numbers and are flourishing. We can say, broadly speaking, that community archives in Indonesia itself has experienced three waves of growth. The first wave was marked by several community archives that emerged in the post-Reform era through 2010, including the Indonesian Visual Art Archive, Warung Arsip/Radio Buku, and KUNCI. The second wave was marked by the emergence of archives initiatives between 2011 and 2021, including—to name a few—Bebaskan Buku!, Perpustaxaan, Ruang Arsip & Sejarah Perempuan, and Queer Indonesia Archive. Meanwhile, the third wave is characterized by archives initiatives that emerged from 2022 to the present, such as Jogja Sonic Index, Pustaka Taratsa (if they can even be categorized as an archive), Pustaka Langka/Logos, Catatan Nusantara, and Puss in Bed Zine Library.

title: Nolan Peltz - Prison, Persecution, and Resistance
content:
Author

: Nolan Peltz

Title

: Prison, Persecution, and Resistance

Subtitle

: The Case of Miguel Peralta

Date

: January 29, 2026

Notes

: 

Translated from Peltz, Nolan, “Prisión, persecución y resistencia. El caso de Miguel Peralta Betanzos”,

 Avispa Midia

, 29 January

, 2026. https://avispa.org/prision-persecucion-y-resistencia-el-caso-de-miguel-peralta-betanzos/ Part of a series of translations in solidarity with Miguel Peralta from a little corner in Chicago known as Blood Fruit Library

Source

: Retrieved 10/19/2026 from https://www.patreon.com/bloodfruit/posts/prison-and-case-165958672




 Miguel Peralta, a community defender and anarchist, exited the Cuicatlán, Oaxaca prison more than six years ago. His original arrest happened on April 2015, and on October 2018 he was sentenced to 50 years in prison for two charges, one of homicide and another of attempted homicide. 




 After an intense legal battle and political pressure, he managed to appeal the sentence. A year later, on October 14, 2019, after almost a month-long hunger strike, Peralta was finally absolved of all the charges and released from prison. In all, he spend a little under 4 years and six months behind bars due to fabricated charges brought against him. 




 Miguel’s arrest came following a sociopolitical conflict that erupted into violence on December 14, 2014 in the Eloxochitlán de Flores Magón municipality in Oaxaca when the Community Assembly was attacked by a violent armed group headed by the petty warlord Manuel Zepeda Cortés. In the conflict that followed, two people lost their life and many were left injured. This attack, although headed and orchestrated by Manuel Zepeda, was used as a pretext to persecute members of the Community Assembly. Thirty five community members were initially charged in the case number 10/2015, and other charges were brought against other members later. Many community members, Miguel Peralta among them, ended up spending time behind bars and, although they are all free now, the persecution against the community members continues on, for more than ten years now. 




 Miguel’s father, Pedro Peralta, had previously been detained on August 10, 2012 when he was taking part in communal work in Eloxochitlán de Flores Magón, Oaxaca. When he was apprehended, he was beaten and tortured. Pedro Peralta spent nearly three years in the Cuicatlán, Oaxaca prison, even spending some weeks alongside his son behind bars before being released on July 30, 2015. 




 Behind the repression and criminalization in Eloxochitlán, there are direct ties between the local petty warlords and State power, including the weaponizing of the legal system against the community defenders. Local petty warlord, Manuel Zepeda, municipal president from 2011 and 2013, used municipal funds to enrich himself, and also extracted stone, sand, and gravel from the community river, materials that furnished his stores and which he in turn sold to carry out municipal projects. When community members raised their voice against his authoritarianism, the theft of community funds, and the ecological destruction of the community, he resorted to flagrant violence. 




 His daughter, Elisa Zepeda Lagunas, used the 2014 conflict as a political springboard, climbing up the hierarchy of public authority using the vocabulary of victimhood. She placed herself as municipal president in the 2017–2019 term before abandoning the position to run as local deputy for the MORENA political party. Since then, she’s been a local deputy, president of the Oaxaca Congress during the LXIV Congress Session, Secretary of Women under the Salomón Jara government, and presently, serves a second term as a local deputy for the MORENA political party. Thanks to her political contacts and power, she has mobilized the repressive State apparatus against members of the community. 




 Indomitable Resistance




 Miguel Peralta’s criminalization, incarceration, and persecution is the aftermath of his struggle for the autonomy and land defense of his community, Eloxochitlán de Flores Magón. Miguel has been an important voice in the condemnation against natural resource extraction and the petty warlord-ism of the Zepeda Lagunas family. He has also been an important voice in the struggle for the community’s autonomy and self-determination against the power grab of petty warlords and political parties alike. The criminalization against him is a direct outcome of his resistance and, despite this, it has not managed to silence his voice. 




 As a prisoner, Miguel Peralta actively took part in the struggle against prisons, in solidarity with other imprisoned men and women and communities in resistance, and for the freedom of his Eloxochitlán de Flores Magón comrades. Between September and October in 2016, Miguel Peralta took part in intermittent fasts in solidarity with a hunger strike launched by anarchist prisoners in Mexico City condemning the prison conditions and the oppressive role of prisons on society. 




 In October 2018, after his first final hearing, Miguel Peralta went on a hunger strike demanding his complete freedom and declaring his body as a weapon of war against incarceration. in March 2019, Miguel Peralta went on a fast in solidarity with indigenous prisoners in Chiapas who had launched a hunger strike demanding their liberty after being false accused under torture. Later, in October 2019, the day of his second final hearing, he went on another hunger strike that lasted 26 days and ended in his release. 




 Beyond hunger strikes and fasts, Miguel Peralta actively participated in discussions and debates around indigenous autonomy, land defense, and against prisons and prison society, taking part in activities organized outside of prison via recordings and writings. He has released statements and analysis dealing with the anniversary of Ricardo Flores Magón’s murder, October 2

nd

 and the Tlatelolco Massacre of ’68, June 11

th

 and the Day of Solidarity with Marius Mason and All Long-Term Anarchist Prisoners, among other subjects. He also organized activities in jail together with other prisoners, in search of spaces of autonomy and self-organization within a facility that sought absolute control and submission.

title: Sea // Fish - Prison Futures
content:
Author

: Sea // Fish

Title

: Prison Futures

Date

: 10/20/2026




Introduction




 Across Turtle Island the network of U.S. prisons stretch from edge to edge in a vast network. The proliferation of prisons across the occupied land gestures towards the racial ordering of the settler society’s long project of of colonialism and coloniality. With the advent of European settlers on Abya Yala and Turtle Island two significant constituent elements emerged. That being the confluence of multiple modes of productions in unison around the accumulation of capital by European settlers, these modes took the form slavery, serfdom, and salaried labor. With this was the sociogenic imposition, codification, and reification of race as both a biological and hierarchical ordering (Quijano 2000: 216). This historical process of human ordering—in the productive and ideological forces—is the coloniality of power. Colonialism begets a global, and specifically trans-Atlantic consideration. With the transferring of capital to the European metropoles colonial projects and the coloniality of power cross germinate into local formulations of race, hence the local construals of race require global considerations (Pierre 2013: 1). I argue that people in prison utilize communication with the outside world to challenge their position as colonial subjects under global white supremacy, and in doing so exercise their agency as counter-normative spatial politics. To do so, I trace the writings of Kuwasi Balagoon and Malik Muhammad as they exercises agency under incarceration and counter the stability of inside/outside through action and communications. 




 Understanding and parsing the U.S. prison system requires attending to the colonial context they emerged in. The ethnic cleansing, genocide, and forced serfdom of Indigenous people of Turtle Island/Abya Yala by Europeans transformed the land into the Americas and in doing so capitalism emerged for the first time. Through the violent force of European settlers, the labor of all Others was aligned in the accumulation of capital (Quijano 2000: 219). The forced migration of Afrikan communities to the newly transfigured Americas as enslaved laborers produced, not only the commodities that made the European and settled metropoles wealthy but also, the bottom of stratified racial taxonomy to which Europeans became white, Indigenous peoples Indian, and Afrikan peoples Black (McKittrick 2013: 3; Quijano 2000: 219; Wynter 2003: 309). Intimately bound to the transformation of Afrikan peoples into a racialized as Black population on occupied Turtle Island is the colonial experience of Afrikan peoples in Afrika. Specifically, in the modes of production and the social formulations under European plantocracies. The economic production of “native labor” being that of agrarian serfdom for Afrikan peoples in Afrika racialized as native, African, and Black (Pierre 2013: 24, 40, 50), specifically recalls the modes of production of Afrikan people on Turtle Island post-emancipation as sharecroppers. 




 In Sylvia Wynter’s “Black Metamorphosis”, the transition out of plantation production to sharecropping is marked by this racial and geographic transformation. Wynter identifies that under capitalism, invented by European colonization of Turtle Island/Abya Yala, three zones of labor control existed that of the peripheral plantation economy, the semi-peripheral serfdom economy, and the wage labor economy exclusive to the core (151). It is thus that from the transition of enslavement to post-emancipation labor configurations to which the labor of Afrikan peoples on Turtle Island became native laborers in the colonial configuration shifting from peripheral to semi-peripheral (Ibid.). With this was Jim Crow, the indirect rule built on bifurcated legal constructions of apartheid, was the continuity of slave laws which reified the Black subject position as human Other (153–154). With the transition of Black labor as enslaved chattel labor to native labor the transition from human animal to human Other implicated the Black subject as a contradictory human, one who was now minimally human, but whose labor must be devalued to maintain the coloniality of power (162–163). 




 This important historical transition of productive forces in the U.S. underscores the transition from Plantation Archipelago to the Archipelago of Human Others, in this is the Prison Archipelago (Wynter 2003: 321,329; Wynter 1970s: 372). Through the coloniality of power, the sharecropping mode of production encroached upon the status of human, dominated by Man as white bourgeoise, and thus access to value of human labor. But as Wynter described the Black subject position was implicated by Jim Crow, as indirect rule, to devalue the labor of Black sharecroppers. In doing so the Prison Archipelago’s growing (in numbers of people) and expanding (across land) since emancipation, is constructed as poverty producers rather than capital producers (Wynter 2003: 329). It is through the social relationships developed by 300 years of plantation economy which would emerge with capitalism as global structures of labor and social organizations (Wynter 1970s: 390–391).

title: Mistral - Iolaus’ Lament
content:
Author

: Mistral

Title

: Iolaus’ Lament

Subtitle

: or Why You Should Move to the Country

Date

: 2020

Source

: PDF provided by librarian




 







Iolaus provided essential help to Heracles in his battle against the Hydra, his second labor. Seeing that Heracles was being overwhelmed by the multi-headed monster (the Lernaean Hydra), who grew two heads in place of each one cut off, Iolaus helped by cauterizing each neck as Heracles beheaded it.







Beginning




 We deny our bodies. We deny each other. We deny ourselves to this world. 




 Cross the river from New Orleans and drive the highway southwest to the edge of the city, to the receding boundary between empire and the wild. The air thickens as the swamp enfolds you in its warm breath. The chemical lawns of poisoned people and cheap geometric boredom, which just a few miles back dominated the landscape, are now intrusions upon it. The swelling symphony of insects crescendos as a blue heron perched at the edge of a property line cranes her head to dark water. Spanish moss sways in a light breeze, almost dripping, over a trio of turtles on a log. Sufficiently warmed by the sun, they plop one by one into the cool bayou. 




 You drive, the car belching exhaust, the engine increasingly alone as its stertorous roars become faint metallic whines, as its mechanized brethren are left behind. A family in a blue SUV is the last to pass. The screaming children in the back are the eternal return of our condition. 




 You accelerate, the scene out your window transitioning like a flipbook: new-finished homes becoming the naked frames of future ones, then Lot For Sale signs, then the fresh stumps of clear cuts, then finally unscathed groves of bald cypress and tupelo and the homes of a kaleidoscope of creatures, from the mycelia in the wet soil to the birds nesting in snags. Fog lifts into stratus clouds, leaving dewdrop whispers on elephant ears and cattails. 




 Now you and the road are what do not belong—the last remaining markers of the living death; you are in a hermetic capsule looking out, a reluctant emissary of this culture. The faster you go, the harder you try to flee, the more strenuous and stubborn your resistance, the more impossible it seems to defy. 




 When you trace this moment, this progressive frontier, back to where you came from in the city somewhere, you realize that today’s boundary is essentially the same one that delimited the crude settlement on the bank of the Mississippi River in 1718—which in the beginning only extended from the river to Rampart Street, the wilderness a great mystery beckoning beyond the wall. There are no words to describe the voracious inertia of our appetite. You realize that this is the same partition as the ramparts that were taken down after the Natchez were subdued and the marais was drained—when the fledgling settlement became a city; it is the same line as it was when the Americans came, and their development flowed upriver of Canal Street before expanding radially in unimpeded degradation—ramifying, eroding. And it is the same boundary, the same corrupted ovule, that sprouted in the Greater Antilles in 1492, Jamestown in 1607, Plymouth in 1620, Hawaii in 1778, and a thousand times elsewhere long before, when the mother countries had been wild: as when France was Gaul and tribes there fought against Caesar’s incursions. The natural world splintered where profitable, and in-waiting where there is not yet a dollar to be made or power to be accrued. 




 And constantly surrounding, impinging, from the maws of billboards to the mouths of intimates, are the cacophonous signs and symbols declaring 

Never Better!

 or 

A Work in Progress!

 or 

We Have Arrived!

 and all the other deceptions, proclamations of supremacy, and self-celebrations that reverberate over the increasingly silenced wild. 




 It is more tangible than any ideology when your throat tightens in the humidity, more profound than any philosophy when the wipers cannot cut through the misting blur. It is so much deeper than politics when the car pulls over, when the head lowers into the hands, when you concede it is tears that fall and run in rivulets. 




 You sit there on the gravel shoulder, pathetic and choking on what we have done and soon will do—the limitless depth of it all. The car takes you here or there, it does not matter. This newly built home is the desert of the Fertile Crescent; this Wolmanized wooden frame is the paved forests of Europe; this real estate plot is the pasture of the Amazon; this clear cut is the soy horizon. This fecund meadow is tomorrow’s photograph of what once was here and who we could have been. 




Symbolic Expiation




 This is for those who see what we have done and are doing to our home, to each other and to ourselves. For those who daily carry this weight and know there is no resolving it, no matter the lies repeated or prayed, the outcome of the next election or how educated or empowered the population is. For those who cannot settle with the easy justifications, the convenient explanations, the self-absolving blaming of others or the cowardly fall-backs. This is for those who know that the real answers do not lie within the parameters allowed to us, like voting, purchasing, protesting, posting and rioting.

Author

: SA

Title

: On Political Ecosystems

Date

: August 5 2026

Source

: Retrieved on 2026-10-21 from 

<organisemagazine.org.uk/2026/08/05/on-political-ecosystems>




 We recently had a few members of National Rebirth in Preston. They popped up with a table and some of their fascy literature and ugly flags, and attempted some conversations with passers by. They were spotted by members of our local antifascist ecosystem, who took photos, shared information in community group chats, and observed. 




 I wasn’t there at the time. Being a more militant organism in our local ecosystem, I would have happily gone down and told them to get the fuck back to whatever rock they crawled out from under and never return. We had a brief chat in one of our groups and opinions on National Rebirth are mixed: some consider them to not be much of a threat, or not a serious threat, but I am not so sure. 




 I took a look at their website and was particularly surprised to find some very transparent writings about their aims, strategies, and branch goings-on. All veiled with the usual fascist dogwhistles and indirections of course. There is one article in particular I found very interesting, and which I want to deconstruct here. 




 In “The Nationalist Ecosystem – It DOES exist, and it is a curse, not a blessing”, Grand Wizard Alek Yerbury develops an analysis of the disconnects between ‘nationalist’ activists and local communities. To briefly summarise Yerbury’s argument, he views “protests, demonstrations and street movements” and “‘Auditing’, ‘Youtubing’, and ‘Streaming’” as “staple activities of this nationalist ecosystem” which is ultimately doing nothing but perpetuating itself, and will “never develop into real political power”. Having recently read D. Hunter’s “Chav Solidarity”, I was surprised to find some parallels with his analyses, of the disconnects between “capital heavy” activists and people who are poor, working class, or criminalised. Hunter makes similar observations of the anarchist and leftist ecosystems from the other side, as a member of a local community trying to participate in what is in effect somebody else’s political ecosystem. He talks about escaping from a violent and racist upbringing, only to find countless activists and activist groups unable to engage with him or people like him with anything but contempt. As he puts so eloquently: 







 I believe that the working class in this country has been thoroughly stratified, in a way which makes revolutionary change almost impossible, but I believe this can be repaired. It requires those who sit at the top of the pile to understand that they are living off bread crumbs, and in many cases I think they do, but what isn’t recognized enough is that when they catch bread crumbs, others are going without. And for sure, we should want the whole fucking loaf, but people are gonna find it hard to fight for that loaf if they’re hungry and it’s gonna be even harder if they’re being told what to do by people who are keeping the crumbs they catch to themselves. 







 Both Yerbury and Hunter point to the ways political activists of all stripes cut themselves off from the very people outside of their movements that they want and need to bring into their movements. For Yerbury, the “parallel society” constituted by the far right’s organising activities are a distraction, “an echo chamber of pre-vetted, pre-screened people”. His point is that the internal cultures we develop through our collective practices might bring us closer together, but are also inherently exclusionary, forming shibboleths, and presenting barriers to audiences and potential new members, who must learn our language, so to speak. For Hunter, radical leftist spaces may preset themselves as inclusive, while also completely lacking all the individual and collective interpersonal and structural skills that are needed to actually include people who are different from us. Further, he shows how this situation is a deliberate construction of white supremacy, cisheteropatriarchy, capitalism, and the class system: 







 If I was unable to pay my rent or feed myself in a socially acceptable fashion, or sub-culturally acceptable by squatting and skipping, would I be treated in comradely fashion? Perhaps. But if I lived with the stress of going day to day without knowing where my next meal would come from or where I would sleep, would I behave in ways that would be acceptable? If I was still being told I was worthless, would I be able to interact with the social movements, filled with those who look, move and sound just like the social workers, judges and those whose houses I robbed. Some of this is in my head, but it was put there by lived experience, and I have witnessed countless interactions and exclusions between capital heavy activists and those struggling for basic survival. 







 Interestingly, both the fascist and Hunter come to similar conclusions on what is to be done. Although this is perhaps not surprising, as both anarchists and fascists tend towards material theories of power. Yerbury highlights the importance of local community activism at the neighbourhood level, and working with people locally across political divides, in order to demonstrate “the value of their ideology”. I find it interesting that he doesn’t consider how that kind of work actually directly refutes all of their fascy nonsense. He continues by connecting local and neighbourhood organising to the typical fascist strategy of “taking power” by also advocating for his troopers to also get involved with community and local government meetings and the like.

content:
Author

: Tom Nomad

Title

: Toward an Army of Ghosts

Subtitle

: Immanence, Conflict and Crisis

Date

: 2017

Source

: PDF provided by publisher




 




 To Emma, the love of my life,

 you’re amazing and you always will be. 




Introduction




 Almost four years ago, when 

Master’s Tools

 was released, I had embarked on a distinct philosophical and political project, one that had grown out of the lessons from past experiences, and that did not have a determinate destination. This project was born as much out of frustration and failure as it was out of a certain conceptual interest and political desire. What was clear at the beginning of this project were the fundamental flaws in the categories we were using to make sense of action, and in our relationship to the space where action occurs. Paradoxical structures, fanciful notions, illusions, and utopian portrayals of our social and political milieu formed the basis of a political practice that was as much separated from the terrain of activity as were the liberals that we decried. Clearly we needed to at least throw out the latencies of the activist era, which we were discussing. But, for all the pages written about this—the problem of activism, the problems of conceptually-driven conflictual practice—all too often we seemed to be replicating the same categories in our attempts at transcendence. This current book is not some attempt to determine the way out of the morass of activism and ideology; it merely points out where some sparks may reside. 

Master’s Tools

 is largely a discussion of immediate questions surrounding tactics; on some level this is a companion text. Some of the ideas will seem familiar to those who have read other writings of mine, but what my earlier writing has not focused on is the larger conceptual context at the base of my previously published works. This has led to misunderstanding by some, and problematic readings by others—some going as far as to retreat into liberal concepts of the rejection of militarism as a form of superficial rejection. I hope that this text clears some of the air, and illuminates a different point of perspective on these earlier works. Though there will be some things in common (the structure of the state, the relationship of logistics to the collection of actions that we term the police) the structure of the discourse here functions in a different mode and exists for a different purpose. 




 These texts exist in relation to fundamentally different, yet intertwined, forms of life and tempos of existence. Previous texts were responses to an immediate question, one that was relevant when they were written. Specifically, they tried to articulate and address the failure of the tactics and methods that we were deploying. This mode of being was at a frenzied pace, with hectic risks, rewards, and activity. It was full of late night meetings, large distances traveled, and complicities formed: a life of immediacy. This formed a project to produce and distribute materials related to specific questions, first to a small group of people within direct proximity, which then leaked out into a wider, but still self-contained readership, and finally was compiled into 

Master’s Tools

 and became one of the foundations for the journal, 

Insurgencies

. It was to cut a line between the current approaches of the time, which were firmly rooted in activism, and address questions relevant to that space, while at the same time critiqueing that paradigm and pointing out some possibilities of escape. 




 The text that you hold, on the other hand, reflects the time in between, a mode of life constructed around study, quiet music, and intimately engaged conversations, stepping back, looking beyond reactionary polemics on some immediate question, and forming foundations to think about the questions themselves. The second project, begun concurrently to the first and proceeding in parallel, was to articulate the grounding for 

Master’s Tools

. Often relevant questions have emerged from those previously published writings, such as the rejection of utopianism, the rejection of activism, the rejection of political absolutism, morality, and the structure of absolute meaning. These questions are left open by much of the post-left literature written within the Western context. This book attempts to address a specific question—what are the implications of a distinctly materialist approach to the foundations of politics—without falling into the trap of pretending to understand some sort of truth about the material, nor rejecting the role or importance of thought as a functioning structure. 




 Previous texts have brought up this question implicitly, but always framed through a discussion of tactics, or of making sense of action-based conflictual dynamics. This text departs from that. First, while previous texts focused on action within events identified as political, and as a result was framed by activism-centered discourse, here we look to a larger context. Second, a number of arguments present in past texts are engaged with here in much more detail, and with more care and nuance. This depth positions these arguments within the wider framework, one between thought and activity, as well as one rooted in a discourse of the ontology of statism.

title: Maureen Wright - Book Review: A Brave and Beautiful Spirit
content:
Author

: Maureen Wright

Title

: Book Review: A Brave and Beautiful Spirit

Date

: 2020

Source

: Women’s History Review. <

https://doi.org/10.1080/09612025.2020.1844413

>







A Brave and Beautiful Spirit: Dora Marsden 1882–1960

, Les Garner, Portland, OR, Union of Egoists, 2019 (first published 1990), 1–486 pp., £19.95 (pb), ISBN 978-1944651-14-5 







 The lives of women who refused to conform to the ‘Vicwardian’ stereotypes of femininity took many forms, but perhaps one of the most individual was that of Dora Marsden (1882–1960), scholar, Freethinker, Egoist and militant suffragette of the Women’s Social and Political Union (WSPU). Les Garner informs us that Emmeline Pethick-Lawrence, long-time Treasurer of the WSPU, wrote of Marsden in 1909 that her ‘brave and beautiful spirit’ exemplified the disposition most valued by the leaders and strategists of the organisation. Yet before too much time had passed, Marsden had left the WSPU behind, writing in a torrent of ‘hurt anger and not a little arrogance’ (122) that its leaders, the infamous Pankhurst women, were insensible to her independent style of regional organisation, and that she obstinately refused to comply with what she saw as their ‘autocratic’ demands. It was an opinion she held for the rest of her life, which came to its close in 1960 in the withdrawn isolation of a mental asylum in Dumfries. It was a tragic end to what, in many ways, was a tragic life. 




 The re-issue of Garner’s 1990 biography of Marsden by the Egoist Press is simply that, a re-issue. Garner writes in a new preface to the book that although it would have been ‘tempting … to … re-write’ (11) he chose not to, on the grounds that his current political activism would have suffered as a result of having to become ‘seldom seen’ (11) as he worked on the manuscript. The pun on the name ‘Seldom Seen’, the name of the Lake District residence Marsden occupied with her mother Hannah in the 1920s, was deliberate, but I feel the work involved would have been worthwhile, particularly in light of the excellent recent scholarship undertaken by Lucy Delap, Tanya Cheadle, Sheila Rowbotham and others on Freethinkers, Socialists and the feminist 

avant-garde

. Dora Marsden is a key figure among such pioneers and a re-write, penned in the midst of new discoveries of the twenty-first century, would have been both appropriate and timely. 




 Marsden was not alone among early twentieth-century feminist pioneers in finding Emmeline and Christabel Pankhurst’s WSPU guilty of moving away from its Radicalliberal and Socialist roots. She was also not alone in pursuing a life that, increasingly, questioned the relationship between the ‘personal and sexual life and social change’ (161). In common with her close friend, the bright and effervescent Mary Gawthorpe (regional Organiser of the WSPU in Leeds), Marsden rose from a poverty-blighted childhood, via the route of probationer and pupil-teacher to the role of an independent woman, earning her own living through teaching. At Owen’s College where she took her degree, she was in the orbit of likeminded women, including scientist Rona Robinson, Eva Gore-Booth and Theresa Billington. It was this ‘network of friends and sympathisers’ which proved ‘vital’ (63) to Marsden, both in the period of her suffragette activism and, latterly, while working on the 

Freewoman

 group of publications from 1912. Following graduation in 1903, Marsden gained her first teaching post in Leeds, later moving to Colchester and Manchester before becoming Headmistress at Altrincham Pupil-Teacher Centre in 1908. Garner informs his readers that Dora’s work had made her ‘well aware of the vast gulf between idealized concepts of women’s lives and reality’ (70), and it was for these reasons she became attracted to the suffrage movement. She was courageous, exceptionally determined and held ‘a strong belief in her own abilities’ (70), but these qualities led her away from the WSPU after only a few years. Ultimately, she also shied away from the designation ‘feminist’, her evolving philosophy leading her to embrace humanism, individualism (especially that form exemplified by the German postHeliganist Max Stirner) and a ‘keenly developed’ (209) egoism. 




 Marsden became the poster-girl of the WSPU; this was after one day in 1909 in which she endured such ‘rough treatment’ at police hands it was like being ‘in the thick of [a] battle’ (102–3). But even though she and Rona Robinson had been awarded the ‘Union’s Victoria Cross’ and Marsden had been sent to Southport as WSPU Organiser, the relationship soured between the physically diminutive Dora and WSPU Headquarters at Clements Inn. While in Southport Marsden’s health declined, but she was independently minded and refused to delegate her work when she became overloaded and ill. Her style of working became heavily criticised from the centre and, when the relationship finally fractured, it surprised no-one, least of all Marsden’s inner circle. In 1912, Marsden found herself bereft of employment and income and physically ill. She turned, as she always, to her mother Hannah for support, but on her recovery began to pursue the dream she had long held— to become a writer and commentator on social questions, in her periodicals 

The Freewoman

 (from 1911), 

The New Freewoman

 (1912) and 

The Egoist

 (1913). But her dreams of literary success turned to nightmares as her ‘elitism, arrogance and … bullying over-confidence’ (216) turned supporter after supporter (and publisher after publisher) away from the papers she sought to succour into success.

title: Aldo Santiago - The Political Persecution Against an Absolved Mazatec Indian, Miguel Peralta, Continues After 11 Years of Legal Battles
content:
Author

: Aldo Santiago

Title

: The Political Persecution Against an Absolved Mazatec Indian, Miguel Peralta, Continues After 11 Years of Legal Battles

Date

: July 13, 2026

Notes

: 

Translated from Santiago, Aldo, "Continúa persecución política contra Miguel Peralta, mazateco absuelto tras 11 años de lucha legal",

 Avispa Midia

, 13 July

, 

2026

. 

https://avispa.org/continua-persecucion-politica-contra-miguel-peralta-mazateco-absuelto-tras-11-anos-de-lucha-legal/

 Part of a series of translations in solidarity with Miguel Peralta from a little corner in Chicago known as Blood Fruit Library

Source

: Retrieved 10/19/2026 from https://www.patreon.com/bloodfruit/posts/new-transl-after-165960159




 Four days after the Oaxaca Third Criminal Division of High Court Justice absolved ex-political prisoner Miguel Peralta Betanzos, accused of homicide and attempted homicide, on March 6, deputy Elisa Zepeda Lagunas presented a new legal appeal to review the sentence of said Mazatec defendants in a legal process that totals more than 11 years. 




 According to a communiqué sent out by family members, collectives, and organizations following Peralta's defense, the constestation against his absolution was presented on March 10, and submitted before the Nation's Supreme Court of Justice (SCJN) as "Amparo Directo in Review 2705/2026." 




 Said appeal was evaluated by the president of the Court, a position filled by minister Hugo Aguilar Ortiz, who approved its admission this past April 17. By June 12, the SCJN gave notice that the case would be reviewed by minister Loretta Ortíz and solicited the previous records in order to form the legal analysis. 




 "Today, once again, we are about to return to the Supreme Court at the whims of deputy Elisa Zepeda and her closeness with the president of said institute. This has nothing to do with justice, but rather with the use of these institutions to persecute and wear down anyone who resists," shared Peralta upon learning of the new contestation. The legal cause stems from the events of December 2014 and, since then it has passed through state trials, Collegiate Tribunals and even the SCJN itself. 




 Miguel Peralta, born in the community of Eloxochitlán de Flores Magón in the Mazatec Mountains, was detained on April 2015 in Mexico City and transferred to Oaxaca, where he remained incarcerated for four and a half years, charged with the killing a person and of supposed attempted homicide against Elisa Zepeda, within a context of aggression of petty warlord groups that belong to Zepeda against the Community Assembly. 




 On October 2019, the Huautla Joint Lower First Instance Courts had absolved him upon considering that the evidence presented in the trial did not prove his responsibility of the crimes, and so Peralta left prison despite the fact that the prosecution appealed the resolution. By March 2022, the Oaxaca Third Criminal Chamber revoked the absolving sentence and emitted one of 50 years behind bars. He remained under political persecution while he continued his legal defense, since, upon issuing an arrest warrant, the possibility for his arrest at any time was kept open. 




 On August 2023, a Collegiate Court granted a direct writ of amparo to Peralta. Without resolving the background case, the sentence was limited to ordering the resumption of part of the legal process, such that the Mazatec defense appealed to the SCJN. On November 2024, The First Chamber revoked the resolution and concluded that the Oaxacan tribunal had infringed Peralta's right to obtain justice by not considering the fact that he belonged to a First Peoples and in failing to analyze the case from an intercultural perspective. 




 The Court returned the file to the Oaxaca First Collegiate Tribunal of Penal Matters so that it may issue a new sentence which took into consideration of the social, cultural, and political context of Eloxochitlán. At this stage, expert anthropological opinions became involved who documented the existence of petty warlords in said community, for which there have been human rights violation against the townspeople and a power imbalance that has placed the townspeople under more than a decade of political persecution. 




Justice Delayed




 On February 20, 2026, the Collegiate Tribunal cataloged just how lacking the evidence against Peralta was. It also pointed out contradictions in the testimonies made against him, making it clear that the charges against him were fabricated, thus determining that the crime of attempted homicide against Elisa Zepeda did not take place. With such a decision, the absolution was partial in ruling out one of the Mazatec's felonies. The full sentence was issued on February 25, and, by March 6 the Third Criminal Chamber completely absolved Peralta, dismissing the charge of homicide as well. 




 The new contestation presented by Elisa Zepeda, who currently holds the position of local MORENA Party deputy, and who presides of over the Standing Commission of Indigenous and Afro-Mexican Inter-culturality, Peoples and Communities in the Oaxaca Congress, raised alarms due to her new attempt to delaying the process after more than 11 years and the issuing of various absolutory sentences. 




 In his communiqué, Peralta and the collectives that have kept up with the case, denounce Elisa Zepeda for having climbed up the ranks of state power given that, in less than 10 months, she's gone from being the municipal president of Eloxochitlán to sitting as the local MORENA deputy, from where she served as the president of the Permanent Commission of Justice Administration and Management; she was chief of the Women's Secretary under Salomón Jara's state government, and presently holds a seat again in the local Congress.

title: Ejército Zapatista de Liberación Nacional - A Declaration... For Life
content:
Author

: Ejército Zapatista de Liberación Nacional

Title

: A Declaration... For Life

Date

: January 1, 2021

Notes

: Translated by Ediciones Bloodfruit/Malvivientes from https://enlacezapatista.ezln.org.mx/2021/01/01/primera-parte-una-declaracion-por-la-vida/

Source

: Retrieved 10/19/2026 from https://www.patreon.com/bloodfruit/posts/new-zine-for-148153724







 First of January, 2021. 




 TO THE PEOPLES OF THE WORLD: 




 TO THE PEOPLE WHO STRUGGLE IN THE FIVE CONTINENTS: 




 BROTHERS AND SISTERS AND COMRADES: 







 In these past months we have established contact among ourselves through various means. We are women, lesbians, gay, transgender, transvestites, intersex, queer and more, men, groups, collectives, associations, organizations, social movements, first peoples, neighbor associations, communities and a long 

et cetera

 that identifies us. 




 We are differentiated and separated by lands, skies, mountains, valleys, steppes, jungles, deserts, oceans, lakes, rivers, streams, lagoons, race, cultures, languages, histories, age, geographies, sexual and non-sexual identities, roots, borders, forms of organization, social classes, purchasing power, social prestige, fame, popularity, followers, likes, coinage, degree of education, ways of being, chores, virtues, defects, pros, cons, howevers, rivalries, enmities, conceptions, arguments, counter-arguments, debates, disputes, denunciations, accusations, disdains, phobias, philias, praises, repudiations, jeers, applause, divinities, demons, dogmas, heresies, joys, dislikes, modes, and a long 

et cetera

 that makes us different and, not infrequently, opposites. 




 We are united only in a few things: 




 In that we make the Earth’s sorrows our own: the violence against women; the persecution and contempt for those different in their affective, emotional, sexual identity; the annihilation of childhood; the genocide against the First Peoples; racism; militarism; exploitation; spoliation; nature’s destruction. 




 The understanding that it is a system which is responsible for these sorrows. The executioner is an exploiting, patriarchal, pyramidal, racist, thieving and criminal system: Capitalism. 




 The knowledge that it is not possible to reform, educate, allay, soften, domesticate, or humanize this system. 




 The commitment to fight, everywhere and at all times —each in their own field— against this system until it is completely destroyed. Humanity’s survival depends on Capitalism’s destruction. We do not surrender, we do not sell out and we do not waver. 




 The certainty that the struggle for Humanity is global. Just as the ongoing destruction recognizes no borders, nationalities, flags, tongues, cultures, races; so, too, is the struggle for Humanity everywhere, at all times. 




 The conviction that many worlds live and fight in The World. And that all pretense of homogeneity and hegemony threatens the human being’s essence: Liberty. Humanity’s equality lies in respecting the different. Its resemblance lies in its diversity. 




 The understanding that it is not the vanity of imposing our gaze, our steps, company, paths and fates what allows us to advance, but rather listening and the sight of the other who, distinct and different, has the same calling to liberty and justice. 




 Due to these convergences, and without abandoning our convictions nor leaving behind who and what we are, we have agreed: 




 First ‒ To realize gatherings, dialogues, exchanging of ideas, experiences, analysis and evaluations amongst the committed we find —from among different conceptions and in different lands— in the struggle for life. Afterwards, each will continue on their own path, or not. Seeing and listening to the other may or may not help us on our way. But to learn of the different is also part of our struggle and our commitment, of our humanity. 




 Second ‒ That these gatherings and activities take place in the five continents. That, with regards to the European continent, these take place in the months of July, August, September and October of the year 2021 with the active participation of a Mexican delegation made up of CNI-CIG, the People’s Front in Defense of the Water and Land of Morelos, Puebla and Tlaxcala, and EZLN. And in later dates to be determined, to support, according to our ability, so that they may be realized in Asia, Africa, Oceania, and America. 




 Third ‒ To invite those who share the same concerns and similar struggles, every honest peoples and all those 

belows

 who rebel and resist in the many corners of the world, so that they join, contribute, support and participate in these gatherings and activities; and so that they may sign off on and make their own this declaration FOR LIFE. 




 From one of the bridges of dignity that joins the five continents. 




 We. 




 Planet Earth. 




 1

st

 of January of 2021. 







 People’s Front in Defense of the Water and Land of Morelos, Puebla and Tlaxcala 










 Indigenous National Congress/Indigenous Council of Government 










 From the Southeastern Mexican mountains. 










 For the women, men, others, boys and girls and the elderly of the Zapatista Army of National Liberation: 










 Comandante Don Pablo Contreras and Subcomandante Insurgente Moisés. 










 Mexico. 










 If you wish to sign this Declaration, send your signature to firmasporlavida@ezln.org.mx. Please give the full name of your group, collective, organization or whatever, in your language, and its location. The signatures will be added as they come.

title: 14 y 21 de octubre. Inauguración de la exposición ‘Una brecha en el silencio: exhumaciones en el cementerio parroquial de Colmenar Viejo’
content:
El miércoles, 

14 de octubre

, a las 

19:00

, se inaugurará en nuestra sede de la FAL en Madrid la exposición fotográfica 

Una brecha en el silencio: exhumaciones en el cementerio parroquial de Colmenar Viejo

, con la cual descubriremos el exhaustivo trabajo de recuperación de las víctimas de la violencia franquista en el cementerio parroquial de Colmenar Viejo.




El mismo 

14 de octubre

, coincidiendo con la inauguración, se celebrarán dos conferencias. La primera correrá a cargo del antropólogo 

Roberto Fernández Suáre

z, bajo el título 

Represión franquista en el Norte de Madrid

. Posteriormente participará 

Carmen Carreras Béjar

, secretaria de la ACVSSR, con la charla 

Las exhumaciones en el cementerio parroquial de Colmenar Viejo: inicio, gestiones y desarrollo del proyecto

.




El día 

21 de octubre

, a las 19:00, se realizará la conferencia 

Exhumaciones en el cementerio parroquial de Colmenar Viejo: resultados y estado del proyecto

, a cargo de 

Elvira García Aragón

, perteneciente a Equipo A de Arqueología.




A través de sus 

fotografías

, conoceremos los trabajos arqueológicos que permitieron localizar a 

77 de las 90 personas desaparecidas

, así como una selección de objetos personales recuperados junto a las víctimas, debidamente restaurados.




Os dejamos con la información detallada de la exposición:




El 

1 de abril de 1939

 se dio por finalizada la Guerra Civil y quince días después se producía el primer fusilamiento en las tapias del cementerio parroquial de 

Col-menar Viejo,

 el de 

Isidoro Marivela Paredes,

 último alcalde republicano de Colmenar Viejo junto a otros tres hombres. El siguiente fusilamiento masivo tendría lugar el 9 de mayo. En los seis meses siguientes los fusilamientos se repitieron hasta matar a un total de 

108 personas.




Colmenar Viejo, como cabeza de partido judicial, fue elegida como sede del tribunal militar que iba a ocuparse de Juzgar a aquellos republicanos y republicanas de todas las localidades pertenecientes a su partido judicial, desde Miraflores de la Sierra al norte hasta Hortaleza (población aún no integrada en la ciudad de Madrid) al sur del mismo.




El proyecto técnico-científico para la recuperación de las víctimas de la violencia franquista del cementerio parroquial de Colmenar Viejo ha sido elaborado por la Sociedad de Ciencias Aranzadi y lo lleva a cabo en colaboración con la Asociación Cultural Equipo A de Arqueología, la Unidad de Antropología Física de la Facultad de Biología de la Universidad Complutense de Madrid y los laboratorios de genética BIOMICs de la Universidad del País Vasco y CITOGEN.




En agosto de 2022 se realizó la primera excavación en la mitad Sureste del antiguo cementerio civil. Fueron localizadas tres zanjas o trincheras en las que estaban dispuestos los cuerpos de 12 de las víctimas buscadas. Se trataba de individuos de sexo biológico masculino, que presentaban traumatismos compatibles con heridas por arma de fuego, principalmente en cráneo y mandíbula. La mayoría estaban enterrados en ataúd, dispuestos hasta en tres niveles. En julio de 2023 se retomaron los trabajos en el cementerio civil, pero no se documentó la presencia de nuevas fosas ni enterramientos relacionados con la represión.




Las exhumaciones realizadas en el cementerio parroquial de Colmenar Viejo se llevaron a cabo a petición de los familiares de las víctimas con el objetivo de identificar los restos y proporcionarles una sepultura digna. El proceso de identificación combina el análisis de testimonios y fuentes documentales con los datos obtenidos mediante excavación arqueológica, estudio antropológico y análisis genético. En la antigua zona civil se localizaron al menos 12 víctimas enterradas en distintos momentos, todas ellas adultos de sexo biológico masculino con evidencias de muerte violenta por arma de fuego. Entre los restos hallados se identificó a Florencio Elipe Sánchez gracias a una amputación previa del brazo documentada históricamente y confirmada por análisis genético. En la gran fosa del espacio conocido como «el paseo» se documentaron 65 inhumaciones, entre ellas los restos de Mar-tina Aparicio Bastero, la única mujer identificada. El acto de entrega de restos a las familias que tuvo lugar en la Universidad Complutense en septiembre de 2024, representó un paso clave en el camino hacia la Verdad y la Reparación.




En «el paseo», sin embargo, fueron sucediéndose los hallazgos a lo largo de sus 47m de longitud y 1,5m de anchura. Se trataba de 65 enterramientos en posición original y 7 conjuntos de huesos desarticulados, que correspondían a alteraciones posteriores. La disposición, orientación y características eran similares a las de los encontrados en el cementerio civil. La memoria colectiva estaba en lo cierto: estaban aquí.




14 DE OCTUBRE

, por

title: 21 de octubre. Charla informativa: hacia la huelga general del 11 de noviembre
content:
Este miércoles 21 de octubre, a las 19:00 horas, nos encontramos en La Cabrera para hablar de la huelga general del próximo 11 de noviembre, resolver dudas y organizarnos colectivamente.




La huelga es una de las herramientas más importantes que tenemos como clase trabajadora para defender nuestros derechos y conquistar mejores condiciones de vida. Frente a la precariedad laboral, la pérdida de poder adquisitivo, la especulación con la vivienda y el deterioro de los servicios públicos, necesitamos organizarnos y unir nuestras luchas.




A la hora de secundar una huelga surgen muchas preguntas: 

¿Puedo hacer huelga en mi trabajo? ¿Tengo que avisar a la empresa? ¿Pueden sancionarme? ¿Qué ocurre con mi salario? ¿Qué reivindicamos?




Para responder a estas cuestiones y debatir sobre la próxima convocatoria de huelga general del 11 de noviembre, organizamos una 

charla informativa abierta a todas las personas interesadas

, junto a la Sección Sindical de Educación de la Comunidad de Madrid de CNT y el nodo Sierra Norte del Sindicato de Inquilinas de Madrid.




¿De qué hablaremos?







El derecho a huelga y cómo ejercerlo.




Quién puede secundar la convocatoria y qué protección legal tiene.




Las obligaciones de las empresas y los derechos de las personas trabajadoras.




Las reivindicaciones de la huelga general del 11 de noviembre.




La importancia de organizarse en los centros de trabajo y en nuestros barrios y pueblos.







No es necesario estar afiliada a ningún sindicato ni tener experiencia previa en movilizaciones. 

La charla está abierta a todas las personas que quieran informarse, compartir inquietudes y participar.




Guía práctica: conoce tu derecho a huelga




Para facilitar el acceso a la información, compartimos también la guía de CNT 

«Derecho a la huelga: te resolvemos 8 dudas frecuentes»

, un material que aborda cuestiones habituales sobre el ejercicio de este derecho fundamental.




En ella encontrarás información sobre la participación en huelgas sin afiliación sindical, los periodos de prueba, las situaciones de becarios y falsos autónomos, los servicios mínimos, la obligación de avisar a la empresa, los descuentos salariales y la protección frente a represalias.




Conocer nuestros derechos es el primer paso para poder defenderlos colectivamente.




La organización, el apoyo mutuo y la solidaridad son nuestras mejores herramientas.




Te esperamos este miércoles. ¡Acude, participa y difunde la convocatoria!




 ¡Unamos las luchas de la clase trabajadora!




 CNT Sierra Norte

 se publicó primero en 

Confederación Nacional del Trabajo

.
