title: Francs-Tireurs Partisans (1991-1999) : s'attaquer à l'extrême droite, autrement qu'avec des mots
content:
Nous avons décidé de revenir sur certains événements marquants de l'histoire de l'antifascisme hexagonal contemporain, pour remettre en lumière une histoire militante parfois méconnue dans nos propres rangs et éclairer les luttes d'aujourd'hui avec les combats d'hier. Voici le premier des trois épisodes d'une petite histoire du groupe marseillais Francs-Tireurs Partisans qui, dans la dernière décennie du XXe siècle, s'en est pris aux intérêts du Front national dans la région de Marseille.




Première partie (1/3) : Les Francs-Tireurs Partisans, genèse d'un combat antifasciste à Marseille.




Marseille, 7h le matin du 15 octobre 1999. Au terme de huit années d'enquête la police arrête à leurs domiciles Yves Peirat et William Ferrari. Ces deux militants libertaires sont accusés d'avoir commis des attentats sous le nom de « FTP » pour Francs-Tireurs Partisans, un acronyme qui convoque l'imaginaire de la résistance à la dictature de Vichy et à l'occupant nazi. Le groupe marseillais qui se réclame de l'antifascisme radical à mis en action une forme de « résistance active ». Il a « officiellement »

 [

1

]

 revendiqué 12 attentats entre 1991 et 1998, en grande majorité dirigés contre les intérêts du FN. Des agissements qui se limitent à des destructions matérielles, les enquêteurs eux-mêmes souligneront qu'aucun engin n'était destiné à tuer. Leur histoire est la collision d'un moment et d'un environnement particulier. La région Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur est alors le terrain de conquête privilégié de l'extrême droite. Elle y trouve enfin l'occasion d'accéder aux affaires, bien aidée par l'inconsistance et parfois la complaisance d'adversaires politiques n'opposant que la vacuité de discours rendus caducs par l'affairisme et le clientélisme ambiant. Le FN progresse à grands pas, emportant par exemple des mairies. Son discours prospère sur un racisme qui n'a rien de latent, hérité de la guerre d'Algérie. Revenir sur l'histoire des FTP c'est se reposer la sempiternelle question de la performativité du militantisme antifasciste et révolutionnaire. Subir les offensives et les offenses de l'extrême droite : jusqu'à quel point ? Ou, pour le dire de manière à la fois explicite et poétique : « Je ne cherche pas à changer les règles du jeu, mais le jeu lui-même. »

 [

2

]

 Une phrase d'André Breton mise en exergue parmi les revendications des FTP. Une histoire récente qui mérite d'être remise sur l'établi parce qu'elle renvoie les militant·e·s pour l'émancipation à des dilemmes politiques et moraux dont nous ne sommes loin de nous départir.




L'extrême droite méridionale : la rage et la revanche en bandoulière




Pour comprendre l'irruption des FTP dans le paysage politique il faut revenir sur une des spécificités de la région Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur : « L'arrivée successive de deux communautés issues du même pays, l'Algérie, mais dont l'une portait sa rage et sa revanche en bandoulière a permis la renaissance d'une xénophobie jamais totalement éteinte depuis les chasses à l'Italien du début du siècle (Franc-Tireur, n°1, février 2000) ». Cette arrivée autour de 1962 et la guerre coloniale qui l'a précédé représente la matrice historique qui a conduit à la création du FN. À l'exemple de Jean-Marie Le Pen, jeune député poujadiste, qui s'engage volontairement en Algérie fin 1956 où il participe activement à ce qui ne peut être qualifié autrement que de torture. Parmi les différentes factions à la création du FN on retrouve nombre de nostalgiques de l'Algérie française (Roger Holeindre, Pierre Sergent) dont d'anciens membres de l'OAS (Organisation Armée Secrète) à l'origine de nombreux attentats en Algérie et en France. L'extrême droite dispose donc d'un terreau favorable en PACA, même si dans les années 1970 le FN stagne à un niveau électoral très faible, encore disqualifié dans les urnes et la vie politique publique par sa filiation avec Vichy, la collaboration et le nazisme. La libération n'est pas si lointaine et les blessures restent vives. Cela n'empêche pas les diverses composantes de l'extrême droite d'affirmer leur présence par des actions clandestines violentes et spectaculaires.

 [

3

]

 En PACA elles sont dirigées vers les immigré.es ou perçu.es comme tel.le.s qu'elle accuse de tous les maux. Posons quelques jalons chronologiques. En 1973, le Groupe Charles Martel organise un attentat contre le consulat d'Algérie à Marseille faisant quatre morts et entre 14 et 20 blessés selon les sources.




 

 




Cet attentat est l'acmé d'un climat de terreur raciste avec des mitraillages de foyers et de bidonvilles. « L'État algérien décomptera près de 50 morts – la France, 16 – et 300 blessés en moins de six mois. » Une histoire traumatique qui mérite une introspection collective mais qui est largement refoulée. En décembre 1977, à Toulon, les Commandos Delta assassinent le gardien de nuit de l'Amicale des Algériens en Europe. En août 1980, à Marseille, l'imprimerie libertaire et coopérative L'Encre Noire est visée par un attentat à l'explosif qui fait un mort et plusieurs blessés. Le 14 mars 1983, deux hommes à moto jettent une bombe à Marseille et blessent grièvement deux enfants. Un attentat attribué au Groupe Charles Martel. Le milieu des années 80 marque un relatif reflux des attentats d'extrême droite mais pas leur disparition. Et en 1987 et 1988, quatre attentats racistes sont perpétrés contre des foyers SONACOTRA (logements sociaux de travailleurs immigrés), causant un mort à Cagnes-sur-Mer. Actes malveillants auxquels il faut ajouter des attentats contre des locaux de la CGT ou du PCF. Des actes impliquant au moins un membre des néonazis du PNFE (Parti Nationaliste Français et Européen) et où durant le procès un avocat des parties civiles dira qu'« on rencontre le Front National à chaque page de ce dossier ». La violence d'extrême droite est une épée de Damoclès qui pèse de manière diffuse mais permanente en PACA. En 1995 l'assassinat du jeune Ibrahim Ali par des colleurs d'affiches armés du FN, un drame central dans l'engagement des FTP, est certes un fait traumatique qui exprime un racisme crasse et une haine froide mais il n'est pas un coup de tonnerre dans un ciel serein. Il se place dans un continuum de violences d'extrême droite installé depuis trois décennies qui favorisent le passage à l'acte. Il faut composer aussi avec la crispation de l'État qui entame sont grand tournant libéral et sécuritaire. La montée de la répression d'État culmine à Marseille avec la manifestation anti-FN du 11 mars 1997. Réunissant 5000 personnes, elle est très violemment réprimée par les CRS. On compte des dizaines de blessés, une vingtaine d'interpellations, des scènes de tabassages et des tirs tendus de lacrymogènes qui « montrent à quel point la limite entre démocratie libérale et régime autoritaire peut vite devenir très floue... »

 [

4

]

. Une répression gravée dans les esprits qui marque localement un tournant dans la perception du simple acte de manifester. L'arrivée du FN aux affaires conjuguée au durcissement de la répression policière incite les acteurs de la lutte antifasciste que sont les FTP en devenir à se reposer la question de la violence (d'ailleurs le terme de violence prête ici à confusion parce que peu opérant dans son usage le plus étroit, rappelons qu'aucune souffrance n'a été infligée à des personnes). Le choix de son emploi politique peut aujourd'hui avec le recul du temps paraître décalé et peu opportun, mais sans mise en contexte ce jugement relève au mieux de la téléologie et au pire de la pure paresse intellectuelle.




 

 




Un collectif au pluriel singulier ?




Les FTP ont souvent été ramenés à la seule personne d'Yves Peirat occultant au passage la place de William Ferrari. Celui qui est alors technicien-journaliste pour Radio Galère, se voit réduit à la loyauté envers son vieux compagnon de luttes à qui il donne un coup de main logistique et de repérages, notamment en amont de la destruction du groupe électrogène du concert de Vitrolles en 1998. Cette réduction des FTP à la personne d'Yves Peirat s'explique en partie par la stratégie de défense lors de leur procès où le « seul et unique membre des FTP » revendique l'entièreté des actions et endosse ainsi la plus grande part de responsabilité opérationnelle pour dédouaner son compagnon. Cette stratégie de défense a, selon Yves Peirat avec qui nous avons échangé, été anticipée. La perspective de finir dans les griffes de la justice étant une hypothèse présente dès les discussions de constitution des FTP. William Ferrari est alors en couple et il a un enfant et « il était hors de question qu'il soit incarcéré trop longtemps et la vérité était que effectivement c'est moi qui ai commis la série d'attentats [...] qu'on nous a reproché. William était mon binôme dans tout ce qui était technique et logistique […]. » Ce serait encore éclipser William Ferrari de le cantonner à la position du « technicien » subalterne. Il a aussi contribué à l'élaboration des revendications des FTP : « Nous avons écrit deux textes de revendications pour expliquer notre démarche. Si je suis l'auteur à 90 % du premier texte « Ami, entends-tu », William est le principal auteur du second dans la même proportion. […] Nous étions sur la même longueur d'ondes politique. » On peut vraisemblablement déduire dans la position de William l'idée qu'un militantisme plus traditionnel (sans être confondu avec un militantisme strictement public et légaliste) n'avait pas tout à fait échoué à empêcher la progression de l'extrême droite. D'où une certaine réserve et une pondération stricte sur la justesse morale et politique des moyens à mettre en œuvre par les FTP. L'écrit que vous parcourez ne lèvera pas toutes les ombres sur l'histoire des FTP, nous n'avons malheureusement pas eu l'occasion d'échanger avec William. Enfin, Albert, le frère cadet de Yves sera lui aussi inculpé pour « destruction volontaire d'un bien immobilier par l'effet d'une substance explosive ». Soupçonné de facto parce qu'il avait un temps travaillé au Stadium de Vitrolles il sera écarté du dossier par la justice. Ce binôme des FTP n'était pas pour autant laissé à lui-même. On y reviendra plus bas, trois personnes ont ajouté par leurs conseils un surplus de conscience politique, éthique et moral.




Parcours de vie avant les FTP




 

 




Les parcours de vie des FTP et les conditions de leur rencontre permettent de situer le centre de gravité de leur combat. Un grand-père d'Yves Peirat avait des responsabilités au sein du POUM (Partido Obrero de Unificación Marxista en castillan et Partit Obrer d'Unificació Marxista en catalan), une organisation communiste indépendante anti-stalinienne qui défend la révolution collectiviste en Catalogne et est active dans la lutte anti-franquiste. Même idéal du côté du grand-père maternel qui fut emprisonné 10 ans sous Franco

 [

5

]

. Né à Marseille en 1959, celui qui deviendra infirmier va durant son enfance baigner dans cette société recomposée des réfugié·e·s espagnol·e·s. Son grand-père l'emmenait à des « réunions qui se tenaient à la bourse du travail dans le quartier de Noailles à Marseille, (…) il y avait des communistes, des socialistes, des anarchistes. Je ne comprenais pas vraiment le fond de leurs divergences, mais je savais par contre que les crispations au sein de la gauche étaient toutes centrées autour du rôle joué par les uns et les autres pendant la guerre d'Espagne. C'est ma matrice, j'ai été élevé dans la guerre d'Espagne […] »

 [

6

]

. L'héritage familial infuse dans l'idéologie et l'imaginaire militant d'Yves Peirat, affermissant la conviction qu'au delà de la propagande, la lutte antifasciste en Espagne était le fait des courants anarchistes et communistes anti-staliniens. Adolescent, il tâtonne et passe par divers groupes militants. Néanmoins, « logiquement » son premier engagement conséquent se dirige vers le soutien à la lutte du peuple basque. Un prolongement évident du combat anti-franquiste arrimé à une perspective d'émancipation libertaire. C'est d'ailleurs dans ce courant libertaire qu'il fait la connaissance de William Ferrari, « à l'occasion d'une soirée agitée à Aix lors d'un meeting de l'Eurodroite (liste présentée par le Parti des Forces Nouvelles) aux élections européennes de 1979. »

 [

7

]

. Lors de cette « soirée agitée » sont lancés pas moins de 150 cocktails molotov et il y a des affrontements très violents avec la police qui protège les lieux. Cette fin remuante des années 1970 correspond au passage à la fac Aix-Marseille d'Yves Peirat, un moment structurant du point de vue idéologique, entre confrontation avec une extrême droite bien implantée et, dans son camp social, la prévalence des Jeunesses Communistes aux pratiques verticales. En 1984 pour un peu plus d'une année, Yves Peirat part en Amérique Centrale, notamment au Nicaragua. Son retour à Marseille en janvier 1986 marque le retour d'une centralité de de l'engagement antifasciste dans sa vie. Depuis 1984 un groupe en particulier est à la pointe du combat contre la progression du FN, le GAF (Groupe Antifasciste) « et bien sûr je retrouve William lors d'une réunion du GAF dont je deviens membre » nous confie Yves. Comme il le rapporte

 [

8

]

, « l'époque est aux manifs-bastons » et les queues de cortège sont imprégnées des pratiques tactiques de l'autonomie d'alors. Le GAF est un assemblage de militant·e·s de tous horizons, depuis des trotskystes plus où moins en rupture de ban jusqu'aux écolos et féministes non-encartées, en passant par les activistes des radios libres, les chômeureu·x/ses totos qui côtoient des syndicalistes et des militant·e·s plus âgé·e·s. des luttes contre le colonialisme. Pour le collectif, William et Yves participent notamment à des discussions en vue d'une coordination antifasciste hexagonale, la CNAF (Coordination Nationale AntiFasciste). C'est en partie cette dynamique qui plus tard débouchera sur la création du Réseau No Pasaran. Pour revenir au GAF, le collectif fonctionne en assemblées générales qui rassemblent parfois une centaine de personnes. La cohabitation de sensibilités hétérogènes n'est pas sans générer des tensions notamment lorsque certains veulent attaquer la responsabilité d'une partie de la gauche (Parti Socialiste et Parti Communiste Français) dans l'instrumentalisation du Front national à des fins électoralistes quand d'autres y voient une erreur de cible. C'est l'époque de la stratégie pyromane de François Mitterrand qui impose la proportionnelle intégrale pour freiner la montée attendue de la droite. Le but est d'atténuer une claque attendue pour le PS, quitte à laisser entrer le loup FN dans la bergerie. Avec pour effet de donner un siège à 35 députés FN, dont Jean-Marie Le Pen, à l'Assemblée nationale. Le parti à la flamme confirme en PACA aux présidentielles de 1988 où il tourne autour des 25 % dans les départements respectifs de la région. Cette poussée enhardi les radicaux qui veulent en découdre. Une vague d'attentats d'extrême droite touche le sud de la France, visant notamment le foyer SONACOTRA de Cagnes-sur-Mer en décembre 1988, tuant un ressortissant roumain. Cette expression désinhibée de la xénophobie, combinée à la déliquescence morale et politique de la gauche institutionnelle (Par exemple à Marseille c'est le très libéral Bernard Tapie qui se pose de manière absurde en barrage contre le FN) questionne nombre de militant·e·s antifascistes sur l'efficacité des pratiques circonscrites à la légalité républicaine. Fin 1989, pour deux petites années, Yves Peirat entame une période parisienne qui marque le début d'« amitiés solides ». Il va militer au sein de l'équipe de la revue d'enquêtes de référence de l'antifascisme d'alors : REFLEXes. Méridional de cœur il revient à Marseille dans cette époque de trouble des cadres idéologiques et de perspectives bouchées. C'est alors que le noyau qui deviendra les FTP acte son parti pris explosif.

author: Clayton Aldern
title: Segundo turno das eleições será referendo sobre futuro da Amazônia
content:
Depois dos resultados do primeiro turno, observadores ambientais acreditam que o dia 25 de outubro não será apenas a disputa final entre Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva e Flávio Bolsonaro: a votação será também um referendo sobre o futuro da Floresta Amazônica.




“Estamos muito preocupados com os riscos para a Amazônia caso Flávio vença a eleição, porque ele nega as mudanças climáticas”, afirmou 

Carlos Nobre

, uma das maiores autoridades na área e um dos cientistas brasileiros mais conhecidos do mundo. 

“Se ele for eleito, certamente o desmatamento na Amazônia vai aumentar. Estamos em uma situação muito grave.”




Flávio Bolsonaro faz campanha com uma 

agenda

 favorável ao agronegócio e à desregulamentação. O candidato do PL, que terminou o primeiro turno à frente de Lula por 2,2 milhões de votos, promete zerar o desmatamento ilegal até 2029. Mas o 

programa de governo

 do filho de Jair Bolsonaro também defende um processo de licenciamento ambiental “ágil e moderno”, que “não servirá mais como instrumento para bloquear quem deseja investir e gerar empregos”.




Monica de Bolle, economista do Peterson Institute for International Economics, nos Estados Unidos, avalia que uma vitória de Flávio repetiria o mandato de seu pai, marcado pelo 

aumento

 do desmatamento, pela queda acentuada no número de autos de infração ambiental e pela quase 

duplicação

 das emissões de carbono na Amazônia em 2019 e 2020, na comparação com a média registrada entre 2010 e 2018.




“Jair Bolsonaro basicamente desmantelou a estrutura de fiscalização. E acho que isso provavelmente aconteceria de novo”, afirmou de Bolle.



















Onipresente, mas sem direito a voto na próxima eleição, a própria Amazônia está em jogo.

 A floresta enfrenta uma série de ameaças, da seca às queimadas, passando pela extração de madeira e pelo desmatamento. Embora o Código Florestal permita que proprietários rurais desmatem até 20% de suas terras na Amazônia, a rede de monitoramento MapBiomas 

estimou recentemente

 que 97% da supressão da vegetação nativa na Amazônia em 2025 apresentava indícios de ilegalidade.




Durante o atual mandato de Lula, as taxas de desmatamento na Amazônia caíram a cada ano. Se o Brasil voltasse ao ritmo registrado durante o governo de Jair Bolsonaro, a floresta perderia cerca de 45.600 quilômetros quadrados nos próximos quatro anos, em comparação com aproximadamente 23.000 quilômetros quadrados caso o ritmo observado em 2025 fosse mantido. A diferença equivale a uma área aproximadamente do tamanho do estado de Sergipe.




Os resultados do primeiro turno sugerem que os interesses do setor agropecuário provavelmente contribuíram para o bom desempenho de Flávio Bolsonaro.

 Lula perdeu votos em quase todos os municípios do país na comparação com seu desempenho em 2022. Mas, como a 

Agência Pública

 

mostrou

, nos municípios onde o agronegócio representa mais da metade da economia local, sua votação caiu quase oito pontos percentuais, três vezes a perda registrada nas áreas onde a atividade não predomina.



















Se o próximo governo acelerar o desmatamento, as consequências podem ser devastadoras para a Floresta Amazônica, para seus moradores e para as atividades econômicas que dependem de sua preservação. 

Há décadas, cientistas que estudam florestas e clima alertam para um possível 

ponto de não retorno

:

 se uma área grande demais da floresta for derrubada, o ciclo da água deixará de ser forte o suficiente para sustentar um ecossistema de floresta tropical.




Em seu lugar, a região se transformaria em uma floresta degradada e em um ambiente seco, como o cerrado, provocando a liberação líquida de carbono que intensifica o aquecimento global e reduzindo as chuvas que abastecem as plantações de soja nas áreas próximas.




O ponto de não retorno em questão depende de vários fatores e é difícil de estimar. No entanto, o limite de desmatamento mais citado é de 20% a 25% da cobertura florestal da Amazônia, intervalo 

proposto pela primeira vez em 2018

, por Nobre e pelo biólogo conservacionista norte-americano Thomas Lovejoy.




Os dois argumentaram que “as sinergias negativas entre desmatamento, mudanças climáticas e uso generalizado do fogo” colocariam a floresta em um ciclo de retroalimentação quando esse limite fosse ultrapassado. Um 

estudo publicado na revista 

Nature

, em maio deste ano, estimou que a faixa do ponto de não retorno estaria mais próxima de 22% a 28% de desmatamento, considerando o aquecimento global de 1,5 a 1,9 grau Celsius que o mundo provavelmente deve registrar até meados deste século.




Cerca de 18% da Amazônia — que se estende por nove países — e 22% da Amazônia brasileira já foram desmatados.



















Nico Wunderling, cientista climático da Universidade Goethe de Frankfurt (Alemanha), liderou o estudo publicado em maio na 

Nature

. Ele estimou que a retomada das práticas adotadas durante o governo de Jair Bolsonaro levaria ao desmatamento de cerca de 1% da floresta da bacia amazônica ao longo do próximo mandato presidencial. Nesse ritmo, “chegaríamos à zona de perigo em meados ou no final da década de 2030”, disse ele à Grist.




Por outro lado, se Lula cumprir sua promessa de zerar o desmatamento até o início da década de 2030, ainda seria possível evitar um processo descontrolado, na opinião de Wunderling. Embora as mudanças climáticas sejam um processo global que exige coordenação internacional, o desmatamento é 

“a alavanca sobre a qual é mais fácil agir para reverter o quadro”, afirmou.




O final da década de 2030 está além do período abrangido pela eleição de 2026, e a ciência ainda não permite determinar com precisão qual será o ponto de não retorno. Mesmo assim, o resultado da disputa pode colocar a Floresta Amazônica em uma trajetória decisiva. 




Ronaldo Christofoletti, oceanógrafo da Universidade Federal de São Paulo, compara a situação à contratação de um seguro para um veículo. “Por que pago o seguro? Porque um acidente pode acontecer. Quando? Não sei.”




Para Christofoletti, o que está em jogo na eleição é justamente como lidar com essa incerteza. 

“Não esperem milagres dos cientistas”, afirmou. “Mas confiem que o ponto de não retorno está cada vez mais próximo.”




A campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro não respondeu ao pedido de comentário para esta matéria.




Enquanto isso, o agronegócio organizado trabalha pela eleição de Flávio no segundo turno. A Frente Parlamentar da Agropecuária (FPA) 

declarou apoio

 ao candidato do PL, que 

prometeu

 deixar a escolha de seu ministro da Agricultura a cargo da bancada.




Mesmo que Flávio não vença o segundo turno, o agro talvez já tenha saído vitorioso. Em 4 de outubro, o PL elegeu 121 deputados federais, o maior número de cadeiras conquistadas por um partido desde a promulgação da Constituição de 1988. 

Reportagem

 da Pública mostrou que a bancada indígena diminuiu no Congresso e lideranças já se preparam para um mandato de desmonte e retrocesso.




Para o agronegócio, isso significa que áreas atualmente protegidas de atividades econômicas poderão em breve ser liberadas para exploração. “Mesmo que Lula seja reeleito”, ele estará muito enfraquecido”, afirmou de Bolle.

author: Julia Conley
title: Trump Admin Backed Alberta’s Separatists. Canadian Voters Rejected Secession.
content:
Separatist leaders sought advice on their “Let Alberta Decide” campaign from Republican operatives.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The leader of the movement that opposed separatists’ efforts to achieve independence for the Canadian province of Alberta said Monday night that voters’ resounding rejection of the secession push would “send a very strong message to the rest of the world,” after Trump administration officials backed the effort.

“Don’t mess with Canada,” said Thomas Lukaszuk, a former deputy premier of Alberta who led the Forever Canadian campaign.

With more than 1.8 million votes counted Tuesday morning, 75.7% of Alberta voters had supported remaining in Canada with no further referendum. Just over 24% voted in favor of holding a second referendum on separating from the country, which would have been binding.

Around 76% of voters in the Canadian province of Alberta have rejected a proposal to hold a referendum on independence, according to unofficial results. It's a victory for PM Mark Carney but more than 300,000 backed the proposal, and separatists say their grievances remain. pic.twitter.com/vZ5gUA7Cwr

Separatist leaders, many of whom came to prominence after leading protests against public health precautions during the coronavirus pandemic, were welcomed to meetings at the US State Department in recent months, where they sought advice on their “Let Alberta Decide” campaign from Republican operatives. The meetings, said British Columbia premier David Eby, amounted to “treason.”

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent expressed support for the separatist movement, which does not have a central leader but is backed by groups in Alberta including the Alberta Prosperity Project and Stay Free Alberta.

Bessent said in January that the province, which holds the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves, could be “a natural partner for the US.”

“I think we should let them come down into the US,” Bessent told right-wing podcaster Jack Posobiec. “They have great resources. The Albertans are very independent people… Alberta has a wealth of natural resources, but they won’t let them build a pipeline to the Pacific.”

Former Trump administration adviser and Republican megadonor Elon Musk also said on social media this month that Alberta “should separate” from Canada.

The referendum came as President Donald Trump has threatened to take over Canada and make it “the 51st state,” accusing the Canadian government of treating the US “very badly.” He has imposed 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian imports, setting off a trade war.

Separatists in Alberta, whose views have long been in the minority, have complained that the province “sends $20 billion more to Ottawa every year than it gets back,” and fumed over any environmental policies that threaten Alberta’s oil industry, one of the most polluting in the world.

Canceled oil pipelines, a bill banning oil tankers from stopping and unloading at ports on British Columbia’s coast, and an emissions cap have been decried as evidence that the federal government has treated Alberta as “a colony,” as one separatist told The Associated Press Monday — despite the fact that the emissions cap was dropped for the province’s oil and gas sector last year.

“They want to take and take and take from us, and not return anything,” Dustin Degenhardt said while voting.

Danielle Smith, the leader of the United Conservative Party and the premier of Alberta, said she supported the province remaining in the country and applauded the vote results.

But at a recent online forum, Smith outlined the concerns of separatists, saying families face growing affordability struggles and asserting the province has been forced to provide hundreds of thousands of immigrants whom the federal government has resettled there.

A report released in June by the Calgary Chamber of Commerce found that seceding from Canada would shrink Alberta’s economy by $62 billion per year.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said after the vote Monday night that the decision by a large majority of voters was “a great result for Canada.”

“Albertans have chosen unity,” said Carney. “They’ve chosen to build together. They’ve chosen to continue to take care of each other, to move forward together.”

Podcast host Laura Babcock said Tuesday that “the separatists and Trump lost. Canada won.”

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

author: Babatunde Opeyemi Salami
title: What Nollywood owes the ancestors
content:
In June 2025, in Lagos, I sat down with custodians of Yoruba masquerading traditions, and I asked each of them a version of the same question: “What do you think about masquerades appearing in Nigerian films?” Each time, the answer was a flat no.

I grew up in Lagos and have spent years studying Yoruba masquerading traditions, particularly 

Eyo

 and 

Igunnuko

. With support from the Ebrahim Hussein Fellowship and the Aliko Songolo Award, I conducted formal interviews at the Bajulaye and Alagbeji palaces and at the Igunnuko shrines in Epetedo and Alaguntan to understand where this resistance comes from. More importantly, I sought to know what it means for Nollywood to keep returning to these figures despite the pushback.

Foundational cultural theorists of the 1930s and 1940s grappled with a similar question of what happens when a sacred or ritual object is copied, restaged, or transferred into a new medium. In 1944, Theodor Adorno and Max Horkheimer believed that mechanical reproduction drains ritual objects of their meaning, while Walter Benjamin had argued the opposite about a decade earlier. For Benjamin, reproduction could free art from ritual’s grip rather than hollow it out. The reality of this tension is a concept that my fieldwork explores.

To understand the resistance to masquerade remediation in film, you first have to understand what a masquerade is to its custodians. In Yoruba tradition, the 

egungun

 is not a costume design. It’s what a family member becomes after death, made visible. 

Ile

, the family compound and infrastructure of domestic life, is what produces a person worth remembering. A properly raised person becomes, after death and burial within that same compound, an ancestor (

alaale

 or 

babanla

). The cloth used to bury them, 

ago

 or 

eku

, is equal to the same cloth a masquerade wears.

Therefore, a masquerader is not an actor playing an ancestor; the masquerade is treated as an ancestral presence, returned. These masquerades are called 

ara orun

 (heaven dwellers), and their presence has two faces: the ancestral side is what is made public, danced and seen at a festival, while 

orisa

 is the sacred essence beneath it, hidden and guarded. None of this starts on the day a masquerade appears. It starts with the 

ile

, a life, a death, a burial, a cloth. Once you skip that, what is left on a screen is the shape of a masquerade without the systems that make one real.

Interestingly, motion has always been the story of Yoruba masquerades. Scholars trace the tradition from the Nupe to the Oyo, who developed traditions like Ololu, still performed in Ibadan today. From Oyo it moved south, reshaped by Ijebu, home to the 

Agemo

 and 

Eyo

 masquerades. Historical accounts credit two Ijebu brothers, Malaki and Ejilu, with carrying Eyo onward to Eko, old Lagos, where it grew into the festival celebrated today. Therefore, studying masquerade in Lagos already means studying something remediated many times over, long before a camera entered the picture.

Following this trajectory, screen media is the newer remediation, and it works differently. Abba Makama’s 

The Lost Okoroshi

 (2019) turned a security guard into a purple ancestral spirit, putting a masquerade at the center of a very modern Lagos story. 

Jagun Jagun

 (2023), the Netflix epic produced by and starring 

Femi Adebayo

, leaned hard on Yoruba spiritual and masquerade imagery and became one of the biggest Yoruba-language releases in years. 

Gangs of Lagos

 is another Nigerian film that significantly employs the image of a masquerade tradition. Masquerades also appear constantly in music videos, almost always as background texture, with no voice of their own.

The rare film attempts have drawn public criticism and lawsuits from masquerade societies and state authorities, as in the case of 

Gangs of Lagos

. However, nothing comparable has happened to a music video. The traditional masquerade falls under the supervision of a secret cult called 

awo

, which sets the pace and protects 

orisa

, the sacred core of the tradition. A film crew doesn’t move at that pace, and it certainly doesn’t answer to that authority.

Furthermore, the filmmakers see it differently. In my interviews with them, both Adebayo and Makama were clear that they aren’t trying to reproduce a masquerade as it exists. They’re making something new, despite drawing on existing traditions. Makama has said plainly that he wants Nigerians, especially younger ones, to reconnect with traditions that colonial-era religion spent decades demonizing. However, that doesn’t necessarily mean consent from the people who consider these figures sacred.

Film isn’t the only place where masquerades reappear. I spent time at the 

John Randle Centre for Yoruba Culture and History

, the National Museums in Onikan and Ibadan, and the 

Nike Art Gallery

, all of which hold masquerade pieces. These vitrine spaces offer another kind of remediation, arguably a stranger one than film. It removes a masquerade from 

ile

 entirely and places it in a non-performative state. There is no dance, no voice, no direct exchange with the living, which is the entire point of a masquerade at a festival. No lawsuits follow a museum acquisition in Lagos. If the objection to film is about skipping the machinery that makes a masquerade real, a glass case skips all of it. In fact, it rarely draws any objection. This evidences the tension I raised earlier.

As I wrapped up the interviews, I realized it might be useful to revisit the classical debate among Frankfurt School scholars. I think Adorno and Horkheimer would read the custodians’ “no” as evidence that mechanical reproduction erodes what makes a masquerade real. Benjamin would push back, insisting that sacrificing authenticity at the altar of accessibility is fine. My take on this is simple. If masquerading traditions have never stood still, then the question is not whether they should be remediated. Perhaps the more important question is how screen remediation can demonstrate genuine care and respect for tradition while remaining committed to social function.

author: admin
title: Activists Release 1,500 Mink From Idaho Farm
content:
Activists called the raid on an Idaho mink farm “liberation” for the 1,500 minks they released. But they can’t take care of themselves, said the farm’s owner, leaving many to die of heat, stress or get run over. “This is an unethical thing to do,” he said.

Intent on liberating caged animals, masked protesters broke into a family-owned mink farm in southeast Idaho, less than 80 miles west of Wyoming, and released 1,500 mink into the wild on Saturday.

Farm owner Jeff Hobbs told Cowboy State Daily that instead of freedom, the activists delivered a death sentence, leaving the animals to perish from dehydration, stress, heat or getting run over on the road.

“This is an unethical thing to do to animals,” Hobbs said. “Regardless of your value system, I haven’t quite figured out how you can claim that you’re doing something for the benefit of the animals that’s so harmful to them.”

When he spoke to Cowboy State Daily on Tuesday, Hobbs said he was still working to gather the loose minks in Franklin County. At this point, he said about 90% of the mink have been caught but still face health risks from the trauma of being temporarily released.

“This stressed them hard,” Hobbs said. “You stress animals and you run into problems. You have to do something to offset that stress so this has created a serious herd health problem.”

Hobbs said the break-in happened around 2:30 a.m. Saturday. Mink were almost immediately killed by passing cars and several more were running around the area, Hobbs said.

“Immediately we started calling out to people that we thought could assist us, and word spread in the community,” Hobbs said. “In a short time, I had almost 100 people here help them to catch animals.”

In a Saturday statement, the Franklin County Sheriff’s Office said it was investigating the incident. The department did not respond to Cowboy State Daily by publication.

On Sunday, the North American Animal Liberation Press Office posted a statement celebrating the release of the mink.

“The animals liberated this weekend have a fighting chance at life,” the statement said. “They faced a 100 percent death rate if they stayed on the farm.”

In an email to Cowboy State Daily, North American Animal Liberation press officer Jerry Vlasak disputed claims from Hobbs and the sheriff’s office that most of the mink had been recaptured.

“Almost surely did not happen,” Vlasak said. “These mink are not domesticated as the farmers claim. Scientific studies have shown them to be easily able to survive in the wild when they are released.”

Challis Hobbs, Jeff Hobbs’ son and executive director of Fur Commission USA, said in a Saturday statement that the action should be handled as a federal offense under the Animal Enterprise Terrorism Act.

“Those responsible for this attack are terrorists, plain and simple,” Challis Hobbs said.

Vlasak threw that same label back at Challis Hobbs and the Fur Commission USA.

“Those who breed, imprison and kill thousands of innocent animals every year to make a profit are the real terrorists,” Vlasak said.

Hobbs said that his fourth-generation family farm has long been the target of animal-rights organizations. In the 1990s and early 2000s, Hobbs said, authorities warned him twice that his farm ranked high on a list of likely targets and recommended he increase security.

Since then, he said, drones have flown over the property and people have driven by with cameras. Hobbs said a drone flew over the farm on Oct. 6, his father’s birthday, and was seen by a family friend who was preparing for a party.

“She didn’t realize that was a threat until after the release,” Hobbs said.

Hobbs said he understands people have different values and are entitled to be against the business of harvesting mink for fur.

“But none of us are entitled to try to press our value system on other people,” Hobbs said.

Moreover, he said the action of releasing 1,500 minks, which have no skills to survive in the wild, is antithetical to the larger goal of animal welfare.

“When people come in and do something this blatant, it’s done a lot of damage,” Hobbs said. “Animals are dying because of it.”

He also said releasing 1,500 mink, which have no skills to survive in the wild, runs counter to the larger goal of animal welfare. For Vlasak, it’s “laughable” for Hobbs, who profits from harvesting and selling mink pellets, to claim concern for the animals.

“The mink are born in February or March and are killed by gassing, clubbing or anal electrocution in November, before being skinned, sometimes while still alive, for their fur,” Vlasak said.

While Hobbs claimed a similar timeline from birth to harvest, he said the nature of how the minks are killed is far from the truth.

“They’re euthanized with carbon monoxide,” Hobbs said. “They just go to sleep.”

Hobbs said the mink live healthy lives on the farm, with constant access to fresh water, a balanced daily diet and warm, dry nests. He said the farm also has a herd-health program to treat animals that get sick.

Susan Curtis, director of Sandy’s Haven, a wildlife rescue service in Preston, Idaho, told Cowboy State Daily the Hobbs Family Farm has a local reputation for farming fur as ethically as possible.

“I would absolutely love it if the mink farming went away forever but I know they’re doing it as humanely as possible,” Curtis said. “I’ve never had any issue with the Hobbses.”

What the activists did, Curtis said, took the mink from a “bad situation and put them in a worse situation.” The release also endangers local wildlife by dropping the mink back into an ecosystem where they can strain the food supply, Curtis said, and it puts domestic animals, including outdoor pets, at risk of attack.

Already, Curtis said she’s heard of one wild goose with bite marks and a resident whose dog was attacked by one of the newly freed mink.

“These are definitely carnivores and predators, these little mink guys,” Curtis said.

That’s something that area resident Deirdre Burgess has learned the hard way.

“I live on the edge of town and I have chickens,” Burgess told Cowboy State Daily. “Or, I had chickens. I had 15 hens and 1 rooster and they killed my rooster and 10 of my hens.”

Burgess said her small flock was more pets than livestock. To lose all at once, and to encounter such a bloody scene in her backyard, was heartbreaking, she said.

“It was so sad,” Burgess said. “And it was just gross.”

Like Curtis, Burgess said she doesn’t agree with the business of fur. But simply freeing the animals, she said, condemned them to an almost certain death, and let the rest of them loose to do more damage.

“Do I buy furs? No,” Burgess said. “But on the other side of that, I wouldn’t turn all of those animals loose. There’s a humane way to do it. Letting them starve or get run over is absolutely no way to fix it. It doesn’t help.”

In 2015, activist Joseph Buddenberg was indicted under the Animal Enterprise Terrorism Act and later served two years in federal prison for his role in a cross-country campaign that released nearly 6,000 mink, including an estimated 1,800 animals from a farm in Burley, Idaho.

Though he does not claim a role in the most recent action, Buddenberg told Cowboy State Daily in an email that the Hobbs raid was justified.

“The fur industry’s days are numbered,” Buddenberg said. “Compassionate activists will continue to open cages and shut these places down.”

Emma Jane Jackson can be reached at emma@cowboystatedaily.com.

author: John Mullen
title: Is France burning down? The French revolt, rioting and the radical left
content:
Rioting is the voice of the unheard, and is completely inevitable once a spark of revolt arrives after months and years of austerity, extreme police violence and racism. Of course that doesn't mean the job of anticapitalists is to make plans about what buildings to burn next week. We don't want our young people to end up in prison for decades! The more organised and effective collective action is at all levels, the less chaos there will be, anyway. Union leaders need to build mass strikes quickly.

“Now that the focus is on all this violence, can you really recommend that school kids continue going to demonstrations?” asked a slimy journalist on France Info, the national 24-hour news radio, of a young activist, the morning after Saturday’s [October 17] day of action. Meanwhile Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, whose public relations team had been up all night racking their brains, managed nothing more sophisticated than to blame the unrest across the country on the radical left France Insoumise (France in Revolt).

Eight hundred thousand people joined demonstrations in dozens of towns on October 17. The protests were characterised by an explosion of popular creativity and anger. Far more people turned up than organisers had dared to hope, flooding into the streets to support the high school revolt, to protest about impoverishment and the cost of living, and to express their desire for rapid change.

Antifascist slogans were everywhere, as were Palestinian flags and placards in favour of voting for radical left FI candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon in next May’s presidential election. People sang the Marseillaise and the Internationale.

Where the police left the protests alone, nothing got smashed up. But the cops had their orders. They beat and injured thousands of protesters and quite a number of journalists and passers-by too, in one more attempt to frighten the masses off the streets.

In Mulhouse, in the East of France, a young woman lost an eye. In town after town, reports tell of completely unprovoked baton charges and teargas attacks. In Paris, demonstrators were massively tear-gassed at the starting point of the demo, as it was assembling. There are few things that make people want to riot more than being attacked while arriving at a rally.

In response, several thousand rioted in a number of towns. The town hall in Limoges in the centre of France and a Tourist Office in Lyon were set afire. Bus Shelters and wheelie bins were burned, and hundreds of shops looted and wrecked across the country (50 shops in Bordeaux, for example). Many of these were luxury shops, but others were ordinary small businesses.

Such events are inevitable in a situation of simmering mass anger, to which President Emmanuel Macron’s only significant response has been mass police violence. Hundreds of videos of the police thugs in action have circulated, including some of severe mutilation imposed deliberately. Is it any wonder that some fight back by smashing up places which make easier targets than the highly trained Robocops?

Others came to the demos so outraged at police violence and Macronite austerity that fighting back with paving stones felt right. More wanted to demonstrate at the Elysee Palace or the Hotel Matignon, whereas police authorities would only authorise protests several kilometres away.

We can add to the mix a certain number of police in disguise, agents provocateurs encouraging rioting. We have plenty of evidence that these are used in France, though it is generally impossible to prove in any specific case. Add, too, a bunch of opportunists hoping to rob pharmacies and computer shops. But an outburst of legitimate rage is the main explanation for Saturday’s rioting.

This obviously does not mean that organised radicals and revolutionaries should be making careful plans about which public buildings, or which cafés, pharmacies or phone shops to loot or burn next week. Denouncing the rioters is a complete waste of time, but the more organised effective action inspires people, the less chaos we will see.

The most influential politician by far among the protestors is Mélenchon. In his statement after the day of action, he insisted that it was President Macron and his ministers who were responsible for the horrific police violence and for the chaos in the streets. “Wherever there were no police [at the demonstrations] calm and joy were all around,” he said.

He added that his organisation did not believe rioting would help: “Whatever the responsibilities of the authorities, whatever their incompetence and their violence, we must refuse to take part in actions which do not have political meaning and which are contrary to our methods,” he insisted.

Green presidential candidate, Marine Tondelier criticised the government for its announcement before the day of action that hardline policing would be the norm. Other left-wing spokespeople trotted out old clichés of denunciation. “A sort of madness has taken over France,” lamented Gregory Doucet, Green mayor of Lyon.

The Powers-that-be are hoping to profit from the situation to damage FI. After Lecornu’s ravings mentioned above, hard right spokespeople demanded the organisation should be banned. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez blamed the disorder on “several thousand ultra-left individuals”. Ex-minister Bruno Retailleau insisted “the only possible response is the implacable force of the state” and demanded that a state of emergency be declared.

At least one of his senior advisors, Jean-Baptiste Moreau, suggested that Macron should resign. Instead, the president commandeered prime time television Sunday evening to moan that, in the six months before the presidential elections, this was just not the right time for a social explosion.

“All those who want to persuade you today that what is urgent is to be on the streets, to demonstrate, to create unrest have one single aim: they want to damage the republic and block the presidential debate,” he complained.

“Nothing can explain, nothing can excuse” the rioting, Macron continued. He promised “action” to respond to people’s “worries”, which he said he “understood”. The usual empty phrases. He has asked his prime minister to meet with political parties and union leaders, but without any suggestion of real concessions. Monday morning a crisis cabinet meeting was underway.

But what of our side? The biggest trade union confederation, the CGT declared in a press release: “Because of its refusal to the demands of a peaceful mass movement, the government is politically responsible for the rise in violence observed today.”

The main union confederation leaderships called two weeks back for mass strikes on November 5, not in any hurry to encourage the revolt. Much more is needed. The situation is such that a general strike is both possible and necessary. Yellow Vest organisations are demanding a general strike on November 5. Union leaderships must be made to build such a strike.

[John Mullen lives in the Paris region and is a supporter of the France Insoumise. Visit his website at randombolshevik.org.]

author: Chris Walker
title: Mahmoud Khalil Files Appeal to SCOTUS to Block Trump Admin From Detaining Him
content:
The pro-Palestine activist says the Trump administration is infringing upon his free speech rights.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Former Columbia University graduate student and pro-Palestine activist Mahmoud Khalil has filed a request to the Supreme Court, asking it to overturn an appellate court’s ruling that could lead to his being detained and deported by the Trump administration in the near future.

Khalil is a legal U.S. resident, and his spouse has citizenship status, making the administration’s attempt to deport him last year an extraordinary move. In March 2025, shortly after he graduated, he was detained by immigration officials, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio utilizing scarcely used powers of his office to do so despite Khalil’s legal residency, citing unfounded claims that the activist was involved in “antisemitic protests and disruptive activities” while studying at Columbia.

Khalil was kept in a Louisiana immigration jail, but was released in June 2025 after a federal judge found Rubio’s actions were likely unconstitutional. The administration appealed, and in January 2026, a 2-1 decision from the Third Circuit Court of Appeals overturned the lower court’s decision, stating that Khalil’s claims couldn’t be addressed at that level of the judicial system, and had to be moved to an immigration court, which is managed by the executive branch.

On Monday, Khalil and his lawyers announced that he was appealing that decision to the Supreme Court, hoping that they will overturn it, allowing him to remain protected from being detained again for the time being. He called the continued efforts by the administration an assault on his free speech rights.

“If the Trump administration can punish someone for their pro-Palestine speech, this or any future administration can punish anyone for any speech, whether it’s pro-Palestine, pro-Israel, or anything,” he said in a statement announcing his appeal.

Khalil will still have legal avenues available to him to challenge the Trump administration’s attempts to deport him, but his options to thwart the White House’s actions would be much narrower if the Supreme Court doesn’t take his case. For a case to be heard, at least four of the nine sitting justices must agree to the writ of certiorari that Khalil submitted to them. Afterward, it would likely be a few months before oral arguments begin, and then it would likely take until the end of the current term — around May or June 2027 — for a decision to be rendered.

Khalil’s case has been rife with irregularities, including being pushed by the Trump administration to proceed at a faster tempo than other similar cases. Khalil also detailed last spring the horrors he faced while he was detained in Louisiana, decrying how his rights were being infringed upon.

“I think about the breakneck speed with which my case was heard and decided, running roughshod over due process,” he wrote in his piece for The Washington Post. “On the flip side, I think about those I am locked up with, many of whom have been languishing for months or years waiting for their ‘due process.'”

“Why should protesting Israel’s indiscriminate killing of thousands of innocent Palestinians result in the erosion of my constitutional rights?” Khalil stated, adding that, “A democracy for some — a democracy of convenience — is no democracy at all.”

In this edition of the Equality Culture Club’s interview series, we speak with Meredith Walker, author and co-founder of Smart Girls, an online community created to help girls learn more about themselves and the world around them. Through a series of questions and answers, she addresses her writing style, the advice that can often feel like a trap, feminist media recommendations, and more.

Q: Was there a specific moment or conversation that made you realize Be Yourself and Other Bad Advice needed to exist?

A: Through years of listening to girls in schools and communities, a pattern emerged. Teens and young women told me how stressful it was to feel so much pressure to achieve and to have their lives mapped out before they even knew what they really wanted or were good at.

That pressure isn’t anything new, but social media has added another dimension. Now it’s continuous, hyper-targeted, and carried around with them all day. There’s a constant stream of content telling them what life should look like and all the ways they could be improving themselves.

It became clear to me that girls need more tools for questioning all of those expectations and pressures. They need some help figuring out what they actually think and want. Getting to know yourself and learning to think for yourself are skills. This book is a way to practice them.

Q: What’s a piece of advice that sounds empowering but can actually be a kind of trap?

It was meant as an expansive message that women didn’t have to accept all the old limits on what their lives could look like. But it can easily become another source of pressure. We’ve turned it into: “You should have it all, and what’s wrong with you if you can’t pull it off?” A great career, meaningful relationships, financial success, a comfy home—and somehow hold it all together without much of a social safety net. Good luck!

We can have an interesting, meaningful life, but probably not every version of it, all at the same time. And that’s okay.

Q: If you could put one line from Be Yourself and Other Bad Advice on a poster in every school hallway, what would it be?

A: “No matter where you go, you’ll always bring you with you—so make sure you like who that person is.”

Q: How do you balance humour and vulnerability on the page?

A: I wanted readers to know the book was going to be honest, and I was willing to be honest about myself, too. I struggled my first year of college, made mistakes, had boring jobs….and had the emotional intelligence to once throw an egg at my brother. Not when I was a toddler. When I was 20.

For me, the balance is being vulnerable (and ridiculous) without making the reader the joke. A little humour lets me write honestly about my mistakes and what I learned the hard way without sounding preachy.

Q: For anyone unfamiliar, how would you describe the mission of Smart Girls?

A: Smart Girls was created to help girls know themselves better and become more curious about the world around them.

We offered web shows, interviews, workshops, summer camps, journalism boot camps, and a friendly digital community. The idea underneath all of it was pretty simple: girls are totally interesting, their ideas matter, and the world is worth being curious about.

Q: Can you point to a moment that confirmed you were doing something important?

A: Well, it was pretty rad when we started Smart Girls Ask. We showed up on red carpets and, instead of asking women what they were wearing, we asked them substantive questions about their craft, their ideas, and what they cared about.

Women standing on a red carpet had interesting things to say. We decided to ask them. Our community loved it—and so did the women we interviewed.

To close, we ask every Equality Culture Club guest about the people, stories, and ideas that shape their vision for a more equal world. From the future they hope to see, to the women who inspire them, to the books and films that have stayed with them, these reflections offer a glimpse into what fuels their work and optimism.

Q: What excites you most about the prospect of a gender-equal future?

A: Under what circumstances is gender inequality acceptable? None. Zero. Gender equality should be so fundamental that we no longer have to make the case for it. It should simply be the baseline in our workplaces, our policies, our communities, everywhere.

Imagine a world where gender has no bearing on who gets to make decisions that affect all of us. Think of what we might notice, fix, or understand differently if everyone actually had an equal say.

And oh my gosh, HALLELUJAH! When the day comes that gender inequality disappears from laws and policies affecting women’s bodies and healthcare, we will dance in the streets!

Q: Who is your favorite feminist icon and why?

A: I can’t pick just one, so I’ll give you three: Barbara Jordan, Kathy Valentine, and Linda Ellerbee.

Barbara Jordan was a brilliant congresswoman from Texas who blew everyone’s minds during Watergate. During the Nixon impeachment hearings, she explained what the Constitution required of us in a way that still makes you want to be a better citizen and a better person. I have a T-shirt with her image on it, and it’s so awesome when someone says, “I love your shirt!” They get it.

Kathy Valentine is a writer, musician, member of the Go-Go’s, and very punk rock. But what I especially love about her is that she keeps challenging herself. She writes music, books, and essays, goes on adventures, and pushes herself out of her comfort zone. She’s just so cool.

And Linda Ellerbee is an award-winning journalist and producer who broke barriers in broadcasting and created Nick News, a model for how to talk with young people about what’s going on in their world. She respected her audience enough to tell them the truth about complicated things and trusted them to think for themselves. She also mentored me and gave me my start in TV, and I love her.

Q: Do you have feminist media recommendations?

A: Yes Please by Amy Poehler, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings by Maya Angelou, This Book is Feminist: An Intersectional Primer for Next-Gen Changemakers by Jamia Wilson, Moxie by Jennifer Mathieu, Ginger Mancino, Kid Comedian by Wendi Aarons, and All I Ever Wanted: A Rock ‘n’ Roll Memoir by Kathy Valentine.

And watch Somebody Somewhere. It’s so good at showing what can happen when you discover more about who you are and find your people.

title: Кому нужен АУЕ? Распространение арестанских идеологий в местах лишения свободы

author: Khushi Arora, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Williams Lake First Nation memorializes history and justice with opening of Sḱulé7ten Park
content:
Williams Lake First Nation Willie Sellars speaks about the significance of Sḱulé7ten park during its official opening.

Photo by Khushi Arora




This story was originally printed in the 

Williams Lake Tribune

 and appears here with minor style edits.







The Williams Lake First Nation (WLFN) celebrated the grand opening of a new memorial park in downtown Williams Lake, unveiling its name as Sḱulé7ten Park.




WLFN, also known as T’exelc, welcomed the community to the park on Oct. 13. The space memorializes WLFN’s journey towards reaching a historic specific claim settlement with “Canada.” The colonial government illegally displaced the First Nation from their traditional village site 165 years ago, in what’s now the City of Williams Lake. 




After guiding attendees through the pronunciation of the park’s name “skoo LET nn,” WLFN member William Lulua explained that the surrounding area included spaces where people did vision quests. Although there was a disconnection from the practice as Williams Lake developed into a city, he said the names of the people received through those places could not be taken away.




William Lulua shares the history and meaning behind Sḱulé7ten park’s name during the official opening on Tuesday, Oct.13. Photo by Khushi Arora




According to the Facebook post by WLFN, the name Sḱulé7ten is the traditional Secwepemcstin word for the area that makes up downtown Williams Lake, and the name translates to “where you find yourself.”




Before the main opening drum song, Elder Virginia Gilbert was called upon to do a prayer. She spoke about attending both day and residential “schools,” expressing gratitude that her five children had not attended those institutions. She gave thanks for her ancestors, family, food, water and medicines, and asked that the park provide a place for rest for people struggling with addictions.




“Great spirit, let this place bless them and look after them,” added Gilbert.




Students from Little Chiefs Primary School performed drumming and songs during the ceremony. 




Little Chiefs Primary School students drum and sing during the official opening of Sḱulé7ten park on Tuesday, Oct.13. Photo by Khushi Arora




WLFN Chief Willie Sellars thanked the students, recognizing the strength it takes to perform and carry forward songs significant to the First Nation and their ancestors.




Sellars also thanked the contractors who helped design and build the park and said, “we couldn’t have done it without all those contractors stepping up and contributing to this project, city representatives, community members and WLFN staff who attended the opening.”




WLFN councillor and director of self-government Chris Wycotte recalled the First Nation’s persistence through decades of pursuing its specific claim.




“We just said, no, we’re going to take it as far as we can,” said Wycotte.




Community members gather to celebrate the official opening of Sḱulé7ten memorial park in downtown Williams Lake on Oct. 13. Photo by Khushi Arora




He described finding documents in the provincial archives that revealed an injustice against the First Nation. After repeated rejections, WLFN continued pursuing the claim through legal proceedings, eventually taking its fight to the Supreme Court of Canada.




“And this is what we end up with today. And this park here is just a memorial to that journey,” he added.




Chief Sellars acknowledged relationships with municipal, provincial and federal governments, saying collaboration had helped bring community to where it is today.




“And that relationship has been tough at times, but where we’re at right now, we’re in a good place,” Sellars added.




“Under the settlement, Canada provided the Williams Lake First Nation with $135 million in total compensation,” the federal government stated in a September 2023 news release about the Village Site Specific Claim.




Sellars said the First Nation’s approach to the settlement honours its ancestors while providing for future generations. He described the opening as an opportunity for the wider community to participate in reconciliation.




“That’s taking care of our generations, four, five, six, seven generations from now, and that is what we are very proud of as Williams Lake First Nation,” he continued.




WLFN manager of culture and language Cecil Sheena introduced a grass dance with Reggie Sandy and Sellars and invited drummers to take part.




Afterward, Sellars thanked Sheena and the drummers and invited another round of applause for Sandy, whom he recognized as an emerging leader and a positive role model.




Williams Lake First Nation leaders, dignitaries and project partners cut the ribbon to officially open Sḱulé7ten Park. Photo by Khushi Arora




Sellars then invited dignitaries such as Williams Lake Mayor Surinderpal Rathor, councillors, WLFN leadership, staff and contractors to participate in the ribbon cutting, officially opening the park. The Sḱulé7ten Park is located at the corner of Yorston Street and Third Avenue.




“It’s open for anyone and everyone, “ he concluded.

Williams Lake First Nation memorializes history and justice with opening of Sḱulé7ten Park

Indiginews

title: Meral Çiçek: Jineology must develop concrete solutions to social problems
content:
Journalist Meral Çiçek, who attended the European Jineology Conference in Haelen, the Netherlands, spoke to ANF about the educational activities carried out across Europe over the past decade, the key discussions at the conference and the work that needs to be developed in the coming period.




Meral Çiçek said that Jineology has brought about significant changes in women's approaches to knowledge and learning. She stressed that, in the coming period, research into social problems must go hand in hand with the development of solutions. She also highlighted the importance of strengthening ties and developing joint projects with women's organisations.







 







‘Knowledge is hidden in every aspect of life’




Meral Çiçek highlighted the methodological diversity of Jineology's educational activities in Europe, conducted through camps, seminars, workshops and conferences. She said these activities have encouraged women to develop new ways of questioning and examining the world around them.




Çiçek explained that education is not regarded merely as the transmission of knowledge, emphasising that Jineology encourages women to question existing knowledge while also transforming their understanding of where knowledge comes from.




Çiçek said: “It is not simply a matter of treating formal educational institutions or written books as the primary sources of knowledge, but of showing that knowledge is actually hidden in every aspect of life. Therefore, the relationship between two people is also a source of knowledge. Our own culture is also a source of knowledge; indeed, it is a fundamental source of knowledge. We can learn from our mothers, from our relationships with children, with women and with men, from social relationships as a whole, and from the relationship between human beings and nature.”




Meral Çiçek stressed the importance of learning to recognise the sources of knowledge found in everyday life. She said that Jineology's educational activities have introduced many women to different ways of thinking, questioning and learning.




‘Findings must be translated into practical policies’




Meral Çiçek said that, considering current conditions and needs, society should be the primary focus of Jineology in the coming period. She stressed that this did not mean that work concerning society had not been carried out in the past.




Çiçek said that the crises deepened by capitalist modernity, changes within Kurdish society and growing social needs demanded a more concrete perspective. She said, “We need to focus more closely on the social problems experienced here, but not merely investigate them from a historical or social perspective. We must also show possible ways out of these problems and identify the paths towards solutions.”




Meral Çiçek emphasised the need to investigate social problems more deeply, particularly those experienced by women, make these problems easier to understand and translate the findings into practical policies. She said that Kurdish women in Europe, as well as women from different peoples, needed such an approach.




Çiçek stressed that a scientific approach centred on social life could not be limited to institutional relations. She said it was necessary to work collectively with grassroots women's organisations and different women's groups.




‘A single method is not enough to reach women’




Meral Çiçek said that different methods must be developed to reach Kurdish women, European women and women from various migrant communities living in Europe. She noted that experiences in this field had also been shared at the conference.




Çiçek highlighted the importance of organising Jineology workshops on a continuous basis. She said that workshops, public panel discussions, seminars and meetings could be used to share research findings with society. She also stressed the need to make more effective use of digital media.




Meral Çiçek pointed out that Europe has a strong institutional foundation for women's studies. She proposed developing relationships with women's studies institutes and gender studies centres at universities, as well as independent research centres and academies.




Çiçek said these relationships should be based on mutual learning, allowing the Jineology perspective to become more widely known while also drawing on different experiences.




‘Jineology belongs to all of us’




Meral Çiçek stressed that Jineology should be represented more widely at women's gatherings and in areas of struggle, not merely as an institutional identity but also as a perspective. She acknowledged that the women's movement also had shortcomings in this regard.




Çiçek said that criticism and self-criticism concerning these shortcomings had been expressed at the conference. She said, “Jineology is not merely an institutional identity. That is one dimension of it. But ultimately, as the science of women and life, or as a science that produces knowledge of free life, Jineology belongs to all of us. Therefore, it must be represented by all of us.”




Meral Çiçek said that all components of the Kurdish Women's Movement in Europe bear responsibility in this regard. She stressed that the Jineology perspective must be developed more comprehensively, both within individuals and in their work.




Çiçek said that this approach could not only help reach Kurdish women more directly but also strengthen the common ground for struggle with European and migrant women.




‘Not merely identifying problems, but producing knowledge of free life’




Meral Çiçek also discussed Jineology's relationship with feminism and the differences between them, noting that feminist theories and women's studies are important sources for Jineology.




Çiçek explained what she considered the fundamental difference: “I think the most fundamental point is that Jineology does not limit itself to researching, examining and clarifying history or the present. It also seeks to produce knowledge of free life.”




Meral Çiçek said that women's reality should not be examined within the confines of a particular historical period or geographical region. She explained that Jineology seeks to understand women's existence in relation to social reality, beginning with the earliest layers of history. She added that the method of women's archaeology forms part of this approach.




Çiçek drew attention to the metaphor of a “dagger in the back of society” used in the perspective Abdullah Öcalan presented to the conference. She said, “The enslavement of women is a dagger in the back of society. Therefore, no social problem can be resolved without removing it.”




Meral Çiçek stressed that this approach aims not only to expose the enslavement of women but also to abolish it and build a free life.




‘A common perspective is needed against attacks on women's gains’




Meral Çiçek called for closer ties with women's movements and the development of a common perspective, warning that women across different parts of the world face systematic attacks on their will, organisation and achievements.




Çiçek pointed to attacks on the achievements of the women's revolution in Rojava and North and East Syria, the exclusion of women from public life in Afghanistan and the killings of women in Europe. She stressed that femicide and the systematic destruction of women must be understood within this broader context.




Meral Çiçek said, “What are we going to do as women's movements around the world? How will we defend our existence and our social bonds, and how will we wage an effective struggle against these attacks? The issue is not simply rejecting something or resisting something.




How will we find a way out? How will we uproot that reality and build a free life in its place? Jineology is the science of this. This science is not limited to a single society. It is not a science developed solely for Kurdish women or Kurdish society.”




Meral Çiçek said that Jineology establishes connections between the local experiences from which it draws inspiration and universal problems, giving it the potential to reach women from different peoples.




‘The decision to establish academies is important for new initiatives’




Meral Çiçek said that Jineology studies have also developed beyond Europe and Kurdistan, noting that institutional structures have been established in Egypt and extensive work is being carried out in Abya Yala.




Çiçek highlighted the importance of women's studies in Asia, particularly their theoretical and practical experiences in overcoming colonialism. She stressed the need to expand contacts with women's movements in different regions, including Africa and the United States.




Meral Çiçek said that the institutional foundations of these initiatives must also be strengthened, describing the conference's decision to establish academies as an important step.




She concluded, “I am hopeful in this regard. I believe that, in the period following this conference, the Jineology Academy in Europe, or other academies that will be established, can play a strong role in this respect.”

title: Whereabouts of five people detained by Iranian forces unknown
content:
A report published by Kolbernews provided information about the disappearance of five mountaineers from Rojhilat (East Kurdistan) following their detention by Iranian state forces.




More than 30 armed Iranian intelligence agents reportedly raided the homes of seven members of the Helo and Sewz Mountain groups, independent mountaineering groups based in Saqqez. The mountaineers were detained following the home raids.




The report stated that the mountaineers Abdullah Amini and Rahim Haqparast were subsequently released. However, Mihemed Hekîmpûr, Mistefa Qadirî, Mihemedsalih Husênî, Husên Ebdulahî, and Xalid Rehemî remain in detention, and their whereabouts and fate are unknown.




It was reported that all the mountaineers had been subjected to torture while in detention. The report also stated that those whose fate remains unknown have been denied the right to meet with their families and lawyers.

title: Rape case in Siverek highlighted at "Women, Justice and Memory" vigil
content:
Organised by the Amed Network Against Violence, the vigil continued for its third week outside Diyarbakır Courthouse. Participants carried photographs of women and chanted slogans including “Femicide is political,” “Protect, exonerate, prosecute” and “Jin, jiyan, azadî” (Woman, life, freedom).




Berfin Elçi, a member of the executive board of the Amed branch of the Human Rights Association (IHD), stated that femicides are not isolated incidents, but are the result of a male-dominated system, impunity and the mentality that seeks to control women’s lives.




Emphasising that women should not have to seek justice only after they have been killed, Berfin Elçi called for reports of violence to be taken seriously, suspicious deaths of women to be effectively investigated, and protection obligations to be fulfilled.




Drawing attention to the release of three defendants in the rape case in Siverek (Sêwereg), as well as the acquittal of the perpetrator tried on abuse charges despite Fatmanur Çelik’s pursuit of justice, Berfin Elçi stated that practices of impunity threaten women’s right to life.




Stories of murdered women were read aloud




During the vigil, the stories of Canan Yıldırım, Naz Aslan, Ebru Serep and Pınar Güneş, who died in different cities in October, were shared. It was reported that Canan Yıldırım was killed by the man she lived with in Antalya, while Naz Aslan died under suspicious circumstances in the Nusaybin district of Mardin (Mêrdîn). Ebru Serep died after her home was set on fire in the Seferihisar district of Izmir, while Pınar Güneş lost her life after shots were fired following an argument in Alaçatı. Participants called for all circumstances surrounding the women’s deaths to be fully clarified and for those responsible to be held accountable.




Policies of impunity must be exposed




Speaking at the vigil, Halide Türkoğlu, spokesperson for the DEM Party Women’s Assembly, said that women’s struggle for equality and freedom was being targeted and stressed the need to continue fighting against policies of impunity.




Türkoğlu underlined that they wanted a country where women could live freely and equally without the fear of being murdered. She added that the vigil taking place in Amed was giving a voice to women murdered across all parts of Turkey.




The event concluded with a “moment of silence in memory” of the women. Participants stated that they would continue to gather every Tuesday to demand justice, truth and remembrance.
