So war es in gewisser Weise nur konsequent, dass im Bericht zu Rüstungsangelegenheiten vom Dezember 2021 die Verspätungen mit 52 Monaten angegeben werden und sich die Kostensteigerungen auf 13,8 Milliarden Euro summieren.




Es ist also nicht gelungen – oder es war wohl eh nie gewollt –, die Rüstungsindustrie stärker an die Kandare zu nehmen. Auffällig war ohnehin, wie entspannt und positiv die Waffenhersteller von Anfang an auf die Agenda Rüstung reagierten. Schon aus der ersten Pressemitteilung der größten Rüstungslobbyverbände zum Gutachten im Oktober 2014 wurde ersichtlich, wohin die Reise gehen würde: »Die Studie bestätigt die Notwendigkeit der industrieseitig bereits seit längerem angemahnten ausreichenden Mittelbereitstellung.« Die Entwicklung der Rüstungsausgaben war dann auch Thema im ab November 2014 tagenden Dialogkreis, der sich aus 70 Vertreter*innen des Verteidigungsministeriums und der Rüstungsindustrie zusammensetzte und im Juni 2015 einen ersten Ergebnisbericht veröffentlichte. Darin wurde unmissverständlich festgehalten, es bestehe weiterhin die »Notwendigkeit einer graduellen Erhöhung des Einzelplans 14 [Verteidigungshaushalt] und seines investiven Anteils«. Wir treten als ver.di gleichzeitig dafür ein, die Diskussion um mehr Sicherheit in Europa nicht in erster Linie aus einer militärischen Perspektive heraus zu führen. Wir brauchen einen breiten zivilgesellschaftlichen Diskurs darüber, wie wir in Europa zukünftig in Frieden und Sicherheit zusammenleben wollen und rufen alle zivilgesellschaftlichen Akteur*innen dazu auf, sich in diesen Friedensdiskurs einzubringen. Unser Ziel bleibt eine Welt mit weniger Waffen, insbesondere streben wir nachdrücklich eine dauerhafte atomare Abrüstung an. Wir wollen keinen neuen Rüstungswettlauf, der auch dazu führt, dass Gelder für die dringlichen Investitionen in den sozial-ökologischen Umbau fehlen oder dem Sozialstaat entzogen werden. Die Erhöhung der Verteidigungsausgaben auf einen dauerhaften Anteil von zwei Prozent am Bruttoinlandsprodukt, wie es das NATO-Ziel vorsieht, lehnen wir daher ab. Die Bundesregierung plant im Rahmen einer Grundgesetzänderung den Aufbau eines Sondervermögens. Dieses soll ausschließlich für die Zwecke der Bundeswehr zweckgebunden sein. Insbesondere sollen zusätzliche Rüstungsgüter beschafft werden. Diese Pläne lehnen wir ab. Sehr wohl notwendig ist in diesem Jahr angesichts der finanziellen Herausforderungen durch die russische Invasion in der Ukraine und ihre Folgen eine erhöhte Nettokreditaufnahme des Bundes. Wir werben für eine umfassende Definition von Sicherheit. Diese umfasst die Versorgungssicherheit durch den Ausbau erneuerbarer Ener-gien ebenso wie den Gesundheitsschutz, auszubauende öffentliche Infrastrukturen einschließlich der IT-Sicherheit sowie mehr Mittel für die internationale Entwicklungszusammenarbeit und den Zivil- und Katastrophenschutz.




All diese längst bekannten und teilweise neuen Herausforderungen und Aufgaben werden über eine erhöhte Nettokreditaufnahme und bestehende Steuereinnahmen allein nicht zu schultern sein. Daher treten wir als ver.di für eine stärkere Besteuerung hoher Einkommen sowie großer Vermögen und Erbschaften ein. Wir fordern zudem eine Lastenausgleichsabgabe für besonders vermögende Privatpersonen und größere und mittlere Unternehmen. Reiche und Superreiche müssen gerade in dieser Zeit einen angemesseneren Beitrag zur Finanzierung des Gemeinwesens leisten.




Gemeinsam mit dem DGB und seinen anderen Mitgliedsgewerkschaften halten wir daran fest, dass die militärische Friedenssicherung nicht zulasten des sozialen Friedens erkauft werden darf. Deutschland muss als wesentlicher Akteur an einer gemeinsamen europäischen Friedens- und Sicherheitsarchitektur arbeiten. Auch wir Gewerkschaften leisten durch unsere transnationale Arbeit einen Beitrag dazu

.“

Bereits beschlossen ist insbesondere die Beschaffung des US-Kampfjets F-35, den Berlin erwerben will, um in der Bundesrepublik gelagerte US-Atomwaffen an ihrem Ziel abwerfen zu können. Der US-Konzern Lockheed Martin erwirtschaftet mit dem Jet, den Militärs wegen seiner zahlreichen Pannen kritisieren, mehr als ein Viertel seines Umsatzes und ist deshalb auf neue Käufer angewiesen. Verteidigungsministerin Christine (…) insistiert, es handle sich nicht um „Aufrüstung“ oder gar „Militarisierung“, sondern nur um „die Ausstattung, die eine wehrhafte Demokratie braucht“. Zu dem Material, das aus dem „Sondervermögen“ finanziert werden soll, zählen nach Aussage der Bundeswehr auch „überjährige Großvorhaben“, so etwa Kampfjets, die die alternden Tornados der Luftwaffe ablösen sollen. Sie werden insbesondere benötigt, um die „nukleare Teilhabe“ zu sichern; darunter wird verstanden, dass deutsche Flugzeuge die US-Atombomben, die in Büchel (Eifel) gelagert sind, im Kriegsfall an einen Zielort fliegen und sie dort abwerfen können. Wie es in einem aktuellen Bericht des Stockholmer Forschungsinstituts SIPRI heißt, stiegen in Europa die Einfuhren von Rüstungsgütern im Fünfjahreszeitraum von 2017 bis 2021 um 19 Prozent gegenüber dem Zeitraum von 2012 bis 2016 – mehr als auf jedem anderen Kontinent. Ursache dafür, so stellt SIPRI fest, sei die Aufrüstung gegen Russland gewesen. 54 Prozent der europäischen Rüstungsimporte kamen demnach aus den Vereinigten Staaten; ein erheblicher Teil davon ging auf den Kauf von insgesamt 71 F-35-Kampfjets durch Großbritannien, Norwegen und die Niederlande zurück. Darüber hinaus hätten weitere Staaten F-35-Jets bestellt, etwa Finnland (64 Stück), die Schweiz (36 Stück) und Polen (32 Stück). Nun kommt die Bestellung durch die Bundesrepublik hinzu.“

(…) Mit anderen Worten: Es stimmt nicht, dass für all diese so radikal oder naiv anmutenden Forderungen kein Geld da ist. (…) Dabei wären etwa Maßnahmen gegen Hunger und eine andere Politik gegenüber Geflüchteten gleichzeitig auch nachhaltigere Investitionen in Frieden, weil sie viel Kriegsgründe an der Wurzel bekämpfen. (…) Einer der ideologischen, affektiven, politischen und ökonomischen Grundpfeiler des Autoritarismus ist gerade der Militarismus. Insofern ist eine militarisierte Demokratie nicht das Gegenteil einer Autokratie – sondern ihre Keimzelle. Darauf wies bereits vor über 100 Jahren, nach der Zustimmung der zum Ersten Weltkrieg führenden Kriegskredite durch die SPD, die dissidente Sozialistin Rosa Luxemburg hin. (…) Es gibt in Russland, in der Ukraine und in der Europäischen Union zivilgesellschaftliche Bewegungen, Graswurzelinitiativen und Support-Gruppen, die jeweils vor Ort gegen den Krieg und gegen die den Krieg bedingenden Verhältnisse kämpfen. Die einzige Aussicht für einen dauerhaften Frieden liegt heute immer noch nicht in einem neuen Wettrüsten, sondern in einer konsequenten internationalistischen und antimilitaristischen Bewegung von unten. Wenn es heute Kräfte gibt, die den Frieden voranbringen, dann sind es ganz sicher nicht Rheinmetall, Heckler & Koch oder die deutsche Bundeswehr, sondern die Initiativen, die gerade in der Ukraine, in Russland und in der EU das Leben und Überleben organisieren – die sich formierende Anti-Kriegs-Bewegung, Menschenrechtsorganisationen, der Kunst- und Kultursektor, Selbstorganisationen von Geflüchteten, feministische Frauengruppen, queere LGBTQ-Initiativen, Initiativen für gegenseitige Hilfe und Solidarität.“

title: روش‌های سازمان‌یابی کمونیستی
content:
This essay is the second part of The Dislocation of Vendémiaire, following Part I, “The Disruptors of the 21st Century and the Ideological Collusion.” While Part I interprets the 2026 France-centered student-led protest wave as a politically dislocated movement—one misread by mainstream discourse as a multi-class coalition when it is in fact an expression of fragmentation within the proletariat—Part II develops the theoretical argument behind that claim. Drawing on Marx’s thesis of society’s polarization into two hostile camps, it distinguishes between “property” and “proletarianization” in the sense of national economics and in the sense of political economy. The essay argues that class should be analyzed through the actual control over the production of labor-power, and that digital capitalism increasingly enables capital to dominate labor-power directly, beyond the mediation of formal ownership of physical means of production. On this basis, it explains why many who appear as middle-class or petty-producer subjects in national-economic terms—scholars, franchise shopkeepers, senior programmers, platform creators—are in political-economic terms being proletarianized, while carrying petty-bourgeois habits of political compromise, individualism, hostility to centralized discipline, and identity- or interest-based linkage. The result is a form of struggle that is radical in appearance but conservative and spontaneous in its core: it completes the first step of linkage through identity and affinity, but fails to return to the common ground of class interests and to connect with the broader industrial working class.

title: Hobby Lobby’s Billionaire Founders Are Building a White Evangelical America
content:
Michael Blanding’s new book documents how the billionaires behind the craft store are funding evangelical propaganda.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

For decades, Barbara and David Green, the billionaire couple behind the craft store chain Hobby Lobby, have tried to shape the country according to their white evangelical worldview. In his book The Gospel According to Hobby Lobby: Inside a Billionaire Family’s Quest to Craft a Christian Nation, investigative journalist Michael Blanding shows how the Greens deliberately used their wealth to build institutions and gain cultural and political influence. They funded missionaries, ministries, and evangelical colleges, produced documentaries, and founded the Museum of the Bible in Washington, D.C., which was filled with tens of thousands looted and stolen antiquities at its founding. According to Blanding, Hobby Lobby was forced to return 17,000 of the looted and stolen artifacts after a raid by federal agents.

The Greens have also backed controversial conservative figures and have been at the forefront of some of the most contentious legal battles of recent decades, including the fight over reproductive rights. In this interview, Blanding — the best-selling author of The Map Thief, In Shakespeare’s Shadow, The Coke Machine, and most recently, The Gospel According to Hobby Lobby (2026) — discusses the beliefs that drive the Greens, the strategy behind their giving, and what it means that they now operate from the center of American political life.

The interview that follows has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Claudia Garcia-Rojas: What was the moment you felt a flicker of interest in writing about the Green family?

Michael Blanding: It was immediate upon reading a 2021 New York Times article that was about the seizure of the Gilgamesh Dream tablet in the Museum of the Bible. Halfway through, it said that the tablet was owned by Hobby Lobby Corporation. It got me curious. What is this big-box craft chain doing with an ancient tablet? Why and how was Hobby Lobby trafficking Middle Eastern antiquities? I started researching and realized they were doing it to prove the truth of the Bible, and they had used their fortune to fund right-wing religious causes. It made me realize there was a much bigger story about this family and the influence and impact that they have in our culture.

Early on, you trace a worldview in which the Greens see their lives as evidence of God’s intervention and believe they possess absolute biblical truth. What happens when that view is combined with enormous wealth and political power?

I wanted to understand where the Green family was coming from and the origins of their beliefs. I found two strains in their beliefs. One was Pentecostalism: speaking in tongues, receiving prophecies, hearing God’s voice direct your every move. The other is fundamentalism, that the Bible is inerrant. What surprised me is that American fundamentalism only goes back about 100 years; before that, the Bible was open to many interpretations. Once you see it as inerrant, there’s only one truth, and anyone that doesn’t follow is going to hell. So, my central question became: how does that sincere belief, and I have no doubt it’s sincere, interact with our pluralistic democracy?

What emerged were questions of accountability. When you believe you have a personal relationship with God and he directs all your actions, you see yourself as privileged, doing God’s work. When things go wrong, the Greens blame their lack of faith in God. But oftentimes they blame others. When they nearly lost Hobby Lobby in the ’80s oil bust, the lesson wasn’t that they’d taken on too much debt, but that they hadn’t been humble enough before God. There’s no sense that their actions are theirs or they need to learn from their mistakes. That lack of personal accountability becomes maddening over time. The Green men are the public face of the family, but the women seem to hold real power behind the scenes. What role do they play?

The Greens were major supporters of Bill Gothard. One of the main Christian ministries the Greens funded was the one founded by Gothard. He had an extremely hierarchical view of the family — God, then the father, the mother, and the children — that the Green family really embraced. Yet, during the Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc. Supreme Court case, [in which the court ruled that certain employers could block their employees access to birth control if it violates the employers’ religious beliefs], Barbara Green became the family’s main spokesperson, I think to shield them from accusations of gender discrimination. When it was convenient, they pushed her to the forefront.

I’m also thinking about David’s mother. His siblings all went into ministry, and she seems to have pressured him not to be the outlier.

His mother had a huge impact. In his books, he barely mentions his father beyond saying he was a pastor, but he talks constantly about his mother and how she was critical of him because he wasn’t doing more for God. When he became a department store manager, she’d ask, “What are you doing for the Lord, David?” When he became a regional manager over six stores, she’d ask again. There’s a Freudian reading here: once he built his wealth, he gave so much to religious causes partly to assuage guilt from her pressure.

In the book you note that despite their strict beliefs, the Greens had their own first child, Mart, out of wedlock?

I was surprised to discover that. They married in February, I believe, and Mart was born seven months later. The birth announcement described a healthy baby at a normal weight. It seems clear they had premarital sex, which I don’t judge, but which their religion did, and which was grounds for excommunication then.

They’ve never acknowledged it. Them not being able to follow their own religion, yet imposing it on other people, telling them what to do with their reproductive freedom. I found that fascinating, if not completely arrogant and hypocritical.

You place the Greens within a movement shaped by figures like R.J. Rushdoony, Jerry Falwell, and Bill Gothard. How direct was their influence on the family?

I wanted to tell of the rise of Christian nationalism alongside the rise of the Green family and Hobby Lobby. Sometimes the influence was direct. The Greens were among Gothard’s biggest financial backers; he was hugely influential in Christian homeschooling and was later accused of molesting young girls. Other influences were a generation removed. They supported David Barton, a self-styled historian who believes the United States was founded as a Christian nation. Barton, in turn, drew on Rushdoony, who established the basis for some of these ideas in the ’50s and ’60s.

There’s a perception that because the Greens are fundamentalist, they’re politically unsophisticated. But your book suggests they understand that controlling institutions that produce knowledge, like schools, museums, and film production companies, can be as consequential as winning elections.

There is something unsophisticated and naive about them. None of them went to college, and nearly all still live near each other in Oklahoma City. Yet, their influence comes through controlling institutions. This is a different model of political influence than the one most of us have, which is about making campaign contributions and controlling politicians. The Greens give only token amounts to candidates. They started with supporting missionaries, then ministries. They’d buy land, wait a year, get it appraised much higher, donate it to a ministry, and pocket a hefty tax break. They gave to evangelical colleges and figures like Falwell and Oral Roberts, then founded the Museum of the Bible. After Burwell, they realized the courts were a way to get their policies established. At each step, they’re controlling these institutions with outsized impact on our culture. Whether or not they fully realize it, they have been far more effective than they would be if they were simply lobbying legislators.

For David Green, making money seems to have become a religious calling in itself. How did his convictions blur the line between building wealth and pursuing a religious mission?

Ultimately, there was no boundary. From his first church donation, David saw the company as a vessel for his worldview. And because his siblings were ministers, I think he lacked a sense of purpose until he realized that making money and giving it the right way could be just as influential. The ’80s crisis crystallized that; in his mind, God became an owner of the company. Yet you don’t see them giving much to the poor, as you might expect Jesus to advocate. Their Christianity aligns with right-wing market capitalism.

Every Christmas, Hobby Lobby runs full-page newspaper ads that don’t sell anything. Instead, they preach the gospel. How did those ads begin, and what do they reveal about the family’s sense of being persecuted?

The origin story of how the Green family became much more public about their beliefs was that on Christmas, around 1994, David Green opened [The Oklahoman] newspaper, saw no mention of Jesus, and was outraged. So, the Greens began placing Christmas ads professing their faith. And when I went back to the newspaper, I found Jesus all over it. There was a picture of Jesus in the manger on the front page above the fold. I can’t explain it outside of the belief, shared by the Greens and those like them, that they’re persecuted. As white Christian evangelicals, they’re at the center of the culture, yet they see themselves in a holy battle against demonic forces, the forces of secularism… It’s a victim mentality.

There’s a distinctly American “bootstraps” story here, but it’s also a story about neocolonial power. A white fundamentalist Christian family builds extraordinary wealth, uses it to amplify its ideology through cultural institutions and political influence, and acquires objects from the “Middle East.”

Many call it white Christian nationalism because there’s no equivalent for people of color. The story of America’s Christian founding is always one of white European colonial powers. The Greens never talk about race, but people with Christian nationalist views are more likely to support deporting immigrants, believing the founders’ white Christian heritage is under attack. Some of that targets other faiths, but much of it is racialized, a belief about who counts as a real American.

You close the book with your visit to Iraq, from which some of the antiquities once held in the Greens’ Museum of the Bible were looted. What was that experience like?

It’s one thing to say the Greens illegally acquired antiquities. It’s another to see what stripping cultural heritage means. Visiting sites pocked with looters’ pits, then museums whose objects now sit in European institutions, drove that home.

What is your own relationship to Christianity?

I grew up devoutly Catholic in Massachusetts. I was an altar boy and thought I’d become a priest, but as a teenager I saw hypocrisy in the people who held themselves up as most religious. I didn’t get confirmed, and eventually found Buddhism, which I practice now.

You read the Bible as part of your research for this book. What did you take away from it?

To sincerely understand the Greens, I spent four months reading the Bible and its commentaries. There are so many Bibles and interpretations, and because it’s inherently contradictory, you have to impose a belief system to make sense of it.

On abortion or homosexuality, there are only a handful of verses, all open to interpretation. A passage in Exodus says that if a pregnant woman is killed, the killer is put to death, but if she’s injured and loses the baby, the penalty is lesser, suggesting the “unborn” wasn’t considered equal to a human life. I think more people should read the Bible. You won’t persuade believers by saying it isn’t true, but you might by knowing it as well as they do.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Luis Feliz Leon
title: Labor Goes on Election Defense
content:
New York City unions representing 1 million members launched a new coalition October 15 to defend the right to vote ahead of the midterm elections November 3. A thousand members rallied outside the city’s main post office, pledging to mobilize the labor movement to defend the elections from Trump administration interference. 




The throng included large contingents from Laborers Locals 78 and 79, the Hotel and Gaming Trades Council, building services and airport workers from SEIU 32BJ, and health care workers from 1199SEIU. There were also union telecom workers, nurses, stagehands, municipal workers, retail workers, postal workers, electricians, grocery workers, office workers, and painters. 




The NYC Central Labor Council initiative, called “Our Voice, Our Vote, Our Democracy,” aims to turn out union members and their communities to protest peacefully and to document intimidation of voters. It was announced just ahead of October 17, when the No Kings coalition held 3,000 events nationwide to promote early voting.




“We are demanding democratic and fair elections,” said SEIU 32BJ President Manny Pastreich in a statement to 

Labor Notes

. “In anticipation of possible election sabotage, unions have hosted dozens of know-your-rights trainings, have organized hundreds of poll-watchers, and have created rapid-response networks.”




32BJ will mobilize members to monitor poll sites in swing districts on Long Island and the Hudson Valley. Pastreich added that if Trump takes unlawful action, unions are prepared for acts of civil disobedience.


In March, Trump issued an executive order to prohibit mail-in voting except by people on a list of eligible voters submitted by states to the Postal Service. But in September, the courts blocked implementation of this order.


The Trump administration has also tried to restrict voting access through the SAFE Act, which passed the House but was blocked in the Senate. It would have banned voter registration by mail, at motor vehicle offices, or online, and required voters to document their citizenship with a passport or birth certificate, along with a marriage license for women who changed their names.




On the steps of the post office, Joseph Martier, president of the New York Metro Area Local of the Postal Workers (APWU), led the crowd in chants: “Whose post office? The people’s post office!”


In the last election, Martier said, 48 million Americans cast their ballots by mail. He argued it’s “not a convenience” but “a vital way to participate in our democracy" for people in the military, students, people with disabilities, flight attendants, and the elderly.




“Our postal workers are trusted public servants,” he said. “They don’t deliver Democratic mail or Republican mail. They deliver America’s mail. Vote by mail is not a partisan tradition. It’s been part of our election system for generations. So we must ask: if this system is working, why are they making every effort to restrict it?”

author: Amy Goodman
title: Nobel Peace Laureate Navi Pillay Calls US’s ICC Sanctions “Totally Unacceptable”
content:
Pillay led the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

We speak with the acclaimed South African human rights lawyer and international jurist Navi Pillay, who was awarded this year’s Nobel Peace Prize. Pillay has been the United Nations high commissioner for human rights and a judge at both the International Criminal Court and at an international tribunal investigating the 1994 genocide in Rwanda. Most recently, she led the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry that concluded Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Hours after Pillay was announced as winner of the Nobel Prize, the United States imposed sweeping new sanctions against the International Criminal Court.

“It’s extremely shocking to me, totally unacceptable, that the United States administration can today impose sanctions against the International Criminal Court,” says Pillay, speaking to Democracy Now! from The Hague.

Navi Pillay is now 85 years old. She was born into an Indian Tamil family in apartheid South Africa in 1941. The first woman to start a law practice in Natal, South Africa, in 1967, Pillay began her legal career defending anti-apartheid activists including Nelson Mandela, exposing torture, and helping establish key rights for prisoners on Robben Island. Mandela, as president, later appointed Pillay to the High Court of South Africa, making her the first woman of color on that bench.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: Later in the broadcast, we’re going to talk about a ballot initiative here in California, which would be, if passed, the first billionaires’ wealth tax. But first, we begin today’s show with this year’s Nobel Peace Prize winner, the South African human rights lawyer, international jurist Navi Pillay. Speaking in Oslo earlier this month, the chair of the Nobel Committee announced the award.

JØRGEN WATNE FRYDNES: This year’s laureate has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted. The Norwegian Nobel Committee has decided to award the Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

AMY GOODMAN: The Nobel Prize Committee said it chose Navi Pillay as this year’s Nobel Peace Prize winner to, quote, “issue a reminder” at a time when “judges and institutions of international law are under political attack,” unquote.

Navi Pillay has served as the United Nations high commissioner for human rights and a judge at both the International Criminal Court and at an international tribunal investigating the 1994 genocide in Rwanda. Most recently, she led the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza.

Navi Pillay was in Nuremberg, Germany, at an annual conference of human rights lawyers and judges when she heard the news.

NAVI PILLAY: Thank you very much. Thank you very much. If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump. … The last thing I did is the delivery of the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide.

AMY GOODMAN: Hours after Navi Pillay was announced as winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, the U.S. imposed sweeping new sanctions against the International Criminal Court that target the institution as a whole. Earlier U.S. sanctions targeted individual ICC judges and court personnel. This is U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

SECRETARY OF STATE MARCO RUBIO: President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans. And that’s why today the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us, because our message is clear: The United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC.

AMY GOODMAN: Soon after winning the Nobel Prize, Navi Pillay visited her former colleagues at the ICC in The Hague in a show of solidarity.

Navi Pillay is now 85 years old. She was born into an Indian Tamil family in apartheid South Africa, the first woman to start a law practice in Natal, South Africa, in 1967. She began her legal career defending anti-apartheid activists including Nelson Mandela, another Nobel Peace Prize winner, exposing torture, and helping establish key rights for prisoners on Robben Island.

To talk more about her remarkable career, from apartheid South Africa to serving on the International Criminal Court, findings of genocide from Rwanda to Gaza, and President Trump’s attacks on international law, we are joined now by the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay, joining us today from The Hague in the Netherlands.

Navi Pillay, welcome to Democracy Now! It’s great to have you with us. Congratulations on winning this global peace prize. If you could respond to its significance and also talk about the significance of you hearing the news when you were in Nuremberg, Germany, so seminal when it came to the establishment of international law so many decades ago after World War II? Congratulations again!

NAVI PILLAY: Thank you so much, Amy. I’m really pleased to be on your program. You know, the discovery now is — I mean, Democracy Now! is well known. I hope you would include my country sometimes. It’s a extremely valuable program. I’m really happy to be on the program.

And to your questions, yes, I’m now at the International Court of Justice. I serve as ad hoc judge in one of the cases. I came to do some work here. And this was a big surprise to me. I was attending, as you’ve just told the audience, that I was attending a conference in Nuremberg in Courtroom 600, when someone shouted — it was Stephen Rapp, an American, actually, the previous U.S. war crimes investigator, and he announced from his cellphone that that’s the news. And, of course, I had not heard from the committee, so I was astonished, and I disbelieved them, until I heard the announcement myself later online. And it turned out that they had been trying to get hold of me, but there was no connection in the inside the courtroom. A wonderful surprise.

Part of the reasons why I was skeptical is, firstly, because we don’t often hear of them giving the award to women. They have given — mine, apparently, is the 21st woman out of 100-some-odd — 90 were men — recipients. So, that was one factor. And the other is, yes, you know, judges and lawyers don’t often get awards, especially not judges. We work quietly in our courtrooms. We speak through the judgments. And we don’t act it out or make speeches thereafter.

For me, the significance of the fact that I was in Courtroom 600, where the Nazis were tried, is very important, because as an 18-year-old, when I was studying in apartheid South Africa, I was studying law, and nonwhite students attended the university separately, in separate facilities, which in our case happened to be a potato warehouse, and I found these copies of the Nuremberg judgments. Nobody else had seen them. They were high up. I climb a ladder, find some of them. And that started my interest in international justice, because in my country the laws were bad. They were immoral. Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher had used the veto to stop U.N. sanctions against apartheid South Africa. Of course, later, they were pressured by civil society to change and not use the vote, so sanctions were applied, and all of which contributed to ending apartheid. So, I was very interested in us having some access to international justice or a system of laws that had values and principles behind them.

And the significance of Nuremberg is, of course, it was mainly a U.S. idea. The person who is always quoted when it comes to the Nuremberg trials is Justice Jackson, who was a United States person. And all of us have learned about Nuremberg through his writings. So, here’s a country so highly committed to international justice, opting to use the rule of law rather than force in dealing with the high-level Nazi criminals. It was such a wonderful idea. All of us lawyers and judges subscribe to that.

And therefore, it’s extremely shocking to me, totally unacceptable, that the United States administration can today impose sanctions against the International Criminal Court. Straight from Nuremberg, I came to The Hague and went to that court to show solidarity with the staff. These sanctions affect all the staff, who are doing such a courageous job in their investigations.

Now, I don’t want to jump too much, but if I may just add that if the objection is that the judges authorize the prosecution to investigate not only the Taliban’s activities but also the activities of U.S. soldiers who were based in Afghanistan at that time, so if the objection is to the ICC even thinking or considering of investigating those U.S. soldiers, the solution for U.S. is simple: You begin investigating, because the ICC statute doesn’t allow that court to intervene as long as the state is investigating, prosecuting these crimes.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Navi Pillay, you chaired the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territories from 2021 to 2025, and as soon as you got news of the Nobel Peace Prize award, you mentioned the decision of the commission there in terms of the genocide committed by Israel in Gaza. Why did you feel it was so necessary to immediately refer to that, especially?

NAVI PILLAY: You know, as I said, I work very well with the U.S. I chaired commissions of inquiry that the U.S. supported, such as two in respect of North Korea. So I know that Americans support the principle of ending impunity for these serious crimes and that they support justice and accountability.

I mentioned the Gaza report because it has been widely covered, and I’ve been accused of being biased and taking sides and speaking lies. That report was mandated by the United Nations Human Rights Council, so it’s a U.N. body. We followed all the U.N. rules, and we worked in cooperation with all the U.N. agencies. We had access to U.N. satellite footage. We did not include a single fact in our report that was not personally verified. So, based on the facts and the statements of the leaders, we named them, the former — the president, the current prime minister and the former defense minister. We said that those three individuals should be investigated and prosecuted for having committed genocide and for the continuing commission of genocide. The report was mentioned — my activities as chair of that commission was mentioned as one of the categories of my life work by the Nobel Committee.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And nearly 20 years ago, back in 2008, you were appointed the U.N. high commissioner for human rights by Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon, and the United States initially opposed your appointment then. Why was that?

NAVI PILLAY: I believe they opposed my appointment because the secretary of state felt I would influence my office, the High Commissioner’s Office, towards supporting reproductive rights for women.

AMY GOODMAN: Speaking of reproductive rights and speaking of overall women’s rights, one of the issues that you have focused on that has been so important, I believe coming out of the Rwanda Tribunal, was talking about rape as a weapon of war. And I’m wondering if you could elaborate on that and that whole body of law coming out of your emphasis.

NAVI PILLAY: So, I’ll deal with the background just now, but the important point is, as all judges know, you need the evidence before you. So, all judges look at the evidence first. So, in this case, we heard from many women and men from Rwanda who gave evidence of rape, sexual violence on women, girls, and even some men. So we had this massive body of evidence.

It’s true that when we first heard the evidence, we realized that it had not been charged, so we would have had to completely ignore all that evidence in the normal course. But this is an international court. We were there to render justice. And so we judges allowed the prosecutor to investigate and apply for an amendment of the charge sheet to add four counts of rape and sexual violence.

And that is the case, which is now very well known, of Jean-Paul Akayesu, the mayor of Taba province. Most of the rapes took place on those premises under his control, and there was also evidence that he encouraged them: you know, “Taste the Tutsi women today, because you’re not going to be able to do that in future.” They were raped and killed, largely.

I first, then, credit the courageous women and men who testified on these matters, which enabled the court to consider them and see whether they fulfilled the requirements of the Genocide Convention, which is proof of the specific intent by the perpetrators to destroy, in whole or in part, a group — in this case, the ethnic group of Tutsis. So, that’s the evidence we established. We looked at statements of incitement made by the leaders. The Rwanda Tribunal tried mainly the leaders, the political leaders, military leaders, religious leaders. One, in fact, was a religious leader of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, and we heard evidence from the head of that church from the United States, who came to plead on behalf of that particular priest, whom we convicted because of the evidence before us of his own involvement in these crimes.

Let me say then that we had no precedent. There was no universally accepted definition of what constitutes rape, what constitutes sexual violence under international law. And we looked at very many jurisdictions, and most of us from the common law system — United States, South Africa — we followed the requirement that there has to be proof of no consent, that there has to be proof of penetration by the male organ in the female — in the vagina. So, how do you use that definition when this is happening to hundreds of women? The prosecutor asked these witnesses, yes, “Was there penetration?” And the witness answered, “Well, that’s not the only thing they did to us. These are children. And they didn’t respect us as mothers, and they said vile things to us. They did terrible things to us.” So, we were influenced once again by the experience of sexual violence as viewed by the victims themselves, in order to create a definition that is gender-neutral. Rape and sexual violence constitute crimes of invasion of a person — that’s gender-neutral — under coercive circumstances of a sexual nature. So, we completely did away with the requirement where the victim or the prosecutor has to deal with the element of consent. These are coercive circumstances.

And we had help, of course, from very many academics, from the U.S. in particular. Professor Catharine MacKinnon was very helpful to us, because we had to, very importantly, say why does sexual violence committed under those circumstances constitute a destruction of the group, which is the key element, what we call the dolus specialis, the special intent, required under the Genocide Convention. Here, I must interrupt myself to point out to you very many judges, then and now, believe that they should only look at killings as destruction of the group, that sexual violence does not constitute destruction. Well, we used what we’ve been advised by Professor MacKinnon to describe rape and sexual violence as the destruction of life itself for the victims.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: Navi Pillay, I’m wondering —

NAVI PILLAY: Yeah, so I’ll stop there. Yeah.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: Yeah, I’m wondering if you could share with our audience, not familiar with the trajectory of your life’s work, your own family origin story. You’ve said your grandparents were shipped from India as indentured laborers to South Africa. They worked on sugar cane plantations. How did this inform your own experiences? And if you could talk about the conditions under which you were raised in Durban that led you to become a lawyer and get involved in social justice work?

NAVI PILLAY: Well, thank you for that question. I still remember my grandfather, who was brought as an indentured laborer, and he lost both his arms in an accident at the sugar mill. Both his arms were cut off, but he still survived ’til age 87 or so. My parents were born in South Africa. Now, Mahatma Gandhi described the indentured system as akin to slavery, so they apparently really suffered. They focused on education as a way out. My parents were not educated. My mother was told by her father that if he let her learn to read and write, she would be writing letters to boyfriends. So, she made sure that her children were — and so did my father — that we — we were seven children in all — that we were educated.

And, of course, then, we didn’t have money. I wanted to do law. I wanted to know what are our rights, because even as children, we experienced discrimination. We couldn’t go to the beach. Our parents said, “No, we can’t take you to that park. You’re not allowed on the swings.” And we would ask, “Why? Why not?” Yeah. And so, they made it out as if it’s written in stone, things will never change, you are a lesser being because you have a dark skin. That’s what children experience, which got to me, as well. I wanted to know my rights. I wanted to study law.

And the teacher in my high school asked the question of all the students, “What would you like to do when you grow up?” And I said I wanted to be a lawyer. And he said, “Well, your father must have a lot of money. You need a lot of money to go to university.” I was the lucky one, one of the lucky ones. The school approached the community. They went door to door, tapping on doors. This is a poor community of Clairwood, a suburb outside Durban. So, they contributed their pennies and sent me to university, because they were told, “We have a student with potential.” And that is how I was able to get a university degree.

AMY GOODMAN: So interesting. It may be you’re the first Nobel Peace Prize winner to represent another Nobel Peace Prize winner, and that was Nelson Mandela. I believe you were the first woman lawyer to set foot on Robben Island, where he was imprisoned for decades. If you can talk about that relationship? And I also believe you were the first nonwhite lawyer to be — nonwhite woman lawyer to be appointed by Nelson Mandela — the first nonwhite woman judge on the High Court. If you can talk about your relationship with Nelson Mandela and one first after another?

NAVI PILLAY: Thank you. Well, that’s true. He did appoint me as the first woman of color to be a judge on the High Court. Until then, they were all white, and they were all male. It was a pretty drastic step on his part. I was also an attorney. We have a split bar, and judges were usually drawn from the Bar Council. And they were almost — they were always white men. The Bar Council held a meeting. Agenda item one was the competence of Pillay. The public took that up because, remember, this is our new, newly emerging democracy. The public then questioned why these advocates in the Bar Council did not question the competence of the apartheid-era judges. Why me? So, I was very heartened by that level of interest from the public.

Let me — let me begin, though, in answer to your question, to make very clear: I was not his defense counsel. There were other lawyers, various lawyers, who represented him. I, you know, engaged about him with my clients who were on Robben Island Prison. I went to see them on an appeal that had been lodged on their behalf. That’s why I got access into Robben Island Prison, where Mandela was serving and eventually served close to 27 years. My clients told me that they didn’t know their rights. They didn’t have the prison regulations. They were being punished for apparent violations of the prison regulations. And one of them, who happened to be a lawyer, was sentenced to six months’ imprisonment in isolation and spare diet, because all he had done is drawn a petition of their requests, one of which was they needed to see the prison regulations. And the other was that they were — they started a small class where they were teaching English to their companions who needed to learn English, for which he was punished in this way. They discussed the matter. And as soon as I turned up there, we secretly, by code, engaged in their problems and challenges, which I was not allowed to discuss. I was there specifically to talk about the appeal.

So, it was a visit within sight, and supposedly out of hearing, but we were all aware that the whole discussions were — the lawyers’ visits were taped anyway. And I was informed that they had consulted Mandela inside the prison, who discouraged them and me from bringing any application, because there was little chance of succeeding in an apartheid-era court. I then went out and consulted other lawyers, and some of them were very senior white male lawyers who readily, very readily, gave me the time. That’s what lawyers do. You get interested in a challenge. They then encouraged me to bring this application, which we did.

And we won, with costs. The court ordered that the prisoners have a right to a lawyer. They have a right not to be further penalized apart from the court sentence. And if they are alleged to have broken any regulation, there must be magistrates brought out of Cape Town, the mainland, onto Robben Island, and trials must be held. So, since their rights were now spelt out, they were able to have visits from their lawyers, and they were able to study, which was a survival necessity for them. And this is how he came to know of me.

AMY GOODMAN: Navi Pillay, we have to end it there, but I want to thank you —

AMY GOODMAN: — so much for taking this time, South African human rights lawyer, international jurist. She was just awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. She will actually receive that prize on December 10th. Navi Pillay has been speaking to us from The Hague.

title: Senate Democrats Demand Trump Administration Reveal Full Costs of Iran War
content:
“Americans deserve to know how much of their money is being burned on Trump’s war,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren said.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Democratic members of the Senate Armed Services Committee are demanding that the Trump administration release official figures about the true economic costs of the war in Iran.

Lawmakers on that congressional committee were recently briefed about the war’s costs, but the administration has not made those figures public. Noting that the Congressional Budget Office estimated the war’s cost at $38 billion in September, Democrats are saying the White House should be forthright with the American people about updated numbers.

In an open letter sent to U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) commander Navy Admiral Brad Cooper, Democrats wrote that the “publicly disclosed costs of the war have already been tragic,” citing the fact that as many as 23 servicemembers have been killed and 861 have been wounded since the start of the conflict.

“Despite a lack of clarity and candor from [the Department of Defense], press reports of attacks, video footage, satellite images, and photos leaked to the media by active U.S. service members have painted a dire picture of U.S. bases and facilities damaged and destroyed by Iran,” the letter stated, adding that the war has also caused “significant damage to the U.S.’s critical infrastructure in the region.”

“The administration’s ongoing efforts to hide the true cost of this war are outrageous and unacceptable,” the Democrats’ letter stated. “DoD has repeatedly tried to cover up the truth about the number of service members hurt and killed since the war began and has not disclosed these deaths and injuries to the public in a timely manner.”

The letter-writers are calling for more transparency from the administration, and a response from CENTCOM by November 2.

In a post on X, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts), a member of the Armed Services Committee, reiterated her and her colleagues’ call for more information.

“Americans deserve to know how much of their money is being burned on Trump’s war with Iran,” Warren said.

Estimates vary, but one examination of household expenses by Moody’s Analytics suggests that the average family’s costs have increased by $2,000 as a result of the war. Energy prices in particular have seen monumental increases, with regular grade gasoline costs going up by 45 percent since late February.

In addition to economic costs for the U.S., the war is having a tremendously negative impact on the region’s environment, with emissions from military activities contributing to the climate crisis, bombings worsening the effects of drought and water scarcity/access in the region, and pollution threatening air quality for much of Western Asia, an analysis from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace shows. In terms of loss of life in Iran, between 3,592 and 11,410 people have been killed, and an estimated 26,500 (or more) are injured, because of the war.

title: Bu yıl ilki gerçekleştirilen Üzümlü Sanat Festivali daha kapsamlı devam edecek
content:
Muğla – Yalınayak Sanat Kolektifi'nin ev sahipliğinde, şair ve yazar Namık Kuyumcu'nun koordinatörlüğünde 2-4 Ekim tarihlerinde düzenlenen 1. Fethiye Üzümlü Sanat ve Edebiyat Festivali büyük ilgi gördü. Festivalin önümüzdeki yıl daha farklı ve kapsayıcı şekilde devam etmesi için çalışmalar yapılacak.

Üzümlü'de ve bölgede ilk kez düzenlenen sanat yürüyüşü festivalin en dikkat çekici etkinliklerinden oldu. Çocuklar, kadınlar, sanatçılar, atölye eğitmenleri, Yalınayak Sanat Kolektifi üyeleri ve sanatseverler; barış, özgürlük, kardeşlik, adalet, eşitlik ve dayanışma temalı pankartlarla yürüdü. Herkesin kendi sesiyle katıldığı buluşma, köy halkının da ilgisini çekti. Üç gün boyunca şiir dinletileri, müzik, mim, ateş dansı ve teatral performanslar izleyicilerle buluştu.

Festival programında şiirleriyle Duygu Kankaytsın ve Namık Kuyumcu ve Neşe Yaşın, akademik ve müzikal çalışmalarıyla Özge Cengiz, şiirleri ve masallarıyla Melek Özlem Sezer; farklı sanat disiplinlerindeki üretimleriyle heykelci Sercihan Alioğlu, ressam Pınar Ceylan Genç, şair ve yazar Semih Çelenk, mim sanatçısı İlker Kılıçer, şair ve yazar Betül Dünder, Özgür Zeybek ve dansçı ve egitmen Emre Coşkuner yer aldı. Şair ve yazar Sezai Sarıoğlu, müzisyen Şenol Morgül, şair, yazar ve çevirmen Tozan Alkan programa katkı sundu; festivalin sunuculuğunu Cansu Akarçay üstlendi.

Festival kapsamında farklı yaşlardan katılımcıların ilgi gösterdiği dokuz sanat atölyesi gerçekleştirildi. Heykel, baskı sanatı, tiyatro, mim, masal, ekoloji, oyunculuk, yazarlık, dans ve jonglörlük atölyelerinde sanatçılar bilgi ve deneyimlerini paylaştı. Atölyeler, birlikte düşünmenin, denemenin ve üretmenin yaratıcı alanlarına dönüştü.

Festivalin özgün çalışmalarından biri, Yalınayak Sanat Kolektifi gençlerinin hazırladığı “Başıkabak” adlı fanzin oldu. Kolektifin adına mizahi bir gönderme taşıyan fanzin, gençlerin bağımsız yayıncılık anlayışını, yaratıcılığını ve festivalin neşeli ruhunu yansıttı.

Festival, sanatçı ile izleyici, eğitmen ile katılımcı, düzenleyen ile konuklar, sanat ile sanatçı, sanatçı ile sanatçının arasındaki klasik ve sahici olmayan mesafeleri ortadan kaldırdı. Olanakların paylaşımını güç ve egemenlik ilişkisi olarak değil, sanata yakışan aidiyet ve liyakat temelinde ele alan festival; gösterişten, hiyerarşik ilişkilerden ve tüketim odaklı popüler kültürden uzak, gönüllülüğe, karşılıklı saygıya ve ortak emeğe dayanan yapısıyla takdir topladı.

Yalınayak Sanat Kolektifi festivalle ilgili yaptığı açıklamada, on yıldır sürdürdükleri sanat atölyelerinin, festivalle yeni ve güçlü bir ivme kazandığını belirtti. Turistik beklentilerin ve popüler kültür kalıplarının dışında, bölgenin doğal ve insani dinamikleriyle buluşan özgün bir sanat ortamını değerli sanat insanları ve sanatseverlerle paylaşmanın düşlerine yeni bir anlam kattığını ifade eden Yalınayak Sanat Kolektifi açıklamasında, "Festival boyunca ortaya çıkan içtenlik, dayanışma ve yaratıcı enerji, gelecek çalışmalarımız için önemli bir umut kaynağı oldu. Yıl boyunca sürdürdüğümüz sanat atölyelerini zenginleştirerek, önümüzdeki yıl daha farklı ve kapsayıcı bir festivalde yeniden buluşacağımıza inanıyoruz. Bu ortak düşe emeğini, bilgisini, sanatını ve yüreğini katan herkese teşekkür ediyoruz" dedi.

1. Fethiye Üzümlü Sanat ve Edebiyat Festivali'nin sanatın büyük bütçelerden ve görkemli sahnelerden önce insana, özgürlüğe, yaratıcılığa ve dayanışmaya ihtiyaç duyduğunu gösterdiği ifade edilen açıklamada, "Üzümlü'de sanat, herkese ulaştı. Edebiyatın, müziğin, yaratıcılığın ve dayanışmanın buluşma noktası oldu" denildi.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

title: Münih'ten Paris'e dayanışma mesajı
content:
Bavyera Öğrenci Hareketi’nin (Bayerische Schüler_innen Bewegung) çağrısıyla, GEW (Eğitim ve Bilim Sendikası) başta olmak üzere birçok kurum ve kuruluşun desteklediği yapılan dayanışma mitingi yüzlerce öğrenci ve yurttaşın katılımıyla gerçekleşti.

Münih Ludwig-Maximilians-Üniversitesi ana binasının önündeki Geschwister-Scholl-Platz'da toplanan kalabalık, "Münih'ten Paris'e: Öğrenciler Sokağa!" sloganıyla eylem yaptı.

Fransa'daki öğrenci hareketine güçlü bir destek mesajının verildiği gösterildiği eylemde, hem Almanca hem de Fransızca hazırlanan pankartlar dikkat çekti. Öğrenciler, Fransızca ve Almanca "Eğitimimize yatırım yapın!" yazılı dev pankartın arkasında kenetlendi.

Eylemde, Fransa'dan gelen temsilci öğrenci konuşmacılar da söz alarak ortak mücadele vurgusu yaptı. Mitingde yapılan konuşmalarda, Almanya ve Fransa'daki öğrencilerin karşı karşıya kaldığı eğitim yetersizlikleri, gençliğin sosyal sorunları ve zorunlu askerlik hizmetine (Wehrpflicht) karşı tepkiler dile getirildi.

"Sınır Tanımayan Dayanışma" (Solidarité sans frontières) mottosuyla düzenlenen eyleme WE ACT, GEW Landesverband Bayern, La France Insoumise, Jusos München, Linksjugend ['solid] Bayern, Nein zur Wehrpflicht! München ve Die Linke Landesverband Bayern gibi pek çok örgütsel yapı destek verdi.

author: Jéssica Ribeiro
title: Empresa ligada a Willer Tomaz foi administrada por diretor da Polícia Civil do DF
content:
Uma empresa ligada ao advogado Willer Tomaz – alvo da segunda fase da operação Sem Descontos, que apura desvios indevidos em aposentadorias e pensões de beneficiários do INSS – teve como administrador um diretor da Polícia Civil do Distrito Federal (PCDF). Durante quatro meses de 2025, Delcimar de Oliveira Silva, que havia assumido a diretoria de Tecnologia da Informação (TI) em fevereiro de 2023, respondeu como administrador da Direção Táxi Aéreo LTDA enquanto era remunerado pela instituição pública, o que é vedado por lei.




A Direção Táxi Aéreo LTDA foi adquirida em maio de 2024 pela Jet Line Locações e Serviços Aéreos S/A, naquele ano representada por Lídia Maria Figueiredo Mazelli, apontada como administradora de empresas de Willer Tomaz. 

Sete meses após a incorporação, a Direção Táxi Aéreo passou a ser administrada pelo então diretor da PCDF, informação que consta no contrato social da empresa, conforme documentos obtidos pela 

Agência Pública

. 




Procurado, Delcimar de Oliveira Silva afirmou ser “policial civil aposentado” e declarou que, “durante o curtíssimo período em que estive no [Direção] Táxi Aéreo, encontrava-me afastado das minhas funções na PCDF”. O servidor saiu da ativa no ano passado. Segundo o Portal da Transparência do Distrito Federal, no entanto, o então servidor recebeu proventos pela função de “diretor/ delegado de polícia” da corporação entre dezembro de 2024 e abril de 2025, como confirmado por cópias dos comprovantes de pagamento, obtidas pela 

Pública

.




Comprovantes de pagamento de Delcimar de Oliveira Silva obtidos pela Pública

Comprovantes de pagamento de Delcimar de Oliveira Silva obtidos pela Pública

Comprovantes de pagamento de Delcimar de Oliveira Silva obtidos pela Pública

Comprovantes de pagamento de Delcimar de Oliveira Silva obtidos pela Pública

Comprovantes de pagamento de Delcimar de Oliveira Silva obtidos pela Pública

Comprovantes de pagamento de Delcimar de Oliveira Silva obtidos pela Pública




A reportagem apresentou os dados das guias de pagamento a Silva. Também questionou o motivo de ter sido exonerado do cargo de diretor em período similar à sua saída da Direção Táxi Aéreo. O ex-diretor, no entanto, limitou-se a dizer que “não tem outras considerações a acrescentar”.




Arranjo incomum




De acordo com o inciso X do artigo 17 da Lei 8.112/1990, é vedado a servidores públicos participação em gerência ou administração de sociedade privada, personificada ou não personificada, e de exercerem o comércio, exceto na qualidade de acionista, cotista ou comanditário. 
















Comprovante da participação de Delcimar de Oliveira Silva na administração da empresa










 




O que a legislação proíbe expressamente é a participação na gestão empresarial, seja formalmente, como administrador designado no contrato social, seja materialmente, por meio da condução efetiva dos negócios. Essa restrição decorre das peculiaridades da atividade policial, que exige dedicação ao serviço público, disponibilidade funcional, imparcialidade e prevenção de conflitos de interesses.”




Vinícius Nascimento

 

Consultor legislativo e professor de direito para carreiras policiais 

 










Segundo a Lei 15.047/2024, que institui o regime disciplinar da Polícia Federal e da Polícia Civil do Distrito Federal e atualiza a legislação de 1965, “participar da gerência ou da administração de empresa, de fato ou de direito, qualquer que seja a sua natureza” é considerada uma das “infrações disciplinares praticadas por servidor puníveis com demissão”. De acordo com Nascimento, a regra não é diferente “quanto ao policial que exerce cargo de confiança”. A lei foi sancionada pelo presidente Lula e entrou em vigor em 17 de dezembro, dois dias antes de Delcimar de Oliveira Silva assumir a administração da empresa ligada a Willer Tomaz.




Procurada para explicar o arranjo incomum que permitiu que o então diretor de TI ocupasse um cargo de administração em empresa privada, a PCDF informou que Delcimar de Oliveira Silva não integra mais o quadro ativo na instituição. A instituição admitiu não ter “conhecimento da situação” e que a questão foi “encaminhada para a Corregedoria Geral de Polícia para conhecimento”.
















Delcimar assumiu a administração da empresa dois dias após a entrada em vigor da Lei 15.047/2024




Sucessão recorrente dentro da família Tomaz




Conforme certidão de inteiro teor da Direção Táxi Aéreo LTDA, o diretor da PCDF deixou a administração da empresa em maio de 2025, quando o cargo passou para Flávia Tomaz, esposa do advogado. No mesmo mês, Delcimar de Oliveira Silva foi 

exonerado da direção da Polícia Civil

 e saiu em licença não remunerada. Um ano depois, ao retornar à ativa, em maio de 2026, o então servidor solicitou aposentadoria. Dias após consegui-la, porém, foi agraciado com 

abono de permanência

 – benefício pago a servidores que cumpriram requisitos para se aposentar voluntariamente, mas escolheram continuar trabalhando.




No mesmo período em que o então servidor se retirou da Direção Táxi Aéreo, Lídia Mazelli deixou a sociedade da Jet Line, passando o controle total da empresa a Flávia Tomaz. Diferentemente da vida luxuosa do casal, Mazelli mora em um prédio de três andares, sobre uma loja de móveis, no Riacho Fundo, região administrativa do Distrito Federal.




Segundo os documentos aos quais a 

Pública

 teve acesso, todas as modificações e alterações no contrato social da Direção Táxi Aéreo foram feitas pela Voga Serviços Contábeis – companhia de Alexandre Caetano dos Reis, sócio do lobista Antônio Carlos Camilo Antunes, o “Careca do INSS”, e irmão de Letícia Caetano dos Reis, administradora do escritório de advocacia de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL).

 Alexandre Reis também faz a contabilidade de empresas do filho 01 de Jair Bolsonaro.
















Trecho de alteração contratual da direção da empresa Táxi Aéreo LTDA




Questionado sobre o período da administração de Delcimar de Oliveira Silva, Willer Tomaz informou que o gestor “encontrava-se afastado de suas funções na Polícia Civil do Distrito Federal durante o período em que participou da administração da empresa de táxi aéreo”. “As empresas às quais Willer Tomaz está vinculado exercem suas atividades em conformidade com a legislação e as normas da Anac, sem pendências perante os órgãos de fiscalização”, declarou o advogado em 

nota

 à 

Pública

.




Empresa “familiar”




Segundo dados públicos, a Jet Line foi constituída em setembro de 2008, com capital social de R$ 1 milhão. Na Receita Federal, apenas os nomes de Flávia Oliveira Correa Tomaz e Christine Tomaz de Souza, irmã de Willer Tomaz, constam no quadro societário da Jet Line. 




A Jet Line funciona no mesmo endereço da empresa que adquiriu em 2024 – a Direção Táxi Aéreo LTDA, aberta em 2021, com capital social de R$ 200 mil, por um servidor público e uma médica.




Apesar de estar oficialmente em nome de Flávia Tomaz, o site oficial da Direção Táxi Aéreo aponta como responsável pelo domínio o advogado Willer Tomaz. 



















Além do diretor da PCDF, a Direção Táxi Aéreo também teve, a partir de janeiro de 2026, um coronel da reserva da Aeronáutica como administrador. O militar Virgínio Augusto Corrieri de Castro permaneceu no cargo por cinco meses até devolver o cargo para a esposa de Willer Tomaz, em maio deste ano.




A 

Pública

 tentou contatar Castro por meio do telefone de uma das empresas pertencentes a ele, mas não obteve retorno. O espaço será atualizado no caso de manifestação.




De acordo com a Receita Federal, a Direção Táxi Aéreo funciona no Hangar 36 do Aeroporto Internacional de Brasília e tem como principais funções o transporte aéreo de passageiros não-regular, manutenção e reparação de aeronaves, comércio atacadista de outras máquinas, além do transporte aéreo de carga e serviços de reservas.




A Jet Line conta com ao menos quatro aeronaves. Uma delas era do DJ Alok e foi vendida à empresa ligada a Willer em setembro de 2024.

 Em 2018, esse mesmo jatinho transportava Alok e convidados quando 

saiu da pista durante decolagem no Aeroporto da Serrinha, em Juiz de Fora

 (MG). Ninguém ficou ferido.




Relação com a Anac




Em 20 de julho de 2026, Willer Tomaz pediu permissão à Agência Nacional de Aviação Civil (Anac) para a construção de um aeródromo de uso privado, denominado WT-01, no interior de uma casa localizada no Conjunto 4 da QI 1 do Lago Sul, onde funciona seu escritório de advocacia e outras empresas vinculadas a ele.




A solicitação foi feita pela WT Administração de Imóveis e Bens S/A, também ligada a Tomaz. De acordo com investigações da Polícia Federal, o CNPJ da WT foi utilizado na compra da 

residência de R$ 6 milhões do senador Weverton Rocha

 (PDT-MA), no Lago Sul, e de um apartamento de Fabiano Zettel, cunhado de Daniel Vorcaro, em São Paulo. O imóvel de Zettel foi utilizado por 

Flávio Bolsonaro durante a campanha

 presidencial, segundo a revista piauí. Foi também a WT Administração que teria recebido 

R$ 136,5 mil do Senado

, pagos como complemento de auxílio-moradia desde 2023 em benefício do senador Ciro Nogueira (PP-PI), ex-ministro da Casa Civil de Jair Bolsonaro.
















Casa localizada no Conjunto 4 da QI 1 do Lago Sul, em Brasília, onde funciona o escritório de advocacia e outras empresas vinculadas a Willer Tomaz




O imóvel de Willer que recebe o aeródromo é uma velha conhecida da política brasileira. Em 2004, a residência ficou conhecida como “República de Ribeirão”, quando servia de ponto de encontro para políticos, empresários e lobistas ligados ao então ministro da Fazenda Antonio Palocci e ocorriam negociações investigadas no episódio do Mensalão.




O pedido à Anac foi feito apesar do histórico da Jet Line junto à agência reguladora. Em 2022, a empresa foi punida por 

“recusa de exibição de livros, documentos contábeis, informações ou estatísticas aos agentes da fiscalizaçã

o”. Naquele ano, a fiscalização solicitou cópia autenticada das páginas do diário de bordo que contém o termo de abertura, páginas e os dados dos voos realizados entre 1º de setembro de 2019 e 31 de dezembro de 2019; além da lista de passageiros de todos os voos realizados nesse período, e os motivos de cada viagem. As informações não foram apresentadas e, apesar de Tomaz recorrer como advogado da Jet Line, 

alegando não obrigatoriedade de manutenção desses registros

, 

teve de pagar R$ 8 mil em multa.




A Anac também instaurou procedimento investigatório após o piloto de uma aeronave da Jet Line 

impedir a inspeção de servidores da agência

, também em 2022. Após o início do processo, a empresa apresentou os documentos solicitados pelos agentes. 

O procedimento foi arquivado

.




A 

Pública

 procurou a Agência Nacional de Aviação Civil, mas não obteve retorno até a última atualização do texto. No caso de manifestação, o espaço será atualizado.  
















Willer Tomaz mantém uma relação próxima com o senador Flávio Bolsonaro




A origem do advogado famoso em Brasília




A trajetória de Willer Tomaz começou no setor de informática. Em 1999, ele abriu uma empresa em Taguatinga (DF), que faliu. Tomaz migrou de área, formou-se em direito e passou a atuar como advogado e empresário.

 Ele acumulou patrimônio com imóveis, propriedades rurais, veículos de luxo e participações em empresas.




Em 2017, Tomaz foi preso na Operação Patmos, que também atingiu o então presidente Michel Temer e o senador Aécio Neves. O advogado foi investigado por suspeita de atuar junto ao procurador da República Ângelo Goulart Villela em favor dos interesses de Joesley Batista e sua empresa, a JBS. O advogado negou as acusações. Dois meses depois, o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) determinou sua soltura.




Tomaz mantém uma relação próxima com o senador Flávio Bolsonaro. Os amigos, como se declaram, são vistos com frequência juntos. Recentemente, além de ter utilizado o apartamento de São Paulo do advogado durante a campanha presidencial, Flávio também usufruiu de propriedade de Tomaz em Angra dos Reis (RJ). 




Algumas das propriedades e negócios de Tomaz aparecem associados a empresários investigados em outros casos, entre eles Daniel Vorcaro, ex-controlador do Banco Master. Em agosto de 2026, a Polícia Federal cumpriu mandado de busca e apreensão na casa do advogado durante a Operação Sem Desconto, que investiga um esquema de descontos indevidos em benefícios do INSS. Tomaz nega participação nas fraudes.




O amigo de Flávio Bolsonaro voltou para a mira da Polícia Federal (PF) depois que foi tornado público um processo que ele moveu contra a empresa de apostas online Blaze. Tomaz alega sofrer de ludopatia e pede ressarcimento por perdas em bets na ordem de R$ 163,2 milhões. O Ministério da Fazenda e a PF se voltaram ao caso para apurar irregularidades da plataforma e verificar a possibilidade de lavagem e dinheiro em operações no episódio. 




A defesa de Willer Tomaz afirma em nota que as empresas às quais o empresário está vinculado “suas atividades em conformidade com a legislação e as normas da Anac, sem pendências perante os órgãos de fiscalização.

 Quanto às locações imobiliárias, os contratos são regulares, celebrados a valores de mercado e sujeitos aos deveres legais de confidencialidade e proteção de dados pessoais. Os pagamentos são realizados diretamente pelos locatários, não cabendo à locadora prestar esclarecimentos sobre a origem de seus rendimentos.”




Além disso, o advogado diz não ter “qualquer envolvimento com as fraudes investigadas na Operação Sem Desconto e ressalta que a denúncia oferecida contra ele no âmbito da Operação Patmos, em 2017, foi definitivamente rejeitada”, além de que “repudia a tentativa de associá-lo a supostas irregularidades por meio da reunião de episódios distintos, sem demonstração de qualquer conduta ilícita de sua parte.”

title: NATO, “Karadeniz'de gemilerin korunması” bahanesiyle bölgeye ek unsurlar sevk edecek
content:
NATO Sözcüsü Allison Hart, X sosyal medya platformundaki hesabından yaptığı paylaşımda, üye ülkelerin daimi temsilcilerini bir araya getiren Kuzey Atlantik Konseyi'nin Karadeniz'in güvenliğini görüşmek üzere toplandığını aktardı.

Hart, NATO'nun insansız hava araçlarına karşı koyma kabiliyetleri dahil doğu kanadındaki duruşunu güçlendirdiğini öne sürerek, İttifak'ın gözetleme, keşif ve adli inceleme destekleri dahil bölgeye ek unsurlar sevk edeceğini aktardı.

Karadeniz'de bir süredir ticari gemilere yönelik saldırılar düzenleniyor.

13 Ekim'de Bulgaristan'ın Karadeniz açıklarında iki gemi insansız hava aracıyla (İHA) saldırıya uğramış, gemilerden biri batmıştı.

Son olarak Romanya'nın Karadeniz kıyısı açıklarında San Marino ve Komorlar bayraklı 2 ticari gemiye İHA ile saldırı düzenlenmişti.

San Marino bayraklı gemide bulunan 12 kişilik mürettebattan 5'inin kurtarıldığı, 7'sinin kaybolduğu belirtilirken Komorlar bayraklı geminin mürettebatının tahliye edildiği ve güvende olduğu aktarılmıştı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Unknown
title: Netanyahu’dan “İran'daki yönetimi devirmeye kararlıyız” açıklaması
content:
İsrail Başbakanı Benyamin Netanyahu, Kiryat Şimona kentindeki Tel Hai Üniversitesi'nin akademik yıl açılışında yaptığı konuşmada, ana hedeflerinin Tahran yönetimini devirmek olduğunu savundu.

ABD Başkanı Trump'la dün gerçekleştirdiği telefon görüşmesinde sarf ettiği “Bitirmemiz gereken bir iş var.” ifadesiyle İran yönetimini saldırılarla devirmeyi kastettiğini söyledi.

İran’da yönetimi devirdikleri takdirde Hizbullah’ın sonunun geleceğini ve Lübnan’la da barışa kavuşacaklarını iddia eden Netanyahu, "İran rejiminin tamamen ortadan kaldırılmasını sağlamalıyız. Temel hedefimiz budur.” ifadelerini kullandı.

Netanyahu, İran'a yönelik yeni saldırılar hakkında Başkan Trump ile 18 Ekim de dahil olmak üzere birden fazla kez görüştüğünü kaydetti.

ABD Başkanı Trump ve Netanyahu’nun ekim ayının ilk haftasında, İsrail'de 27 Ekim'de yapılacak genel seçimler ve ABD'de 3 Kasım'da gerçekleştirilecek Kongre ara seçimlerinden önce İran'a yeni bir saldırı düzenleme ihtimalini görüştüğü öne sürülmüştü.

author: Unknown
title: Max Oelschlaeger - The Wilderness Condition
content:
Author

: Max Oelschlaeger

Title

: The Wilderness Condition

Subtitle

: Essays on Environment and Civilization

Date

: Jun 1, 1992

Source

: <

press.princeton.edu

> & <

www.archive.org

>




 




 In this age of heightened sensitivity to environmental problems, the popular press inundates us with the issues of the moment. We hear of the immediate threats to our groundwater supply, to the rain forest, to the ozone. Yet nowhere do we find coverage of the fundamental issues of environmentalism, those elements such as philosophy and history that, though less dramatic, constitute the foundation from which we can reverse ecological breakdown. 




 This vital collection of essays by some of the environmental movement’s preeminent thinkers addresses these deeper, neglected issues. Written from a broad range of perspectives, the authors explore the dynamic tension between wild nature and civilization, offering insights into why the relationship has become so conflicted and suggesting creative means for reconciliation. 




 Introducing the concept of the wilderness condition, the essays probe the effects of history, psychology, culture, and philosophy on the environment. Included is commentary from Gary Snyder, award-winning author of 

Turtle Island,

 who discusses how our prevailing assumptions about “nature” and “wilderness” impede conservation. Paul Shepard, author of 

Man in the Landscape,

 presents his compelling, controversial theory that the seeds of our current ecological crisis were planted in the New Stone Age. And George Sessions explains how the two major schools of thought in the environmental movement differ on its most basic issues, again thwarting opportunities for change. 




 Other essays discuss how Western philosophy has erroneously divorced humankind from nature; why Sierra Club founder John Muir’s early writings remain eminently relevant; and how elements of Eastern philosophy may hold the key to sucessful change. 




 The contributors eloquently demonstrate why we can no longer take nature for granted, or assume that its existence is somehow second to humankind’s. They argue convincingly that no amount of technology will ever displace our primal connection to nature. But rather than simply deploring the prevailing attitudes toward our imperiled environment, the essayists offer fresh, realistic, and inspiring ideas for alleviating the crisis. 




 Three themes unify the collection: the essayists, though they represent different traditions, share an evolutionary perspective that confirms why humankind and nature are by necessity interdependent; sensitive to language, the writers reveal how the words we choose when we consider environmental issues reflect our sometimes naive understanding of them; and most important, the essayists share the conviction that al! is not lost—and that we can initiate a worldwide trend toward recognizing the environment as a vital entity in its own right, thereby preserving its integrity. 




 




 MAX OELSCHLAEGER teaches philosophy of ecology, environmental ethics, and wilderness studies at the University of North Texas. He is author of the influential and critically acclaimed The 

Idea of Wilderness,

 which explores Western culture’s persistent attempts to separate humankind from the natural world. 




 




 The Sierra Club, founded in 1892 by John Muir, has devoted itself to the study and protection of the earth’s scenic and ecological resources — mountains, wetlands, woodlands, wild shores and rivers, deserts and plains. The publishing program of the Sierra Club offers books to the public as a nonprofit educational service in the hope that they may enlarge the public’s understanding of the Club’s basic concerns. The point of view expressed in each book, however, does not necessarily represent that of the Club. The Sierra Club has some sixty chapters coast to coast, in Canada, Hawaii, and Alaska. For information about how you may participate in its programs to preserve wilderness and the quality of life, please address inquiries to Sierra Club, 730 Polk Street, San Francisco, CA 94109. 




 







For A. E. Koenig, in memoriam







Introduction: The Wilderness Condition Today




 by Max Oelschlaeger 




 During 1989 the popular press rediscovered the environment. After almost a decade of neglect, during which time disasters such as “Bhopal” and “Chernobyl” or the misadventures of various Reagan appointments such as James Watt dominated environmental news coverage, less dramatic but substantive conservation issues again attracted attention. 1989 became the “Year of the Environment,” with newspapers and magazines running races to stay on the breaking front of the news. Today the outlines of a global ecological crisis are well known (although scientists always hasten to warn that our knowledge remains sketchy and imprecise in some areas). With so much attention in the print media to “things environmental,” especially to issues of pressing importance, the reader may wonder what function is served by this collection of articles on environment and civilization. 




 Reflective essays dealing with conservation issues have never reached a wide audience, and perhaps understandably so. The press has constitutional safeguards for its freedoms, and the for profit context in which publishers compete largely precludes any simultaneous combination of mass appeal and intellectuality. The media provide what the reading public will buy, and sober intellectual deliberations therefore have a relatively small market, since what sells newspapers and magazines tends to be crisis or scandal oriented. Clearly this collection of essays on “the wilderness condition” does not compete with publications that deal with issues of the moment, with the factual underpinnings of global ecological malaise, with considerations of public policy, and with detailed proposals for a “green future.” And yet just as clearly it is in relation to the “re-greening of consciousness,” engendered in large measure by the popular press, that 

The Wilderness Condition

 finds its justification.
