author: Publicación Abierta
title: España: Los que nunca han cogido una pala nos dan lecciones de absentismo
content:
Abascal presume de representar a la España que madruga. Un hombre que ha vivido siempre de cargos, fundaciones y chiringuitos políticos, y que no sabe lo que es fichar a las siete de la mañana. Lo mismo vale para Feijóo, Ayuso, Rueda y cualquiera de estos señores que no sabrían por qué lado se coge una pala. Y son precisamente ellos quienes hablan de absentismo laboral.




¿Qué sabrán ellos de trabajar enfermos?




¿Qué sabrán de tener una hernia, una discopatía o una tendinitis y seguir yendo a trabajar? Lo máximo que hacen para herniarse es levantarse del sillón. Y, aun así, tenemos a un Feijóo que, en plena campaña electoral, dejó de dar mítines porque tenía un pinchazo en la espalda y no podía hablar. Para él, el dolor propio justifica parar. El de la dependienta, el reponedor o el albañil con la espalda destrozada, en cambio, no. Esos sí pueden trabajar y, además, más horas.




El bulo de las bajas del fin de semana




Nos cuentan que la mayoría de la gente se coge la baja los viernes, los sábados o los domingos. Vamos a ver: para coger una baja hay que acudir al médico de cabecera. En urgencias, lo que te dan es un informe sobre lo que te pasa y, con ese informe, tienes que acudir después a tu médico de cabecera del Sergas, que es quien te da la baja y quien te va expidiendo los partes de confirmación cada semana, cada quince días o cada mes.




Yo he ido a urgencias muchas veces y nunca, jamás, me han dado la baja allí. ¿Cómo vas a ir a tu médico de cabecera un sábado o un domingo si los centros de salud están cerrados? Ese argumento no se sostiene desde la base. Si alguien quiere vendernos que los trabajadores somos unos caraduras, que enseñe los datos. Porque el gran caradura, el que lanza bulos y mentiras, es quien los difunde sin comprobar nada.




Hablan de trabajo sin conocerlo




¿Cómo van a hablar de faltas y de absentismo quienes no faltan al trabajo porque no trabajan? Cobran un buen sueldo por hacer prácticamente nada. Ni siquiera se preparan los discursos. Recordemos a Feijóo explicando que Orwell escribió 1984 en el año 84. Si no eres capaz de documentarte sobre lo que vas a decir, ¿me vas a dar lecciones de esfuerzo? ¿Me las va a dar Abascal, que no domina un solo dato y cuyo repertorio se reduce a gritar «¡Viva España!» y a llamar «menas» a unos menores?




Respeto a la clase trabajadora




A personajes como Abascal, Ayuso o Feijóo les exigiría respeto hacia los trabajadores y las trabajadoras de este país. No somos unos mangantes. Somos trabajadores y trabajamos más horas que en Alemania, Francia, los Países Bajos o Dinamarca, con salarios bastante peores. Los precios se han disparado y los sueldos se han devaluado, de modo que a la mayoría no nos llega para vivir con dignidad. Más horas por menos dinero que en los países más avanzados de la Unión Europea: esas son nuestras condiciones.




El despido ya es libre y barato




Para colmo, las instituciones europeas llevan tiempo avisando de que los trabajadores españoles están desprotegidos ante el despido. El Consejo de Europa, por ejemplo, ha señalado que la indemnización prevista en la legislación española es insuficiente. Y, mientras tanto, Vox pide el despido libre y gratuito, y el PP habla de facilitar un despido que, según ellos, es demasiado caro.




Es todo lo contrario: despedir en España ya es muy barato, y lograr la nulidad de un despido, aunque tengas toda la razón, es complicadísimo, incluso con la reforma de este Gobierno «de progreso», que en tantas cosas no lo es. Con ellos será mucho peor, porque su mensaje es que ya tenemos demasiado: que el salario mínimo es alto, que tenemos demasiados derechos. Nada más lejos de la realidad.




Repartir la riqueza, no privatizarla




Somos un país avanzado, uno de los que más crecen, según el FMI y los organismos internacionales. Entonces, lo que toca es repartir esa riqueza para que la brecha entre ricos y pobres no sea tan brutal y para que quienes se están forrando aporten más, de modo que el Estado del bienestar, las pensiones, la educación y la sanidad no corran peligro.




No se trata de privatizar los servicios públicos y ponerlos en manos de quienes solo buscan ganar dinero, convirtiendo nuestras vidas en un negocio.




Patriotas de verdad




Eso sí es ser patriota: no de la cartera, ni de la pulserita, ni de la banderita, sino de tu pueblo. Y eso es precisamente lo que no son ninguno de estos.




Ya está bien de que nos falten al respeto quienes no han trabajado nunca, de que nos llamen mangantes cuando los mangantes son ellos. Ya está bien de que nos digan que tenemos que trabajar enfermos en una sociedad envejecida, donde cada día hay más trabajadores mayores de cincuenta años que se han roto la espalda y el pecho levantando este país.




¿Cómo van a saber lo que es vivir trabajando enfermos quienes no lo han hecho jamás ni conocen a nadie de su entorno que haya tenido que hacerlo, porque todos ellos se han enriquecido gracias a su paso por la política?




Dejemos de votar a quienes nos insultan




¿Qué futuro queremos para nuestros hijos? Cuando se oponen al salario mínimo, cuando piden el despido libre y cuando hablan de recortar derechos, ¿en qué mercado laboral van a trabajar nuestros hijos?




No somos de hierro. Nosotros también enfermaremos, también envejeceremos y, si no nos morimos antes, también tendremos que jubilarnos y vivir de una pensión.




Ya está bien de votar a quienes nos insultan y amenazan los pocos derechos que tenemos, así como el presente y el futuro de nuestros hijos y el nuestro propio. Empecemos a pensar en nosotros mismos, a defender nuestros intereses y nuestros derechos, y dejemos de confiar en mangantes que no saben lo que es trabajar y solo saben faltarle al respeto a la clase trabajadora.




¡Até a vitoria sempre!




André Abeledo Fernández

España: Los que nunca han cogido una pala nos dan lecciones de absentismo

author: Publicación Abierta
title: La Matriz Ideológica de la Dominación Occidental y el nuevo cerco a los pueblos rebeldes de Nuestra Améfrica Ladina
content:
A 534 años de la Resistencia Indígena Planetaria, en homenaje al maestro Saúl Rivas Rivas: guerra cognitiva, tecno feudalismo y soberanía algorítmica cimarrona frente al cerco electoral, espiritual y epistémico del imperio.




Por Argenis José Delgado Vegas 

| @ArgJoDel | 10 de octubre de 2026




Nuestra Améfrica Ladina despierta. En el marco de una resistencia que lleva más de cinco siglos frente a la colonización y la neocolonización, los pueblos de México, Cuba, Haití, Brasil, Colombia, Nicaragua, Bolivia, Venezuela, Ecuador y Argentina —con mayoría de población indígena y afrodescendiente— han impulsado en las últimas décadas procesos de liberación y descolonización estatal. Unos se han aproximado al zapatismo, panafricanismo, socialismo, comunismo, comunitarismo… No importa la etiqueta: importa que se atreven a caminar fuera del guión que Occidente les tenía reservado. Y cuando los pueblos rebeldes se mueven, el imperio afila sus armas. No solo las militares. Las armas más letales son las ideológicas.




La densidad afroindígena de Colombia, Brasil y Venezuela: el corazón demográfico de la rebelión




En Nuestra Améfrica Ladina hay tres países donde la matriz colonial muestra su rostro más descarnado porque allí se concentra una de las mayores densidades de población afrodescendiente e indígena del continente. Brasil, con más de la mitad de su población autoidentificada como negra o parda y cerca de 1,7 millones de indígenas; Colombia, con millones de afrocolombianos, raizales y palenqueros y más de un centenar de pueblos originarios; y Venezuela, con una presencia afrodescendiente que atraviesa la región norte costera frente al Caribe, los llanos y los Andes, el Sur y con 2,8 % de población indígena reconocida. No son datos menores: son la prueba viviente de que la colonialidad no terminó. Son también el sujeto histórico que el imperio teme, porque su memoria colectiva guarda el cimarronaje, el Cumbe, el resguardo, el conuco, el territorio y la espiritualidad como formas de libertad.




Esa densidad afroindígena explica por qué estos países son blanco prioritario de la Matriz Ideológica de la Dominación Occidental. En Brasil, el bolsonarismo no solo disputa el Estado: disputa el relato sobre la esclavitud, los quilombos y los pueblos indígenas. La bancada evangélica ultraconservadora, el agronegocio y la minería ilegal avanzan sobre tierras indígenas y quilombolas mientras se boicotea Durban y se criminaliza el racismo estructural. En Colombia, el giro a la derecha de Abelardo de la Espriella se monta sobre el miedo, el extractivismo y la guerra cognitiva contra el Acuerdo de Paz, justo en el país con mayor población afrodescendiente del mundo después de Brasil y con pueblos indígenas que han sido víctimas del conflicto armado. En Venezuela, el cerco financiero, el secuestro del presidente legítimo Nicolás Maduro y su esposa la diputada Cilia Flores, la ofensiva contra los cultos populares apuntan al corazón afroindígena del proyecto bolivariano.




 Estos tres países son, además, la demostración de que las Causas Comunes de la Humanidad no son abstracciones: la causa indígena, la causa de la diáspora africana, la causa del planeta, la de la mujer, la del trabajo y la intergeneracional se intersectan en la Amazonía, el Pacífico colombiano, el Cerrado brasileño, Barlovento y la Guayana venezolanaa ( incluye el Esequibo). Allí la colonialidad de los datos se vuelve concreta: los algoritmos de Silicon Valley clasifican, vigilan y expropian los saberes de pueblos que han cuidado la vida durante milenios. Por eso la soberanía algorítmica cimarrona no es un lujo teórico: es la continuación digital del palenque y del resguardo. Sin ella, la gran población afro e indígena de Colombia, Brasil y Venezuela seguirá siendo materia prima de la guerra cognitiva, del tecno feudalismo y del viejo Dios blanco que no tolera la pluriversalidad.










 













Marco Teórico: 

«Saúl Rivas Rivas lo advirtió con claridad: existe una Matriz Ideológica de la Dominación Occidental, un entramado histórico, cultural, social y espiritual cuyo fin es ‘dar continuidad a toda una opresión capitalista occidental’. Esa matriz no es un invento reciente. Es la misma que construyó un ‘Dios blanco y europeo’ frente a un ‘Diablo negro, indio o árabe’, justificando la dominación como un acto de perfeccionamiento racial.»
















Ramón Grosfoguel desmonta el mecanismo con precisión quirúrgica. El “universalismo abstracto” es aquel que, “desde un particularismo hegemónico, pretende erigirse en diseño global imperial para todo el mundo”. Se presenta como “descarnado”, como si no tuviera cuerpo, como si no hablara desde ningún lugar. Pero sí habla: habla desde la geopolítica y la corpo-política del conocimiento eurocéntrico, desde el “punto cero” que se arroga el derecho de nombrar la verdad universal. Ese universalismo no es universal: es el particularismo de Occidente disfrazado de destino de la humanidad.




Enrique Dussel completa el cuadro al señalar que el eurocentrismo consiste exactamente en “haber confundido la universalidad abstracta con la mundialidad concreta hegemonizada por Europa”. Europa no fue el centro del mundo hasta que la conquista y la colonización la pusieron allí. Pero una vez instalada, su particularidad se transfiguró en universalidad. Lo que era un momento regional se convirtió en la medida de toda civilización. El mito de la Modernidad convirtió al victimario en inocente y a la víctima en culpable.




Frente a esa matriz, Rivas Rivas no solo denuncia: propone. Sus tesis sobre las Causas Comunes de la Humanidad parten de una premisa fundamental: “La humanidad toda se encuentra afligida por razones de género, luchas de pueblos por su liberación, ambiente y explotación de clases. Lejos de entender estas causas por separado, describimos la intersección de las mismas como una lucha común de la humanidad toda por alcanzar su emancipación”. No son causas aisladas, sino “pies distintos del mismo cuerpo que caminan en torno a la descolonización, la anticonquista, el antiimperialismo y la liberación definitiva”.




Entre esas causas, Rivas Rivas enumera la del planeta —porque “el Planeta puede vivir sin nosotros, nosotros no podemos vivir sin Él”, como dicen las filosofías indias del Buen Vivir—; la de la mujer y la familia, señalando que el patriarcalismo no ha existido siempre, sino que aparece con el Estado y la sociedad patriarcal hace 7.000 a 10.000 años; la del trabajo y los trabajadores; la causa indígena de América en conexión con los pueblos originarios de todos los continentes; la causa de la diáspora africana; y la causa intergeneracional en el diálogo de civilizaciones. El autor insiste en que “cada una de estas causas es específica e irreductible unas a otras”, pero todas confluyen en un mismo horizonte emancipatorio.




Esa matriz sigue operando. Y su expresión más reciente y descarnada es el boicot a la conmemoración del 25.º aniversario de la Declaración de Durban. La administración estadounidense, a través de su embajador ante la ONU, Mike Waltz, calificó el evento como una reunión “vergonzosa”, “antioccidental y antisemita”, y agradeció explícitamente a los Estados que se unieron al rechazo del “legado pernicioso de Durban” (Insurgente, 2026). Ese boicot —al que se sumaron 48 Estados, incluyendo a Venezuela (por omisión) y Argentina— es una expresión concreta de la Matriz Ideológica de la Dominación Occidental. Condenar como “antioccidental” todo esfuerzo por visibilizar el racismo estructural, la colonialidad y la reparación histórica es precisamente el gesto que la matriz prescribe. Y es, sobre todo, un golpe directo contra los pueblos afrodescendientes e indígenas de Colombia, Brasil y Venezuela, que son los que más han exigido reparación histórica y los que más han visto cómo sus territorios, sus saberes y sus vidas siguen siendo expropiados.




El laboratorio cubano: fundamentalismo evangélico y cerco espiritual




Pero la contraofensiva no se limita a los foros internacionales. Se expresa con crudeza en los procesos electorales, los cambios políticos de la región y, de manera cada vez más alarmante, en la esfera religiosa. Cuba, que ha sido faro de resistencia anticolonial durante más de seis décadas, enfrenta hoy una ofensiva silenciosa pero profunda: el crecimiento acelerado del fundamentalismo evangélico ultraconservador, un fenómeno que no es casual ni espontáneo, sino que responde a la misma lógica de la Matriz Ideológica de la Dominación Occidental.




En un continente históricamente católico, con diversidad de espiritualidades ancestrales, se expande con fuerza un evangelismo de corte ultraconservador, de cuya mano también han crecido las fuerzas políticas de ultraderecha. Cuba no es en absoluto una excepción a este fenómeno. Desde los años 90, coincidiendo con la crisis económica derivada del derrumbe del campo socialista, las iglesias evangélicas de corte ultraconservador crecieron en la isla y se convirtieron en un actor político contrario al proyecto revolucionario. Lo que comenzó como un florecimiento religioso legítimo en un contexto de vacíos existenciales, fue progresivamente capturado por redes neoconservadoras con financiamiento y respaldo desde Estados Unidos.




El analista cubano Iramis Rosique Cárdenas, en un artículo publicado por el diario español Diario Red, sostiene que ese fenómeno “parece ser el mayor adversario interno que haya tenido el proyecto social cubano”. No es una exageración. Las iglesias evangélicas ultraconservadoras fueron el frente más relevante de oposición al proyecto de Constitución de 2018 —que incluía el matrimonio igualitario— y articularon un bloque de al menos 16 denominaciones contra el Código de las Familias. Su presión logró que el programa de educación sexual del Ministerio de Educación, aprobado en 2021, nunca se aplicara. Estamos ante una ofensiva que no solo disputa el alma, sino que legisla sobre el cuerpo y la subjetividad de todo un pueblo.




La pregunta clave es: ¿cómo se financian? La mayoría de las iglesias evangélicas en Cuba tienen una “iglesia hermana” en Estados Unidos, de la cual reciben apoyo financiero. El Evangelismo Cristiano Humanitario para Cuba, por ejemplo, recibió aproximadamente USD 2,3 millones del Gobierno de Estados Unidos entre 2009 y 2017, y ocupó uno de los primeros puestos entre los proyectos relacionados con Cuba que han recibido mayor cantidad de fondos desde que Trump asumió el cargo. La mano del “Tío Sam” existe, actúa e influye, intentando desmovilizar a los sectores populares y/o producir cambios en los Gobiernos.




El patrón es conocido: donde el Estado revolucionario no puede ser derrotado por la vía militar ni por el bloqueo económico, se activa la guerra cognitiva y espiritual. El fundamentalismo evangélico opera como una tecnología de modelación de subjetividad que, bajo la apariencia de salvación espiritual, instala un imaginario anticomunista, individualista y pro-mercado. En diciembre de 2023, 15 líderes evangélicos cubanos divulgaron una carta en apoyo a Israel durante el conflicto con Hamas, contrariando la posición oficial del gobierno cubano. No es teología: es geopolítica disfrazada de fe.




Y hay un elemento adicional que conecta directamente con la guerra cognitiva: estos grupos no operan solo desde el púlpito. Utilizan tecnologías digitales modernas —altavoces, TVs modernas, redes sociales— para transmitir su mensaje. Son influencers evangélicos que ya no se limitan a combatir la llamada “ideología de género”, sino que tienen un discurso abiertamente anticomunista, cercano al libertarismo argentino o al movimiento MAGA, y que piden derrocar el orden constitucional o una intervención militar de Estados Unidos. Es la misma matriz: el Dios blanco y europeo que no tolera la pluriversalidad, ahora armado con algoritmos y plataformas digitales. Y es la misma arremetida que en Brasil ataca los terreiros de candomblé y umbanda, en Colombia estigmatiza las espiritualidades indígenas y afro, y en Venezuela pretende silenciar el Culto a María Lionza.




La Revolución Cubana, que en los años 90 rectificó su política de ateísmo estatal y abrió un diálogo con las denominaciones religiosas —reformando la Constitución para transformar el Estado de ateo a laico—, se encuentra hoy ante un dilema: cómo garantizar la libertad religiosa sin permitir que esa libertad sea instrumentalizada como caballo de Troya del imperio. La respuesta no puede ser la represión indiscriminada, que solo alimentaría la narrativa de persecución religiosa. La respuesta es la soberanía epistémica y espiritual: desenmascarar las redes de financiamiento, visibilizar la agenda política oculta tras el discurso de la fe, y fortalecer las tradiciones religiosas autóctonas —la santería, el espiritismo, las iglesias comprometidas con la justicia social— que forman parte del tejido cultural cubano y que no responden a los designios de Washington.




Cuba no es un caso aislado. Es el laboratorio donde la Matriz Ideológica de la Dominación Occidental ensaya su nueva modalidad: la conquista espiritual por vía evangélica. Lo que ocurre en la isla es una advertencia para toda Nuestra Améfrica Ladina, y muy especialmente para Colombia, Brasil y Venezuela, donde la población afro e indígena es el principal blanco de esa ofensiva.




Brasil, el epicentro del cerco electoral




El mismo patrón se repite en el resto del continente. En Brasil, la primera vuelta del 4 de octubre dejó un resultado que estremece: Flávio Bolsonaro obtuvo el 47,03 % de los votos válidos frente al 45,16 % de Lula da Silva. El ultraderechista, que promete amnistiar a su padre condenado a 27 años por intento de golpe de Estado, llega a la segunda vuelta del 25 de octubre con el impulso de una “ola” reaccionaria que Trump celebró como una “gran victoria”. El Partido Liberal casi duplicó sus escaños en el Senado y avanzó en la Cámara de Diputados. La campaña de Flávio exhibe banderas estadounidenses e imágenes de Trump, mientras Lula denuncia que del otro lado están “aquellos que aman la bandera estadounidense” y quieren que “los estadounidenses vengan a explotar nuestras riquezas”. Brasil, el último reducto progresista de la región, está en juego. Y no es cualquier país: es el país con la mayor población afrodescendiente fuera de África y con la mayor diversidad indígena del continente. Allí, el cerco electoral es también un cerco racial y territorial: la avanzada del agronegocio, la minería y la bancada evangélica ultraconservadora busca desmantelar las políticas de cuotas, los derechos quilombolas y la demarcación de tierras indígenas. Derrotar a Lula es, para la matriz, derrotar al sujeto afroindígena que ha osado disputar el poder.




El mismo patrón se repite en el resto del continente. En 2025 y 2026, el llamado “giro a la derecha” ha recorrido la región: José Antonio Kast en Chile, Daniel Noboa en Ecuador, Rodrigo Paz en Bolivia, Abelardo de la Espriella en Colombia, Keiko Fujimori en Perú, Laura Fernández en Costa Rica. En Argentina, el gobierno de Javier Milei fue sostenido por una condicionalidad explícita de Washington: Trump advirtió que el rescate financiero dependía del triunfo electoral de ¡Viva La Libertad Carajo!. La consigna #PatriaOColonia se volvió tendencia: el viejo dilema colonial actualizado en pleno siglo XXI. La matriz opera aquí como disciplinamiento: los pueblos que osan salirse del guión son castigados con la asfixia financiera o la intervención directa, como ocurrió con la captura del presidente Nicolás Maduro en Caracas. Y en Colombia, con su enorme población afrodescendiente e indígena, el giro a la derecha amenaza con sepultar el capítulo de paz y reparación que esas comunidades arrancaron a duras penas.




El 12 de octubre: la disputa por los espíritus




Y mientras el imperio aprieta el cerco electoral, se aproxima el 12 de octubre, Día de la Resistencia Indígena en Venezuela y Día de la Celebración del Culto a la Reina María Lionza en la Montaña de Sorte, Yaracuy. Cada año, miles de devotos peregrinan a Quibayo para el “Baile en Candela”, rindiendo culto a las cortes indígenas, africanas y libertadoras. Pero este año las tendencias religiosas ya se muestran polarizadas. Las autoridades católicas denuncian un “aumento de ritos esotéricos” y la “Marcha para Jesús” —que desde 2004 se realizaba cada 12 de octubre “para hacer frente al ocultismo”— ha cambiado de fecha. Grupos evangelistas han destruido altares marialionceros en el pasado, y la tensión entre espiritualidad popular y ofensiva confesional se exacerba. Es la misma matriz: el Dios blanco y europeo que no tolera la pluriversalidad de los espíritus. Lo que en Cuba se expresa como cerco evangélico al proyecto revolucionario, en Venezuela se manifiesta como ataque a las espiritualidades populares y afroindígenas. Y en Brasil y Colombia, esa misma ofensiva se disfraza de “guerra espiritual” contra terreiros, pagamentos y rituales ancestrales.




Guerra relatora, tecno feudalismo y guerra cognitiva




Todo este entramado adquiere hoy una dimensión que trasciende los foros y las urnas: la guerra relatora, el tecno feudalismo y la guerra cognitiva. La guerra relatora es la disputa por el relato, por la narrativa que define qué es verdad y qué es desinformación. Los centros de poder occidentales —y sus plataformas digitales— imponen un sentido común que criminaliza la rebeldía y naturaliza la sumisión. El tecno feudalismo, como lo describe Yanis Varoufakis, es la mutación del capitalismo hacia un orden donde unos pocos señores de la nube —Google, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft— extraen renta de la vida entera, convirtiendo a los usuarios en siervos digitales. En Nuestra América, esa lógica se traduce en la colonialidad de los datos: nuestras vidas, nuestros territorios y nuestros saberes son expropiados por algoritmos diseñados en Silicon Valley. La guerra cognitiva busca que la gente “piense muy simple o deje de pensar y deje de recordar”. Es la modelación coercitiva de la subjetividad periférica: “el triunfo más invisible y letal de la nueva imperialidad cognitiva”. Y la diplomacia coercitiva —sanciones, bloqueos, injerencia electoral, persecución judicial y acciones militares— es el brazo visible de esa guerra total.




Soberanía algorítmica cimarrona




Frente a ese cerco, sostengo una salida: la soberanía algorítmica cimarrona. No se trata de una consigna tecnológica más, sino de una categoría que hunde sus raíces en el cimarronaje: la fuga del orden impuesto, la construcción de un territorio propio donde las reglas las ponemos nosotros. La pedagogía cimarrona —”el conjunto de técnicas y métodos que la diáspora africana utilizó para transmitir códigos culturales, éticos y espirituales bajo el oprobioso sistema esclavista”— es la garantía de una soberanía duradera. Aplicada al algoritmo, significa apropiarnos de la infraestructura digital, producir nuestros propios datos, gestionar nuestros propios nodos, disputar el sentido en las redes. La producción y gerenciamiento de datos propios sobre la microfísica territorial “son los únicos insumos capaces de restar centralidad al comando corporativo”. Soberanía algorítmica cimarrona es que ningún señor de la nube decida qué pensamos, qué consumimos o qué recordamos. Es la fuga hacia el monte digital, la construcción de CUMBES de datos libres.




Y esa soberanía algorítmica cimarrona debe aplicarse también a la disputa espiritual. Si el fundamentalismo evangélico ultraconservador utiliza plataformas digitales para modelar subjetividades y expandir su agenda geopolítica, la respuesta no puede ser solo la denuncia. Es necesario construir redes de comunicación propias, producir contenidos que visibilicen las tradiciones religiosas emancipadoras —la teología de la liberación, el ecumenismo comprometido con la justicia social, las espiritualidades afroindígenas— y disputar el espacio digital con narrativas de dignidad y pluriversalidad. La guerra cognitiva se libra en los algoritmos, y allí también debemos plantar nuestras tiendas. Especialmente en Colombia, Brasil y Venezuela, donde la población afro e indígena es mayoría o fuerza decisiva, la soberanía algorítmica cimarrona es la condición para que su voz no sea filtrada, clasificada y vendida por el tecno feudalismo.




Conclusión: la pluriversalidad como horizonte




La avanzada hegemónica no es solo militar o económica. Es, fundamentalmente, epistémica y espiritual. Los pueblos que se acercan al socialismo, al panafricanismo o al progresismo se convierten en blanco de una guerra ideológica que busca deslegitimar sus proyectos mediante la imposición de un “universalismo” que niega la pluriversalidad. Grosfoguel lo dice sin rodeos: frente al universalismo abstracto, la alternativa es el “pluri-versalismo transmoderno decolonial”, un diálogo horizontal entre mundos donde ninguna particularidad se arroga la representación de toda la humanidad. El boicot a Durban, el cerco electoral —con Brasil como epicentro—, la ofensiva contra los cultos populares, el cerco evangélico en Cuba y la guerra cognitiva son caras de una misma contraofensiva que apunta a sepultar el legado anticolonial de Nuestra América.




Pero la matriz no es inexpugnable. Las Causas Comunes de la Humanidad nos recuerdan que las luchas por el planeta, por el agua, por la mujer, por los pueblos indígenas, por la diáspora africana y por la clase trabajadora no son compartimentos estancos: son un solo cuerpo que camina hacia la liberación definitiva. Los pueblos rebeldes de Abya Yala llevan quinientos años resistiendo, y su memoria es más larga que la arrogancia imperial. Colombia, Brasil y Venezuela, con su enorme densidad afroindígena, son la prueba de que la descolonización no se detiene con un boicot. La pluriversalidad no se apaga con un twitters. Y la soberanía algorítmica cimarrona es la garantía de que la dignidad de los pueblos no se mide en ninguna reunión de alto nivel.




Argenis José Delgado Vegas




@ArgJoDel

author: Publicación Abierta
title: España: Trump se hunde en Estados Unidos y aquí nos quieren vender el trumpismo como futuro
content:
El trumpismo se hunde en su propia casa




Faltan pocas semanas para las elecciones de medio mandato en Estados Unidos y el panorama para Donald Trump es, como mínimo, vertiginoso. Las encuestas llevan meses diciendo lo mismo: su aprobación ronda el 37-39 %, el rechazo a su gestión alcanza máximos históricos desde que se formula esta pregunta y los demócratas aventajan a los republicanos en la papeleta genérica por entre 6 y 9 puntos, según el sondeo. Hasta en estados que Trump ganó con holgura en 2024, como Texas, Ohio, Alaska o Iowa, hay una batalla abierta.




Y lo más elocuente: los propios candidatos republicanos empiezan a marcar distancias con él. Saben que su nombre ya resta más de lo que suma. Cuando el presidente les pide que voten «como si él estuviera en la papeleta», muchos de los suyos piensan lo contrario: que cuanto más lejos de él, mejor.




Un fracaso en lo económico y en lo social




Trump prometió prosperidad, empleo y precios más bajos. Lo que ha llegado es otra cosa: la inflación, el empleo y la sanidad encabezan las preocupaciones de la gente, y es precisamente en esos ámbitos donde su aprobación es más baja. Los republicanos han perdido incluso su vieja ventaja como «mejor partido para la economía». En el ámbito social, el balance es un retroceso de derechos, una persecución sistemática de los migrantes y un país cada vez más crispado y desigual.




A eso se suma lo peor: las guerras. Guerras comerciales, guerras sociales y guerras reales que siempre pagan los mismos: la clase trabajadora. No es solo que no mejore la vida de la gente, sino que, además, empeora.




Y mientras tanto, aquí, a contramano




En este panorama, con el trumpismo perdiendo terreno en su propia casa, resulta que aquí, en el Estado español, quienes beben de esa misma fuente se perfilan como posibles ganadores de las elecciones. ¿En serio? Parece que vamos siempre a destiempo, sin mirar hacia dónde soplan los vientos de la historia. Cuando el modelo fracasa allí donde nació, aquí hay quien nos lo quiere vender como el futuro.




Es una lástima que, como pueblo, nos falte esa visión global: la capacidad de entender lo que ocurre a nuestro alrededor y lo que está en juego en el ámbito geopolítico.




Los que se arrodillaron




Feijóo, Abascal y Ayuso le hicieron la ola a Trump y a Netanyahu, sobre quien pesa una orden de detención internacional, mientras callaban ante las agresiones que llegaban desde el Washington trumpista y desde el Israel genocida. Se plegaron y se arrodillaron ante unos poderes fácticos que han intentado imponerse por la fuerza. Eso tiene un nombre: vendepatrias.




Trump pasará a la historia como uno de los peores presidentes de Estados Unidos y como uno de los mandatarios más ridículos de nuestro tiempo, junto a otros como Milei y a quienes aspiran a imitarlos aquí. Y cuando el proyecto se agota, también caen quienes se apoyaron en él.




Despertar a tiempo




Que no nos pase lo de siempre. Que no demos el paso de apoyar a quienes han estado una y otra vez en manos de Trump y Netanyahu. El trumpismo no sirve, no vale: no mejora la vida de la gente, sino que la destruye. Ojalá despertemos a tiempo y veamos dónde estamos.




¡Até a vitoria sempre!




André Abeledo Fernández

España: Trump se hunde en Estados Unidos y aquí nos quieren vender el trumpismo como futuro

 se publicó primero en 

Indymedia Argentina Centro de Medios Independientes (( i ))

.

author: Mada Masr
title: Parliament puts off vote on authorizing Sisi to send troops to Saudi Arabia until Tuesday
content:
After a closed session on Sunday that ran for nearly three hours, the House of Representatives postponed a vote on authorizing President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi to send troops on a combat mission to defend Saudi Arabia, putting it off until after Monday’s and Tuesday’s sessions.




Sisi had called for an emergency parliamentary session during the Egyptian Military Academy graduation ceremony on Saturday, asking lawmakers to authorize him to take any measures necessary to protect Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks “if we are asked to do so.”




The delay came after MPs demanded details of the Armed Forces’ role in Saudi Arabia beyond the National Defense Council’s 

statement

, asking that every MP get a chance to express their views on the matter, according to three lawmakers who spoke to Mada Masr.




MP Ehab Mansour, the Egyptian Social Democratic Party parliamentary bloc head, told Mada Masr after the session that members were instructed not to share details of the discussions with the media.




“We are not looking for a role to play, but it makes no sense whatsoever for us to allow any harm to come to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, its security or its stability,” Sisi said during the graduation ceremony.




He appealed to “everyone in the Gulf” to stop the war. “Regardless of this appeal, whether it is heeded or not, Egypt, in line with His Majesty King Salman and Crown Prince Mohamed bin Salman’s directives, will carry out any measure to protect and defend you,” he added.




Sisi stressed that he is not speaking “in order for us to fight anyone or attack anyone. We are speaking only in defense.”




Following Sisi’s remarks, House Speaker Hesham Badawy called an emergency plenary session for Sunday morning.




Article 152 of the 

Constitution

 requires the president to consult the National Defense Council before declaring war or sending armed forces on combat missions outside the country. It also requires approval from two-thirds of the members of the House of Representatives, voting in a closed session under Article 130 of the House’s bylaws.




Before Parliament convened, the presidential spokesperson 

announced

 three points agreed upon by the National Defense Council at a meeting chaired by Sisi earlier on Sunday morning. The council declared Egypt’s full solidarity with Saudi Arabia, out of a belief that Saudi national security is tied to Egyptian and Arab national security, and pledged to provide the country with all necessary and available forms of support to defend its security and stability, protect its resources and territorial integrity and safeguard Islamic holy sites.




The council also called for continued and intensified political and diplomatic efforts, coordinated with relevant regional and international parties, to de-escalate tensions across the region and peacefully resolve the crisis affecting it.




A senior judicial source criticized the wording of the presidential request. “No state takes directives from another state,” he told Mada Masr on condition of anonymity.




The source explained that the Constitution requires Parliament’s approval before troops are sent on combat missions outside the country, meaning the president must specify the nature of the mission, its strategic value to the country and the number of soldiers needed to carry it out. That “authorize me and I’ll handle it” matter, the source said, is “unconstitutional.”




In a video 

posted 

to his personal Facebook account, MP Reda Abdel Salam, an economics professor at Mansoura University, laid out his view of the president’s authorization request, saying he was unable to express it during the session as each MP was allotted only two minutes. “If Egypt takes part in defending Saudi Arabia, it is only defense, with no Egyptian soldier sent onto Yemeni soil and no Egyptian strike or bullet fired at brotherly Yemen,” he said. “We are defending, alongside Saudi Arabia, the property, wealth, vital sites, airports and water and power stations. Egypt’s participation is defensive only, while mediation efforts continue.”




An MP with military background who spoke to Mada Masr on condition of anonymity expected Egypt’s involvement to be limited to deploying air defense forces and missiles, while also replacing some Saudi units with Egyptian forces and carrying out limited airstrikes against naval targets, without deploying troops in ground combat.




The source said that Egypt’s military doctrine since former President Gamal Abdel Nasser’s experience in Yemen has been shaped by the principle that the military “does not kill Arabs with its own hands.”




A governmental source echoed this view. “What we will do is send defensive forces to Saudi Arabia and naval forces to the Red Sea,” he said. “That will benefit us in our relations with both Saudi Arabia and 

Ethiopia

, as it sends a very strong message to Ethiopia about our presence in that area.”




Similarly, an informed political source explained that the understanding is for the Egyptian military support to be purely defensive and confined to protecting Saudi Arabia. Forces would enter Yemen from the Saudi side only if the Houthis launch a ground invasion, the source said, adding that such action is unlikely as the Houthis lack the capacity to do so. They can send drones, or engage in battles against the Yemeni military, but at the same time, they are under growing pressure on the ground, he added.




This official stress on purely defensive aims and on staying out of any offensive, which Sisi’s announcement affirmed and the various sources emphasized, fits the state’s broader stance of avoiding entanglement in regional wars, even when circumstances call for openly supplying military support.




This was plain to see when Egypt sent a “

detachment

” — a limited military formation drawn from one or several corps — to the United Arab Emirates in May. Sources at the time said that the word “detachment” came to “signal the limited size of the formation and the limited duration of the presence,” a gesture of Egyptian support for the UAE against Iranian attacks that stopped short of real Egyptian involvement in the war.




Egypt has historically had reservations about any ground intervention in Yemen, dating back to the 1962-1967 war, when Nasser sent troops to back the republicans in North Yemen against the Saudi-backed royalists. The intervention began small and grew to around 70,000 soldiers. Estimates of Egyptians killed range from 10,000-26,000. Nasser himself 

described 

the war as his own Vietnam, since it drained both the military and the economy, and a large share of the troops were still in Yemen when Egypt was defeated in 1967.




The intervention ended with the withdrawal of troops late that year, after Nasser and then- Saudi King Faisal reached an agreement on the sidelines of the Khartoum summit. Since then, a conviction to avoid getting entangled on the ground in Yemen has become ingrained in the military’s memory, something some analysts call the “Yemen complex.”




Egypt has previously 

taken 

part in the coalition Saudi Arabia has led in Yemen since 2015 under Operation Decisive Storm. It dispatched four naval vessels to secure the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the Gulf of Aden, alongside air force participation. Cairo 

said 

at the time that it is prepared to send ground troops “if the situation warrants,” but it never did.




Ahead of Parliament’s emergency session, the speaker of the Houthi-controlled House of Representatives in Sanaa, Yahya al-Raei, sent Badawy a letter urging him not to be pulled along by the policies of the Saudi regime, warning that “Egypt’s slide down this path would pose a grave danger to its national security and internal stability.”




In the letter, of which Mada Masr obtained a copy, Raei wrote, “We categorically reject that the Egypt of Arabism and history be dragged into a battle that does not resemble its values,” adding, “We have always known Egypt as a supporter of Yemen’s unity and stability.”




Raei accused the Saudi regime of waging “aggression and a blockade on Yemen for more than 12 years,” of shirking implementation of the roadmap by circumventing understandings and political efforts aimed at peace and of tightening the blockade on the Yemeni people to the point of famine in some areas.




He stressed that “the Saudi regime is the one that proceeded to end the de-escalation phase by targeting the Sanaa airport and chose to escalate through air raids on most Yemeni regions, targeting civilian infrastructure.” He also accused it of involvement in backing and financing groups he described as “Takfiri,” including the Islamic State, in their war against the Yemeni people.




An Egyptian government official previously told Mada Masr that Egypt has kept an open channel of communication with the Houthis, especially since they took control of Bab al-Mandab in September.




The front between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis is seeing its most violent 

escalation 

since the 2022 truce collapsed. In July, the Houthis declared a “naval blockade” of the kingdom and attacked Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea. In September, they launched a ground attack, capturing the Yemeni Mokha Port, which had been under the control of the Saudi-led coalition’s joint forces, effectively controlling Bab al-Mandab. By early October, the two sides were escalating: the internationally recognized Yemeni government launched the Fajr al-Yemen Operation to retake Sanaa, backed by extensive Saudi air support, while the Houthis attacked facilities belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco and 

struck 

King Khalid International Airport, killing 12 people and wounding hundreds.




The crisis comes amid shifts in the map of regional alliances. In August, Riyadh signed a joint defense pact with Turkey and Pakistan, in what came to be known as the Mecca Pact. Cairo, a member of the Quad formed by the pact’s signatories, didn’t join. According to diplomats and officials in Cairo who 

spoke 

to Mada Masr at the time, Egypt was not willing to sign up for what it saw as a Saudi-authored political bloc that would undermine its own ability to maneuver regionally.




On September 10, Axios 

reported

, citing United States officials, that bin Salman called US President Donald Trump twice, urging him to launch strikes against the Houthis, but Trump rejected. The officials said the US administration “does not intend to take direct military action against the Houthis at this time” and that Trump’s directives are to keep US forces focused on Iran and the Strait of Hormuz and to avoid opening another front.




Five days later, bin Salman 

visited 

Egypt at the head of a delegation that included Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud and Saudi National Security Advisor Musaed al-Aiban. The Saudi Royal Court said the visit was made at the direction of King Salman to discuss ways of strengthening bilateral relations and issues of common interest.




On September 20, CIA Director John Ratcliffe 

met

 with Sisi in Egypt. Iranian 

outlets 

took the visit as feeding speculation that Washington wants to hand Cairo a larger role in regional security arrangements.




On Tuesday, Foreign Minister Badr Abdel Atty said Egypt would respond to any Saudi request, and joining the “Mecca treaty” is now “under serious consideration.”




Saudi Asharq Bloomberg 

cited 

on Friday an official source saying Cairo is negotiating with Riyadh to renew deposits to the Central Bank of Egypt worth US$5.3 billion, which mature this month. According to the source, the talks are focused on how long the renewal should last, with no final agreement yet.




The next day, at the Military Academy graduation ceremony, Sisi 

called 

on the military parade leader, the Armed Forces’ commanders and the rest of the state officials in attendance to give a military salute to the Gulf states, in appreciation of their economic support for Egypt after “the events of 2011,” as he put it.

The post 

Parliament puts off vote on authorizing Sisi to send troops to Saudi Arabia until Tuesday

 first appeared on 

Mada Masr

.

title: Danny Evans - ‘Ultra-left’ anarchists and anti-fascism in the Second Republic
content:
Author

: Danny Evans

Title

: ‘Ultra-left’ anarchists and anti-fascism in the Second Republic

Date

: 2016

Source

: 

International Journal of Iberian Studies

, 29: 3, pp. 241–56, doi: 10.1386/ijis.29.3.241_1




ABSTRACT




 This article investigates the anarchist understanding of fascism during the Second Republic, and particularly during the abstention campaign of 1933, when the practice of radicals in the National Confederation of Labour (CNT) has been described as ‘ultra-left’ in view of its sectarianism and insistence on the need for an insurrectionary response to the threat of the right. The article explores the comparison made to the German Communist Party (KPD) during the so-called ‘Third Period’, and the lessons that anarchists in Spain attempted to draw from the rise of Hitler. 




INTRODUCTION




 The Spanish general election of November 1933 resulted in the formation of a centre-right government presided over by Alejandro Lerroux with the support of the Spanish Confederation of Autonomous Right Wing Groups (CEDA). Thus began the so-called ‘bienio negro’ of the Second Republic, characterized by the reversal of the reforms of the previous two years and the repression of left-wing and labour organizations. The elections had been preceded by a campaign orchestrated by the anarcho-syndicalist union, the National Confederation of Labour (CNT) which called on Spanish workers to abstain from voting. Following the elections, that same organization initiated a short-lived and disastrous uprising, which left over a hundred dead. This marked the beginning of a period of repression in which thousands of CNT activists were jailed and the day to day functioning of the organization was jeopardized. 




 Understandably, the historiography has not been kind to the CNT in this period. Its actions have been considered a consequence of ‘impatience and revolutionary mysticism’ (Gómez Casas 1973: 172), its propaganda dismissed as ‘the radical discourse of a minority’ of anarchists within the organization (Casanova 2005: 46). Thus the abstention campaign and the rising of late 1933 have generally been considered to be consequent upon the internal dynamics of the CNT, and the culmination of the process of radicalization within the organization during the first bienio of the Second Republic (1931–1933). This radicalization had already produced two uprisings, in January 1932 and January 1933, and the December revolt has been considered the closing act of a ‘cycle of insurrections’. In contrast to the Asturian insurrection of October 1934, the anarchist revolt of late 1933 is not normally considered a response to the increasing perception of an international and domestic fascist threat. On the contrary, the CNT’s insistence on pursuing a lonely insurrectionist tactic has been taken as evidence of ultra-left indifference among radicals as to the specific danger posed by fascism. According to Chris Ealham, anarchist radicals in this period ‘downplayed the danger of the far Right’, and acted in a sectarian manner that undermined attempts at anti-fascist unity: 







 Playing an ultra-leftist, divisive role that had much in common with the German Communist Party (KPD) prior to Hitler’s electoral triumph, the radical anarchists argued that there was no difference between the various electoral options, even suggesting that fascism was already in power […] like the KPD, the CNT and the FAI [the Iberian Anarchist Federation, a federation of anarchist affinity groups] blocked united anti-fascist action, directing their fury against what they regarded as the ‘fascism’ of their enemies, be they treintista [moderate syndicalist], socialist, republican or bloquista [dissident communist], all of whom were regarded as variants of authoritarianism. (2010: 134) 







 Using this suggestive comparison as a starting point, in this article I examine the roots of the commonalities between the approaches of the KPD and the CNT, specifically their sectarianism and revolutionary maximalism, while also fleshing out the differences that marked the anarchist approach to fascism in theory and in practice. 




 The ‘anti-fascist epic’ (Southworth 1996: 310) was finally won in 1945 by an alliance of imperial, Communist and democratic forces. This alliance contrasted with the ‘divisions and ineffectiveness’ of those who had opposed Hitler in Germany, identified as a contributing factor in his accession to power (Bullock 1973: 253). As such, the ‘object lesson’ of the rise of Nazism has been taken to be the need for unity among anti-fascists (Salter 1987: 21). History has not been forgiving, therefore, of the ‘ultra-left’ refusal of such alliances. However, the need for unity was not the only possible lesson to draw from Hitler’s coming to power. For the anarchists in Spain, more attuned to developments in Europe than is sometimes suggested, the rise of Nazism confirmed their critique of the electoral tactic and the corruption inherent in a democratic system that had acquiesced in the establishment of tyranny through ‘a shoddy political deal’ (Bullock 1973: 253). By returning to the anarchist interpretationof fascism in the pre-civil war period, therefore, I not only intend to bring fresh light to bear on our understanding of anarchist activity in 1933, but also to suggest that this interpretation has some merit. In paying attention to the Spanish anarchists in this period, we might recover a lesson from history that has been glossed over, and which has continued relevance for how we think about democracy, fascism and the state today.

Whether it’s a coincidence or a sign of the times, it is in the midst of a youth revolt and on the eve of a possible “return of the Yellow Vests” that the Invisible Committee is releasing its new book, Survival Manual, on October 16.

For twenty years now, through its many textual interventions (The Coming Insurrection, To Our Friends, Now...), it has both inspired, and produced the critical balance sheets of, successive waves of revolt and the situations that followed. With its “survival manual,” the group offers a stringent, unflinching, self-critical perspective — one free of flattery, yet also capable of being generous and honest.

Many of the questions the book raises are also, at times, our own, just as they are, ultimately, those of many people frustrated by defeat and a feeling of powerlessness: How should we make sense of repeated defeats, even despite the persistence of conflictual forms of action? What conclusions are we to draw from this? How are we to “survive” the present moment? How do our enemies continue to prosper? How can we confront capital with seriousness and strategy and truly reinvigorate revolutionary ethics and perspectives? In line with their explicit critique of the public sphere, their public statements remain rare. However, two contributors to the Invisible Committee’s Survival Manual answered our questions about the book, while offering their own analysis of the current moment.

Survival Manual argues that the Yellow Vests carried out a form of insurrection long awaited by autonomists, yet they did so without them: a movement born out of the encounter between singular, previously-isolated experiences, rather than from any preexisting forms of organization. Are there any similarities with the current youth revolt, or is this just yet another left-wing mobilization destined to be channeled, co-opted, or even sabotaged by unions and political parties?

What is shaking the country right now is not a social movement, it is a vital movement. The world of the “adults” in charge is hurtling headlong toward a wall — it’s even accelerating. It doesn’t care about anything; it wants to keep enjoying itself until the very last drop of oil. Claiming to be “responsible,” “reasonable,” and the custodians of “authority” is the height of their ferocious infantilism. A society of geriatrics can only be youth-obsessed, if not actually young. It wants all the trappings of youth, but detests its vitality. High school students have no reason to feel solidarity with such a civilization of suicidal people. They’ve seen their parents and teachers submit to all the humiliating aberrations of COVID management, then spout vague justifications to lock them down and subject them to the same treatment in turn. So much so that, when they speak up, it’s as if we were hearing the parents of their own parents. “Just because you accept being treated like worthless dogs, getting paid peanuts, unable to afford a full month of groceries doesn’t mean everyone else has to suffer because you didn’t have the guts to speak up — I’m sorry,” a student explodes. The reverse is also true. That infamous Nazi, Henry Ford, used to say, ““It is well enough that people of the nation do not understand our banking and monetary system, for if they did, I believe there would be a revolution before tomorrow morning.” If students knew what — with very few exceptions, and all the more precious for it — their teachers say about them in the teachers’ lounge, there’d be few high schools left standing in France. Governing a world with no promise other than that of its own collapse is shaping up to be more complicated than expected. It’s not clear that parental geolocation will suffice.

In an administered society, what we call “youth” is simply the free element, those who are not yet bound by a career, a boss, a loan, or a social circle, and who can therefore afford to say aloud what the rest see but prefer to keep quiet about. We generationalize the revolt in order to prevent it from generalizing. The current revolt of “young people” is primarily over our common condition. What is the point of pursuing a career in a world where temperatures reach 45°C — and therefore of pursuing an education in it? How dare this society treat its untenable contradictions as a “psychological problem,” like it’s our responsibility, and thus call on us to be “resilient” in the face of our “eco-anxiety”? How long will we tolerate the sifting process occurring at every level of the population — and thus systems like Parcoursup and MonMaster? Does life consist in caring for oneself as “human capital” — and thus as an aggregate of skills? When will we stop working toward our own replacement by AI — a fate already promised to teachers by the ministry’s startups? And above all, how can we bring about a revolution in a world entirely designed to prevent us from doing so? All these questions—and a few others — were our starting point in writing Survival Manual. For two years, we sought to answer them, to draw up a strategic balance sheet of the failure of the movements in which we had participated, and to clear the ground for the beginning of a new revolutionary process. We knew this task was necessary, but no one was talking about revolution anymore. We wondered if we were even writing for anyone at all. Now we know who we wrote for. We didn’t do all this for nothing.

The first thing the Yellow Vests and the current high school revolt have in common is that they come from sectors most removed from militant socialization, with its codes, its endless ruminations, its gloom, and its scowling radicalism. These are revolts that still know how to say “I.” Honestly, until last week, we hadn’t felt such joy in being out on the streets — joking, dancing, singing, tagging, and rioting — since the Yellow Vests. Another common trait is the way they challenge the humiliation that serves as the norm for social integration, which forms the very foundation of French culture. In other words, they defy judgment. Problems with toilets aren’t just “shit” problems, but a clear sign of contempt. They must therefore stop. “Gen Z, because we’ll be the last generation to be treated like shit,” a sign read last Tuesday. Needs are no laughing matter — whether it’s the need for sleep, cash, respect, meaning, or love. Everything in French culture seeks to make us ashamed of our needs, to the point that “meeting one’s needs” is synonymous with “shitting.” High school students, like the Yellow Vests, brazenly defy this taboo. Needs, in their materiality, in their singularity, are ungovernable: as soon as they’re brought up, governments no longer know what pretext to use to change the subject. A third common trait between these two uprisings is their refusal of governmental double binds, a refusal to let those in power drive us mad with paradoxical injunctions; it is, therefore, the same way of taking them at their word. “You told us to come holler at you; well, here we are, Macron: we’re down on the Champs-Élysées, we’ll be at the Élysée Palace soon!” “You drone on year round about how we need to work, pass our exams, and sacrifice ourselves for our ‘future’ — so, give us the conditions to do so, you sons of bitches!” All of a sudden, the powers that be are rendered naked, and begin to stutter. Then they shows their true colors and blurt it all out. They treat a blockaded high school as “urban violence” and explain, on public radio, that there are too many high school students, that many of them don’t belong in high school, and that, anyway, even if they pursue an education, it will never be enough for them to compete with AI in the job market. Now everything becomes clear.

The activists’ guilty conscience over having “missed out on the Yellow Vests” — a movement they took three weeks to join after initially labeling it “fascist” — is so strong that they have since been constantly trying to “recreate the Yellow Vests” at every opportunity. And in fact, as Survival Manual points out, this purely proletarian, anti-union, anti-political, and anti-representative insurrection took place without them. This did not prevent the Yellow Vests, after their first clashes with the CRS, from adopting the “black bloc” as a technique — a technique for rioting that had its origins in the German autonomist movement of the 1980s, but was not popularized in France until much later, in 2016. They adopted the technique, not the identity. But it was less through this particular feature, striking though it was, that the Yellow Vests acted autonomously than through their constant refusal of any representative, any spokesperson, any outside organization, or any form of institutional mediation. “Power for no one!” was the rallying cry of German autonomists in 1981. The Yellow Vests embodied that “autonomy beyond the autonomists” of which the Metropolitan Indians had dreamed in 1977. If the Yellow Vests wounded the pride of the autonomists, they were a nightmare for the trade unions: workers rising up, taking to the streets and speaking out directly, without going through their designated, salaried representatives. We need only recall Laurent Berger’s speeches in 2023, at the beginning of the movement against pension reform. All he talked about was his contempt for the Yellow Vests. Indeed, taking revenge on them was the sole motivation of the union leadership in that movement — not winning the fight through a series of stop-start protest days in the face of government provocations, but simply getting back in the saddle after such an affront. It was, in other words, a restoration movement. For all sorts of reasons, the current high school and student movement is less well equipped to defend itself against union and political maneuvering. Last Tuesday, a march on Matignon — the prime minister’s residence — from City Hall, a march decided upon by thousands of high school and university students, was quietly sabotaged by the trade union organizations and transformed into a march that ended with protesters being kettled in Place Vauban, without anyone making a scandal of it. Trade unions, the media, left-wing organizations — false friends are far more dangerous than genuine enemies. If they manage to fuck us over, it is precisely because, for a time, they pretended to be on our side. As for the Mélenchon supporters, with their strategy of bringing everything that moves under their hegemonic control and their PANG! tactic (“Nobody to Our Left!”), they are merely cynically preparing the biggest political hangover since Mitterrand. They feed on other people’s hopes as ticks feed on blood. Is this an excuse not to join the high school students? Certainly not. “Joining the high school students” means less following them and lending them support than extending their refusals and the forms of becoming that their gestures make possible: refusing to let ourselves be crushed. Refusing to become victims of the system. Becoming alive, autonomous, explosive. We are confident: in any case, there is no electoral solution to this civilizational impasse.

Important sections of Survival Manual are devoted to "governance through trauma.” This includes, in particular, a scathing critique of the strategic stupidity of the organizers of the Sainte-Soline mobilization, whose actions resulted in deliberate “traumatization.” To “begin again” would therefore mean drawing the appropriate lessons and breaking out of traumatic repetition. Here again, we are faced with police repression that is as predictable as it is massive. Are we once again throwing ourselves into a trap?

When you send 7,000 high school students into police custody over the course of three weeks and charge at them on horseback or with grenades with their pins pulled, this is obviously no longer a matter of “maintaining public order” or a problem of “unit deployment.” It is a strategy. “The aim of the operation was to frighten students and their parents in order to put an end to the rebellion as quickly as possible,” a police commissioner explains matter-of-factly. What this ordinary admission illustrates is the extent to which governments have, in recent years, become accustomed to manipulating trauma — whether its source is a catastrophe, a terrorist attack, a war, or their own police force. In the latter case, the Survival Manual speaks of “strategic traumatization.” The repression of the high school student movement unfortunately confirms this thesis. In France, the Yellow Vest uprising marked a turning point in this new configuration. During the week of December 8, 2018, the government and the media never stopped stoking the threat of people being killed. It was then that they threw the “Malik Oussekine doctrine” overboard. The strategy of “maiming one to deter a hundred” had already been tested in the context of the ZADs (Zones à défendre, or “Zones to Defend”), whether at Sivens, at Bure, or during the eviction of Notre-Dame-des-Landes. Taking advantage of the non-urban terrain, the police and gendarmerie rained down offensive grenades that exploded indiscriminately. This is apparently what happened in Lens. As for the tactic of ramming protesters with vehicles, it has long been tested in the banlieues. What is its purpose, from the standpoint of crowd management? None. The point is to traumatize. The shock and terror are amplified by videos — one way, among others, of turning the protesters’ own tools against them. Their videos become the means through which trauma spreads and, consequently, through which deterrence is achieved. To blame the fascisization of the police serves only to obscure how profoundly democratic this mode of governance actually is.

Sainte-Soline, in March 2023? The trap was visible from everywhere, from every vantage point and every point of view. Anyone who had taken part in the wildcat demonstrations during the pension protests — with their decapitated effigies of Macron, their threats invoking Louis XVI hurled from Place de la Concorde, or the administrative court attacked in Nantes — knew that something was slipping beyond the deadly grip of union control. For those in power, it was urgent to crush at birth the generation that was emerging there. So they installed their gigantic trap for the militant mice on this conspicuous mound. Anyone standing in front of that hill of earth, surrounded by trucks forming a defensive wall, with the general of the opposing forces parading along the battlements of the keep, could immediately recognize the trap. Anyone who had heard Darmanin’s provocations in the preceding days, like the pre-fight taunts before a boxing match, could smell the ambush. A few days after our complete rout, the gendarmes were crowing in the newspapers about the success of their campaign of traumatization. That was the term they used. The movement was abruptly broken. The organizers’ political maneuvering and calculations are not enough to explain why such an obvious trap worked. Until we confront this kind of failure head-on, along with the whole web of reasons that led to it, we condemn ourselves to repeating it. We remain prisoners of the cycle of traumatic repetition. At the demonstration in Paris on October 6 last year, the small riot that erupted just before the march reached Place de la Nation was precisely an attempt to avoid falling victim to the police deployment waiting there to crush the usual end-of-demonstration skirmishes. Every revolt of any real consequence invents its own forms, which are also tactics. It is impossible to imagine everything that can exist beyond the idiotic union-led transhumance! On every occasion, the event never lies on the side of mere “demonstration.” Otherwise, we would not have heard LeCornu congratulating himself in the National Assembly on “these demonstrations [which] the government welcomes with great respect [...] and with relief, because at last we have a legal, declared, democratic framework within which disagreements can be expressed.” At the beginning of this month, high school students showed that they could place their own school under siege, using fire and “delirium” to hold it. Nobody expected them there, least of all their wardens. On October 6 in Lyon, rather than endure confinement within the Trotskyist general assembly, the march spread into the surrounding streets and erected barricades there. There was probably more dancing around these improvised fires than on the benches of the Bourse du travail.

Every eruption finds its own repertoire, one that ultimately always runs counter to what aspiring leaders prescribe. All this bears witness to the persistence of the tactical intelligence that was so sorely lacking at Sainte-Soline. Fortunately, there is no general staff directing high school blockades across France, unlike what happened that day in Deux-Sèvres. The strategy of traumatization has, moreover, failed to produce the intended effect on the high school student movement. Quite the contrary: it has added yet another grievance to a movement that already had no shortage of them. And it has hardened the very determination it was supposed to weaken. Caramba, another failure!

There is a certain amount of anticipation surrounding October 17, which is supposed to mark the return of the Yellow Vests. In Survival Guide, the illusion that social media alone could generate a revolutionary dynamic is severely criticized, including through the example usually cited to support this idea (that of the Arab Spring). The failure of September 10, 2025 — considered a “militant speculative bubble” — illustrates this thesis. Are we still in this kind of bubble, or does this call, combined with the youth revolt, create a more open scenario?

A few weeks before the dissolution of the National Assembly in June 2024, Macron’s close advisors gathered at the Élysée Palace to watch the series “La Fièvre” together. The June 9 address announcing the dissolution would, in fact, refer to this same “fever.” The series was conceived by a former member of the Socialist Party (PS) aligned with Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s movement. In it, opponents, whether pro- or anti-government, compete using the power of communication to quell or stoke revolts across the country. Communications strategists from all sides scrutinize giant control panels, where they monitor tensions emerging in real time on social media. It is a fantasy of cybernetic power, that of the Control Room. Readers of the Polytechnique journal know that the Prime Minister’s office, in 2024 to be precise, tested software for a real-time mapping of risks of social fragmentation, a map derived from digital noise. What matters in this mapping are not the ideas circulating or who is spreading them (activists or Russian bots), but the deviations from the norm, how they coalesce, form abscesses, and how to puncture them. It should come as no surprise that governments are turning communication tools into tools of control. What should concern us, however, is that so many revolutionaries have ended up adopting a similar conception of revolt. After weaving a web of real or fake accounts and amassing followers, after crafting a highly viral call to action, all they would need to do is press a big arrow to launch the insurrection. This communicational conception of the uprising did not emerge just last year. Facebook and Twitter were already applying this narrative to the “Arab Spring.” But, as Survival Manual details, there was no Facebook Revolution. Just as May 1968 was not an “RTL Revolution” [Radio Télé Luxembourg], nor was Genoa in 2001 a “Wanadoo riot.” This is not to deny the role of communication channels in these events, and particularly in their rhythm. The multiplicity of narratives, the idea that anyone could show their world to everyone else, is literally an invention of the anti-globalization movement, born from the convergence of the first hackers and the Zapatista movement. We must admit that this idea has been turned against us, like many other weapons from the cycle of insurrections over the last quarter-century. We are only just beginning to take stock of our arsenal.

Deep down, ever since the Yellow Vests movement wore itself out with the repetition of Saturday marches, “Yellow Vests” has become a way of saying “insurrection” without actually saying the word. And in fact, insurrection is the only response commensurate with the suffocation, humiliation, impoverishment, and outright mockery that the government apparatus has in store for us. However, since December 8, 2018, this apparatus has tooled up to defend itself against a new surge of the Yellow Vests, after being caught off guard on November 24 and December 1 of that year. We therefore need a new element of surprise. The vitality of high school students can change the game and complicate the repressive equation for government forces, but an insurrection is not merely a series of demonstrations. Rather than speculating about this date, we prefer to draw strategic lessons from past defeats and build on what remained unaccomplished. In retrospect, the craziest thing about the Yellow Vests’ days of insurrection was that we marched past the headquarters of Lazard, the UIMM, and LVMH, or beneath the Publicis offices, without realizing that it was there — far more than at the Élysée — that the enemy lay in wait: capital. Things are clearer now. Capital’s arrogance has laid it bare. The addresses are circulating. Insurrection is the only way to escape the electoral trap looming on the horizon. Everyone senses that the moral and financial pressures to bring us to heel will only intensify in the coming months. Lockdown through gas prices is no more acceptable than previous lockdowns. Moreover, we cannot let the Macronist regime fade away without making it pay the price for its abuses. They demand vengeance. In any case, we will be in the streets on October 17.

The entire text is a nuanced analysis of contemporary forms of capitalist domination and how they have evolved over the past fifteen years or so. It shows how so-called “revolutionaries” have fallen into every trap set for them and are thereby reinforcing their dependence as well as their powerlessness. It critiques the analytical and strategic weaknesses of these circles. What, then, are the paths of resistance, the lines of flight and subversion, the right strategy for all those — and there are many — who, though likely caught up in their own contradictions, can no longer stand the world as it is, but who, isolated and cornered by the entire machinery of capital described here in such precise detail, can’t see where to begin?

When we step out of our shell and finally rise up, we still find in our paths a whole little activist world standing in our way, trying to intimidate us. It claims to have the right practices, the right rhetoric, the necessary organization, and a whole range of ready-made solutions. It even has a sound system and media contacts; can you believe it! What Survival Manual documents is that this entire little scene is rich only in its failures, and its determination to repeat them. If it had even the slightest solution, we wouldn’t be where we are today. We’re in France, a country where there’s always someone claiming to educate you. When it’s not the government, it’s the anti-government crowd. Activist circles are a cul-de-sac, not a point of departure. There’s no such thing as a bad starting point; the best one is undoubtedly right where we are, with those we love and the things we hold dear — provided we stop telling ourselves stories, stop playing along with social lies and their so-called “values,” and provided we stop being terrified, deep down. Terrified of being banished. This is what the Survival Manual calls the “process of singularization.” It has no end. This is what it means to truly live. No one wants to sacrifice themselves anymore. No “collective value” can command sacrifice anymore. Collective realities must be founded on something other than suffering. It is precisely to prevent this that the specter of war is now being held up before us. But the real war is between all these processes of singularization and the crumbling yet still-reigning order that intends to continue vampirizing every form of life on earth. At this point, all legalistic options have been swept aside — on the mega-reservoirs, the A69 highway, the Duplomb Law, labor law, and international law alike. “Burn it all down since everything’s already burning,” read a sign in the Paris march last Tuesday. “Fuck almost everything!” another one put it more subtly. The echoes currently reverberating between the French, Belgian, Spanish, and Albanian uprisings are no coincidence. A war is underway between us and capital, against the backdrop of the thousand forms of dependence through which it believes it holds us captive. The entire Survival Manual is an effort to update our understanding of the theater of operations. We cannot summarize it in a few sentences. Noting, shortly before his death, the fatal course the Soviet regime was taking, Lenin wrote: “Those communists who do not give in to illusions or discouragement, who retain the strength and flexibility to start over from scratch and tackle one of the most difficult tasks, are not lost (and most likely will not perish).” Amidst the apocalypse of capital, this advice remains solid.
