author: Unknown
title: Из колонии вышел Василий Куксов, осужденный по делу «Сети» в 2020 году
content:
По данным «Медиазоны», вчера, 16 октября, 38-летний Василий Куксов освободился из колонии №16 в Нижегородской области. Сегодня утром он доехал на поезде до Сердобска в Пензенской области и встретился там с родными.

В 2020 году Куксова, музыканта и инженера-конструктора, приговорили в Пензе к девяти годам колонии по делу «террористического сообщества "Сеть"» (всего обвиняемые по этому делу получили до 18 лет заключения).

Дело возбудили в октябре 2017 года. Сотрудники ФСБ тогда обвинили антифашистов и анархистов, многих из которых объединяло увлечение страйкболом, в том, что они создали «террористическое сообщество» и планировали «раскачать народные массы для дальнейшей дестабилизации политической обстановки в стране».

Тогда в течение месяца силовики задержали Куксова, а также Илью Шакурского, Дмитрия Пчелинцева, Андрея Чернова, Армана Сагынбаева и Егора Зорина. Формальным поводом для начала уголовного преследования стала явка с повинной Зорина. Молодого человека задержали с наркотиками, и он дал показания о террористическом сообществе. Впоследствии дело против него прекратили. В январе 2018 года в Петербурге по тому же делу были задержаны Виктор Филинков и Игорь Шишкин. 11 апреля обвинения предъявили еще одному петербуржцу — Юлию Бояршинову.

Сначала большинство фигурантов дали признательные показания, но позже отказались от них, заявив о пытках. О насилии и применении тока со стороны силовиков сообщали Виктор Филинков, Дмитрий Пчелинцев, Илья Шакурский, Арман Сагынбаев и Андрей Чернов. Следственный комитет не возбудил дело ни по одному заявлению обвиняемых о пытках. О пытках и давлении со стороны силовиков также рассказывали пятеро свидетелей по делу.

Василий Куксов говорил в суде, что сотрудники ФСБ при задержании избили его со словами: «Ты попал, жизнь твоя кончена», — и угрожали отрезать палец. Несмотря на это, он никогда не давал признательных показаний. Во время следствия в пензенском СИЗО-1 у него перед приговором диагностировали открытую форму туберкулеза. Его не госпитализировали и продолжили содержать c другими фигурантами дела. После вступления приговора по делу «Сети» в силу Куксова в ноябре 2020 года доставили в нижегородское ЛИУ-3 для больных туберкулезом. Его выписали в январе 2022 года. В нижегородской ИК-16 после этого его несколько раз отправляли в штрафной изолятор.

author: Marcus Baram
title: Aging Coal Plants Turn Into a Midterm Fight Over Energy Costs
content:
Climate and energy battles are running through campaigns in Michigan, Colorado, Indiana, and beyond.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Craig Unit 1, a coal-fired power plant distinguished by tall exhaust smokestacks that rise above a rolling landscape in northwestern Colorado, was scheduled to close for good at the end of 2025 amid pressure from environmental advocates, public interest groups and state officials.

But on Dec. 30, Energy Secretary Chris Wright ordered it to keep burning coal. The unit had suffered a mechanical failure 11 days earlier and was not even running. Wright has since renewed the order three times — most recently on Sept. 25, extending the plant’s life through Christmas Day, a full year past its retirement date.

Its operator, Tri-State Generation and Transmission, is a nonprofit rural cooperative, and in January it joined co-owner Platte River Power Authority, a public power agency, in arguing that Wright’s orders violate the Constitution and federal law — a fight that has since reached a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C. A co-op and a municipal utility suing the executive branch for the right to close their own coal plant was not what Congress had in mind in 1935, when it wrote the emergency provision that the Energy Department is now leaning on.

Data centers and gas pump prices have dominated the energy story in this midterm cycle — polls show broad opposition to the artificial intelligence build-out over utility bills and grid strain. But with just weeks until Election Day, a second tier of climate and energy battles is running through campaigns in Michigan, Colorado, Indiana and beyond: forced coal plant extensions, canceled plans for offshore wind farms, repealed clean energy tax credits, drought, state preemption of local climate rules and a drumbeat of federal rollbacks. None of these issues poll as high as affordability. But all of them, say the people trying to turn them into votes, are essential to the affordability debate.

Starting in May 2025, the Energy Department invoked Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act to order Consumers Energy’s J.H. Campbell plant in West Olive, Michigan, to stay online past its planned retirement, then renewed the order five more times.

Similar mandates followed for Craig and for the Schahfer and Culley plants in Indiana, each justified by grid reliability. On Sept. 11, a unanimous D.C. Circuit panel, in an opinion written by Judge Cornelia Pillard, ruled that the first two Campbell orders were illegal — no genuine emergency existed to justify overriding Michigan’s regulators.

Ari Peskoe, director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard Law School, said the provision had been dormant for decades after some early wartime use. “Over the past 20 to 30 years it’s really been used almost exclusively for weather-related events,” he said, “and it only lasts a few days.”

Nothing like Wright’s coal orders had been tried. “In every prior instance there’s been some entity, whether a utility, a grid operator or a state regulator, that’s asked for these orders. Here it’s [the Department of Energy] acting on its own,” he said. “No one had asked for it. And to the contrary, some had said, ’Please don’t do this.’”

The administration has until roughly the end of October to decide whether to appeal. If it lets the ruling stand, Peskoe said, “I think the other orders for the other plants will fall pretty quickly.”

Utility giant Consumers Energy put the net cost of running Campbell from May 23, 2025, through June 30 of this year at $295 million, after wholesale market revenue. Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel’s office has cited that figure, against nearly $600 million in savings the retirement was supposed to deliver. In August, federal regulators let Consumers Energy spread the costs across the grid’s north and central regions — from North Dakota to Indiana. That means Wisconsin ratepayers, whose share one estimate puts at $117 million, could wind up paying for a Michigan coal plant. The recent appeals court decision overturning the Energy Department’s order could spare taxpayers those costs.

Brian Wheeler, spokesperson for Consumers Energy, said the utility would work to ensure “everyone who benefits from power from the Campbell plant across the Midwest pays their fair share.” Nessel, who has challenged all six orders, said, “This administration does not get to invent fake emergencies to bypass the rule of law.”

The coal plants have become a factor in the midterm elections for a key seat in Michigan. The Campbell plant sits in the 4th Congressional District, where Rep. Bill Huizenga, a Republican, is defending a traditionally red seat against Democratic state Sen. Sean McCann of Kalamazoo.

Huizenga cheered the first order; constituents answered with marches on his office under signs reading, “My asthma and my wallet can’t afford coal.”

“If you’re seeing your electric bills go up, that has happened because of this,” McCann told a crowd in Saugatuck in August. “This should be shut down.”

Huizenga blamed Gov. Gretchen Whitmer “and her Green New Deal cronies in the state Legislature like Sean McCann,” arguing that “forcing the premature closure of cheap, reliable power plants is punishing hardworking Michiganders who just want to keep their lights on without going broke.”

The fight runs up the ballot. Nessel, who recently joined McCann at a roundtable on the Campbell plant, is term limited, and the race to succeed her as attorney general has become a referendum on whether Michigan should keep suing. Democrat Eli Savit, the Washtenaw County prosecutor, pledged to continue the Campbell litigation, while Republican Doug Lloyd, the Eaton County prosecutor, has declined to take a position on the plant and accused Nessel of politicizing the office.

Climate Power senior adviser Jesse Lee said the issue had ripened with time and is starting to galvanize voters.

“The longer these decisions have sat out in the sun, the worse they stank,” he said. “It might have a ring of common sense — oh, we need more energy — but people caught on to that: ’Wait, this is actually costing me more money. There’s one guy who supports it and one guy who’s against it.’”

A poll commissioned by the Environmental Defense Fund in West Michigan found 71% of respondents said their utility bills had risen too much, and 51% favored closing the Campbell plant, as opposed to 32% who want it kept open. But the coal industry insists otherwise, with a September National Mining Association poll in which 58% of Americans supported government efforts to keep coal plants open.

Colorado’s version runs through the 3rd Congressional District, where Rep. Jeff Hurd, a Republican and former co-op lawyer, asked the Energy Department to intervene and keep Xcel’s Comanche plant in Pueblo running. Hurd praised the Craig order as a correction to a state energy policy “driven by ideology instead of reality.” His Democratic challenger, Dwayne Romero of Aspen, is running on affordability, accusing Hurd of “rubberstamping reckless policies that raise our costs.”

Statewide, Sen. Michael Bennet called the Energy Department order part of a federal “revenge tour” against Colorado, and Attorney General Phil Weiser, the Democratic nominee for governor, has challenged every coal-fired plant renewal, warning it “will result in unnecessary costs passed onto Coloradans in higher electric bills and more pollution in the region.” But in Craig, a small coal town near the Wyoming border, Mayor Chris Nichols welcomed the short-term jobs resulting from the order. The cost so far is unknown: Tri-State spokesman Mark Stutz said generator-specific data is confidential.

Indiana is the outlier — the orders have a cheerleader in the governor’s office and no competitive race to carry them, since both plants sit in safe Republican House seats. Gov. Mike Braun praised the latest renewal, saying it would “help protect Hoosiers from higher energy costs and keep the power on.”

But the utilities disagree, with CenterPoint asking the Energy Department in February to let the Culley order lapse, calling the power plant “inefficient and increasingly unreliable.” NIPSCO, one of Indiana’s largest power companies, said both Schahfer units covered by the orders remained offline for maintenance, and asked federal regulators in August to approve about $38 million in cost recovery for the first quarter — a bill for a plant that was not running. On top of that, the utility has outraged customers, who experienced a more than 25% jump in their bills last year. The pushback has come from statehouse Democrats like Rep. Carey Hamilton, who said Hoosiers were “being asked to foot the bill for a decision they had no say in.”

As to other climate and energy issues, their impact on the elections depend on whether a voter can feel the issue, such as dwindling water supplies. Federal cuts to Arizona’s Colorado River supply in August pushed water to the top of the state’s campaign messaging — Gov. Katie Hobbs is running an ad declaring, “Arizona’s water is for Arizonans,” while Republicans accuse her of failing to negotiate a fair water rights deal.

Along with Colorado farmers getting no water after a dismal snowpack and Corpus Christi potentially owing Texas $235 million for a desalination plant that was never built, the crisis highlights how climate change is being experienced by many Americans through higher water bills, exacerbating the affordability challenge.

The electric vehicle tax credit repeal has galvanized donors more than voters. The One Big Beautiful Bill’s elimination of the credit cast a pall over 2026 sales, and its wind and solar phaseout spawned a super PAC, the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, that bills its work as a “Revenge Tour” and has already claimed five Republican primary casualties — including Rep. Chip Roy, who lost a runoff election in May for Texas attorney general. Four House Republicans, among them Rep. Mike Lawler of New York, have introduced a bill to restore the EV credits and House Democrats have made reinstating such credits a major part of their governing agenda.

Offshore wind is a courtroom story more than a voting booth one. Nine states have sued over federal deals paying developers more than $1.5 billion to abandon leases on the condition they reinvest in oil, gas or geothermal instead. The League of Conservation Voters’ David Shadburn put the estimated taxpayer tab for blocking cheaper power at nearly $4 billion.

Florida’s HB 1217, which stripped cities of climate authority and outraged Democratic mayors, has been duplicated across the country but seems to have little visible traction with voters. And on Sept. 14 the EPA finalized its repeal of most Biden-era power plant rules, while the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act, which the League of Conservation Voters dismissed as window dressing. Neither one seems to have galvanized voters, though some Democratic candidates have mentioned them in their campaigns.

Whether voters can parse any of it is another matter.

“To some extent it’s all a bit of a blur for voters,” said Lee, the Climate Power adviser. “But it’s all kind of accumulated into one cloud of corruption. They just understand that they’re paying more every which way they look.”

As for what lands last, he pointed north. It is getting chilly, and people are starting to read about what it will cost to heat their homes — a problem for Lawler in New York and Sen. Susan Collins in Maine, and for anyone else on the ballot above the Mason-Dixon line.

“That’s the kind of story voters are going to be reading about right before they head into the voting booth,” noted Lee.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Andrés
title: No soy amigo de los que cooperan, los quiero fuera fuera fuera
content:
La pierna de un jubilado que cae por el chorro de un hidramte




La decadencia moral y generalizada de un país se mide por la cantidad de recursos empleados en contra de la propia población, y de la vida misma. Que todo gobierno autoritario invierte onerosos recursos en las Armas es un hecho más que probado. De lo que se habla bastante menos es que en países donde el trabajo formal se viene erosionando desde hace tanto, los puestos en las policías y fuerzas armadas los ocupan en amplia mayoría las clases socioeconómicas más vulnerables. Y entonces la extorsión del trabajo estable opera sobre los sujetos al punto de quebrar todo principio, cortar los trazos democráticos y convertir a los “servidores del orden” en cómplices de un poder que no los quiere más que dentro de una institución cuyo funcionamiento mafioso los subordina, los presiona. Y en muchos casos termina descerebrándolos al punto en que ni siquiera pueden abrir los ojos ante la traición que cometen cada vez que apuntan un arma, empuñan un palo, empujan a un compatriota, golpean a un viejo, gasean a una niña, ahorcan entre varios a un hombre solo, disparan a un joven, lo esconden, gasean a la población y lastiman toda posibilidad de concordia. El todos contra todos y cada uno contra sí mismo está a la orden del día bajo esta gestión fascista. 

Por Andrés Manrique (ANRed).







El  jubilado golpeado por la presión del hidrante, apuntado por la Policía Federal




Quienes cobran para ir a pegar, disparar y ahogar a estudiantes, a discapacitados, a viejos se cuentan entre lo más bajo de los traidores. Si era el último círculo, cuando además se detenta la fuerza física, se suma una vuelta más.




“Vos te pasaste al otro lado de la vereda”




Tirarle gas a un viejo de camperita, empujarlo.




Pegarle con el puño a toda carrera y por la espalda a un fotorreportero en la cara.




Echarle la moto de alta cilindrada a alguien que va en paz por la vereda.




La Policía Federal agolpeando con el hidrante al jubilado de espaldas




Acorralar a dos fotógrafos en un zaguán y dispararle a quemarropa: contra el abdomen, a las piernas, a la cabeza: en la cara y a los ojos.




Clavarte la rodilla en la espalda cuando estás en el piso, boca abajo, desarmado, reducido por el sobrepeso de aquel al que un trote lo haría infartar, mientras otro te lastima las muñecas con el precinto, y un tercero apoya todo su odio contra las vértebras de tu cuello.




Amedrentar con los escudos, con las tonfas, acelerando las motos, haciendo chasquear las  escopetas, con  bombas de estruendo, postas de goma y armas mal llamadas no letales, con las que no se cansan de matar o herir de gravedad. Revolear bastones, batiendo el aerosol de gas pimienta sobre la cara de una nena, de una anciana, de una vecina que pierde su  bolsa de compras.







“Esa es la diferencia entre la gorra y la visera”




Gasear a pibes con carteles, irse encima de discapacitados. Golpear con la escopeta, salir a cazar a compatriotas que protestan. Salir a cazar fantasmas en manada. Seguir órdenes, aunque vayan en contra de todos los principios. Golpear a alguien indefenso, lastimar entre muchos a uno solo.




Miserable soldadesca del brazo tilingo del poder que nos ahoga. Dése vuelta, reconozca dónde está su enemigo. Identifiquelo, usted sabe que la mano que le pone el sueldo es la misma que lo va a someter a la mazmorra cuando no sirva más.







¿Más traidor que un desclasado?




¿Peor traidor que alguien al que han entrenado para que se odie a sí tanto que odia a todo el que tiene a su alrededor?




Fotos: Andrés Manrique

author: Aallyah Wright
title: Organizers Are Pushing to Reach “Forgotten” Black Voters Ahead of the Midterms
content:
The efforts target college students, first-time voters, and the formerly incarcerated, particularly in the South.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Kamora Greggs returned to her college campus with voting on her mind. She’d just visited her home in Jackson, Mississippi, about three hours away, when her mom encouraged her to exercise her right.

“And don’t have anybody change your mind about what you want to do,” Greggs recalled.

As a first time voter, the 19-year-old health and kinesiology major wanted to know more about the process, the role of government, and hear directly from her peers about why they thought voting is important.

She and dozens of other Coahoma Community College students participated in a September town hall – playing games like Levels, learning history and the power of the ballot box — at their school in Clarksdale.

“It’s a good way to learn with your friends,” Greggs said. “It really impacted me and made me want to actually get out there and spread the word and make sure other people my age know that it’s a good idea to get registered to vote.”

With Election Day just weeks away, the experience is part of the Voting Is No Laughing Matter Tour. Rita Brent, an Emmy-winning comedian from Jackson, partnered with the Southern Poverty Law Center to host the five-stop campus initiative, which aims to empower students at the ballot box.

“To witness young people who are not only civically engaged but genuinely concerned about the state of our communities, our country, and the world gives me tremendous hope,” Brent said. “Their passion for justice, thirst for knowledge and their commitment to creating meaningful change remind me that our future is in capable hands.”

It mirrors renewed energy in civic engagement nationwide. It is one of several efforts focused on what some are calling the forgotten voters: college students, first-time voters, and the formerly incarcerated.

In another effort to mobilize younger voters, companies and groups transformed campus spaces into art installations, alongside on-site voter registration. And in North Carolina, a group is working to engage more with formerly incarcerated people who don’t always utilize their right to vote.

Since the weakening of the Voting Rights Act, attention has shifted to the South, where many communities are underserved, organizers told Capital B. The region is both a battleground and testing ground for voting rights. Decades of voter suppression, gerrymandering or redistricting, and landmark decisions such as Louisiana v. Callais have shaped the current political landscape.

In Mississippi, citizens don’t have an option when it comes to whether to vote or not, said Waikinya Clanton, the state’s director for the SPLC. Despite the decline in voter participation, it’s more about conditions, racism, and restricting access and opportunity.

In the Magnolia State, an appeals court recently refused to overturn a centuries-old lifetime voting ban for those with certain felony convictions, which was embedded in the state’s constitution. Nearly 60% of people who lost their right under this law were Black. Mississippi also does not offer early voting or drop boxes.

“So many people have felt disillusioned by the fact that they don’t feel like their vote matters. It can be depressing for people who are really trying to find their way out,” Clanton said. “For folks to be working so adamantly to make people feel like their votes don’t matter, that’s a problem.”

Over the past five years, 86 million eligible voters — about one-third nationwide — live in states that have passed more restrictive voting and election-related laws, according to a new report by the Movement Advancement Project. It is disproportionately impacting Black adults in the South, said Brian Hinkle, author of the report and senior democracy program manager for MAP.

“It was really striking that we saw that the Americans who live in the states with the most restrictive voting laws are disproportionately Black. While that was also true in 2021, the proportion has nearly doubled in the last five years, from 27% to over 48%,” Hinkle said.

According to the MAP report, the 2020 election and subsequent Jan. 6 attack prompted an unprecedented wave of state legislation limiting voter access. For example, 13 states passed laws that gave state legislatures the power to interfere in elections, which allowed them to replace or remove election administrators locally. At least eight states passed stricter voter ID laws. Sixteen states banned drop boxes, which is more than triple the number in 2021.

“I think it mirrors the broader kind of polarization in our society. With some states taking one view of what free and fair elections look like, and other states taking a different view,” Hinkle told Capital B. “Heading into the midterms, for example, a voter that lives in Atlanta or a voter that lives in Denver are going to head to the polls under fundamentally different sets of rules.”

The report is the result of a yearslong effort called the Democracy Maps, which tracks policy areas in all 50 states and the District of Columbia. Some of the policies such as restrictions on mail voting, drop boxes and voter ID can acutely impact rural communities, too, he added.

From his home in North Carolina to Georgia and Tennessee, Daryl Atkinson witnesses firsthand how difficult it is for people with criminal records and their families to navigate voting systems. As executive director of Second Chance Federation, Atkinson leads a team providing legal services, leadership development, community organizing, and civic engagement.

There are 19 million people convicted of felonies in North Carolina. A person with a felony conviction can vote after they complete their sentence or supervision. People in this demographic, Atkinson said, are considered low-propensity voters and often show up to the polls around 50%. He believes this is why most political parties don’t engage with this population. As a result, they suffer the “collateral consequences” of arrest and conviction, which impact their civic participation.

“We believe those people are sleeping giants to a more inclusive, vibrant, and multiracial democracy.” Atkinson said. “They are really high opportunity voters.”

Atkinson approaches the work as quid pro quo: if a justice-involved person needs legal services to help get a driver’s license or fees reduced, for example, Second Chance may ask them to show up to a community event or participate in a phone bank.

“We engage our people year-round, and we engage our people around their most pressing legal needs. But we do that in a way that’s not charity,” he added.

Back in Mississippi, college students like Madison Nichols-Harris, 19, say it feels like they are an often-overlooked population when it comes to voting. More times than she can count, she’s heard people say “Just go vote,” without any context or information about why it matters.

For a while, she didn’t take it that seriously. She said she will cast her first ballot in November, and she’s been seeking more information about voting.

Nichols-Harris said she believes social media is causing additional distractions, which she said may contribute to lack of engagement around elections by some in her generation. Instead of running to TikTok or Instagram, she attended the event at Coahoma Community College.

She listened to a panelist who explained how difficult it was for Black people, and women, to obtain the right to vote. She walked away energized in a way she couldn’t explain, she said.

“She emphasized that our present is what’s going to affect our future, so we should at least share the message and create the change we want to see,” Nichols-Harris added. “If we bring more conversations about voting and about what’s going on in the world today, I feel like it can change minds.”

It’s why the SPLC says it has doubled down its efforts to reach young people. There are children’s books, workshops, and even physical games to create an opportunity for learning, Clanton said. It’s not about going out to the polls for one day but to be inspired, whether it’s signing up to be a poll worker or speaking out at a local city council meeting.

“Voter suppression impacts everything from your healthcare, your quality of education, to your roads, your bridges, your water that’s coming out of your faucet to being able to determine whether or not you want a data center in your community,” Clanton said. “All of that is connected to your vote. If we’re not engaged in each and every election, we’re missing out on opportunities to transform the way that our state exists and how we exist within it.”

After attending the campus event, Greggs said she is motivated to get more students involved in the electoral process.

“Homecoming is coming up, and I can talk with an adult that can help me plan something that can have more people ready and prepared before voting time starts in November,” she added. “If that’s not the case, I’ll just continue to walk around and encourage my fellow Coahoma students to vote.”

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: groundxero
title: Another One Bites the Dust: Construction Workers’ Not So Quiet Battle For Survival Ahead of Delhi’s Long Winter
content:
The ‘annual ban’ on construction work through the winter seasons in Delhi that has become tradition over the last half a decade due to an acute air pollution crisis in the city, has this year, become a starvation sentence.




 




by 

Mouli Sharma




 




15 October 2026, New Delhi:

 The rain falls in sheets on Thursday morning, ice cold and sudden like it can only get during mid-October weeks as Autumn bleeds into Winter. The wide, planned roads of Delhi’s Civil Lines region don’t flood quite so much as Shankar Road and its tributaries (or, god forbid, Gurgaon) but it’s enough to drench the lower halves of even the umbrella havers stuck underneath foot-over bridges and bus stops. 




 




Needless to say, the roads are abandoned. At the T-Point facing the DRDO office, a lone rickshaw puller stops abruptly, shivering as he holds the thin gamchha protecting his head tighter over him and runs to the shelter of the bridge. I stand there, too. Water has been steadily gathering at the top, and has now begun flooding down the stairs, soaking his sandalled feet and into my socks and shoes. When the rain slows, for a minute, I make to leave, aiming for the bus stop 50 metres away in case it starts up again.




 




The rickshaw puller warns me not to do that. I tell him I have somewhere to be. He asks me where I’m trying to go. I tell him there’s a protest today at Vikas Bhawan. 




 




“Look at the weather. No one’s protesting in the middle of this. Only a lunatic would be out there today.”




 




He is, of course, wrong. 




***




 




At Thursday noon, nearly 50 construction workers led a march from Vikas Bhawan to the Sushruta Trauma Centre, led by the AICCTU’s Building Workers’ Union, many of them travelling from faraway districts like Burari and Okhla. This was ahead of an announcement by the Delhi government that construction work in the city would be banned for a period of three months between November and January, ostensibly due to air pollution concerns, except the Supreme Court’s directions that such a blanket ban on work must be accompanied by the provision of minimum wages to aggrieved workers are not only nowhere close to being fulfilled, but are in fact being violated for a consecutive season since the Rekha Gupta led BJP came to power in 2025. 







 




“The Welfare board website has been down for nearly four months now,” said Ranjan Kuswaha, a mason and secretary of the local Burari unit of the Building Workers’ Union. “They said they were making a new one. And now that they have, they’ve already announced a seasonal ban less than two weeks away, beginning on November 1st and ending on January 31st. And till now this website is taking neither new registrations nor renewals. How on earth is the worker supposed to survive?”




 




Kushwaha further highlighted the plight of the migrant worker, so many of whom come to Delhi to work contractually on the many building and developmental projects undertaken here annually, who will now be left destitute. 




 




Advocate Surya Prakash Union said that a majority of the workers associated with the BWU hail from Supaul and Saharsa, two of Bihar’s poorest districts. 




“Most of our workers come from the poorest regions,” Surya Prakash, AICCTU; Infographic via BWU.




“We demand that this website be fixed at the earliest, and that registrations and renewals be completed as soon as possible and the workers be provided their labour cards,” Kuswaha said. 




 




There is also the matter of alleged gross corruption within this “welfare board” itself—the Delhi Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Board (DBoCWWB), an organisation founded in 2002 in reference to the 1996 BoCW Act, which is apparently as much of a handful as it as a mouthful, according to the workers whose welfare it proclaims to oversee.




 




“On paper, the welfare framework for Delhi’s construction workers promises them wide-ranging support in almost all spheres of life: from maternity care, pension, housing, healthcare, education and even free daily commute on govt buses,” wrote Ishita Jairath for the Times of India in her scathing January 2026 report, 

Hands That Build Delhi Brick By Brick Out Of Welfare Framework. 




 




The ground reality, however, was that the intended beneficiaries she asked about the schemes meant for them had nothing more than a “blank look”.




 




“Bitto, a marble and tile worker from Mangolpuri, didn’t know his children are eligible for education assistance,” Jairath wrote. “Preeti, a construction worker and mother of two who received a subsistence allowance during the recent GRAP-enforced restrictions, asked, “Yeh kya hota hai?””




 




The harsh reality is, despite the city employing over 2.7 registered construction workers, the DBoCWWB has repeatedly come under fire over the 24 years since its foundation due to its failure to bridge the gap between statutory safeguards, provisions, and entitlements to their actual beneficiaries. And come the BJP era, it along with employers have been granted even more impunity than before, as the legislation that mandated the board’s creation, has itself been axed.




 




The 1996 Building and Other Construction Workers, Act, was one of 29 labour statutes that were subsumed and consequently repealed by four controversial parliamentary acts passed between 2019 and 2020, infamously known now as the “New Labour Codes”: The Code on Wages, 2019, the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the Code on Social Security, 2020 and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020.




 




The third and fourth of these repeal the provisions within the 1996 Act. The first, CoSS (2020), allows employers to “self assess” their own cess liabilities—cesses that are meant to finance the minimum subsistence wages owed to workers in a situation like a blanket ban due to GRAP III/IV restrictions. 




 




“Employers can now self-assess liabilities in respect to Building and Other Construction Work, previously assessed by the notified Government authority,” the Labour Ministry said on the subject through a PIB release in 2025. “It reduces procedural delays and official intervention.”




 




The fourth decriminalises the labour offences listed in the repealed Act(s) (12 others along the BoCW, 1996) and replaces them with civil penalties, allowing employers to get away with violating ostensible safeguards with monetary fines, increasing the thresholds for employers’ compliance, and enabling abuse in a myriad other ways, hollowing out pre-existing laws. 




 




As things stand, the current laws are being flagrantly violated by both the employers they are meant for and the constitutional bodies that are meant to enforce them, and the laws that once would have enabled stringent action and criminal proceedings against said violators have been nixed despite unilateral uproar against them from labour rights organisations, workers’ unions, economists, and political analysts at large. 




 




This is the context that allows Rekha Gupta to announce in August a 42 day ban on construction work in the capital despite 2.6 lakh registered workers not still waiting on the minimum wage compensation due to them from 

last year, 

which she has now extended to a 90 day ban while the website meant to register and entitle them to reparations—after an arduous and alienating bureaucratic process that requires mobile-Aadhaar linkages and documents that a significant number of migrant workers don’t possess, mind you—and 

doesn’t even work

. 




 




***




 




As Jairath wrote, though, even when those safeguards did exist, a vast majority of workers within the capital were not aware of them, and unlike the prohibitions in Central Delhi due to the ongoing SIR protests, in which the State has spared no expense in making people aware of their authority to violate citizens’ constitutional freedoms, no similar mass notification or awareness drive seeks to bring workers into the know of all they can and should be doing to safeguard them.




 




“How is it that these kinds of things can be allowed to escape people’s notice?” JNU SFI President Nadia said later the same day, at a protest commemorating the forced disappearance of the missing JNU student Najeeb alongside 12 days of an indefinite hunger strike by the University’s student union against what appears to be a crackdown on campus politics and democracy in its entirety. 




 




Neha Bora had just left after delivering her own speech on the enduring legacy of JNU as India’s conscience and spirit of dissent, as had MP John Brittas. Both took much of the crowd with them, but much to the chagrin of the security personnel tasked with ‘observing’ such protests within the campus, the program went on. These security personnel, for those who don’t know, are also contract workers, employed through private security firms like A.E. Securitas, who are so aware of their own impunity in a labour dispute that they did not even show up to a recent meeting with a labour conciliator about wage theft and worker endangerment. As Nadia went on, I could see some of them zoning back in.




 




“You need to fill out a form by such and such date, or you aren’t going to be able to vote anymore. How is it that a right like Universal Adult Franchise, or something equally basic,” say, three months of minimum wage, “can possibly be made subject to being lost by accident or negligence. If you walk down central Delhi right now, you will know you can’t be there. Why isn’t the same done for these bureaucratic processes? We know the answer. It’s not incompetence. It’s very intentional,” she said. 




 




At the protest, no worker knows the ins and outs of what the government owes them, or even the ballpark of all the things that have been stolen from them. The New Codes mentioned above have expanded the previous statutes for 40-hour workweeks for 48-hour workweeks, but the ordinary day’s work has still been capped out at 8 hours as per the landmark ILO treaty. Every hour past that constitutes overtime, which requires both the workers’ consent as well as double-pay from the employer. 




 




None of that is real. These are fairytales that when relayed to the BWU workers on ground accomplish little more than making them laugh.




 




“I work 12 hours a day at the least,” says Rampyari, a 26-year-old mason tender. Everyone around her agrees. 




 




“Somedays I start working at 7 in the morning and work till 8 or 9 at night,” says 35-year-old Arun Kumar Yadav, a mason. None of them has ever received overtime. They are paid by the day, and the hours are not negotiable. 




 




Further, women are paid exorbitantly less than the men. While Rampyari makes Rs. 500 per 12 hour shift, Arun Kumar makes Rs. 700 or even Rs. 800, making their monthly earnings miles apart. The workers tell this reporter that this is because masons are seen as more skillful than mason tenders (centering masons like Ranjan are seen as even more skillful), and the women tend to get assigned the lowest paying jobs despite the differences in the skill requirements of the roles being negligible in their practical experiences. 




 




“It’s all the same process,” Arun Kumar confesses. “One person mixes the masala, another applies it and lines the bricks, another checks the centering of the wall. All of us can do all of it, if it comes down to it.”




 




Obviously, the rates are unlawful. The New Codes have weakened the pre-existing regulations around wages just as they have all others, with the Cosen on Wages, 2019 having replaced the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, and placed wage notification processes entirely in the hands of individual states’ and the formula for their assessment within the discretion of individual actors. The recent labour upheaval throughout the North Indian industrial belt saw the governments of Haryana and UP both being compelled to renew wages after decade long delays, but despite the acknowledgement of extended failures, the updated wages followed no transparent declaration of methodology, and fell far short of the recommendations made by researchers under the landmark Reptakos judgment. A detailed analysis of the embedded corruption and irregularities within the new wage codes as well as outstanding delays in the wage renewal process can be read 

here

.




 




Recently though, the phenomenon went from intra-state to national, with the Karnataka High Court directing the Union Government itself to renew central minimum wages the way UP and Haryana had been forced to after tens of thousands of workers took to the streets.




 




“The Union government had last revised minimum wages in the year 2017 and despite the statutory mandate to do it within the year 2022, the Union government kept delaying the same,” said AICCTU, who repeatedly moved court on the subject and recently found victory in September earlier this year, when the Union of India, through the Ministry of Labour and Employment was directed to complete the process of revision of minimum wages and to issue the necessary notification within five months from the date of the order, i.e. 16 September 2026.




 




The minimum wage as directed to be calculated according to the previously mentioned landmark Reptakos Judgment (which laid provisions for a five-part calculation of the bare minimum subsistence amount necessary for a worker and their family’s survival) would sit at around Rs. 40,410. 




 




Given the five month deadline, the construction workers’ season of starvation will long since have passed, but a requirement for the payment of backwages and arrears from 2022 onwards means that the rates being paid to workers like Rampyari, Anil Kumar and Lal Shah can be qualified as legally exploitative.




 




The gender disparity on the other hand, the law is not so vocal about.




 




***




 




The youngest protester this reporter had the pleasure of meeting on the 15th was Shyam Babu, asleep in his mother Rita Devi’s arms under a banner (“Stop starving workers in the name of stopping pollution!”) repurposed as a small shelter from the rain. He was six years old, and fast asleep. 




 




Shyam looks small for his age; very small. Rita, 30, tells me his health has been delicate since he was born, and his muscles never quite developed since.




 




“There’s something wrong with his bones. His arms won’t lift up properly. We don’t really know what to do.”




 




Under the current wage administration system, the consumption units assigned to an adult male minimum wage earner are one whole of the calculations made based on daily calorie consumption of the average adult Indian by Dr. Wallace Akroyd, the first director of the Department of Nutrition at the Food and Agricultural Organisation, in 1948. Come 2026, minimum wage provides for only 0.8 of this whole unit to adult women, and only 0.3 for a child. 




 




AICCTU called out this bias in a press note announcing the 16 September Karnataka High Court Order, and seeks to move court for an increase in consumption units (also including a demand for two full additional units for senior citizens).




 




“Assigning only 0.8 consumption units to women is not only arbitrary but also inherently discriminatory, as it undervalues their nutritional requirements and perpetuates gender bias,” the note said. “Hence, an adult woman must be assigned 1.0 consumption unit, equal to their male counterparts. Similarly, providing only 0.6 consumption units for children grossly underestimates the nutritional needs of growing children in vulnerable age groups. In view of growing malnutrition, it is necessary that each child should be allocated at least 0.8 consumption units.”




 




But down on the ground, not a single worker fighting for her right to survive is aware that 20% of her food is being taxed away at the source by virtue of her assigned sex.




 




“The person who cooks always gives less to herself to begin with,” Rampyari says. “A woman would go hungry before letting her family want.”




 




Ruminating upon the health problems running throughout her family, though, she wonders if she’s been handed the short end of the stick from the start. 




 




“My brother-in-law is also mentally ill,” she says. “Treatment in government hospitals is a nightmare.”




 




Such conversations reveal more and more holes within the ostentatious framework of India’s labour law (now its 

new 

labour law): the third and fourth new labour codes formally entitle professionals to free annual health check ups, employee-state insurance and other health and maternity benefits. But till date, only one ESIC hospital stands functional in Delhi, in Basai Darapur, and even there, insured treatment is capped at 21,000 rupees. 




 




And anyway, there’s only so much health insurance can do when a child grows up on 30% of an average person’s nutritional requirements and the mother who births them survives on 80% of the same. 




 




“Food is everything,” Arun Kumar says. 




 




“What else is there?”




***




 




By 2 o’clock, the crowd begins to dissipate. There’s a brief bout of drama near the tail end of the hour: a politician from a rival party, the Indian Inclusive Party, based in Bihar where most of the BWU’s workers hail from, which focuses on Pan caste politics, arrives to speak to the workers, leading to a brief tiff between him and a CPI-ML Liberation leader.




 




“I am simply talking to members of my caste,” he said. 




 




“Why are you bringing up caste?” Asked CPI-ML’s Ajay Pal. “Why can’t you look beyond caste in this day and age?”




 




While the man left soon after, those speaking to him said in his defence. “He means no harm. We hail from the same place, that is why he was speaking to us.”




 




A significant proportion of the population that migrates to Delhi for construction based contractual work from Bihar, Odisha, Jharkhand, and even West Bengal hails from the Pan community, a Scheduled Caste in all four states. The IIP’s symbol itself, for what it’s worth, is a brick trowel. 







 




“They’re all politicians at the end of the day,” a worker said. 




 




Red Mic’s

 Niraj Pandey, who works at the intersection of gender, caste, class and land issues, asked why the workers could not unionise themselves. Simply put, the answer is not so simple: In 2022, the grant of union membership to a contract labourer in Manesar’s Bellsonica Auto Components Private Limited was declared “illegal” by the State’s labour commissioner, under whose protection the management then demanded not only the cancellation of the workers’ membership, but a dissolution of the union itself. 




 




Till date, contract workers across organised and unorganised sectors stand dependent on central trade unions like the Liberation’s AICCTU or other kinds of political backing to generate any sort of bargaining power with the state. With the further weakening of labour laws since the institution of the new codes, their employment and existence has become more precarious than ever, and such relations hardly remain a choice. 




 




At any rate, Delhi’s building workers plan to continue their battle for this season’s survival till the ban takes over, questioning why they must bear the brunt of the country’s pollution crisis while factory and vehicle owners continue to contribute the lion’s share of pollutants to the city’s air. The next strike is set to take place on 1 November 2026 again at Vikas Bhawan, Civil Lines. 




 







 




Mouli Sharma

 is a journalist based in New Delhi. She currently writes for

 

GroundXero

, and her work has appeared in various publications.




 




All Images are by photographer and filmmaker 

Vivek

. He was the DOP for the documentary, Sanitised Republic, which has been heavily censored and banned from screening by the Indian Censor board.

author: Said Alsaloul
title: My Study of Dystopian Fiction Never Prepared Me for Reality Here in Gaza
content:
As a teacher of English literature in Gaza, I’ve seen my relationship to books be overturned by the violence around me.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

As a 27-year-old English literature graduate and English teacher from Gaza, I have always been passionate about teaching. I enjoy helping my students learn to speak English by reciting stories aloud.

I connect with them through English, so I collected every English-language book my hands could reach. Before October 7, 2023, during my fourth year in university, I used to visit a bookshop in Gaza City to buy English novels for enhancing my linguistic link with my job and the students. In 2022, shortly before I graduated, I wrote a short story about our tough conditions in Gaza and submitted it to a writing competition. It ranked seventh out of 80 stories, and I received a reward. What began as a practice to improve my English turned into a way of life. Whenever I had money, I bought a few novels until I gathered a large collection and built my own English library. Sometimes I purchased novels I would never open, but it felt satisfying to have them on my shelf. I could sense linguistic progress: a future.

After lectures, I went to a park near the university where I enjoyed the shade from trees and a soft breeze. It was my place where I could sit on a bench under a big tree, a cup of coffee in one hand, a novel in my bag. The novels were all fiction. What I loved was the way the writers chose words. That gave me the literary sense to generate a unique language over time.

In that shady spot, I opened The Alchemist by Paulo Coelho and began to read: “Tell your heart that the fear of suffering is worse than the suffering itself.”

I recalled Gaza’s 50 percent unemployment rate. I would graduate after a few months and start desperately seeking a job, competing with tens of thousands of unemployed graduates who were also fighting over the same positions. Young men used to dream of building families and marrying the girl they loved. Now they watch their hopes crumble under occupation and blockade. I recalled the constant wars every two years, the terror and psychological traumas they inflict. The patient people who can’t leave because of the blockade and the exorbitant travel fees. The eight-hour daily electricity cuts that devastated us for years.

Thinking about these forms of suffering is unavoidable. They deteriorate your life. But coexisting could be our only key to survival. We learned to carry the weight without collapsing. We learned to read between the lines of our own destruction. Knowing that everyone is suffering gives one a strange kind of comfort.

“And that no heart has ever suffered when it goes in search of its dreams, because every second of the search is a second’s encounter with God and with eternity,” Coelho wrote.

I believed it. Tomorrow will be better. The suffering is temporary. I let out a breath I didn’t know I was holding and turned the page.

When I closed the novel, I was certain Coelho had written it for Gaza. For us. For the young people who struggle so much until we believe it is part of life to keep suffering. For those who are still dreaming no matter what.

Then I saw the word on the cover: fiction.

What was fiction to the world was not fiction to us.

I took a pen and crossed it out. I wrote: reality.

I started to read fiction not just to escape, but to understand, to see how fictional worlds were constructed, to learn how to change our reality, or at least adapt to it. Reading became my life, not just for language, but as a chain of subplots that I recognized in my own existence.

One day I turned to Shakespeare:

To be, or not to be: that is the question:

Whether ’tis nobler in the mind to suffer

The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune,

Or to take arms against a sea of troubles…

I once saw Shakespeare’s words as distant, beautiful meditations on grief — something to study, not to live by. In university lectures, the beloved professor Refaat Alareer, who was killed by an Israeli airstrike in 2023, always asked us: “How can you relate to this as a Palestinian?”

“We lack freedom, suffer the devastating blockade and limited resources to thrive. We are the exception case for the world’s rules,” students would reply. “So shall we stay silent and say it is okay to suffer or shall we rebel?”

Refaat took up arms with a pen. He wrote our suffering in stories that couldn’t be ignored. He co-founded the We Are Not Numbers project to help young Palestinian writers narrate our stories. We lived the suffering and chose to write about it, to open the world’s eyes.

On October 7, 2023, the war began. My job disappeared overnight. So did everything else. Before October 7, I assumed I was collecting fiction novels for escapism. Now I realize I was collecting novels that could never instruct me for what would come next. We entered a constant state of suffering and destruction with no exit gate.

The genocide in Gaza surpasses the horrors imaginable through fiction.

All the parks where I used to sit were destroyed. My university was bombed. The places where I built connections with my novels’ characters no longer exist. Cities became ghosts. Displacement emptied everything. Hunger struck hard. Death tolls rose in thousands.

Some of this was familiar to me from horror novels I read, but what I witnessed went beyond anything fiction could conjure. We have lived through horrors that no book could ever capture.

Death in Gaza is nothing like fiction. It has a smell. It sounds like a muffled mouth under the rubble. It looks like blood-soaked concrete and disfigured bodies. My eyes cannot endure it; my mind cannot bear the terror.

As Hamlet decided to rebel against his oppressive uncle, he paid with his life. That was the cost Refaat paid too for his rebellious, courageous writings.

I remember my neighbor Rahaf — a child calling her father’s name from under the rubble, her voice growing weaker. Her father couldn’t reach her. He could only listen until her calls stopped.

Hemingway never prepared me for the smell of death, or for what it could feel like to wait for a child to die under stones while she called for help, or for seeing the corpse of a baby lifted from under the rubble. T.S. Eliot’s Wasteland could not capture the sound of silence broken by the deathly intonations of an aerial drone. George Orwell’s fictional portrayal of surveillance in 1984 never imagined a child’s head shattered, brain matter exposed, under the eyes of a human-driven drone.

Horror novelists don’t write such scenes, not because they protect readers, but because they never imagined reality could be this dark. We in Gaza experience what lies beyond fiction’s limits.

And I couldn’t stop remembering those moments: mothers emerging from under the rubble with blood streaking their cheeks, smoke filling their lungs, screaming, rummaging through the stones for their families, begging us to rescue their children while aircraft still hovered above our heads.

For Shakespeare, “a sea of troubles” was a metaphor for the difficulties of life. For us, it is an actual sea of rubble, of bodies turned into ashes. Compared to Gaza, Shakespeare’s words are a romanticized whisper. The war has shattered the ostensible timelessness of his art.

Before the war, we could analyze literary suffering from a distance. Now we live in a reality that surpasses even the bleakest plays.

The classics were gentle. Gaza is the opposite.

I don’t read to understand anymore. I read to forget I ever did. I read until my eyes blur, until sleep takes me. The words become shapes — nothing more. Humanity dies, and the world watches. Indifferent. What could be more fictional than this?

In our world there will be no emotions except fear, rage, triumph, and self-abasement. Everything else we shall destroy — everything. We have cut the links between child and parent, and between man and man, and between woman and man. No one dares trust a wife or a child or a friend any longer.

I turn pages I’ve already read, searching for a sentence that might make sense of what we are experiencing. I never find one. No line promises the creeping “Yellow Line” will stop its westward crawl to devour more lands. No sentence assures me that this tragedy has an ending.

There is no fiction left to escape into. There is only Gaza.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Marianne Dhenin
title: California Is Home to 200 Billionaires. Organizers Say It’s Time to Tax Them.
content:
If passed, California’s Proposition 40 would generate funding for health care, education, and food assistance programs.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Thousands of volunteer canvassers are hitting the streets across California, fighting for a first-of-its-kind wealth tax on the state’s ballot on November 3. Those mobilizing for Proposition 40 — which would generate revenue to backfill federal funding cuts to health care, education, and food assistance programs — are up against hundreds of millions in spending on competing ballot measures from the billionaires who would be taxed by Proposition 40. Whether or not it passes, experts told Truthout the citizen-led ballot initiative is a historic measure that could serve as a model for future efforts to tax the ultra-rich.

“Either way, even if it doesn’t, but definitely if it wins, it’s going to set a new standard for the type of tax that people can demand via ballot initiative,” Benjamin Case, project lead on the Ballot Initiatives Project at Arizona University’s Center for Work and Democracy, told Truthout. “It’s the first wealth tax in the U.S., and first wealth tax of its kind in the world, and it’s also the first tax specifically on billionaires.”

The ballot measure was announced last October by high-profile progressive economists Emmanuel Saez and Robert Reich, as well as the Service Employees International Union’s (SEIU) United Healthcare Workers West, which represents 145,000 health care workers across California. Proposition 40, also called the Billionaire Tax Act, would levy a one-time 5 percent tax on the total net wealth of each of the state’s billionaires, using a retroactive residency date of January 1, 2026. It would apply to roughly 200 billionaires, including Silicon Valley titans like Mark Zuckerberg and Peter Thiel. These individuals have seen their average annual income rise 7.5 percent on average per year over the last four decades, while wages for the average American stagnate and a growing number struggle to meet their basic needs.

Most taxes are levied on income or real estate, not wealth. The latter is meant to capture a person’s net worth, including real estate, cash, and stock holdings, minus debts. Wealth taxes remain relatively novel, outside of some examples in European nations. A recent analysis of a similar wealth tax implemented in Norway found that it did not spur significant outmigration of the ultra-rich or deter founders from starting their companies in the country. The relatively few business owners who did leave Norway under the new tax program maintained their businesses and did not stop investing in the country, according to the analysis.

“If you think about the wealthiest billionaires in California, they have a net worth of somewhere in the range of $250 billion, and our highest income tax bracket applies to everybody who makes essentially more than a million dollars. The difference between a million dollars in income and $250 billion in wealth is just astronomical,” Chris Hoene, executive director of the California Budget and Policy Center, told Truthout. “It’s an innovation to try to tax wealth, and you can do it at a very small margin and produce a lot of revenue quickly.”

Proposition 40 is expected to generate about $100 billion over the next five years. About 90 percent of that revenue would be used to replace the tens of billions of dollars that will be stripped from California’s 15 million Medicaid recipients over that same period under President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. That bill slashed taxes for the wealthiest Americans and is expected to undercut health care and social services programs nationwide. The cuts are expected to create a $100 million shortfall in California’s Medi-Cal program alone over the next five years, stripping over a million Californians of coverage and forcing clinics to shutter. SEIU estimates 145,000 health care workers could lose their jobs. The bulk of the cuts are expected to hit after the midterm election, but many across California are already bracing.

“Frontline health care workers that are in the facilities with the patients are already seeing this,” Renee Saldaña, United Healthcare Workers West’s press secretary, told Truthout. “Patients are already getting nervous about things like ‘Am I going to be able to afford my medicine? Am I going to be able to see my doctor? Some are even telling [their doctors] they’re worried about having to ration food and how they’re going to afford food along with their medical expenses.”

Julie Van Winkle, American Federation of Teachers vice president for United Teachers Los Angeles, has been canvassing for Proposition 40 alongside many more of her union’s 37,000 members. “We’re just feeling an urgency right now,” she told Truthout. “It just seems like those basic things that our parents and generations before them had as middle-class, working-class people, are slipping out of reach.”

About 10 percent of the revenue that would be generated under Proposition 40 would be used to fund K–12 education and food assistance programs, which the federal government has also slashed.

Proposition 40 has strong support from unions, health care groups, and economic and social justice organizations statewide. The California Democratic Party has also endorsed it, and prominent mainstream Democrats are mobilizing their constituents to back the measure alongside progressives like Sen. Bernie Sanders, who headlined rallies in San Francisco and Los Angeles in early October to drum up support.

However, California’s Democratic governor, Gavin Newsom, has broken with the state’s Democratic Party by condemning the measure and urging voters not to back it. On October 9, he endorsed Proposition 42, a competing measure that Hoene told Truthout amounts to “a direct assault on Proposition 40.”

Newsom joins a chorus of the ultra-rich who have spent almost a quarter of a billion dollars to block Proposition 40 through advertising campaigns and by bankrolling Proposition 42, as well as Proposition 41, another competing measure that would undermine the billionaire tax.

Proposition 42 is meant to ban new taxes based on the ownership of certain assets — the same assets Proposition 40 aims to tax. It would also prohibit the imposition of new retroactive taxes. The proposition would kill the billionaire tax if it passed with a greater margin.

Meanwhile Proposition 41 is designed to make it more difficult to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review such proposals before going to voters. It would also prohibit revenues raised through special taxes from being excluded from the state’s spending cap, which could trigger automatic refunds.

Hoene told Truthout that the language of the competing measures and their advertising campaigns seem designed to sow confusion among California voters. “The people running the campaigns opposing Proposition 40 are running a particularly misleading campaign,” he said.

Come Election Day, the best-case scenario for proponents of the billionaire tax would be for Proposition 40 to pass, and for Propositions 41 and 42 to fail. Generally, if a pair of competing propositions pass, the one with the most votes prevails. Recent polling suggests the campaigns to undermine Proposition 40 could be working and results will be tight. The Public Policy Institute of California found in September that slim majorities of likely voters support all three propositions. Proposition 42 had the largest margin of support in that poll at 54 percent. Proposition 40 lagged just behind at 52 percent.

Organizers statewide remain committed to grassroots mobilization in the face of a flush and unscrupulous opposition. “We’re being outspent hand over fist,” Van Winkle told Truthout. “They have the money, but we have the people that are willing to go out and talk to people.”

Many of United Healthcare Workers West’s members are also hitting the streets and signing up to text or phone bank to urge their neighbors to back Proposition 40. “It is incredibly all-hands-on-deck. Everybody in the union has a task of phone banking, talking to their own personal contacts, and we all gathered signatures,” Saldaña told Truthout. “The enthusiasm and will to get this done, especially from the frontline health care workers we represent, is completely off the charts. And I think it’s because they, more than anybody else in our society, know firsthand what’s going to happen if Prop. 40 doesn’t pass.”

Saldaña told Truthout that the union’s canvassers have found proponents of the billionaire tax behind most of the doors they’ve knocked. “Sometimes you don’t even have to really convince people, just ask them about Prop. 40 and they’re like, ‘Yes, tax them,’” she said. “There’s a sense that, ‘This economy is not working for me,’ [and] people are starting to get sick of billionaires trying to buy their way in terms of our elections and in terms of them not being held accountable.”

Van Winkle said she expects organizers statewide to be out fighting for the tax until polling sites close on November 3, in what feels like an existential campaign to protect the lives of frontline workers, students, families, and other community members across the state. “If you’re one of the richest people in the richest state in the richest country in the history of the world, you ought to pay your fair share,” she told Truthout. “So that working people who are increasingly facing increased prices with gas, housing, groceries, everything, can live in dignity.”

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Unknown
title: Whereabouts of man summoned by Iranian Revolutionary Guards remain unknown
content:
A 40-year-old man has been detained in the city of Piranshahr in East Kurdistan (Rojhilat) after being summoned by the intelligence service of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). His whereabouts have remained unknown since his detention. The man, Ahmad Mostafanejad, has been denied access to legal counsel and contact with his family.




According to the human rights organization Kolbarnews, Mostafanejad was summoned by telephone to the Revolutionary Guards’ intelligence department in Piranshahr on Wednesday, October 14. After complying with the summons, he was detained and taken to an undisclosed location.




No information has yet emerged about the reasons for his detention or any possible charges against him. His health condition and detention conditions also remain unknown. Iranian authorities have neither disclosed his whereabouts nor allowed him to contact his family.

title: Das öffentliche Bildungswesen wurde nicht nur in Frankreich marode gespart – die Proteste dagegen breiten sich international aus
content:
„

Argentinien, Albanien und 

Frankreich

: Proteste für das Bildungswesen füllen die Straßen und stellen die Regierungen vor eine Herausforderung. Drei Länder, unterschiedliche Konflikte und doch dasselbe Bild, das sich in diesen Tagen wiederholt: Studierende und Beschäftigte im Bildungswesen strömen auf die Straßen, um öffentliche Mittel einzufordern, die Verschlechterung ihrer Arbeitsbedingungen anzuprangern und Entscheidungen ihrer Regierungen abzulehnen. In Argentinien endete der fünfte „Marcha Federal Universitaria“ am Donnerstag mit Tränengas, Wasserwerfern und 31 Festnahmen. In Albanien finden seit drei Tagen in Folge Studentenproteste statt, die zu Zusammenstößen mit der Polizei und Forderungen nach dem Rücktritt des Ministerpräsidenten geführt haben. In Frankreich bereiten die Mobilisierungen von Schülern der Sekundarstufe und Studenten mit Unterstützung von Gewerkschaften neue Kundgebungen für diesen Samstag, den 17. Oktober, vor

…“ span. 

Beitrag vom 16. Oktober 2026 auf sindicalismo.org
