title: the reason why you don’t see women raping or sexually exploiting men as often as the other way…
content:
the reason why you don’t see women raping or sexually exploiting men as often as the other way around, isn’t because women have the divine aura of femininity that prevents them from thinking rapist thoughts, or because cis women lack the Evil Rape Organ or whatever. it is because rape isn’t really purely individual form of violence, but a systemic one. it is also not necessarily done only for personal sexual gratification, but a reassertion of social position through violence.

women hold a lower position compared to men within patriarchy. if you hold a position lower than someone else, then violence against them is not typically something you can get away with, nor can you assert your power over them if you don’t have it.

this is also why the vast majority of cases of women raping or sexually exploiting men are done when a woman holds a higher social position than the man in question. you see this with disparity in class, age (in the case of women sexually abusing children), between white and racialised, and between imperialist and imperialised. most notable examples are the women abusing and torturing prisoners in Abu Ghraib as much as their male colleagues, or the female Israeli prison guards torturing Palestinians.

and of course, women sexually exploiting or abusing other women is done on similar grounds. it is more common for cis women to sexually exploit or abuse trans women than the other way around for example.

Accordi libertari: grande partecipazione alla prima edizione del Canto Anarchico a Massenzatico, 2-3-4 ottobre 2026




Si è conclusa domenica sera la prima edizione del festival del canto anarchico tenutasi alle Cucine del Popolo di Massenzatico (RE). Sono stati tre giorni intensi di conferenze, presentazioni di libri, concerti dal vivo con cantautori, band e cori, allietati dal buon cibo e dall’immancabile lambrusco, che hanno registrato la partecipazione complessiva di oltre 600 persone. Venerdì sera abbiamo aperto ricordando Francesco Guccini, come uomo e come artista, mettendo l’accento sulla Locomotiva, indimenticabile brano con cui è stato anche concluso il concerto finale della Ciurma del Galeone di domenica. Prima di ascoltare i 100 canti anarchici di Alessio Lega, è stata abbozzata da Enri Volta una proposta interpretativa e di studio del canto anarchico oggi. Sabato poi è stata presentata la mostra discografica, con Lp e 7” originali dagli anni ’70 ad oggi sul tema, e Franco Schirone ha presentato il fondamentale libro sul canto anarchico in Italia, giunto ormai alla terza edizione e scritto insieme a Santo Catanuto. Le presentazioni sono poi proseguite con gli approfondimenti di Claudio Piccoli e Tiziana Oppizzi sulla rivista Il Cantastorie di Vezzani e quello di Alessia Masini sul rapporto tra musica e politica nel punk, a cavallo tra gli anni ’70 e ’80. Tra il pomeriggio e la sera si sono esibiti Mars on pluto, Francesco Pelosi e Riccardo Dodi, che ci hanno fatto cantare a pugno chiuso il vasto repertorio che va dagli Arditi del popolo alla Resistenza passando per la Spagna del 1936 e non solo. La serata si è poi chiusa con lo scatenato dj set di Naon Grrrl che ci ha fatto ballare a suon di post punk. La giornata conclusiva di domenica si è aperta con le presentazioni dei libri “Cantare la piazza” sui cantastorie, e “Pino Pinelli un racconto musicale”, che raccoglie i canti per Pino e sulla Strage di Piazza Fontana. Nel pomeriggio Marco Fincardi ha ripercorso le evoluzioni delle serenate alla rovescia raccolte nel suo volume “Derisioni notturne”. La musica dal vivo è poi proseguita con i Cantografi, Donato Landini e Roberto Ruberti, che hanno interpretato rispettivamente l’ampio repertorio libertario sia popolare che d’autore, le canzoni per Giovanni Marini e Franco Serantini e i brani scritti da sua madre Paola Nicolazzi. C’è stata poi un’incursione rap, rigorosamente legato al dialetto reggiano, con La Kattiveria, e la serata si è conclusa con i Quarto Podere e il finalone con tutta la ciurma del Galeone. Ad ogni pasto poi si è esibito un coro. L’amata Rossa, Stazione Rossa, i Malfattori, Oltrecoro e i Violenti Piovaschi hanno intonato canti di lotta e resistenza da tutti i continenti. Un grande ringraziamento va a coloro che hanno reso possibile questo evento tramite il loro lavoro volontario e a tutte le persone che sono venute da ogni dove per partecipare. Un buon primo passo quindi, per continuare con “lo sguardo rivolto all’aurora”, oltre che alla prossima edizione!




Il comitato organizzatore




Reggio Emilia 5/10/2026




DISCORSO INAUGURALE




Subito dopo la “Locomotiva” direi che la miglior citazione di Guccini sugli anarchici si trova in “Canzone di Notte N.2”, quando li definisce come “gente che finisce male: o in galera od ospedale…” – di questi tempi ancora attualissima. Da qui forse si può partire per inaugurare questo festival della canzone anarchica. In questa introduzione proporrò un po’ di ragionamenti: abbozzati, magari provocatori, spero non sterili né deliranti. Beh, innanzitutto parlando di canto anarchico possiamo partire dicendo che esiste ancora. Il fatto che sia esistito non significa che per forza continui ad esistere, per esempio i canti repubblicani esistevano, ma non mi pare che oggi godano di buona salute… Oppure movimenti e realtà politiche non per forza lasciano una produzione canora. Come se guardiamo al movimento anarchico degli anni ’50 del Novecento in Italia, c’è un vuoto: cioè gli anarchici c’erano ma c’è poco o nulla a livello di canti. Anche queste carenze vanno interrogati. Se volessimo categorizzare per forza, – ammesso che sia lecito in ambito anarchico – ma almeno quando è utile credo sia giusto categorizzare, credo che il canto anarchico si possa dividere in: 1) canti DEGLI anarchici (scritti da anarchici, es. quelli di Pietro Gori); 2) canzoni SUGLI anarchici (canzoni che raccontano le loro vite e/o lotte, non per forza – soprattutto in tempi recenti – scritte da anarchici). Poi volendo potremmo individuarne una terza, ovvero la “MUSICA ANARCHICA”

1

 . Ma si tratterebbe di una categoria eterea, troppo fumosa e dai confini poco chiari, dato che ogni persona avrebbe la “sua” musica anarchica, e qui non la tratterò1 . Resta dunque da capire dove sia oggi il canto anarchico. Credo infatti sia utile, se non necessario, allargare la visione quantomeno a livello conoscitivo, per evitare di credere che “il canto anarchico che io conosco” sia per forza “tutto il canto anarchico”. Ma il problema ovviamente non è individuale, cioè che una persona non conosca un singolo artista o una specifica canzone. Il problema si dà ignorando interi generi musicali, intere sottoculture, intere produzioni artistiche, intere sensibilità e operazioni di memoria su fatti, idee, biografie e lotte anarchiche. E oggi è sempre più difficile “perdersi per strada”, pezzetti o interi filoni, perché non sono “organizzati”, ma magari spuntano qui e là su internet. E anche questa è una questione da porre. Per estremizzare: – ma senza prendervi in giro – ecco io credo che per trovare il canto anarchico oggi dobbiamo anche tendere l’orecchio sia verso i gruppi crust-black metal. E se vi fidate vi dico anche perché. Io ho scoperto chi fosse Renzo Novatore ascoltando un disco di Crust mescolato al Black Metal di una band canadese: gli Storm of Sedition, forse dovrei ma di per sé non me ne vergogno. Il disco “Howl of dynamite” del 2019 suona un “genere estremo”: un punk a squarcia gola, purulento e tremendo, mescolato con un metal non-americaneggiante secco e tagliente. Il risultato non può che essere brutale, ma ciò che ci interessa di più sono i testi, infatti, è un album totalmente ispirato alle poesie di uno dei più importanti poeti anarchici futuristi di lingua italiana

2

. Per Novatore forse ci voleva un disco così vista la sua biografia

3

 : individualista che disertò durante la Grande Guerra, si scontrerà con i fascisti e morirà nel 1922 in uno scontro a fuoco con i carabinieri mentre era ricercato per le rapine fatte con la banda di Sante Pollastro – quest’ultimo citato in una celebre canzone di De Gregori. Se in Italia Novatore è conosciuto a livello storico, di musicale c’è davvero pochissimo su di lui… per avere un concept album sulla sua produzione poetica dobbiamo arrivare fino in Canada. Credo sia una cosa davvero pazzesca, che ha dell’incredibile, semplicemente magnifica. Credo che questo sia uno dei più begli esempi di PRODUZIONE CULTURALE. Perché dietro una cosa come questa c’è un intreccio non indifferente di lavoro/cura/passione immenso, che va anche oltre i singoli componenti della band. Perché se loro hanno potuto leggere Novatore per poi musicarlo ci deve essere stato qualcuno che l’ha tradotto in inglese, che lo ha pubblicato o diffuso online. C’è quindi un “lavoro” precedente fatto da case editrici, fanzine, sale prove, etichette discografiche, che tramite gli artisti e le canzoni arriva a noi che ascoltiamo. Tutte queste cose che stanno “nel retroscena” – se non “nelle retrovie” – sono inestimabili e non vanno assolutamente date per scontato. Ricapitolando: per trovare oggi canzoni che hanno a che fare con l’anarchia dobbiamo anche sondare la musica estrema proveniente dell’altra parte del mondo, e gli Storm of Sedition ce lo hanno dimostrato, adesso tocca a Sanremo: il covo per eccellenza della musica mainstream del belpaese. Conto ogni pronostico ebbene sì, anche qui possiamo trovare interessanti sprazzi di anarchia. Nell’edizione del 2022 Giovanni Truppi porta a Sanremo nella serata delle cover “Nella mia ora di libertà” di Fabrizio De André, e già partiamo bene. Truppi ha come ospiti Capossela e Mauro Pagani. Tutti si presentano vestiti di nero e rosso, con un abbinamento cromatico impeccabile. In particolare, Truppi – sempre in canottiera – ha appuntato sul petto un cuore rosso-nero. Ma non si tratta di una spilla qualsiasi, gliel’ha regalata Gogliardo Fiaschi (militante anarchico carrarino che combatté anche nella Spagna franchista e pagherà con lunghi anni di detenzione in Spagna e in Italia le sue azioni, a cui oggi è intitolato un circolo a Carrara

4

 ) in persona. Lo ha dichiarato l’artista stesso, e se ne trova notizia su tutti i giornali

5

. Vi sfido a trovare un momento di più alta diffusione del nome di Gogliardo – ve lo avevo detto che c’erano delle provocazioni eh! De Andrè e Gogliardo sono andati letteralmente in mondovisione, mica male no? Ecco che a tendere bene l’orecchio, e ad avere pazienza, il canto anarchico fa capolino anche da Sanremo. Quindi credo che non dobbiamo aver paura del pop, e non dobbiamo chiuderci a prescindere. Dall’altra parte poi non basta andare a Sanremo, De André è letteralmente l’artista preferito di Matteo Salvini – e vista la situazione ho paura di sapere quale sia quello di Vannacci… Ci contendono già la nostra musica, e anche questa è una battaglia a cui non possiamo sottrarci nascondendoci dietro a un dito. Venendo poi alle canzoni SUGLI anarchici credo che negli ultimi decenni possiamo registrare la nascita di un gran numero di canzoni su anarchici italiani, o meglio “di lingua italiana”. Credo che sia una cosa molto importante, e forse che tutto sommato ci possa anche sorprendere positivamente. Troviamo infatti canzoni su Gogliardo Fiaschi (appena citato), ma anche per Umberto Tommasini, Argo Secondari, Oreste Ristori, Anteo ma anche Mammolo Zamboni, Gino Lucetti, Angelo Sbardellotto (di questi ultimi mi sono tra l’altro occupato recentemente in un’autoproduzione che uscirà a breve). Ancora oggi poi continua la memoria cantata per Bresci, Pinelli, Serantini. E sono citati in canzoni, credo per la prima volta, di Bruno Filippi e Antonio Cieri. Anche se sparpagliate in micro-autoproduzioni o su qualche piattaforma online, comunque queste canzoni esistono. Soprattutto si può registrare un fiorire di canti per Bakunin e Malatesta, quantomeno in Italia o in italiano. Credo sia interessante perché una volta le canzoni raramente erano dedicate a ideologi, pensatori o organizzatori del movimento, per esempio Malatesta viene citato nei canti coevi direi solo quando viene arrestato, quindi nel raccontare la repressione subita in seguito a una lotta. Le canzoni quindi si concentravano sui fatti, sulle lotte, sulle azioni, gli esempi più celebri restano sicuramente la Comune di Parigi, e poi gli atti di Passannante, Caserio e Bresci. Oggi le canzoni fanno anche memoria, e quindi il loro registro e il loro senso è cambiato, alle volte per dire ti spiegano chi erano Bakunin e Malatesta, cosa che “non serviva” mentre questi erano in vita e attivi. Questa operazione di “conoscenza”, da fare sia individualmente che collettivamente, o se vogliamo di mappatura è importante perché ci porta a indagare anche l’humus che fa vivere e prosperare le canzoni e in generale le produzioni culturali. Come nasce infatti una canzone? Come arrivano le storie anarchiche e la Storia dell’anarchica agli artisti che poi decidono di orientare il loro repertorio in quella direzione? L’intreccio storia-memoria-cultura credo sia ancora ampiamente da indagare. Oggi questo rapporto non è sicuramente organizzato, gestito o programmato ma comunque accade che nascano canzoni per fare memoria in questa direzione. Il fatto che succeda e che il nesso storia-memoria-cultura “funzioni”, credo sia molto interessante. L’altra “somma” citazione di Guccini sul canto politico credo che sia: “a canzoni non si fan rivoluzioni”. Non tanto per smentire quanto detto fino ad ora riguardo l’importanza del canto di lotta, ma per dare il giusto peso, il “senso” a quanto stiamo facendo con questo festival. Ovviamente non sarà una canzone che “dice cose rivoluzionare” a “fare la rivoluzione”. La cultura non basta. Come ci insegna Bermani: i canti politici e di protesta proliferano “nei momenti di maggior vigore rivoluzionario”

6

, e questo le tante ricerche storiche ce lo hanno ampiamente dimostrato. E quindi come collocarci oggi? Siamo all’interno di un paradosso? Sicuramente non viviamo tempi rivoluzionari ma possiamo comunque registrare una produzione interessante di canti, per certi aspetti inediti, a cui prima facevo riferimento. Come porci allora? È solo cultura? È tutto inutile? La frase di Bermani sopracitata ci dice anche però che a volte ci sono canzoni che “non sono solo canzoni”. Alcune di esse, infatti, possono riassumere intere visioni, idee, programmi, immaginari, pulsioni, drammi collettivi, paure, speranze, come rabbia, odio, gioia e aspirazione. Possono raccontare interi movimenti politici o spaccati di classe. Sicuramente almeno ci sono stati dei periodi storici in cui è stato così. Oggi sembra tutto più complicato. Credo che esclusivamente attraverso la musica non riusciamo a cogliere esattamente lo stato delle persone oppresse e sfruttate, e spesso nemmeno le condizioni, o le pulsioni, di chi lotta. E questo è un problema da porre. Se non sono le canzoni “a far rivoluzioni” è infatti la lotta a produrre i canti, e ancora oggi credo ci siano dei casi, soprattutto nei cortei, di cori collettivi che ricorrono e che rappresentano i movimenti stessi che li cantano. Due esempi per tutti possono essere: No Tav e GKN (Con “Grida forte la Valsusa che paura non ne ha…” e “Occupiamola, fino a che ce ne sarà…”). Dunque le canzoni, o più in generale la produzione musicale, possono ancora servire per sondare come e quanto le aree sociali e politiche si muovono, e magari in che direzione. Dal momento che non viviamo in un “periodo rivoluzionario” significa anche che ascoltando gli ultimi, gli oppressi, gli sfruttati, o anche le produzioni underground o alternative non troveremo per forza contenuti libertari, radicali o rivoluzionari; figuriamoci poi se sondiamo quelle apolitiche, mainstream o proprio di regime. A volte però vi si possono scorgere quelle ansie, paure, desideri ecc. a cui prima facevo riferimento. Già negli anni ’70 Muzak

7

 si proponeva di fare un’operazione analoga ascoltando la musicaccia, per “sentire il polso” del popolo, della massa o della minoranza che ascolta quella musica. Credo che questo “sforzo” di rivolgere l’orecchio verso lidi inesplorati – per non dire “inascoltati” – potrebbe infatti essere importante, se non proficuo. Concludo con un esempio per me molto evocativo. Qualche anno fa una band molto famosa e amata nella scena punk-Oi! ha scritto una canzone che si chiama e tratta di “Ansia”

8

. Ecco io non sono un esperto, ma credo che in due secoli di Movimento operaio e più in generale in millenni di oppressione e sfruttamento, oppressi e sfruttati abbiano provato letteralmente di tutto, ma mai “ansia”. Sapere che degli skinhead provano ansia può suonare quasi bizzarro, e forse sicuramente lo è in riferimento al secolo scorso, ma evidentemente c’è un cambiamento non indifferente in questo tempo. Ecco che allora la musica ci dice ancora qualcosa. Ha ancora senso cantare, come ce l’ha ascoltare, tendere l’orecchio proprio a quei “lidi inascoltati”, perché anche lì troviamo la voce di chi subisce sfruttamento e oppressione.

author: Mag
title: „So kann man nicht mehr leben“: Auch in Portugal wird gegen steigende Lebenshaltungskosten und Wohnungsnot protestiert
content:
Dossier




„

Seit Jahren werden wir durch steigende Immobilienpreise und Lebenshaltungskosten ausgebeutet. Wir arbeiten uns zu Tode und rackern uns ab, um mit unserem Gehalt bis zum Monatsende durchzukommen, die steigenden Kraftstoffpreise und die Grundausgaben zu bewältigen und unsere Wohnung nicht zu verlieren. Uns bleiben nur Schulden und Sorgen, während die Aussicht auf eine bessere Zukunft schwindet. 

Coimbra bleibt nicht außen vor! Wir rufen alle dazu auf, sich am kommenden *Mittwoch (14.) ab 17:30 Uhr auf der Praça da República* zu einer Malaktion sowie zum Anbringen eines Transparents und anderer Materialien zu versammeln

.“ portug. 

Aufruf zur Demo am 10. Oktober

 

 der Instagram-Plattform „Não dá mais para viver assim“ („So kann man nicht mehr leben“) und mehr dazu:







Nach Protesten am 10. und 15. Oktober schließen sich am Samstag, 17. Oktober die Kämpfe gegen Lebenshaltungskosten und für öffentliche Infrastuktur zusammen 







Die von der CGTP einberufenen Demonstrationen begannen heute Vormittag in Porto, Coimbra und weiteren Städten. In Lissabon ist die Kundgebung für heute Nachmittag angesetzt.




„

Der D. João I-Platz in Porto, Schauplatz der jüngsten Demonstrationen für bezahlbaren Wohnraum, füllte sich am Samstagvormittag erneut mit Menschen – bei einer von der CGTP organisierten Demonstration, bei der verschiedene Forderungen auf der Tagesordnung standen, wie „Höhere Löhne, bessere Renten und öffentliche Dienstleistungen“ oder „Gegen den Anstieg der Lebenshaltungskosten“ und „Ein neuer Kurs für Portugal“. Auch in Coimbra gingen viele Bürger auf die Straße, um zu protestieren, wobei das Thema Wohnen ebenfalls eine wichtige Rolle spielte, obwohl zu diesem Thema neue Zeltlager in Lissabon und Porto geplant sind

.




Die weitreichenden Themen erklären, warum die Demonstrationen junge Menschen, Berufstätige und Rentner zusammenbringen.


In Porto wurden mehrere Tausend Menschen, darunter etwa 100 Jugendliche der Wohnungsbewegung, bei ihrer Ankunft auf der Praça D. João I mit Applaus empfangen, wo der Marsch, der auf der Praça da Batalha begonnen hatte, seinen Höhepunkt fand

…“ portug. 

Bericht von Rosa Soares vom 17. Oktober 2026 auf publico.pt

 

 (maschinenübersetzt)




Proteste in Portugal wegen der Wohnsituation: niedrige Löhne und überhöhte Mieten




„

Die Proteste in Porto bringen die Wohnungskrise in Portugal erneut ins Rampenlicht: niedrige Löhne, explodierende Mieten und Preise, die jährlich um 16,5 % steigen. In Portugal spitzt sich eine Krise zu, die sich immer schwerer verbergen lässt: bescheidene Löhne stehen im Gegensatz zu Mieten und Immobilienpreisen, die rasant steigen. (…)


Die Demonstrationen, die diese Woche in Porto stattfanden, haben ein Gefühl auf die Straße getragen, das in vielen portugiesischen Familien schon seit Langem herrschte. Die Demonstranten fordern erschwinglichere Mieten, mehr öffentlichen Wohnraum, die Wiederbelegung leerstehender Wohnungen und Schutz vor Zwangsräumungen.


Ein auf dem Platz D. João I errichtetes Zeltlager wurde schließlich von der Polizei geräumt, was die Spannungen rund um das Problem noch weiter verschärfte. Die Proteste sollen am kommenden Samstag auch nach Lissabon übergreifen und damit eine Mobilisierung ausweiten, bei der es längst nicht mehr nur um die Quadratmeterpreise geht. Es geht um Löhne, Selbstständigkeit und die zunehmenden Schwierigkeiten, sich ein unabhängiges Leben aufzubauen

…“ portug. 

Artikel von Alessandro Elia am 17.10.2026 in El Folio online

 

 (maschinenübersetzt)




Auf zur nationalen Demonstration | 17. Oktober




„

Am 17. Oktober findet eine landesweite Demonstration gegen die steigenden Lebenshaltungskosten, für den Erhalt des öffentlichen Gesundheitswesens (SNS) und für den Erhalt der Sozialversicherung statt, die von der CGTP-IN organisiert wird – in Porto um 10:30 Uhr und in Lissabon um 14:30 Uhr. Die CGTP-IN organisiert Busse in der Nähe Ihres Wohnorts

…“ port. 

Aufruf vom 14. Oktober 2026 der CGTP-IN

 




Siehe bei der Bündnis-Plattform auf Insta den 

Aufruf zum Protestcamp

 

 in Lissabon, das offenbar schon aufgelöst wurde (s.o.)




Protest in Porto gegen die geplante Mietreform




„

Porto. Tausende Menschen sind am Donnerstag in Porto auf die Straße gegangen, um gegen die rasant steigenden Immobilienpreise in Portugal zu protestieren. »Jeden Monat haben wir Angst, aus unserer Wohnung geworfen zu werden«, sagte eine Aktivistin am Donnerstag abend gegenüber jW. Auf der Praça D. João I protestierten rund 3.000 Menschen gegen Wohnungsnot und die geplante Mietreform der in Lissabon regierenden Mitte-rechts-Koalition Aliança Democrática. Das Protestcamp, das dort seit Sonnabend gestanden hatte, war in der Nacht zuvor gewaltsam von der Polizei geräumt worden. 39 Verletzte gab es nach Angaben der Bewegung. »Als das Fernsehen weg war, kam die Polizei«, berichtete eine Teilnehmerin auf der anschließenden Vollversammlung. Die Aktivisten beschlossen, die Nacht über zu bleiben. Gegen 1.20 Uhr machten die Organisatoren jedoch Schluss, da es zu einer Konfrontation mit einer Gruppe, laut Berichten der rechten Szene angehörig, kam. Aufgeben will die Bewegung nicht und ruft für diesen Sonnabend erneut auf den Platz. In Lissabon soll zudem ein Protestcamp entstehen

.“ 

Artikel von Nikolas Sisic in der jungen Welt vom 16.10.2026

 










Portugiesen protestieren auf den Straßen gegen die steigenden Lebenshaltungskosten




„

Die Proteste wurden von einer Instagram-Plattform namens „So kann man nicht mehr leben“ organisiert und sind von ähnlichen Demonstrationen inspiriert, die sich in Spanien wiederholt haben und durch die Zwangsräumung der inzwischen verstorbenen älteren Dame Maricarmen Abascal ausgelöst wurden.




Tausende Menschen versammelten sich an diesem Samstag in den beiden größten Städten Portugals, Lissabon und Porto, um gegen die steigenden Lebenshaltungskosten und Wohnkosten zu protestieren.




Die Proteste, die auch in Aveiro, Braga und Funchal geplant waren, wurden von einer Plattform namens „So kann man nicht mehr leben“ organisiert. Die Demonstranten skandierten Parolen zu den Löhnen und hielten Plakate mit Aufschriften wie „Von diesem Lohn kann man nicht leben“ hoch.




Andere hielten Plakate mit Slogans wie „Ich möchte vor meinem 50. Lebensjahr aus dem Elternhaus ausziehen“ hoch. (…)




In einem Beitrag eines Instagram-Accounts, der für die Demonstrationen geworben hatte, hieß es, die Menschen würden seit Jahren „von den steigenden Immobilienpreisen und Lebenshaltungskosten erdrückt“

…“ port. 

Bericht von Nathan Rennolds und Ricardo Figueira vom 11/10/2026 von Euronews.com

 

 

 mit Video




Die Plattform „Não dá mais“ organisiert landesweit Proteste wegen der Wohnungskrise




„

Die Bewegung „So kann man nicht mehr leben“, der rund 40 zivilgesellschaftliche Organisationen angehören, bereitet für diesen Samstag eine Reihe von Protesten gegen die steigenden Lebenshaltungskosten und die sich in Portugal verschärfende Wohnungskrise vor. Die Demonstrationen werden in fünf Städten stattfinden.




In fünf Städten Portugals findet an diesem Samstag eine Demonstration gegen die Wohnungskrise statt, die von einer Plattform organisiert wird, in der sich rund 40 zivilgesellschaftliche Organisationen zusammengeschlossen haben.




„Wir arbeiten ununterbrochen und schuften uns ab, um mit unserem Gehalt bis zum Monatsende durchzukommen, um die steigenden Kraftstoffpreise und die Grundausgaben zu bewältigen und um unsere Wohnung nicht zu verlieren“, schreiben die Organisatoren auf ihrem Instagram-Account.




Die steigenden Lebenshaltungskosten und die immer höheren Mieten machen das Leben der Portugiesen unerträglich. „Es ist unmöglich, in einem Land zu leben, in dem die Miete die Hälfte des Gehalts verschlingt und die andere Hälfte für lebensnotwendige Güter ausgegeben wird“, schreibt die Organisation. (…)




Das Bündnis, dem unter anderem Gewerkschaften, Verbände für Geschlechtergleichstellung, für den Schutz und das Recht auf Wohnen, für Klimaschutz und für soziale Inklusion angehören, kritisiert die Art und Weise, wie die Regierung auf die Wohnungskrise reagiert, und fordert eine „stärkere Kontrolle der Preise für lebensnotwendige Güter und Kraftstoffe“ und fordert „Maßnahmen zur Bewältigung der Wohnungskrise“, schreibt die Zeitung „Correio da Manhã“

.“ port. 

Artikel von Manuel Ribeiro vom 10/10/2026 von Euronews.com

 




Portugal: In Lissabon und Porto protestieren Tausende gegen steigende Lebenshaltungskosten




„

Am Samstag, dem 10. Oktober, gingen in Lissabon und Porto Tausende Menschen auf die Straße, um gegen die steigenden Lebenshaltungskosten, unbezahlbaren Wohnraum und Niedriglöhne zu protestieren. Organisiert wurden die Demonstrationen von der Plattform „Não dá mais para viver assim“ (So können wir nicht weiterleben), die auch zu Protesten in Aveiro und Braga aufgerufen hatte. In Lissabon versammelten sich Menschen unterschiedlichen Alters am Largo do Intendente, um ihrem Frust über den wachsenden finanziellen Druck auf die Haushalte Ausdruck zu verleihen. Der Platz war bereits kurz vor dem geplanten Beginn der Demonstration dicht gefüllt; die Protestierenden machten lautstark auf die Schwierigkeiten aufmerksam, mit dem Einkommen über die Runden zu kommen. Die Organisatoren forderten Preiskontrollen für Grundnahrungsmittel und Kraftstoffe, Steuern auf Zufallsgewinne großer Unternehmen aus dem Banken-, Energie- und Einzelhandelssektor sowie Maßnahmen zur Bewältigung der Wohnungskrise. Die Plattform vereint mehr als 30 Organisationen, darunter Gewerkschaften sowie Gruppen, die sich für das Recht auf Wohnraum, Geschlechtergerechtigkeit, ethnische Gleichstellung, Klimaschutz und soziale Inklusion einsetzen

.“ 

Meldung vom 13.10.2026 auf rf-news.de

 




Instagram-Plattform „Não dá mais para viver assim“ („So kann man nicht mehr leben“): 

https://www.instagram.com/manif.janaodamais/

„So kann man nicht mehr leben“: Auch in Portugal wird gegen steigende Lebenshaltungskosten und Wohnungsnot protestiert

author: Sasha Draeger-Mazer
title: Texas Woman Sues Anti-Abortion Group Under Law It Helped to Pass
content:
The woman is suing Students for Life for the cost of raising the children of two unplanned pregnancies.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

A Texas woman is using a state law banning the transport of abortion pills to sue members of the anti-abortion organization Students for Life of America.

In the suit filed Tuesday in a Harris County district court, plaintiff Maria Puerto, a 26-year-old mother of two using a pseudonym to protect her family, alleges that four anti-abortion activists had ordered abortion medication on their phones in March 2026 outside of the Space Center Houston. The lawsuit cites, among other things, a now-expired social media post by one of the defendants captioned “Guess what we are doing? Ordering abortion pills undercover? Yep. Stay tuned.”

Known as the Woman and Child Protection Act, House Bill 7, which went into effect in December, prohibits providing an “abortion-inducing drug” to or from anyone in the state of Texas. The law is enforced by allowing almost any person, regardless of whether they have been impacted by the incident, to bring a civil suit against a provider of abortion medication. Plaintiffs may seek an injunction and a minimum of $100,000. If the person bringing the suit has no connection to the incident, the plaintiff receives $10,000, with the remainder of the award going to a charity selected by the plaintiff.

The lawsuit does not specify how the defendants violated HB 7. While the law does not explicitly bar the ordering of abortion medication, it does prohibit the transport of the drug within the state.

“What the statute says is that transporting abortion drugs from one location to another within the state is a violation of HB 7 … By the plain language of the statute, this would seem to be a violation,” Puerto’s attorney Molly Duane told The Texas Tribune. “This is the problem with writing such a confusing and vague law.”

While pregnant women cannot be prosecuted under HB 7 for actions taken to have an abortion, none of the four defendants — Kristan Mercer Hawkins, Lydia Taylor Davis, Jamie Curry and Megan Roos — were pregnant at the time, according to the lawsuit.

Duane, who is with Amplify Legal, the legal arm of advocacy group Abortion in America, said she and her client are hoping that the lawsuit will eventually surface more about what the defendants did with the abortion pills once they ordered them.

Hawkins is the president of Virginia-based Students for Life, which lobbied heavily for the passage of HB 7 last year. In a video posted to X on Tuesday, Hawkins called the lawsuit “frivolous” and a “publicity stunt,” and urged Texas Child Protective Services to investigate Puerto.

Puerto is suing for $459,782, “the average cost of raising two children from birth to age 18 in the state of Texas.” According to the lawsuit, both of Puerto’s pregnancies were unplanned and occurred despite the use of contraception, and she was unable to end the pregnancies due to the state’s abortion ban and the expenses associated with traveling out of the state. The suit also says that her first pregnancy directly resulted in her having to quit college and losing her job.

If she wins the lawsuit, Puerto would be entitled to $10,000 of the award, as she has no connection to the defendants. According to a Tuesday statement by Abortion in America, she plans to give the remaining award to Jane’s Due Process, a nonprofit that helps young Texans confidentially access abortion and birth control.

In an essay she published Tuesday, Puerto said Texas laws regulating her pregnancy effectively controlled her future, and described the financial struggle she has faced as a result.

“I’ve filed a lawsuit against those who helped build these horrible laws — and then had the privilege to break them in an attempt to trap women like me who still need help,” Puerto wrote. A statement by Students for Life Vice President Kristi Hamrick called the suit a “backhanded compliment” and vowed to fight it in court.

A request for comment from the defendants was directed to Students for Life’s initial statement on the lawsuit.

At least two other lawsuits have been filed using HB 7, and each of those lawsuits have targeted out-of-state abortion providers and alleged that women have actually taken the abortion pills they provided. A case filed by Texas resident Jerry Rodriguez and his daughter against California-based abortion care provider Remy Coeytaux alleges Coeytaux provided the medication used to end his girlfriend’s pregnancy on two occasions. In another case, Davis v. Cooprider et al., the plaintiff accused the organization Abortion Access of providing pills to defendant Christopher Cooprider, who used them to terminate the plaintiff’s pregnancy against her will.

The lawsuit filed Tuesday does not say if the abortion medication allegedly ordered by the defendants was actually consumed.

“Texas is a strange place filled with vigilante statutes, vigilante laws that seek to turn Texans against each other,” Duane, Puerto’s attorney, said. “But if anyone should be benefiting from these legal regimes, it’s people like our client. So it was putting those two things together that might be unusual, but this is the situation that Texas has put its citizens in.”

The Texas Tribune is a nonprofit, nonpartisan media organization that informs Texans — and engages with them — about public policy, politics, government and statewide issues.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Progressive International
title: When the Bargain Breaks
content:
On 23 September, Spanish police evicted 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for 71 years. After buying her flat, property company Urbagestión had sought to increase Abascal’s rent to more than her monthly pension. Neighbours had prevented three previous attempts to evict her. The fourth succeeded. Abascal was carried out of her home on a stretcher and taken to hospital. The eviction was lawful.

Tens of thousands marched through Madrid in outrage. Protesters occupied Puerta del Sol, erecting more than 1,200 tents, complete with named streets and a makeshift medical centre. They demanded rent controls, protection against eviction and an end to housing speculation. Parliament rejected two emergency housing decrees, prompting Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to call a snap election for 29 November. On 7 October, Abascal died in hospital, one day before she was due to sign an agreement allowing her to return home.

Across the Pyrenees, a protest that began at a secondary school in a Paris suburb has become a national uprising. Lycée Saint-Exupéry was missing 13 teachers, a deputy head and essential support staff. Students and teachers walked out. Within days, blockades and other disruptions had spread to more than 1,000 schools. At Lycée Paul-Éluard in Saint-Denis, students described rats in the corridors, collapsing ceilings, windows sealed for fear they would fall on pupils, and one nurse for 2,000 students.

On 6 October, over 250,000 people marched across France, as teachers, parents, trade unions and university students joined the school children. Police used tear gas and made hundreds of arrests. The government promised 3,000 substitute teachers, but the protests continued. As one student put it: “We ask for teachers, they send us police.”

On the Indian subcontinent, 6,000 kilometres away, the capital city of Delhi is under siege by its own government. The Modi regime deployed nearly 35000 police to lockdown the city against student protests. More than 2.2 million students sat the national medical entrance examination in May, competing for far fewer places. When questions were found to have circulated in advance, the examination was cancelled. Students who had spent years preparing, and families who had spent their savings supporting them, erupted in anger.

These unemployed graduates and disenchanted youth called themselves the Cockroach Janta Party, reclaiming a disparaging remark from the Chief Justice about unemployed youth as a badge of pride. What began as an Instagram joke with an AI-generated cockroach logo became a mass movement. In July, the protests forced the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. By October, the movement had joined the struggle against the removal of some 130 million names from India’s electoral rolls, which critics accuse the Election Commission of manipulating to benefit Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party.

On 10 and 11 October, police and paramilitary forces sealed roads, closed metro stations and detained protesters demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Denied access to Jantar Mantar, Delhi’s designated protest site, demonstrators regrouped at markets, intersections and flyovers across the capital.

In Albania, that fire was sparked from a stretch of barbed wire. This May, developers fenced off access to the coast at Zvërnec, where a luxury resort backed by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner threatens the protected Vjosa-Narta wetlands. Villagers produced property deeds and a 2013 court ruling recognising their claim to the land. When residents and environmental activists confronted the development, private security guards dragged them away.

The injustice struck a nerve. The capital, Tirana, has repeatedly been brought to a standstill by protestors carrying inflatable flamingos, the birds whose habitat the development threatens, declaring that “Albania is not for sale”. The protests grew into a revolt against corruption and the grip of oligarchs on the country’s economy and political system. This week, tens of thousands of students protesting over education and living costs have joined the movement, with clashes leaving dozens injured and arrested. Footage is circulating on social media of citizens being abducted into unmarked vans. Prime Minister Edi Rama refuses to resign.

The historian E. P. Thompson described the moral economy of the eighteenth-century English crowd: shared expectations of legitimate conduct whose violation could turn hardship into rebellion. A fair examination, a functioning school, security in old age, access to public land: in each country, a particular injustice exposed years of accumulated grievances.

The protests have brought down an Indian minister, forced France to promise thousands of additional teachers, removed the fences at Zvërnec and helped precipitate a general election in Spain. But the institutions that produced the grievances — from India’s electoral systems to the power of property in Spain and Albania — remain intact. The forces united against a particular injustice may have very different ideas about what should come next.

How can these new rebellions acquire the organised power to change the conditions that produced them?

In Spain, the tenants’ movement is already joining forces with the labour movement. At the tenants’ unions’ initiative, Spain’s two largest labour confederations, UGT and CCOO, are backing a 24-hour general strike on 11 November — the first in fourteen years with their joint support. The Madrid Sindicato de Inquilinas has demanded a Decreto Maricarmen to protect tenants against eviction and rent increases, while their allies in Congress have now called for the expropriation of hundreds of thousands of homes held by investment funds for conversion into social housing. General elections in Spain are set for 29 November.

In India, the Cockroach Janta Party is forging links with the organised left and workers’ movements. At a joint press conference in Delhi on Thursday, founder Abhijeet Dipke appeared alongside leaders of three Left student organisations — AISA, SFI and AISF — as well as PI Cabinet member Nikhil Dey of the workers’ and farmers’ organisation MKSS, and Shaik Salauddin of the Telangana Gig and Platform Workers Union, both of whom are also PI Members. Together, they demanded the resignation of the chief election commissioner and an end to the repression of protesters. Opposition parties in the INDIA bloc are pursuing a parallel campaign against the electoral roll revision.

In France, the Union Syndicale Lycéenne has coordinated blockades and demanded €10 billion in emergency education funding. Its president, Ryad Rani, has called on students to join Saturday’s Gilets Jaunes mobilisation against the cost of living. Meanwhile, La France Insoumise has challenged police violence against the students in the streets and in parliament and is taking their demands for investment and an end to university selection into the 2027 presidential election.

In Albania, Progressive International’s member Lëvizja Bashkë is building on years of organising among workers, tenants and students to challenge the country’s oligarchic order. After winning its first parliamentary seat in 2025, the party has stood alongside the protesters defending the coast, contesting both the luxury development and demanding the repeal of the 2024 legislation that opened protected areas to construction. Many of its members have been beaten and arrested in the protests.

These are the forces that the Progressive International is working to support and connect. Tenant organisations bringing trade unions into a housing struggle. Student movements joining wider coalitions for democratic rights. Political parties emerging from years of workplace and community organising, developing programmes and contesting elections.

Popular anger can spread across a country in days. Building organisations that can confront entrenched interests, withstand repression and win control over political and economic decisions takes years.

Maricarmen Abascal’s neighbours stopped three evictions. On the fourth attempt, the property company prevailed with the police enforcing its claim. The task now is to build the power to resist the next abuse, change the laws that enforce them and the ownership they defend.

author: Admin101
title: Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense
content:
Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN) is excited to announce the publication of 

Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense

.




Drawing on organizing experiences of Black Rose/Rosa Negra members across the United States, this pamphlet explores how workers, neighbors, and communities are building collective resistance to ICE and defending their immigrant coworkers, classmates, and loved ones. By connecting struggles across workplaces, schools, and neighborhoods, the 

transversal organizing

 approach we prioritize builds solidarity across different sectors of society to confront the interconnected structures of domination that shape our lives.




You can find a downloadable PDF version of the pamphlet at the end of this text.







Two Years of Trump II: Immigrants in the Crosshairs, Resistance Under Attack




Upon returning to office, Donald Trump wasted little time fulfilling his white supremacist campaign pledge of “Mass Deportations Now.” Via a flurry of executive orders and congressional acts his administration reinstated the reviled “family separation” policy; directed virtually unlimited resources to stop a fictitious “invasion” of the country’s borders; and sought to end birthright citizenship. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents blitzed Los Angeles in June 2025 with spectacular raids, followed shortly by similar operations in dozens of cities across the country including New York City; Chicago, IL; New Orleans, LA; and Durham, NC. This “shock and awe” strategy culminated in Operation Metro Surge, a months-long invasion of the Minnesota Twin Cities that deported over 2,000 residents. 




Meanwhile, support for the deportation machine plummeted as collective action against it swelled. Everyday people covered their cars, lawns, and lips with the slogan “Abolish ICE;” as of July 2026, nearly 50% of US adults support such a measure. Both May Days since Trump’s second inauguration centered immigrant defense in their celebrations. Rapid-response networks that keep watch for ICE, document kidnappings, and sometimes disrupt them spread wildly. Know-your-rights training flourished at worksites and community centers. Millions of Red Cards–wallet-sized cards outlining the holder’s constitutional protections around interactions with ICE and other police–were distributed at schools, churches, restaurants, and municipal buildings. Children and their parents caged in concentration camps went on hunger strike as constituents bombarded politicians’ hotlines and town halls demanding humanitarian treatment and release outside their walls.




Popular responses in St. Paul and Minneapolis demonstrate the possibilities of mass resistance. Like the Los Angeles Tenant Union’s community defense centers that countered ICE’s Southern California invasion, organizers reactivated dormant neighborhood networks from the 2020 uprising and began building new ones when word spread that Commander-at-Large Greg Bovino was bringing his paramilitary forces to town. Once Operation Metro Surge launched, everyday Minnesotans refined sophisticated systems to track, delay, and disrupt arrests. ICE agents retaliated by killing rapid-responder Renée Good and shooting Julio C. Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan immigrant targeted for deportation. Instead of cowering from the naked clampdown, neighborhood networks coordinated with unions, churches, and other civil societal organizations to shut down their cities on January 23rd. In its wake, Trump ousted Bovino and immigration enforcement plummeted.




But July 2026 saw record high immigrant detentions since Trump’s return to office with little public opposition. What explains it? ICE’s tactical shifts undoubtedly played a role. Bovino replacement and “Border Czar” Tom Homan traded provocative street operations with quiet detainers at jails and prisons and “targeted operations” at sites protected from activist impediment like airports. Escalating repression has also raised the costs of resistance. ICE’s bevy of brutality has included intimidation, beatings, and shootings, culminating in murdering Good and rapid-responder Alex Pretti. Federal grand juries fish from the shadows for information about our movements, stoking fears of informants that slow our organizing. From the Prairieland defendants to the Minnesota 15 and more, indictments and convictions on flimsy charges could make prosecuting dissidents even easier. Evidentiary discovery in the Minnesota 15 case has even revealed how the Department of Homeland Security subpoenaed thousands of records from the local AFL-CIO, other unions, veterans organizations, and liberal non-profits to chill community defense. Although shootings by ICE agents still spark spontaneous protests, these momentary outbursts remain largely contained to their immediate locales.




In short, mass resistance briefly but seriously disrupted the administration’s campaign of ethnic cleansing that forced strategic shifts to cut its losses. How can we adapt to these changing conditions and renew blows to the state, its borders, and the machinery that upholds them?




Immigrant Defense as Transversal Struggle




Members of Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation have fiercely organized defense of our immigrant coworkers, neighbors, and classmates over the last several years. We have facilitated mass assemblies and built neighborhood councils to keep ICE out of the California Bay Area. In Austin, TX, we’ve brought workers and tenants together to fight for wages stolen from immigrant workers. Public school educators in Durham and Chicago forged ICE watches to protect themselves, their students, and their students’ caregivers. Healthcare workers even won added protections at their workplace that helped free patients from unlawful deportations.




We approach immigrant defense as a “transversal issue.” Pioneered by Chilean feminists to confront femicide in all its subtle and overt sexist manifestations, transversal issues span the sectors where we organize—the sites and actors of struggle we prepare to supplant bourgeois-statist institutions with our own mass organizations. Our movements come together at these intersections to wage a frontal assault on the structures of domination that run our lives.




Thus, we do not organize “immigrants” as a category of struggle unto itself. Especially in the wake of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrival (DACA), such framing has extended limited, primarily legal protections to “deserving” groups of immigrants while withholding them from “undeserving” ones. Instead, we defend our immigrant coworkers, neighbors, and classmates as one step in a broader fight for greater control of our workplaces, our communities, and our schools. 




This sectoral perspective critically allows us to cut across the multiple sources of domination immigrants face while concretely attending to their specific needs. Rooted mass organizations that enable immigrant self-determination, rather than solely relying on narrowly focused campaigns, organizations, and formations, can better maintain defense initiatives while empowering people to sustain and expand struggle across all sectors of the lives of dominated classes. 




Based on our own and related experiences defending immigrant coworkers and community members in the articles linked below, we share some lessons and strategic directions to get our movements off the ropes and keep them fighting back around this pivotal transversal issue.




1.

 

Defensive initiatives can spark movements; offensive campaigns can sustain them.




Righteous, reactive defensive efforts mobilized thousands to take on ICE. Take Northern California: organizers throughout the region grew neighborhood-based rapid-response networks, foot and car patrols, and more to prepare for ICE deployments. To their surprise, sustained preparation successfully thwarted a planned insurgency in October 2025. But without confrontational raids, it has been less readily useful and the wide pool of activated residents largely demobilized.




Conversely, offensive campaigns that sprouted from defensive initiatives have won measurable gains and sustained momentum. Shan in Durham, NC explains how collective bargaining by educators renewed protections for immigrant students and staff amidst Operation Charlotte’s Web. Morgan’s union colleagues in healthcare similarly seized protective policies from their hospital administrators that when paired with legal support freed a patient from an unlawful ICE detention. To be certain, these organizers will admit these victories are modest. Confronting the routine operations of ICE lay the groundwork for consistent, widespread participation.




2.

 

Cultural “herd immunity” alone will not protect us through repression. We must foster movement structures and practices that can widely inoculate against it.




Organizers tried to prepare activated participants for the realities of repression. For example, rapid-response, legal observer, and other direct-action training often explores some of the risks that participants should anticipate, and know-your-rights literature circulates widely. Repression has  undoubtedly chilled organizing, though. Outbursts to ICE’s murders of Good and Pretti were relatively short-lived. Mobilizations since the Prairieland verdicts have largely stalled, and rapid-response networks have slowed their vigilance.




Relying on a “herd immunity” of cultural diffusion that grows individual tolerance to withstand repression is not enough. As the state strategically mutates to repress our movements, we must build infrastructure that can inoculate against intimidation as well as fight off coordinated governmental attacks. Decentralized, federated defense committees that become bases for continued revolutionary activity point to how we might go beyond narrow, reactive vessels for legal support. Like with immigrant defense, we must tie together mass organizations in our workplaces, neighborhoods, schools, and sites of confinement into the social antibodies that can take on repression as the transversal plague it is.




3.

 

We must continue going beyond non-profits. In the short-term, though, we are unlikely to go completely without them.




In many urban centers, non-profit organizations dedicated to immigrant defense have played a limited but notable role against ICE. Across the country, the National Day Laborer Organizing Network (NDLON) published how-to guides and led training on “adopting corners” to watch for ICE while the Immigrant Legal Resource Center (ILRC) has distributed more than 10 million Red Cards since Trump’s reelection. Similar organizations have also affected on-the-ground initiatives. Overstretched immigrant support nonprofits in Austin, TX shepherded wage disputes to a budding solidarity network. Siembra NC in Durham similarly supported educators and parents of students to assemble ICE watches at schools. In Northern California, a network of liberal nonprofits mobilized hundreds of people to stop ICE from setting up a base of operations at a local Navy station. 




This diverges from their modus operandi since the social service boom in the 1970s, wherein nonprofits have been an effective counterinsurgent cudgel against social movements for liberation. But federal criminalization, popular discontent, and radical rhetoric have pushed many of these institutions to take a more confrontational posture than previous eras. We should acknowledge that opening for collaboration, drawing on the resources and networks they may be able to provide budding movements. Even if we don’t embrace their participation, at minimum we must brace for their interventions. If we are to build robust, independent movements, militants must prevent these law-fearing organizations from corralling discontent into tried-and-true avenues for demobilization and disorganization like election campaigning and deference to liberal leadership.




4.

 

Broaden and connect the struggle against immigration enforcement to policing more generally.




Immigration enforcement is both a mechanism for reasserting white supremacy and policing the working class in the United States and across its borders. For decades, Black residents, workers, and students have led struggles against the expanding carceral state, from confrontations with police to opposing jail construction and prison expansion. These arenas of struggle are one in the same, and yet the lessons from and relationships between these movements remain largely underdeveloped.




As more and more people are pushed into deportation proceedings by police arrests and custodial transfers, rooted social movements and mass organizations need to take on local police departments and county sheriffs. Every time a “false alarm” mistakenly identifies a different agency deploying into our communities as ICE is an opportunity to learn how to document, disrupt, and disorganize policing operations. Moreover, taking on policing and winning protections against a specific form of policing can encroach against all 

forms of it, as Heather in Chicago and Morgan in Northern California highlight. Making links between all-too-often disparate transversal struggles mutually expands their scopes and consolidates a pole of opposition to the central way the state is reasserting its might in our authoritarian era.




5.

 

Keep rooting movement democracy in independent, durable, and nimble mass organizations we can pivot on shifting terrain.




Defending one another is not solely about the correct tactical techniques or strategic steps. Defined at the broadest level, collective self-defense invites shared participation in our self-emancipation. In all of the cases below, you will read how rank-and-file workers and everyday neighbors collectively identified unique needs among their immigrant neighbors, coworkers, patients, and students, and devised plans to fulfill them. They dedicated lots of time, attention, and effort to make their struggles and victories possible; in some cases, these initiatives grew from organizing that stretches back years. 




Rather than a particular organization or even network of organizations working on our behalf, we can grow self-confidence, initiative, and popular power when we directly act around transversal issues like immigrant defense through our own organizations. Durable mass organizations like the labor unions, neighborhood assemblies, rapid-response teams, and solidarity networks create containers to learn from our defeats, build on our victories, and navigate shifting terrains of struggle towards a world where we can freely move and live.






















Download Pamphlet













If you enjoyed this article, we recommend reading our previous writing from which these lessons were distilled, such as: 

How Everyday Organizing Stopped Trump’s Bay Area ICE Surge

; 

“A Dense Web of Solidarity”: Chicago Public School Workers Defend Students Against ICE and the Feds

; and 

Healthcare Workers Freed a Patient from ICE – You Can Do the Same




The post 

Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense

 appeared first on 

Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation
